pw:QF8.title: CCHC / Larent (IG Risk, Z-Spread vs OAS, International and Structured Products)
pw:QF8.text:
Central County History Center (CCHC) is a not-for-profit history museum that recently completed fundraising for a new permanent gallery. CCHC plans to contribute a portion of the funds raised to an endowment whose income will support the permanent gallery.

Bill Ronane (CCHC’s president) and Amy McDown (CCHC’s vice president of finance) are meeting with Elizabeth Larent (chief investment officer of Snavely Capital Management). The purpose of the meeting is to discuss the creation of a corporate bond portfolio that is suitable for the endowment.

McDown asks Larent to describe the risk considerations for investment-grade bonds. Larent responds by stating that the primary component of credit risk is loss severity. Furthermore, she states that credit rating migration can cause spread risk to become realized. Larent then states that interest rate risk reflects the positive correlation between risk-free interest rates and credit spreads.

Ronane asks Larent to disclose her methodology for credit security selection. Larent explains that she uses various credit spread measures to ensure that the securities she is considering for purchase are fairly priced. Larent illustrates by providing data for three $100 par value A rated corporate bonds that mature in five years and whose benchmark yield to maturity is 4.00%.

**Exhibit 1 Data on Corporate Bonds**

|  | Credit Rating | Coupon | YTM | G-Spread | Z-Spread | OAS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bond A | A | 6.00% | 5.00% | 100 bps | 112 bps | 112 bps |
| Bond B | Baa | 6.50% | 5.50% | 150 bps | 163 bps | 152 bps |
| Bond C | Ba | 7.00% | 6.00% | 200 bps | 213 bps | 213 bps |

McDown expresses concern about the timing of the credit cycle as it relates to constructing a corporate bond portfolio for CCHC. Larent explains that she uses a bottom-up approach to determine which corporate bonds offer the best relative value should the credit cycle deteriorate. Larent then provides the data in Exhibit 2 for three corporate bonds in which the holding period is assumed to be one year.

**Exhibit 2 Data on Corporate Bonds**

|  | Credit Rating | Probability of Default | Spread Duration | Z-Spread | Expected Change in Z-Spread | Loss Severity |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bond D | A | 0.25% | 3.0 | 0.75% | +0.25% | 40% |
| Bond E | Baa | 0.50% | 3.5 | 1.00% | +0.25% | 50% |
| Bond F | Ba | 0.75% | 4.0 | 1.25% | +0.25% | 60% |

Larent explains that another approach to portfolio construction is top down. She says, “I believe that global economic conditions are going to improve. Credit portfolios that are overweight lower-quality bonds in industry sectors that are highly correlated with the economic cycle, such as industrial metals, will likely outperform a global benchmark. We can use effective duration to assess the impact of a likely steepening in the yield curve. Within credit rating categories, we can underweight longer-maturity bonds given my expectation that the relatively widespread curve will flatten.”

Ronane asks Larent to discuss the factors that CCHC should consider before investing in the bonds of international companies. Larent replies that the international bond universe consists of companies that are located in both developed markets and emerging markets. In term of factors to consider, Larent states that a company’s credit ratings are independent from the sovereign rating of its domicile and that bankruptcy laws apply equally to all investors of any particular company’s bond issuances. Larent adds that being able to accurately predict credit cycles is important because of regional differences across the global credit universe.

McDown asks whether structured financial instruments should be considered for CCHC’s portfolio. Larent replies yes and states, “The credit cycle is expected to improve. For purposes of diversification, both collateralized debt obligations (CDOs) and their underlying corporate bonds should be included in the portfolio. AA rated CDOs currently offer significant relative value for long-term investors as the yield spread reflects a BB default rate expectation for the underlying collateral. Moreover, the value of the senior tranches should increase by more than the value of the mezzanine tranches since default correlations are expected to increase.”

pw:QF12.title: Hale / Choate (Strategy, Risk, Spread Measures, Tail Risk, Emerging Markets)
pw:QF12.text:
Spencer Hale is a reporter for “Advisor’s Monthly,” a newsletter that features select mutual fund managers and is circulated to registered investment advisers (RIAs). Hale reports on managers who have performed well over a three-year period. He focuses on their investment style, philosophy, and process while highlighting some personal traits to make the reading entertaining. Because the newsletter is educational for RIAs who are generalists across asset classes, Hale also incorporates some technical material in the story. He published the following article subsequent to a recent interview:

Harlow Choate is the portfolio manager of the Credit Opportunities Fund (COF) at Ipswich Advisors, LLC. Choate navigates his fund with the same dexterity as his 46-foot sloop, scouring the markets for attractive credit securities. He describes his strategy approach as having “an objective to beat the Barclays US Investment-Grade Corporate Index by 100 basis points (bps) annually with a tracking error volatility of 200 bps. We evaluate the relative value of securities within countries and sectors using our own assessment of credit-related risks and use expected excess return as the measure to make relative value decisions. We consider overall corporate profitability, default rates, and industry trends to allocate to industry sectors and when adding an asset class, such as high-yield bonds. Investments are not restricted based on companies’ business practices.”

Choate elaborates on the different risk considerations he attributes to investment-grade bonds compared to high-yield bonds, “Relative to high-yield bonds, investment-grade bonds are more sensitive to interest rate changes and credit migration risk, resulting in credit spread volatility. High-yield bonds are not as sensitive to interest rates, and, given the potential for actual credit losses caused by default, monitoring outright market value of the position is more critical with high-yield bonds than with investment-grade bonds.”

Choate is nimble with seafaring tools, such as the compass and sextant, so it is no wonder that he employs a number of specialized tools when investing in bonds. He shares his favorite measures to assess how much he is being compensated for the credit-related risks he takes, saying “There are a number of credit spread measures that can be used when evaluating risky bonds. My preference is to use a measure at the security level that uses a spread over a linear interpolation of the yields of two on-the-run government bonds. At the portfolio level, I prefer to use a measure that applies to a diversified group of securities, whether they have embedded options or not.”

Similar to many fixed-income investors, Choate envisions the glass half empty. He is concerned about the challenging market environment, liquidity, and a number of black swan or tail risks that could potentially impact the performance of his investments. He outlines for Hale the precautions he can take in the portfolio and specifically outlines three key considerations:

- **Consideration 1:** Liquidity risk has increased markedly for corporate bonds, particularly since the global financial crisis. We assess liquidity through a number of measures, such as the bid–ask spread, trading volumes, and the impact of funds flows. We manage liquidity through position sizes, the use of Treasuries, exchange-traded funds, and derivatives.
- **Consideration 2:** Tail risk events are challenging to model or predict ahead of time. Scenario analysis can provide an indication of how a portfolio would perform under certain conditions, such as spreads widening by a certain amount across the credit curve. The positions in a portfolio can be stressed in scenario analysis assuming similar outcomes of a past crisis recur.
- **Consideration 3:** It is difficult to hedge tail risks through portfolio diversification, and it can also prove too costly. We prefer to hedge using such derivatives as credit default swaps, which have a very low cost.

Choate does not limit his investments strictly to domestic issuers. He prefers to traverse the global waters for opportunities. His rationale is fairly straightforward: “The credit market is global in nature. We evaluate opportunities across regions and countries, which include emerging markets. We are especially keen on emerging market credits, which can provide excess returns that outperform the domestic and global developed market indexes. Because the emerging market credits are not included in the performance benchmark, we limit the maximum exposure to this asset class and buy them in either USD or the local currency depending on the total expected return of the transaction.”

Choate’s final comments to Hale detail how he also looks for structured financial instruments that offer diversification benefits and attractive expected returns. These are listed in Exhibit 1, which shows recent COF portfolio positioning relative to the benchmark and reflects various opportunities Choate has uncovered across several markets.

**Exhibit 1 COF Portfolio Holdings as of 12/31/xx**

| Collateralized Debt Obligations |  |  |

pw:QF13.title: West / Stone / Palma (Risk, Spread Quotes, Top-Down Reports, Liquidity, Out-of-Benchmark)
pw:QF13.text:
Ashley West is the Managing Director of Credit Strategies at Mt. Pleasant Advisers (MPA). She oversees a group of strategists, analysts, and traders who contribute to managing more than $50 billion in fixed-income securities. She has gathered her group for their weekly investment strategy meeting, where they are currently focused on higher expected volatility in the markets. West makes the following comments:

- **Comment 1:** Relative to high-yield bonds, investment-grade bonds of the same duration are more sensitive to changes in interest rates.
- **Comment 2:** Credit investors can use the four Cs of credit as a framework to assess both the probability of default and the estimated loss given default.

**Comment 3:**

Spread duration is a measure of risk that is more useful for high-yield bonds than for investment-grade bonds.

West begins a discussion with her trader, Daniel Island, regarding return compensation for investing in corporate bonds. Island tells West, “When I am evaluating the price of a corporate bond, the screen on my Bloomberg terminal shows several spread measures. Some measures are better than others. Dealers often will quote me a spread to Treasuries whose maturity does not match the bond’s maturity.”

Charles Stone joins the conversation. He is MPA’s credit strategist and coordinates the recommendations of the analysts to portfolio managers. The analysts have provided him with data for three corporate bonds in the media sector that include the credit rating, spread duration, z-spread, and expected loss severity. He asks the analysts to provide data for three additional measures that he feels are required for the portfolio managers to select the most attractive bond using relative value analysis. The measures include expected probability of default, rating agency credit outlook, and historical sector default rates.

West likes to balance the bottom-up approach for portfolio construction with a top-down approach. She provides portfolio managers with a macro factors report containing two sections that they use as part of their investment process. Section 1 shows macro factors that she considers relevant for credit investing and includes corporate profitability, economic growth, currency movements, changes in expected market volatility, key rate durations, and default rates. Section 2 contains risk measurements that are used for credit portfolio management and includes average credit rating, average spread duration, duration times spread, average OAS, duration, and effective convexity.

West is concerned about liquidity risk in the credit markets. She believes that since the Great Recession, liquidity has declined, and she asks Stone for his opinion on the topic. Stone replies, “First, trading volume has declined across credit markets, even for higher-quality sectors. As a result, liquidity management has become less relevant to portfolio managers as a means of adding alpha to portfolios. Second, spread changes are more pronounced during times of outflows in high-yield markets relative to investment-grade markets, particularly during times of stress. Therefore, macro forecasting of the economic and credit cycle would aid in positioning the portfolio to compensate for liquidity risk. Third, bid–ask spreads can vary over time and are a good indicator of liquidity. Wider bid–ask spreads in a market downturn create opportunities for portfolio managers to add value to portfolios.”

Stone fields a call from Edisto Palma, an MPA portfolio manager in the Madrid office. Palma is frustrated with the negative interest rate environment present in the European Union (EU) debt markets resulting from the European Central Bank’s quantitative easing programs. He tells Stone he is considering buying securities outside of the EU market to pick up additional yield. Stone informs Palma that he is sympathetic with the situation but that there are implications to buying securities outside his EU benchmark, whether they are from developed or emerging markets. Stone outlines three suggestions for Palma. First, he should evaluate whether the spread advantage is negated by the cost of a currency hedge. Second, he should avoid local currency investments in countries where the exchange rate is pegged. Third, he should ensure that the timing of the credit cycles across markets coincides.

pw:QG1.title: Harding / Yellow (Trading Strategy, Benchmarks, Algorithms, Costs, Policy)
pw:QG1.text:
Robert Harding is a portfolio manager at ValleyRise, a hedge fund based in the United States. Harding monitors the portfolio alongside Andrea Yellow, a junior analyst. ValleyRise only invests in equities, but Harding is considering other asset classes to add to the portfolio, namely derivatives, fixed income, and currencies. Harding and Yellow meet to discuss their trading strategies and price benchmarks.

Harding begins the meeting by asking Yellow about factors that affect the selection of an appropriate trading strategy. Yellow tells Harding:

Statement 1:
Trading with greater urgency results in lower execution risk.

Statement 2:
Trading larger size orders with higher trade urgency reduces market impact.

Statement 3:
Securities with high rates of alpha decay require less aggressive trading to realize alpha.

After further discussion about Yellow’s statements, Harding provides Yellow a list of trades that he wants to execute. He asks Yellow to recommend a price benchmark. Harding wants to use a benchmark where the reference price for the benchmark is computed based on market prices that occur during the trading period, excluding trade outliers.

Earlier that day before the meeting, Yellow believed that the market had underreacted during the pre-market trading session to a strong earnings announcement from ABC Corp., a company that Yellow and Harding have been thoroughly researching for several months. Their research suggested the stock’s fair value was $90 per share, and the strong earnings announcement reinforced their belief in their fair value estimate.

Right after the earnings announcement, the pre-market price of ABC was $75. Concerned that the underreaction would be short-lived, Harding directed Yellow to buy 30,000 shares of ABC stock. Yellow and Harding discussed a trading strategy, knowing that ABC shares are very liquid and the order would represent only about 1% of the expected daily volume. They agreed on trading a portion of the order at the opening auction and then filling the remainder of the order after the opening auction. The strategy for filling the remaining portion of the order was to execute trades at prices close to the market price at the time the order was received.

Harding and Yellow then shift their conversation to XYZ Corp. Harding tells Yellow that, after extensive research, he would like to utilize an algorithm to purchase some shares that are relatively liquid. When building the portfolio’s position in XYZ, Harding’s priority is to minimize the trade’s market impact to avoid conveying information to market participants. Additionally, Harding does not expect adverse price movements during the trade horizon.

Harding and Yellow conclude their meeting by comparing trade implementation for equities with the trade implementation for the new fixed-income, exchange-traded derivatives, and currency investments under consideration. Yellow tells Harding:

Statement 4:
Small currency trades and small exchange-traded derivatives trades are typically implemented using the direct market access (DMA) approach.

Statement 5:
The high-touch agency approach is typically used to execute large, non-urgent trades in fixed-income and exchange-traded derivatives markets.

The next day, Harding instructs Yellow to revisit their research on BYYP, Inc. Yellow’s research leads her to believe that its shares are undervalued. She shares her research with Harding, and at 10 a.m. he instructs her to buy 120,000 shares when the price is $40.00 using a limit order of $42.00.

The buy-side trader releases the order for market execution when the price is $40.50. The only fee is a commission of $0.02 per share. By the end of the trading day, 90,000 shares of the order had been purchased, and BYYP closes at $42.50. The trade was executed at an average price of $41.42. Details about the executed trades are presented in Exhibit 1.

**Exhibit 1**
BYYP Trade Execution Details

| Trades | Execution Price | Shares Executed |
|---|---|---|
| Trade 1 | $40.75 | 10,000 |
| Trade 2 | $41.25 | 30,000 |
| Trade 3 | $41.50 | 20,000 |
| Trade 4 | $41.75 | 30,000 |
| Total |  | 90,000 |

While the buy-side trader executes the BYYP trade, Harding and Yellow review ValleyRise’s trade policy document. After reviewing the document, Yellow recommends several changes: 1) add a policy for the treatment of trade errors; 2) add a policy that ensures over-the-counter derivatives are traded on venues with rules that ensure minimum price transparency; and 3) alter the list of eligible brokers to include only those that provide execution at the lowest possible trading cost.

pw:QG2.title: Morris / Ogive (Strategy Aggressiveness, Cash Management)
pw:QG2.text:
Lindsey Morris is a trader at North Circle Advisors, an investment management firm and adviser to a suite of value-oriented equity mutual funds. Will Beamon, portfolio manager for the firm’s flagship large-cap value fund, the Ogive Fund, is explaining its investment strategy and objectives to Morris. Morris wishes to know how the Ogive Fund’s underlying trading motivations may impact trade urgency and alpha decay. Beamon notes the following relevant characteristics of the Ogive Fund:

Seeks long-term outperformance vs. S&P 500 by investing in undervalued companies

Evaluates company fundamentals to identify persistent mispricing opportunities

Has a three-year average holding period

pw:QG3.title: Sailors (Valley Ranch vs North Circle, Execution Risk)
pw:QG3.text:
Last year, Larry Sailors left his trading position at Valley Ranch Partners, a multi-strategy hedge fund, to join North Circle Advisors. Discussing his job experiences with a colleague, Sailors remarks that, prior to starting at North Circle, he didn’t fully appreciate the significant differences in trading motivations between the two firms and how such motivations feed into trade strategy. In particular, he notes the following trade characteristics:

**Exhibit 1**
Features of Trades by Sailors’ Employers

| Feature | Valley Ranch Partners | North Circle Advisors |
|---|---|---|
| Investment Philosophy | Short-term long and short alpha trades across equity and non-equity securities | Long equity value investing |
| Trade Size | Small | Large |
| Risk Appetite | Low | Moderate to high |
| Trading Venue | Listed securities only | Listed and non-listed securities |
| Bid–Ask Spreads Experienced in Downturn | Moderate-to-wide | Very wide |

pw:QG4.title: Wong / SWM (Benchmarks, Algorithms, Implementation Shortfall)
pw:QG4.text:
Michelle Wong is a portfolio manager at Star Wealth Management (SWM), an investment management company whose clients are high-net-worth individuals. Her expertise is in identifying temporarily mispriced equity securities. Wong’s typical day includes meeting with clients, conducting industry and company investment analysis, and preparing trade recommendations.

Music Plus
Wong follows the music industry and, specifically, Music Plus. After highly anticipated data about the music industry is released shortly after the market opens for trading, the share price of Music Plus quickly increases to $15.25. Wong evaluates the new data as it relates to Music Plus and concludes that the share price increase is an overreaction. She expects the price to quickly revert back to her revised fair value estimate of $14.20 within the same day. When the price is $15.22, she decides to prepare a large sell order equal to approximately 20% of the expected daily volume. She is concerned about information leakage from a public limit order. Wong’s supervisor suggests using algorithmic trading for the sell order of the Music Plus shares.

West Commerce
Later the same day, West Commerce announces exciting new initiatives resulting in a substantial increase in its share price to $27.10. Based on this price, Wong concludes that the stock is overvalued and sets a limit price of $26.20 for a sell order of 10,000 shares. By the time the order is released to the market, the share price is $26.90. The share price closes the day at $26.00. SWM is charged a commission of $0.03 per share and no other fees. Selected data about the trade execution are presented in Exhibit 1.

**Exhibit 1**
Selected Trade Data: West Commerce Sell Order

| Trades | Execution price | Shares executed |
|---|---|---|
| Trade 1 | $26.80 | 6,000 |
| Trade 2 | $26.30 | 3,000 |
| Total |  | 9,000 |

The value of the market index appropriate to West Commerce was 600 when the West Commerce sell order was released to the market, and its volume-weighted average price (VWAP) was 590 during the trade horizon. West Commerce has a beta of 0.9 with the index.

Trading Policies
At the end of the day, Wong meets with a long-term client of SWM to discuss SWM’s trade policies. The client identifies two of SWM’s trade policies and asks Wong whether these are consistent with good trade governance:

Policy 1:
SWM works only with pre-approved brokers and execution venues, and the list is reviewed and updated regularly.

Policy 2:
SWM is allowed to pool funds when appropriate, and executed orders are allocated to the accounts on a pro-rata basis.

pw:QG5.title: North Circle / LIM (Benchmarks, Delay Cost, Market-Adjusted Cost)
pw:QG5.text:
Although focused on long-term value, North Circle Advisors will exploit temporary mispricings to open positions. For example, portfolio manager Bill Bradley pegged LIM Corporation’s fair value per share at $28 yesterday; however, LIM’s stock price seems to have overreacted to a competitor announcement prior to market open today. The follow events unfold over the course of the morning:

PRIOR CLOSE: LIM closed at $30.05

PRE-MARKET: LIM priced at $20.34

MARKET OPEN: LIM opens at $22.15

10:00 AM: LIM trading at $23.01

10:00 AM: Bradley confirms the overreaction with target price of $28

10:05 AM: Bradley instructs trader to buy 25,000 shares, with a limit price of $28 when LIM is trading at $23.09

10:22 AM: Trader finishes the buy with an average purchase price of $23.45

Bradley and the trader conduct a post-trade evaluation. In picking an appropriate reference price, the trader asks Bradley if that would be a pre-trade, intraday, post-trade, or price target benchmark.

pw:QG6.title: Minchow / EEP (Algorithms, Dark Pools)
pw:QG6.text:
Beatrice Minchow designs and implements algorithmic trading strategies for Enlightenment Era Partners LLC (EEP). Minchow is working with Portfolio Manager James Bean on an algorithm to implement a sell order for Bean’s small position in the lightly-traded shares of public company Dynopax Inc. In a conversation with Minchow, Bean states the following:

I have no expectations of adverse price movements during the trade horizon and would like to use a scheduled algorithm.

I want to minimize market impact, but I’m more concerned about getting the sell order completely executed in one day.

Based on Bean’s comments, Minchow considers three algorithms: POV, VWAP, and TWAP.

pw:QG7.title: Swanson / Russell (Trade Policy)
pw:QG7.text:
Karen Swanson and Gabriel Russell recently co-founded Green Savanah Securities, an asset management firm conducting various equity and fixed-income strategies. Swanson and Russell are formulating Green Savannah’s trade policy. During a meeting, they agree on an initial set of themes regarding trade policy formation:

Theme 1: We should determine an optimal execution approach and apply that approach to each asset class managed.

Theme 2: In aggregating trades for pooled accounts, any partially executed orders need to be allocated on a pro-rata basis.

Theme 3: The principles behind our process to find a broker should be consistent across each asset class managed.

Theme 4: To act in our clients’ best interests, we need to disclose all trade errors to them.

pw:QG8.title: Morales / Bahk (Trading Risks, Delay and Arrival Cost, Implementation Shortfall)
pw:QG8.text:
Hector Morales is a research analyst at Prime Investments, a US-based hedge fund. Prime invests in various asset classes, including equities, fixed income, and derivatives. Morales works closely with his colleague Xiu Mei Bahk, a portfolio manager at the firm.

Bahk makes the following statements regarding risks in various trading strategies:

- **Statement 1:** A trader is exposed to lower execution risk when an order for a security with a wide bid–ask spread is executed over a longer time period.
- **Statement 2:** A trader is exposed to increased market impact cost for trades with higher rates of alpha decay.
- **Statement 3:** The best strategy for a trader seeking to minimize information leakage is to execute faster on exchanges, using market orders before other market participants can adjust the prices.

Bahk then mentions to Morales a trading opportunity in the communications company Salesfirst (SRM). SRM’s stock has underperformed relative to its peers for the last two quarters.

SRM opened the trading day at $245.00. Bahk believes that SRM stock is undervalued and will soon increase. At 10:00 a.m., Bahk instructs Morales to place a buy order for 50,000 shares, good for one day, when SRM’s stock price is $245.10. The trading desk reviews the stock’s volatility, market conditions, and spread, and determines that Pinnacle Brokerage Services (PBS) is the best broker to execute the trade. At 11:00 a.m., Morales releases the order when SRM’s stock price is $246.50. During the day, PBS executes 46,000 shares at an average price of $249.75 per share for an overall fee of $46. At the end of the day, shares of SRM close at $253.00 and the buy order for the remaining 4,000 shares is canceled.

The stock price of Trade Stop (TS), a meme stock, has increased substantially in the past month due to a short squeeze. Bahk and Morales agree that the stock is overvalued and decide to place a sell order for 20,000 shares when the price is $122.60. The TS share price declines to $121.90 by the time the order is received by the broker. Execution details for the TS order are presented in Exhibit 1. No commission or fees are charged by the broker for the TS trades. TS shares close at $118.00 at the end of the day.

**Exhibit 1**

| Trade | Shares Executed | Execution Price |
|---|---|---|
| Trade 1 | 11,500 | $121.80 |
| Trade 2 | 2,500 | $120.50 |
| Trade 3 | 3,000 | $120.20 |
| Total | 17,000 | --- |

pw:QG9.title: Miller / BBIM (Advanced Trading, Expanded Implementation Shortfall, Governance)
pw:QG9.text:
Mark Miller is the CIO at Bulls and Bears Investment Management (BBIM). At the beginning of every quarter, Miller performs an extensive review of portfolio holdings to find rebalancing opportunities. His analysis focuses primarily on changes in macroeconomic factors. He prefers to execute all rebalancing trades within one month after the rebalancing opportunities are identified.

BBIM uses Morgan Traders as a prime broker to execute large orders. Miller meets with Jack Farina, a senior trader at Morgan, to discuss trading strategies. To be consistent with the firm’s investment objective, Miller mentions that he would like to integrate trade execution with the portfolio management process. Farina makes the following statements about advanced trading strategies that may align with Miller’s interests.

- **Statement 1:** To avoid adverse price movements and capture alpha on the rebalancing trades, you should implement an arrival price strategy.
- **Statement 2:** To avoid information leakage and significant market impact, you should use dark aggregator algorithms for large rebalancing orders.
- **Statement 3:** To achieve best execution for the rebalancing trades without market impact, you should use smart order routers to electronically send large market orders.

After reviewing his research and analysis, Miller decides to reduce his position in Schwingate Materials (SM), one of the largest holdings in the portfolio. SM is currently trading at $71.00 per share. Miller sends to Morgan Traders an order to sell 100,000 shares of SM with a limit price of $68.25. The arrival price when the order was submitted to the market by Morgan was $70.75. Order execution details are summarized in Exhibit 1. SM closed the trading day at $67.25 per share.

**Exhibit 1**

| Trade | Shares Executed | Execution Price |
|---|---|---|
| Trade 1 | 24,000 | $70.60 |
| Trade 2 | 31,000 | $69.60 |
| Trade 3 | 20,000 | $69.40 |
| Trade 4 | 25,000 | $68.80 |

Miller then turns his attention to trade governance, including trading policy, procedures, processes, disclosures, and record keeping. He understands the importance of having a trade policy document that clearly and comprehensively articulates the firm’s trading policies and escalation procedures. He requests that the investment committee include the following recommendations when formulating the trading policy.

- **Recommendation 1:** Ensure that partially executed orders are fairly allocated on a pre-trade and post-trade basis to individual clients with similar investment goals.
- **Recommendation 2:** Use the same broker and trading venues for all asset classes to consistently achieve best execution for all trades.

pw:QG10.title: Mulaney / Inflection (Algorithms, Implementation Shortfall, Benchmarks)
pw:QG10.text:
Derek Mulaney is the head trader at Inflection Capital, a Boston-based investment management firm offering traditional and alternative investment strategies. Mulaney leads a three-person trading team consisting of himself, Feng Shui, and Abagail Morrison. The trading team works closely with Inflection’s portfolio managers, analysts, and compliance team in the execution of the firm’s investment strategies.

As part of his morning team meeting, Mulaney often reviews trading situations with Shui and Morrison. He brings up an example that recently occurred while trading for Inflection’s hedge fund. The portfolio manager, Chris Largent, was listening to a 10:00 a.m. earnings call for NeuvoGen (NGEN), a midsize biotech company, during which management announced additional unfavorable news. Largent determined the market had significantly underreacted to the news and wanted to set up a trade to exploit this potential alpha opportunity. Largent communicated a sell order to Mulaney to establish a short position for the fund representing approximately 3% of expected trading volume for the stock that day. Mulaney describes how he used a trading algorithm to sell the shares, adding that some algorithms are more suitable to use than others, depending on the situation.

Morrison has been working on executing a sell order to liquidate shares in Acme Industrials (ACME). The closing price on Tuesday was $79.90. Morrison received the order from Wright before the market open on Wednesday morning to sell 50,000 ACME shares with a day limit of $80.00. No part of the order is filled on Wednesday, and the stock closes the day at $79.60. On Thursday morning, Morrison instructed a new day order to sell the 50,000 shares at $79.50; 30,000 shares were sold at $79.50 per share, with resulting commissions and fees for the trade of $0.02 per share. Shares for ACME closed the day Thursday at a price of $79.40 per share. No further attempts were made to sell the unfilled 20,000 shares, which were canceled.

Shui is instructed to execute a buy order of TeXelence (TEXX), a small-cap technology stock. Shui is able to execute the order over the course of 30 minutes and received an average price of $50.55. The price at the time the order was placed is $50.45. The volume-weighted average price (VWAP) over the trading horizon was $50.52, and the time-weighted average price (TWAP) over the horizon was $50.57, with a closing price later that day of $50.60. The market rose during the trading horizon, with an index arrival price of 1,010 and a VWAP of 1,015. Shui calculates that TEXX has a beta to the index of 1.30.

At the end of each trading week, Mulaney holds a strategy meeting with Shui and Morrison to evaluate trade execution and to discuss strategies for improvement in the future. They are discussing trade implementation in different markets as they begin to support a new macro-hedge fund that frequently trades in emerging market equities and often uses derivatives to implement its strategy.

Morrison is discussing trading trends and makes the following observation: “In recent years, average trade sizes appear to be increasing, and in emerging markets, a similar volume of equity trading is now taking place on dark pools as on ‘lit’ exchanges.”

Shui comments, “For exchange-traded derivatives, market transparency is similar to that of exchange-traded equities, with trade price, size, quote, and depth of book all publicly available. I believe we should explore algorithmic trading in futures markets, where it is more evolved than it is for options markets.”

Mulaney adds, “We can also explore the use of over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives. Liquidity has increased for OTC instruments, even for those not suited to central clearing, and average trade size is still relatively small, which could align well with the needs of the fund.”

pw:QG11.title: Holt / Quagmire (Expanded Implementation Shortfall, Trading Options)
pw:QG11.text:
Steve Holt is the manager for Quagmire Funds. Quagmire has a number of funds under management to meet different client needs.

In the UPX Fund, an investment in the new technology sector has performed well and is expected to continue to do so. However, the proportion of the fund invested in the new technology sector is now larger than what is permitted in the fund prospectus. Holt intends to reduce the holdings in the sector to comply with the prospectus over the next two months before the quarter ends. The volume of shares that need to be sold is approximately 20% of the daily volume in their respective individual markets.

To execute the trades in the new technology sector, Holt asks his team to consider three possible options:

- **Option 1:** Have a broker act as a principal for the entire amount that needs to be sold.
- **Option 2:** Use a scheduled algorithm to execute the trade based on available daily liquidity over eight weeks.
- **Option 3:** Trade in a “dark pool” so as not to reveal any information about the amount to be traded.

Upon completion of the trades, Holt calculates an expanded implementation shortfall to evaluate trade costs. The data are provided in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1 Expanded Implementation Shortfall Information ($) for the Trades in the New Technology Sector
Value of shares sold based on:

- **decision price:** 5,124,300
- **arrival price:** 5,175,800
- **actual trade execution prices:** 5,545,600

Note: All share were sold
Holt asks his team to determine whether trading with a new securities brokerage, Zavier Brokerage (ZB), appears to be viable. The team sent ZB a buy order for 5,000 shares of XTV stock to test the brokerage’s trading abilities. The anticipated trade execution cost was 110.00 basis points (bps), based on previous trading with other brokerages. Exhibit 2 displays ZB’s execution performance.

**Exhibit 2 ZB Trade Execution Performance**

|  | XTV ($) | Index ($) |
|---|---|---|
| Decision price | 25.45 | 12,750 |
| Arrival price | 25.50 | 12,740 |
| Average trade price | 25.75 | 12,775 |
| CAPM beta | 0.85 | 1.00 |

questions.topic: Economic balance sheet
questions.title: Economic Net Worth — Law Family
questions.context:
Financial assets: equities $800,000 (80% is WS stock), fixed income $450,000, real estate $400,000 with a $225,000 mortgage.
Extended: human capital (PV of pre-retirement earnings) $1,025,000. PV of consumption $750,000. PV of children's education $275,000. PV of endowment gift $500,000.
questions.stem: Using the economic balance sheet approach, the Laws’ economic net worth is closest to:

B.text: $1,425,000 = $2,675,000 − $1,250,000, i.e. it leaves out the $500,000 endowment liability. *(My reconstruction; the key doesn't explain B.)*

C.text: $1,675,000 = $2,675,000 − $1,000,000, i.e. it leaves out the $750,000 PV of consumption. *(My reconstruction; the key doesn't explain C.)* Consumption is an extended liability and has to be on the sheet.

questions.keyPrinciple: Economic net worth = (financial + extended assets) − (financial + extended liabilities). Extended assets: human capital. Extended liabilities: PV of consumption and of each goal (education, gifts).

questions.topic: Economic balance sheet
questions.title: Most Concerning Asset
questions.context: Equities $800,000, of which 80% is stock of Whorton Solutions (WS). Both Laws work at WS. Real estate $400,000 (mortgage $225,000). Fixed income $450,000.
questions.stem: Using an economic balance sheet, which of the Laws’ current financial assets is most concerning from an asset allocation perspective?

A.text: Concentration in WS stock plus both Laws' human capital tied to WS: one bad outcome for WS hits the stock and the income stream together. Diversify the equity portfolio.

B.text: Nothing in the vignette ties the real estate to WS or describes a concentration problem there.

C.text: Fixed income is the diversifying piece of the portfolio. Nothing in the vignette ties it to WS.

questions.keyPrinciple: Check correlation between financial assets and human capital. Employer stock + employer salary = doubled exposure.

questions.topic: Asset class specification / factor-based approaches
questions.title: Asset Class Criterion Violated by Debt
questions.context:
Previous adviser's asset class specification:
- Equity: US equities
- Debt: global investment-grade corporate bonds **and real estate**
- Derivatives: primarily large-cap foreign equities

Equity and derivatives returns are highly correlated. Debt has low correlation with both.

*Ignore: the correlation data. That is for the next question.*
questions.stem: Raye believes the previous adviser’s specification for debt is incorrect given that, for purposes of asset allocation, asset classes should be:

C.text: Debt is defined to include both corporate bonds and real estate. Assets in an asset class should be **relatively homogeneous** with similar attributes.

A.text: The diversifying criterion is about correlation with other classes. Debt has *low* correlation with equity and derivatives, so it passes.

B.text: Mutually exclusive is about overlap between classes. The problem with debt is what is inside it (bonds + real estate), not overlap.

questions.keyPrinciple: Homogeneous = similar attributes inside one class. Mixing bonds with real estate fails it.

questions.topic: Asset class specification / factor-based approaches
questions.title: Asset Class Criterion Violated by Equity and Derivatives
questions.context:
Previous adviser's specification: Equity = US equities. Derivatives = primarily large-cap foreign equities. The report notes equity and derivatives returns are **highly correlated**.

*Ignore: the debt specification (previous question).*
questions.stem: Raye believes the previous adviser’s asset class specifications for equity and derivatives are inappropriate given that, for purposes of asset allocation, asset classes should be:

A.text: High correlation means the two classes duplicate risk exposure. An asset class should be **diversifying** (no extremely high correlation with other classes).

B.text: Mutually exclusive is about overlapping holdings. The stated issue is the high return correlation.

C.text: Homogeneity concerns what is inside a class. That was the debt problem, not this one.

questions.keyPrinciple: Diversifying: avoid very high correlation with other classes or with a linear combination of them (a pairwise correlation above 0.95 is undesirable).

questions.topic: Asset class specification / factor-based approaches
questions.title: Fixing Overlapping Risk Factors
questions.context: Raye is concerned the previous adviser's approach produced **overlap in risk factors** among asset classes. He plans to examine the portfolio's sensitivity to risk factors such as inflation, liquidity and volatility to determine the desired exposure to each factor.
questions.stem: To address his concern regarding the previous adviser’s asset allocation approach, Raye should assess the Laws’ portfolio using:

choices.text: a homogeneous and mutually exclusive asset class–based risk analysis.
a multifactor risk model to control systematic risk factors in asset allocation.
an asset class–based asset allocation approach to construct a diversified portfolio.

B.text: A multifactor risk model controls systematic risk factor exposures and exposes overlap across asset classes. Risk factor approaches rest on the observation that asset classes often overlap in sources of risk.

A.text: Homogeneous, mutually exclusive asset classes can still share underlying risk factors. This is the asset-class lens that missed the overlap.

C.text: An asset class–based approach is what the previous adviser used. It is the source of the concern.

questions.keyPrinciple: Overlap in risk factors across asset classes → use a multifactor (factor-based) risk model.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Portfolio for Education Goal
questions.context:
Education goal: PV $275,000. The children start college soon and the Laws have a *very strong* desire to fund it.
Exhibit 1 (diversifying strategies = hedge funds):

| | Cash | Fixed income | Global equities | Diversifying strategies |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Portfolio 1 | 35% | 55% | 10% | 0% |
| Portfolio 2 | 10% | 15% | 65% | 10% |
| Portfolio 3 | 10% | 30% | 40% | 20% |
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, which portfolio best meets the Laws’ education goal for their children?

A.text: Short horizon and high priority → liquidity and stability. 90% in cash and fixed income.

B.text: 65% equities plus 10% hedge funds: growth-oriented, too volatile for a goal starting almost immediately. *(Reasoning from Exhibit 1; key doesn't discuss B.)*

C.text: 40% equities plus 20% hedge funds: still a meaningful risk exposure for a near-term, high-priority goal. *(Reasoning from Exhibit 1.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Match each sub-portfolio to the goal's horizon and required probability of success. Near and critical → conservative and liquid.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Portfolio for Endowment Goal
questions.context:
Endowment gift: PV $500,000, in **20 years**, with a *high probability* of success desired. Raye's baseline for most moderately important 20-year goals is 75% global equities / 25% bonds.
Exhibit 1 allocations: P1 = 35% cash / 55% FI / 10% GE / 0% DS. P2 = 10 / 15 / 65 / 10. P3 = 10 / 30 / 40 / 20.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, which portfolio best meets the Laws’ goal to fund an endowment for their alma mater?

B.text: Portfolio 2 has the greatest growth emphasis (65% equities + 10% diversifying), closest to the 75/25 baseline, which fits a 20-year horizon.

A.text: Portfolio 1 is 90% cash and fixed income. It suits the education goal, not a 20-year horizon.

C.text: Portfolio 3 has only 40% equities, so less growth than Portfolio 2 for the same long horizon.

questions.keyPrinciple: Long horizon → highest growth allocation among the options. Don't pick the middle portfolio just because it is diversified.

questions.topic: Rebalancing ranges
questions.title: Rationale for Wider Equity Rebalancing Range
questions.context: Raye uses a **cost–benefit approach** to rebalancing and recommends global equities have a wider rebalancing range than the other asset classes.
questions.stem: Raye’s approach to rebalancing global equities is consistent with:

choices.text: global equities’ having higher transaction costs than other asset classes.
global equities’ having lower correlations with other asset classes.

B.text: Cost–benefit approach: higher transaction costs → wider range.

A.text: Greater risk aversion generally argues for narrower ranges. *(Curriculum; key silent.)*

C.text: Lower correlation with the rest of the portfolio → *narrower* range (see S1-31 key).

questions.keyPrinciple: Wider ranges: higher transaction costs, higher correlation with rest of portfolio, higher taxes, momentum beliefs. Narrower: lower correlation, higher volatility of the rest of the portfolio, mean-reversion beliefs.

questions.topic: Asset class specification / factor-based approaches
questions.title: Asset Class Specification Criteria
questions.context: Bonnela is considering the criteria for asset class specification to use in constructing Client 1's (retired individual) strategic asset allocation.
questions.stem:
Describe two criteria for asset class specification that Bonnela should use in constructing Client 1's strategic asset allocation.

Note: Each description should be in a separate paragraph.
questions.modelAnswer:
Five criteria in the key (any two):

| Criterion | Description |
|---|---|
| **Homogeneous** | Assets within a class have similar attributes. E.g. equities defined to include both real estate and common stock is non-homogeneous. |
| **Mutually exclusive** | No overlap between classes. Overlap reduces risk control and complicates return expectations. E.g. for a US investor, world ex-US equities pairs with domestic equities; global equities (which include US) would overlap. |
| **Diversifying** | No extremely high expected correlation with other classes or with a linear combination of them, otherwise it duplicates risk exposure. Pairwise correlation above 0.95 is undesirable. |
| **Preponderance of world investable wealth** | The classes as a group should cover most of world investable wealth. Raises expected return for a given risk and widens active opportunities (subject to regulatory/foreign-ownership limits). |
| **Capacity to absorb a meaningful portion** | Liquidity and transaction costs are significant. If they are unfavorable for an investment of meaningful size, the class is not practically suitable. |
questions.keyPrinciple: Five criteria: homogeneous · mutually exclusive · diversifying · preponderance of world wealth · capacity to absorb.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Why the Endowment Model Doesn't Suit Client 2
questions.context: Client 2: recently widowed, 65, new to investing. Wants a traditional **stock-and-bond** portfolio on a **passive** strategy. Needs **liquidity** for unplanned expenses in the coming years. Bonnela decides the endowment model is not appropriate.
questions.stem:
Discuss two reasons that support Bonnela's decision not to use the endowment model approach to asset allocation for Client 2.

Note: Each discussion should be in a separate paragraph.
questions.modelAnswer:
The key gives these reasons (any two):

1. **Traditional vs non-traditional.** The endowment model emphasizes large allocations to non-traditional investments. Client 2 wants traditional stocks and bonds, and her portfolio is probably small.
2. **Illiquidity premium vs liquidity need.** The model seeks illiquidity premiums in non-traditional investments, which conflicts with her need for liquidity.
3. **Active vs passive.** The model emphasizes active strategies driven by manager skill (e.g. private equity). She wants passive.
questions.keyPrinciple: Endowment model = alternatives + active + illiquidity premium + long horizon. Needs size, expertise, and liquidity tolerance.

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: Client 3: Short/Medium-Term Bonds
questions.context: Client 3 (35): had planned to retire early and needed liquid assets for the next five years. Now he will work **10 more years**, no longer has near-term liquidity needs, and is **less risk averse**. Current allocation: equities 60%, short- to medium-term bonds 15%, long-term bonds 25%.
questions.stem: Determine, given the changes in Client 3's circumstances, how Bonnela should adjust his allocation to short- to medium-term bonds. (Decrease, Increase) Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer: **Decrease.** Longer horizon and no immediate liquidity needs reduce the need for liquid short/medium-term bonds. Lower risk aversion is consistent with the same shift.
questions.keyPrinciple: Longer horizon + lower liquidity need + higher risk tolerance → less in liquid/low-risk assets.

questions.topic: Asset class specification / factor-based approaches
questions.title: Least Correct Factor-Based Statement
questions.context:
Ramos on factor-based approaches:
- Statement 1: Asset classes can be described with respect to their sensitivities to each of the factors.
- Statement 2: Factors are often directly investable.
- Statement 3: Multifactor risk models can be used both in selecting individual assets and in controlling systematic risk exposures in asset allocation.
questions.stem: Which of Ramos’s statements regarding factor-based approaches to asset allocation is least likely correct?

B.text: Statement 2 is incorrect. Factors are **not directly investable**. Factor portfolios that isolate exposure to a factor are constructed with long and short positions.

A.text: Statement 1 is correct, so it's not the answer.

C.text: Statement 3 is correct, so it's not the answer. Multifactor models have a history of use in selecting assets and in controlling systematic risk exposure.

questions.keyPrinciple: Factors are not directly investable; you build factor portfolios (long/short) to isolate them.

questions.topic: Risk budgeting (MCTR)
questions.title: Risk-Free Rate from Excess Return/MCTR
questions.context:
EM equities: expected return 8.5%, std. dev. 14.2%, MCTR 12.5%, ratio of excess return to MCTR **0.27**.

*Ignore: std. dev. The ratio divides by MCTR.*
questions.stem: The risk-free rate used to calculate the ratio of excess return to MCTR in Exhibit 1 was closest to:
questions.keyPrinciple: Ratio = (E(R) − Rf) / MCTR. Optimal when equal across assets and equal to the tangency portfolio's Sharpe ratio.
questions.flag: Key doesn't say how A or C were built; I only show they don't reproduce 0.27.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Approach for a Global Bank
questions.context: Bank wants to estimate the probability that its **current capital** can withstand losses in trading units **while liabilities are increasing**. The CRO prefers a **multi-period** model.
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate liability-relative asset allocation approach for the large global bank?

C.text: Integrated asset–liability (ALM for banks): multi-period, decides composition of liabilities together with assets, fits stress testing of capital.

A.text: Surplus optimization is single-period.

B.text: Hedging/return-seeking is single-period.

questions.keyPrinciple: Multi-period + liabilities changing + capital adequacy → integrated asset–liability.

questions.topic: Taxes and asset location
questions.title: Account for Short-Term Bonds (Wiley)
questions.context: Wiley has taxable, tax-deferred and tax-exempt accounts. New money will be invested in **short-term corporate bonds** and **withdrawn within a year** for a house. Short-term gains and bond interest are taxed at a higher rate than long-term gains. She **can't withdraw from retirement accounts without penalty**.
questions.stem: In which of the following accounts should Wiley hold the investments purchased with her new money?

A.text: Taxable bonds normally go in tax-exempt/tax-deferred accounts, but near-term liquidity is the exception. Retirement accounts aren't accessible without penalty, so the funds sit in the taxable account.

B.text: The general-rule location for taxable bonds, but withdrawal before retirement age costs a penalty. Doesn't work for a one-year need.

C.text: Same access problem: not accessible without penalty.

questions.keyPrinciple: Asset location exception: money needed soon stays in an accessible (taxable) account.

questions.topic: Economic balance sheet
questions.title: Economic Net Worth — Nichols
questions.context: Nichols (60, retiring in 5 years): equities $1,350,000, investment-grade bonds $625,000, home $750,000 with $130,000 mortgage. PV of pre-retirement earnings $320,000. PV of future consumption $1,900,000.
questions.stem: Using the economic balance sheet approach, Nichols’s economic net worth is closest to:

A.text: $695,000 = $1,015,000 − $320,000, i.e. it leaves out human capital. *(My reconstruction.)*

C.text: $1,145,000 = $3,045,000 − $1,900,000, i.e. it leaves out the mortgage. *(My reconstruction.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Home is an asset; the mortgage is a liability. Human capital is an asset; PV of consumption is a liability.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Approach for Nichols
questions.context: Nichols' objectives: maintain her current lifestyle and fund each of her various interests and hobbies. She wants her overall allocation to reflect her **required probability of achieving each individual objective**.
questions.stem: Which asset allocation approach would be most appropriate for Nichols?

B.text: Goals-based: each goal gets its own sub-portfolio with a time horizon and required probability of success. Sub-portfolios sum to the overall strategic allocation.

A.text: Asset-only doesn't model liabilities or goals; it maximizes the Sharpe ratio for acceptable volatility.

C.text: Liability-relative models legal and quasi-liabilities and is mostly institutional.

questions.keyPrinciple: Individual with multiple objectives, each with its own probability of success → goals-based.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: MVO Utility for Baker
questions.stem: Which strategic asset allocation considered by Sanchez would be most appropriate for Baker?

C.text: U(C) = 6.0 − 0.005(8)(25) = **5.00%**. At λ = 8 the lowest-risk allocation is not automatically best; C gives up too much return.

questions.keyPrinciple: Compute U for all three. High λ doesn't automatically mean the lowest-risk portfolio.

questions.topic: Tactical / dynamic allocation
questions.title: Sanchez's Short-Term Adjustment
questions.context: Sanchez suggests Baker make a short-term adjustment to address **uncertainty around an upcoming election** and its anticipated impact on economic and financial market conditions.
questions.stem: The short-term adjustment Sanchez proposes to Baker is best described as:

B.text: A qualitative interpretation of political, economic and market conditions = discretionary TAA.

A.text: Systematic TAA relies on quantitative signals.

C.text: Trend-following extrapolates recent trends (a systematic signal).

questions.keyPrinciple: Discretionary TAA = qualitative judgment on political/economic events. Systematic = rules/signals.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Radell's Statements on Option 1
questions.context:
SPP objectives: fully funded in 5 years, minimize fluctuations in required contributions, minimize costs.
Option 1: 25% global FI / 20% developed equity / **20% EM equity** / 10% real estate / 10% PE / 15% hedge funds. E(R) 5.5%, vol 13%, Sharpe 0.19 (current 0.17, Option 2 0.175).
Radell:
- Statement 1: Based on its Sharpe ratio, Option 1 is most consistent with Sabonete's objectives.
- Statement 2: The 10% real estate allocation is too high given the company's recent African real estate acquisitions.
- Statement 3: The 20% EM equity allocation is too high given the sensitivity of the firm's revenues to emerging markets.
questions.stem: Which of Radell’s statements regarding asset allocation Option 1 is most appropriate?

C.text: EM equity is volatile, offers limited diversification versus global equity, and moves with the firm's own revenues. A weak EM environment stresses plan assets and sponsor revenue at once, which conflicts with stable year-to-year contributions.

A.text: Option 1 does have the highest Sharpe ratio, but Sharpe ignores funded ratio, horizon and contribution predictability, which are Sabonete's objectives.

B.text: The land is owned by the company outside the pension fund, so it isn't part of the SPP's extended balance sheet.

questions.keyPrinciple: Sponsor's own risks (revenue, assets outside the plan): only those correlated with plan assets/contributions matter. Sharpe alone isn't the objective for a liability-driven plan.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Approach for SPP Objectives
questions.context:
SPP objectives: reach fully funded (100%) in five years and then fully hedge liabilities; minimize fluctuations in year-to-year contributions; minimize administrative and investment costs.
Fund is **90% funded**: €5B in assets, €5.55B accrued benefit obligation (5/5.55 = 90.1%). €75M contribution this quarter.
questions.stem: From the description of Sabonete’s objectives for the SPP, the most appropriate asset allocation approach is:

C.text: Integrated asset–liability: plan is underfunded and has a funding path and contribution objectives over multiple periods.

A.text: MVO is asset-only and ignores the funding goal.

B.text: The basic two-portfolio approach assumes a surplus to allocate to a return-seeking portfolio. The plan is underfunded.

questions.keyPrinciple: Underfunded + multi-period funding and contribution goals → integrated asset–liability.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: What Wouldn't Hurt Funded Status
questions.context: SPP facts: salary growth rate 3.2%. Liability discount rate 3.5%, benchmarked to **10-year AA corporate bonds**. Risk-free rate 3.0%, **short-term rates expected to remain stable**. Average participant is 45.
questions.stem: If a revision of Falana’s key facts and assumptions regarding Sabonete and the SPP were to occur, which would least likely result in the plan’s funded status deteriorating?

B.text: Liabilities are discounted at 10-year rates, and little of the fixed income would be in short-term assets. A drop in short-term rates is least likely to affect funded status.

A.text: Higher salary growth raises projected liabilities → funded status worsens.

C.text: Older average participant → benefits are paid sooner → PV of withdrawals rises → funded status worsens.

questions.keyPrinciple: Liability PV rises with: higher salary growth, lower discount rate, earlier payments (older participants).

questions.topic: Rebalancing ranges
questions.title: Radell's Rebalancing Range Justification
questions.context: Radell: *"A wide rebalancing range for global fixed income is appropriate because of its **low volatility**, **low transaction costs**, and **low correlation** with other asset classes in the portfolio."*
questions.stem: Which of Radell’s justifications for the proposed rebalancing ranges for Option 2 is most accurate? The one based on:

A.text: Correct. Lower volatility relative to the rest of the portfolio → wider range.

B.text: Lower correlation with the rest → **narrower** range, to preserve its risk-reduction contribution.

C.text: Low transaction costs → rebalancing is cheap → **narrower** range.

questions.keyPrinciple: One-line check of each reason: volatility (own) → wider; transaction cost low → narrower; correlation low → narrower.
questions.flag: Exhibit 3 (Option 2 ranges) shows hedge funds at 5% but Exhibit 2 shows 10% for Option 2, and the Exhibit 3 targets sum to 95%. Doesn't affect this question.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Private Equity Modeling Statement
questions.context: Radell: *"The allocation for private equity is challenging because a low-cost passive investment vehicle does not exist and modeling with a private equity index captures only the return aspects of private equity without an appropriate representation of risk."*
questions.stem: Radell’s statement about the portfolio allocation of private equity in Exhibit 3 is most likely:

choices.text: incorrect in regard to a low-cost passive investment vehicle.
incorrect in regard to modeling risk and return with a private equity index.

C.text: The index part is wrong: PE indexes capture neither the risk nor the return attributes accurately (illiquid constituents → understated volatility).

A.text: Not fully correct, since the index part is wrong.

B.text: The passive-vehicle part is correct: no low-cost passive vehicles exist.

questions.keyPrinciple: Illiquid assets: indexes misstate risk (and return); no low-cost passive vehicles.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Response to the Endowment Model Proposal
questions.context: D'Alessandro prefers Option 1 because the best pension funds adopted the **endowment model** (higher allocation to alternatives). Sabonete plans to hedge its liabilities in **five years** and wants to minimize investment and administrative costs.
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is the best response to D’Alessandro’s rationale for justifying Option 1 for the SPP’s asset allocation? The proposed model:

choices.text: is not well suited to the SPP given its objective of fully funding and hedging its liabilities.
has an inherent illiquidity premium, which will help Sabonete achieve its objective of fully funding the pension plan.
would benefit the SPP because it can be expected to generate higher returns, more than offsetting the higher costs.

A.text: Endowment model seeks illiquidity premiums, which need a long horizon. A 5-year path to full hedging is too short, and its higher costs conflict with the cost objective.

B.text: The premium exists in principle, but the horizon is too short to capture it.

C.text: Higher returns from the illiquidity premium may offset costs in general, but not here (short horizon; cost objective).

questions.keyPrinciple: Endowment model suits long horizons and high tolerance for cost and illiquidity.

questions.topic: Economic balance sheet
questions.title: Endowment Underfunding
questions.context:
Exhibit 1 ($ millions): immediately available funds 50.2. Available funds restricted to scholarships 53.2. Current endowment obligations 89.5. PV of future endowment obligations 502.4. PV of pledged contributions, unrestricted 505.4. PV of pledged contributions, restricted to scholarships 87.8.
Proposal: capital project costing **$210.3M**. Clement donates **$50M** if the project is undertaken. No new campaign.

*Ignore: the $300M campaign figure.*
questions.stem: Based on an economic balance sheet, the answer to Wong’s question about the underfunding of the endowment (in $ millions) is closest to:

B.text: 105.6 = 802.2 − (746.6 − 50.0). It leaves the $50M donation out of assets (the proposal includes it).

C.text: 196.6 = 802.2 − (746.6 − 53.2 − 87.8). It strips out the $141M of scholarship-restricted funds.

questions.keyPrinciple: Economic balance sheet for an endowment: available funds and pledges (including the new gift) vs current obligations, future obligations, and the new project.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Approach Suggested by Black
questions.context: Black suggests a heavy emphasis on fixed-income securities with cash distributions, to offset future cash disbursements needed to cover university costs in excess of tuition revenue.
questions.stem: Which asset allocation approach best describes the asset allocation choice suggested by Black to the board?

A.text: Investing specifically to generate cash flows that offset liabilities is liability-relative.

B.text: Mean–variance is an asset-only approach and doesn't consider liabilities.

C.text: Per the key, asset segmentation is also an asset-only approach that doesn't consider liabilities.

questions.keyPrinciple: Assets chosen to fund specific future outflows → liability-relative.

questions.topic: Tactical / dynamic allocation
questions.title: Deviation Within 5% of Targets
questions.context: Black: weightings should be able to deviate within 5% of the target weights to take advantage of **short-term market opportunities** for additional return.
questions.stem: Black’s suggestion to the board in regard to the asset weightings in the endowment portfolio is best described as allowing for an asset allocation that is:

A.text: Short-term deviations from the strategic targets to capture opportunities = tactical asset allocation (active).

B.text: Indexing is passive.

C.text: Dynamic asset allocation is a long-term active strategy, not short-term.

questions.keyPrinciple: Tactical = short-term deviations from SAA. Dynamic = long-term, multi-period active.

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: UPPC Governance
questions.context: UPPC = six tenured faculty (3 arts, 3 sciences; two-year, non-renewable terms) and three final-year students. UPPC drafts the IPS; the board approves; UPPC then directs the advisory team and managers. Progress reports and governance audits go to the board **upon request**.
questions.stem: The process for creating and implementing the investment policy statement (IPS) by the University Planning and Priorities Committee (UPPC) most likely follows best governance practices in regard to:

choices.text: expertise for developing the asset allocation.
transparency of decision rights for approving a proposed asset allocation.

C.text: UPPC needs the board's approval for any allocation, so decision rights are transparent. That is good governance.

A.text: Audits "upon request" are inconsistent with best practice. Governance audits should be periodic.

B.text: Short terms (two years for faculty, one year for final-year students) and apparent lack of financial expertise are inconsistent with best practice.

questions.keyPrinciple: Governance elements: clear decision rights, expertise, continuity, periodic audits.

questions.topic: Safety-first / Monte Carlo
questions.title: Highest Probability of Meeting 5% Target
questions.stem: The asset allocation choice in Exhibit 2 that has thehighest probability of meeting the committee’s desired return criteria is allocation:

B.text: Highest probability of reaching the target → highest (k − kT)/σ (Ratio 2, the safety-first ratio): Allocation 2 at 0.077.

A.text: Allocation 1 has the highest Ratio 1 (Sharpe), which is relative to Rf, not the target.

C.text: Allocation 3 has the highest Ratio 3 (Treynor).

questions.keyPrinciple: Ratio 1 = Sharpe. Ratio 2 = safety-first (Roy). Ratio 3 = Treynor.

questions.topic: Safety-first / Monte Carlo
questions.title: Monte Carlo for Rebalancing Costs and Non-Normality
questions.context: Black says the UPPC should also consider rebalancing costs and that future asset returns may not be fully characterized by expected return and volatility. His preferred method: **Monte Carlo simulation**.
questions.stem: When addressing the University Planning and Priorities Committee, Black’s preferred approach for dealing with the additional allocation issues is most likely:

choices.text: incorrect because it is unable to address rebalancing costs.
incorrect because it is unable to address distributions that are dependent on parameters other than expected return and volatility.

A.text: Monte Carlo can handle many scenarios, including rebalancing costs and non-normal distributions.

B.text: It can address rebalancing costs.

C.text: It can handle distributions needing parameters beyond mean and volatility.

questions.keyPrinciple: Monte Carlo: path dependence, cash flows, costs, taxes, non-normality.

questions.topic: Economic balance sheet
questions.title: Economic Net Worth — Lennon
questions.context:
Financial assets ($M): investment portfolio 8.0, restricted employer shares 1.0, residence 2.0 (no mortgage), vacation property 3.0 (mortgage 1.0), DC pension 2.5. Human capital (PV of pre-retirement income) 4.5.
Extended liabilities ($M): Everett's education 1.5, special needs trust 2.0, endowed chair (PV) 1.75, PV of consumption 9.0.

*Ignore: age, current $1M salary, 30/70 split of the portfolio.*
questions.stem: Based on the information in Exhibit 1, Lennon’s economic net worth (in $ millions) is closest to:

A.text: 1.25 = (21 − 4.5) − 15.25. Leaves out human capital.

B.text: 4.75 = (21 − 1) − 15.25. Leaves out the restricted shares.

questions.keyPrinciple: Restricted shares still count as an asset. Include human capital and all extended liabilities.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Sub-Portfolio That Can Tolerate Most Risk
questions.context:
Aspirational goals:
- Everett: education and help funding his future practice, PV $1.5M. Funding extends over the longest horizon.
- Marshall: special needs trust, $2M, funded **within the year**.
- Endowed chair: PV $1.75M, funded in **two years**.
questions.stem: Which of the sub-portfolios dedicated to Lennon’s aspirational goals is in the best position to tolerate the greatest risk exposure? The one dedicated to:

B.text: Education has the longest horizon (key: possibly 8–10 years), so its sub-portfolio can take the most risk.

A.text: The trust provides lifetime benefits but needs funding immediately, so it should be liquid and low-risk.

C.text: The endowment is funded in two years (short horizon), so little risk.

questions.keyPrinciple: Risk capacity of a sub-portfolio is set by the horizon to when the money is needed, not by how long the beneficiary lives.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Institutional Approaches (Trainor and Kelly)
questions.context:
- Trainor: A goals-based approach is appropriate for individual investors, but institutions need to focus either on the asset or liability side of the balance sheet, depending on the nature of their business.
- Kelly: A typical objective of some institutions is to maximize their Sharpe ratio for an acceptable level of volatility, and they rely on the law of large numbers to assist them in modeling their liabilities. Other institutions behave much like individuals by segmenting general account assets into sub-portfolios associated with specific lines of business with their individual return objectives.
questions.stem: The most appropriate statement in regards to approaches to asset allocation by institutions is made by:

choices.text: Kelly, regarding the Sharpe ratio and modeling of liabilities.

B.text: Kelly's second comment is correct. Some institutions (e.g. insurers) segment general account assets into sub-portfolios for lines of business, each with its own return objective (a goals-based pattern).

A.text: Trainor is incorrect (key: asset-only is one option, liability-relative another).

C.text: Kelly's first comment is incorrect: an institution maximizing Sharpe for acceptable volatility is following an asset-only approach and wouldn't be modeling liabilities.

questions.keyPrinciple: Goals-based can also be used by institutions that segment assets by line of business.
questions.flag: Key's reason for A is weak, since Trainor already mentions the liability side. The cleaner reason (my reading): Trainor says goals-based is only for individuals, which Kelly's second comment contradicts.

questions.topic: Asset class specification / factor-based approaches
questions.title: Least Accurate Asset Class Statement
questions.context:
- Kelly: Asset classes should have high within-group correlations but low correlations with other classes. Also, because investors need to rebalance to a strategic allocation, asset classes need sufficient liquidity and low transaction costs.
- Trainor: It is important that asset classes should be diversifying. I always look for low pairwise correlations with other asset classes.
questions.stem: In the candidates’ responses to Fox regarding the relevant characteristics of asset classes, the statement that is least accurate is:

A.text: Low *pairwise* correlations aren't enough. A class can be highly correlated with a linear combination of the others even when pairwise correlations are low.

B.text: Kelly's correlation comment is correct (high within-group, low between-group).

C.text: Kelly's rebalancing comment is correct. It is the "capacity to absorb a meaningful portion" criterion: liquidity and transaction costs.

questions.keyPrinciple: Diversifying is tested against a linear combination of other classes, not just pairs.

questions.topic: Asset class specification / factor-based approaches
questions.title: Asset Classes vs. Strategies
questions.context:
Fox's unattributed comments:
1. Emerging market equities should not be considered a separate asset class from global equities.
2. Asset classes differ from strategies in offering a non–skill-based ex ante expected return premium.
3. Asset classes should be defined so that there is no overlap in sources of risk.
questions.stem: In the general comments about asset classes that Fox noted, the most accurate comment is the one regarding:

choices.text: the overlap of sources of risk.
the return premiums from asset classes.

C.text: Asset class return premiums come from an underlying market risk factor (beta), not investor skill. Strategies combine asset classes to earn a return based on skill.

A.text: EM equity is a distinct class: different diversification potential, informational efficiency, corporate governance, taxation, currency convertibility.

B.text: Some overlap in risk sources is unavoidable (US vs non-US equities, large vs small). The goal is as few common risk factors as possible and modest correlations.

questions.keyPrinciple: Asset class = market (beta) premium. Strategy = skill (alpha).

questions.topic: Behavioral biases
questions.title: Lennon's Bias
questions.context: Lennon has a tendency to **sell winning investments** to avoid the risk of giving back gains, and to **retain losing investments** even with little chance of recovery.
questions.stem: The behavioral bias that Lennon’s past investment experience illustrates is best described as:

B.text: Loss aversion: losses hurt more than equal gains please. She sells winners early and holds losers to avoid realizing the loss.

A.text: Self-control bias is a lack of discipline in pursuing long-term goals. She has taken steps to save for her goals.

C.text: Mental accounting is about separate buckets for different purposes. Not what Exhibit 1 describes.

questions.keyPrinciple: Sell winners early / hold losers = loss aversion (disposition effect).

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: Investment Governance
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the governance of an investment fund is most accurate?

choices.text: Effective investment governance should include periodically undertaking a governance audit
Governance focuses on the execution of the plan to achieve the agreed-on goals and objectives
Investment governance structures are more relevant to institutional investors than to individual investors

A.text: One of the six common elements of effective governance models is periodic governance audits.

B.text: That describes management. Governance clarifies the mission, creates the plan and reviews progress; management executes.

C.text: Governance structures matter for both institutional and individual investors.

questions.keyPrinciple: Governance ≠ management. Applies to individuals and institutions.

questions.topic: Economic balance sheet
questions.title: Target Date Funds
questions.stem: Target date funds seek to coordinate asset allocation with:

B.text: Life-cycle (target date) funds coordinate asset allocation with human capital, the PV of future labor income.

A.text: Expected inheritances are an extended asset, but not what target date funds coordinate with.

C.text: Social security benefits are an extended asset, but not what target date funds coordinate with.

questions.keyPrinciple: Individual's extended assets: human capital, PV of pension income, PV of expected inheritances.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Separate Allocation per Sub-Portfolio
questions.stem: The asset allocation approach that designs a separate allocation for different sub-portfolios is best described as the:

B.text: Goals-based: goals map to sub-portfolios, each with an allocation reflecting its horizon and required probability of success.

A.text: Asset-only uses one allocation for the whole portfolio.

C.text: Liability-relative allocates relative to liabilities, not separate sub-portfolios per goal.

questions.keyPrinciple:
| Approach | Primary risk measure |
|---|---|
| Asset-only (MVO) | Volatility of portfolio return |
| Liability-relative | Shortfall: insufficient assets to pay obligations |
| Goals-based | Probability of failing to achieve each goal |

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Approach Using Volatility as Primary Risk
questions.stem: Which of the following asset allocation approaches uses the volatility of the portfolio's return as its primary measure of risk?

A.text: Asset-only (MVO) uses standard deviation of portfolio return as its primary risk measure.

B.text: Goals-based is concerned with the risk of failing to achieve goals (max acceptable probability of not achieving a goal).

C.text: Liability-relative focuses on the risk of having insufficient assets to pay obligations (shortfall risk).

questions.keyPrinciple: Volatility = asset-only. Shortfall = liability-relative. Probability of failure = goals-based.

questions.topic: Asset class specification / factor-based approaches
questions.title: Asset Class Granularity
