questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the classification of asset classes is most accurate?

choices.text: Historical data for broadly defined asset classes are less reliable
Using broadly defined asset classes make it difficult to achieve a well-diversified portfolio
Effective portfolio optimization and construction may be hindered by excessive asset class granularity

C.text: Excessive granularity can hinder effective optimization and construction.

A.text: Historical data for broadly defined classes are usually *more* available/reliable.

B.text: Broad classes with fewer overlapping risk sources are consistent with a well-diversified portfolio.

questions.keyPrinciple: Too many narrow asset classes → overlap in risk sources and unreliable inputs.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Efficient Use of Asset Risk
questions.stem: Which of the following asset allocation approaches is based on selecting portfolios that make efficient use of asset risk?

A.text: Asset-only allocation selects portfolios that make efficient use of asset risk; mean–variance optimization is the mainstay.

B.text: Goals-based disaggregates the portfolio into sub-portfolios for individual goals or mental accounts.

C.text: Liability-relative chooses an allocation relative to the objective of funding liabilities.

questions.keyPrinciple: Asset-only → efficient use of asset risk (Sharpe/volatility). Not about liabilities or goals.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Tilts in the Global Market Portfolio
questions.stem: A common tilt when implementing the global market portfolio is to overweight:

choices.text: growth stocks relative to value stocks.
large capitalization stocks relative to small capitalization stocks.
the investor's home-country market relative to non-home-country market.

C.text: Common tilts: home-country market, value, small cap, emerging markets.

A.text: Tilt is toward value, not growth.

B.text: Tilt is toward small cap, not large cap.

questions.keyPrinciple: Global market portfolio tilts: home country · value · small cap · emerging markets.

questions.topic: Taxes and asset location
questions.title: Portfolio Management Statement
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about portfolio management is most accurate?

choices.text: Portfolios tracking fixed-income indices do not incur ongoing transaction costs
The cost–benefit analysis of tactical asset allocation should exclude the expected costs of simply following a rebalancing policy
When taxable investors hold both passive and active investments, they should in general hold their active investments in available tax-advantaged accounts

C.text: Taxable investors holding both passive and active investments should generally put the active ones in tax-advantaged accounts.

A.text: Index tracking still incurs ongoing costs. Securities move in and out of the index; fixed-income holdings mature, default or get called.

B.text: The cost–benefit analysis of TAA should *include* the expected costs of simply following a rebalancing policy.

questions.keyPrinciple: Tax location: active (high turnover) in tax-advantaged accounts; passive/low-turnover equity in taxable accounts.

questions.topic: Rebalancing ranges
questions.title: Considerations for Narrower Ranges
questions.stem: Which of the following considerations would support a narrower rebalancing ranges for an asset allocation?

choices.text: Less correlated assets in the portfolio

C.text: Less correlated assets → narrower range. A highly correlated asset is closer to a substitute for the rest of the portfolio, so larger deviations matter less.

A.text: Higher taxes → wider ranges. Taxes are a much larger cost than other transaction costs.

B.text: Belief in momentum/trend following → wider ranges. Mean reversion → tighter ranges.

questions.keyPrinciple: Narrower: lower correlation, higher volatility of the rest of the portfolio, mean-reversion beliefs. Wider: taxes, transaction costs, momentum, higher correlation.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Source of the Exhibit 1 Allocation
questions.context:
MVO allocation for an institutional client (MVO details lacking) vs investable global market weights (%):

| Asset class | Allocation | Global market weight |
|---|---|---|
| Cash | 0 | — |
| US bonds | 30 | 17 |
| US TIPS | 0 | 3 |
| Non-US bonds | 0 | 22 |
| Emerging market equity | 25 | 5 |
| Non-US developed equity | 20 | 29 |
| US small/mid-cap equity | 25 | 4 |
| US large-cap equity | 0 | 20 |
questions.stem: The asset allocation in Exhibit 1 most likely resulted from a mean–variance optimization using:

A.text: MVO with historical inputs gives concentrated allocations: heavy weights in 4 of 8 classes, none in the other 4, far from global weights.

B.text: Reverse optimization starts from market-cap weights, so results would sit close to global weights and be less concentrated.

C.text: Black–Litterman starts from reverse-optimized (market-implied) returns and adjusts for views. It would be less concentrated and closer to global weights.

questions.keyPrinciple: Concentrated, far-from-market weights = MVO on historical inputs. Near-market weights = reverse optimization or Black–Litterman.

questions.topic: Rebalancing ranges
questions.title: Corridor Width and Transaction Costs
questions.context:
Policy: rebalance when a weight falls outside a corridor around target; width customized per client and proportional to target. Beade recommends:
- wider corridors for **high-risk** asset classes
- **narrower** corridors for **less liquid** asset classes
- **narrower** corridors for **taxable** clients with **high capital gains tax** rates

Client is concerned about rebalancing-related transaction costs.
questions.stem: For clients concerned about rebalancing-related transactions costs, which of Beade’s suggested changes in the corridor width of the rebalancing policy is correct? The change with respect to:

choices.text: taxable clients with high capital gains tax rates.

A.text: In practice corridor width is set proportionally larger for higher-volatility classes, which avoids frequent, costly rebalancing.

B.text: Less liquid classes get *wider* corridors to avoid frequent rebalancing costs.

C.text: Higher capital gains tax rates → *wider* (not narrower) corridors, since each sale triggers tax.

questions.keyPrinciple: When the concern is cost: wider corridors for volatile, illiquid, or heavily taxed holdings.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Funding Ratio After Rate Rise
questions.context: DB plan: PV of liabilities **$241M**, market value of assets **$205M**. Beade expects rates to rise; both PV of liabilities and assets fall by **$25M**.
questions.stem: Based on Beade’s interest rate expectations, the pension plan’s funding ratio will:

A.text: Funding ratio = assets / liabilities. Before: 205/241 = **0.8506**. After: 180/216 = **0.8333**. It decreases.

B.text: Equal dollar moves don't leave a ratio unchanged unless it is 1.0.

C.text: Subtracting the same amount from numerator and denominator of a ratio below 1 pushes it further below 1 (a smaller base for the same dollar loss).

questions.keyPrinciple: Funding ratio = MV assets / PV liabilities. Underfunded plan: equal dollar declines lower the ratio.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Surplus Optimization Utility
questions.context:
Objective: U = E(Rs) − 0.005·λ·σ²(Rs), with λ = 1.5 *(formula image didn't paste; this is the form used in the key)*.

| | E(Rs) | σ(Rs) |
|---|---|---|
| Portfolio 1 | 13.00% | 24% |
| Portfolio 2 | 12.00% | 18% |
| Portfolio 3 | 11.00% | 19% |
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, which portfolio provides the greatest objective function expected value?

A.text: P1: 13.00 − 0.005(1.5)(576) = **8.68**. Highest return but variance 576 costs 4.32.

questions.keyPrinciple: Surplus optimization = MVO on surplus return: U = E(Rs) − 0.005·λ·σ²(Rs).

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Approach for Kealoha
questions.context: Kealoha has a large **fixed obligation due in 10 years**. She has substantially more funds than needed to meet it. She wants a competitive risk-adjusted return while keeping high certainty that the obligation is met.
questions.stem: The asset allocation approach most appropriate for client Kealoha is best described as:

C.text: Hedging/return-seeking: a hedging portfolio of riskless bonds pays off the obligation, and the balance goes to a risky return-seeking portfolio. A two-step process.

A.text: Surplus optimization is a single-step MVO on the surplus. It does not set aside a fixed hedge for the obligation. *(Key silent; curriculum.)*

B.text: Integrated asset–liability is a multi-period approach for institutions deciding assets and liabilities together. More than a single fixed obligation needs. *(Key silent; curriculum.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Overfunded + fixed obligation + wants certainty → hedging/return-seeking (hedge first, then invest the surplus for return).

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Subportfolios for Rodríguez's Goals
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 3, which subportfolios best meet the two goals expressed by client Rodríguez?

choices.text: Subportfolio A for Goal 1 and Subportfolio C for Goal 2
Subportfolio B for Goal 1 and Subportfolio C for Goal 2
Subportfolio E for Goal 1 and Subportfolio A for Goal 2

A.text: Goal 1 (95% row): highest is A at 2.05%. Goal 2 (85% row): highest is C at 3.26%.

B.text: B at 95% gives 1.75%, less than A's 2.05%.

C.text: E at 95% gives −0.60%. A at 85% gives 3.00%, less than C's 3.26%.

questions.keyPrinciple: Goals-based: read the row for the required success rate; pick the sub-portfolio with the highest minimum return (lowest funding cost).

questions.topic: Risk budgeting (MCTR)
questions.title: Risk Parity Weight on Domestic Bonds
questions.context:
Risk parity with four asset classes. Domestic bonds have the lowest expected return and the lowest covariance with the other classes.

*Ignore: expected return. Risk parity doesn't use it.*
questions.stem: In the risk parity asset allocation approach that Müller uses, the weight that Müller places on domestic bonds should be:

C.text: Risk parity: each class contributes equally (here 25%) to total portfolio risk. Bonds have the lowest risk, so they need a *larger* weight to contribute 25% → greater than 25%.

A.text: Less than 25% would apply to a high-risk class, not the lowest-risk one.

B.text: Equal *risk* contributions require unequal *weights* when risks differ.

questions.keyPrinciple: Risk parity: wᵢ·Cov(rᵢ, r_p) / σ²_p = 1/n. Low-risk assets → overweight.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Heuristic Models
questions.context:
Müller's comments:
1. An advantage of "120 minus your age" over 60/40 is that it incorporates an age-based stock/bond allocation.
2. The Yale model emphasizes traditional investments and a commitment to active management.
3. A client's allocation using the 1/N rule depends on the investment characteristics of each asset class.
questions.stem: Which of Müller’s comments about the other approaches to asset allocation is correct?

A.text: 120 − age lowers the equity share as the client ages; 60/40 is fixed.

B.text: Yale emphasizes **alternatives** (hedge funds, private equity, real estate), not traditional assets.

C.text: 1/N gives equal weights regardless of mean, volatility, correlation.

questions.keyPrinciple: Yale/endowment = alternatives + active + illiquidity premium. 1/N = ignores characteristics. 120 − age = age-based equity weight.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Preferred Allocation for Perkins
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1 and the risk aversion coefficient, the preferred asset allocation for Perkins is:
questions.keyPrinciple: Risk aversion of 8 penalizes variance heavily. The low-risk allocation wins despite lowest return.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Illiquid Asset Classes in MVO
questions.context: Velky wants to add direct real estate, infrastructure and private equity to VP's $500M portfolio and discusses the issues of applying common techniques like MVO to them.
questions.stem: In their discussion of the asset classes that Velky is interested in adding to the VP portfolio, Monteo should tell Velky that:

choices.text: these asset classes can be readily diversified to eliminate idiosyncratic risk.
indexes are available for these asset classes that do an outstanding job of representing the performance characteristics of the asset classes.
the risk and return characteristics associated with actual investment vehicles for these asset classes are typically significantly different from the characteristics of the asset classes themselves.

C.text: Actual investment vehicles (real estate, infrastructure, PE funds) differ significantly in risk and return from the asset classes themselves.

A.text: Illiquid classes can't readily be diversified to eliminate idiosyncratic risk.

B.text: There are far fewer indexes for illiquid classes, and they do a poor job of representing them.

questions.keyPrinciple: Illiquid assets: no good index, no low-cost passive vehicle, idiosyncratic risk not diversified, vehicles ≠ asset class.

questions.topic: Risk budgeting (MCTR)
questions.title: Velky's Risk Budgeting Statements
questions.context:
- Statement 1: An optimum risk budget minimizes total risk.
- Statement 2: Risk budgeting decomposes total portfolio risk into its constituent parts.
- Statement 3: An allocation is optimal from a risk-budgeting perspective when the ratio of excess return to MCTR is **different** for all assets.
questions.stem: Which of Velky’s statements about risk budgeting is correct?

B.text: A risk budget identifies total risk and attributes it to its constituent parts.

A.text: The goal is to maximize return per unit of risk, not minimize total risk.

C.text: Optimal when the ratio is the **same** for all assets (and equals the tangency portfolio's Sharpe ratio).

questions.keyPrinciple: Optimal risk budget: (Rᵢ − Rf) / MCTRᵢ equal across assets.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Criticisms of MVO
questions.context:
Chaterji's criticisms:
1. The allocations are highly sensitive to changes in the model inputs.
2. The allocations tend to be highly dispersed across all available asset classes.
questions.stem: Which of Chaterji’s criticisms of MVO is/are valid?

A.text: Only criticism 1 is valid.

B.text: Criticism 2 is backwards: MVO allocations tend to be highly **concentrated** in a subset of classes.

C.text: Fails because criticism 2 is not valid.

questions.keyPrinciple: MVO: input-sensitive and concentrated. Resampling and Black–Litterman try to fix both.

questions.topic: Asset class specification / factor-based approaches
questions.title: Factor-Based Approach Characteristics
questions.context:
Chaterji's characteristics:
1. Factors commonly used generally have low correlations with the market and with each other.
2. Factors commonly used are typically **different from** the fundamental or structural factors used in multifactor models.
questions.stem: Which of the characteristics put forth by Chaterji to describe the factor-based approach is/are correct?

A.text: Only characteristic 1 is correct: factors are typically zero-dollar (long/short) portfolios, which strips out most market exposure.

B.text: Characteristic 2 is wrong: factors are typically **similar** to fundamental/structural factors in multifactor models.

C.text: Fails because characteristic 2 is wrong.

questions.keyPrinciple: Factors: self-financing long/short → low correlation with market and each other; similar to multifactor-model factors.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Utility-Maximizing Allocation — Youngmall
questions.context:
Youngmall: λ = 7. Utility function: U = E(R) − 0.005·λ·σ² *(formula image didn't paste; this is the form used in the key)*.

| | Allocation A | Allocation B |
|---|---|---|
| Expected return | 6.7% | 5.9% |
| Expected std. dev. | 11.9% | 10.7% |
questions.stem: Determine which allocation in Exhibit 1 Tomb should recommend to Youngmall. Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Allocation B.**

- A: 6.7 − 0.005(7)(11.9²) = **1.74%**
- B: 5.9 − 0.005(7)(10.7²) = **1.89%**

B has the higher expected utility (certainty-equivalent return), so recommend B.
questions.keyPrinciple: U = E(R) − 0.005·λ·σ² (σ in %), or E(R) − ½·λ·σ² (σ in decimals).

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Reverse Optimization vs. MVO — Patel
questions.context:
Rf = 2.0%. Global market risk premium = 5.5%.

| Asset class | Mkt cap ($T) | Beta | Expected return | MVO allocation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cash | 4.2 | 0.0 | 2.0% | 10% |
| US bonds | 26.8 | 0.5 | 4.5% | 20% |
| US equities | 22.2 | 1.4 | 8.6% | 35% |
| Global equities | 27.5 | 1.7 | 10.5% | 20% |
| Global bonds | 27.1 | 0.6 | 4.7% | 15% |
| Total | 107.8 | | | |
questions.stem: Contrast, using the information provided above, the results of a reverse optimization approach with that of the MVO approach for each of the following: (1) the asset allocation mix; (2) the values of the expected returns for US equities and global bonds. Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**1. Allocation mix.** Reverse optimization takes market-cap weights as *inputs* (assumed optimal). In MVO the weights are *outputs*. The two mixes differ significantly.

| Asset class | Reverse opt. (cap weight) | MVO | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cash | 3.9% | 10% | −6.1 |
| US bonds | 24.9% | 20% | +4.9 |
| US equities | 20.6% | 35% | −14.4 |
| Global equities | 25.5% | 20% | +5.5 |
| Global bonds | 25.1% | 15% | +10.1 |

**2. Expected returns.** In reverse optimization, returns are *outputs* (implied equilibrium returns, linked to CAPM): Rf + β × market risk premium. In MVO they are *inputs*.

- US equities: 2.0% + 1.4(5.5%) = **9.7%** (MVO input: 8.6%)
- Global bonds: 2.0% + 0.6(5.5%) = **5.3%** (MVO input: 4.7%)
questions.keyPrinciple: Reverse optimization: weights in (market cap), returns out (CAPM-like implied). MVO: returns in, weights out.
questions.flag: Key says the MVO returns were 'forecasted using historical data'. The vignette doesn't say that. Arithmetic matches the key.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Hedging/Return-Seeking Allocation — Johansson
questions.context:
Fund assets **$10B**, PV of liabilities **$8.5B**. Liability returns are driven by index-linked government bonds. Johansson recommends the hedging/return-seeking portfolios approach.

| | Alloc 1 | Alloc 2 | Alloc 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cash | 15% | 5% | 0% |
| Index-linked govt bonds | 70% | 15% | 85% |
| Corporate bonds | 0% | 30% | 5% |
| Equities | 15% | 50% | 10% |
| Expected return | 3.4% | 6.2% | 3.6% |
| Std. dev. | 7.0% | 12.0% | 8.5% |
questions.stem: Determine which asset allocation in Exhibit 1 would be most appropriate for Johansson given her recommendation. Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Allocation 3.**

- Surplus = $10.0B − $8.5B = $1.5B.
- Hedging portfolio = PV of liabilities = $8.5B = **85%** of assets, held in the assets that drive liability returns (index-linked government bonds).
- The remaining $1.5B goes to a return-seeking portfolio (here corporate bonds and equities).

Allocation 3 has exactly 85% in index-linked bonds.
questions.keyPrinciple: Hedging portfolio size = PV of liabilities / assets. Remainder (the surplus) is return-seeking.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Module for Each Armstrong Goal
questions.stem: Select, for each of Armstrong's three goals, which sub-portfolio module from Exhibit 1 Abbott should choose in constructing a portfolio. Justify each selection.
questions.modelAnswer:
Choose the module with the highest minimum expectation return for each goal's horizon and success rate (lowest funding cost).

| Goal | Row | Best module | Return |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1: $5M home | 5 yr, 85% | **C** | 4.4% (B, D 4.3%; A 3.7%) |
| 2: $100k/yr | 10 yr, 99% | **B** | 2.2% (A 2.1%, C 2.0%, D 1.7%) |
| 3: $10M gift | 25 yr, 75% | **D** | 7.5% (C 7.3%, B 6.9%, A 5.7%) |
questions.keyPrinciple: Don't default to the lowest-risk module for the high-probability goal. Read the actual row.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Overall Goals-Based Allocation — Armstrong
questions.context: Same Armstrong facts (assets $8M). Selected modules: Goal 1 → C (4.4%), Goal 2 → B (2.2%), Goal 3 → D (7.5%). Any surplus → Module A.
questions.stem: Construct the overall goals-based asset allocation for the Armstrongs given their three goals and Abbott's suggestion for investing any excess capital. Show your calculations. *(Enter % of total assets in each module.)*
questions.modelAnswer:
Discount each goal's cash flows at its module's minimum expectation return; the PV is what that sub-portfolio needs today.

| | Goal 1 | Goal 2 | Goal 3 | Surplus |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Horizon / success | 5 yr / 85% | 10 yr / 99% | 25 yr / 75% | |
| Module | C | B | D | A |
| Discount rate | 4.4% | 2.2% | 7.5% | |
| $ invested | $4,031,508 | $1,013,670 | $1,639,791 | $1,315,032 |
| % of $8M | **50.4%** | **12.7%** | **20.5%** | **16.4%** |

- G1: N = 5, FV = 5,000,000, I/Y = 4.4% → PV = $4,031,508.
- G2: $100,000 at t = 1 growing 3% per year thereafter, discounted at 2.2% → PV = $1,013,670. *(The key doesn't show this step; I reproduced it by script: $1,013,670.)*
- G3: N = 25, FV = 10,000,000, I/Y = 7.5% → PV = $1,639,791.
- Surplus = 8,000,000 − 4,031,508 − 1,013,670 − 1,639,791 = $1,315,032 (my recompute: $1,315,031.5; rounding) → Module A.
questions.keyPrinciple: Goals-based allocation: weight of each module = PV of its goal / total assets. Surplus → module chosen for excess capital.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Lowest Funding Cost — Mueller Goal 3
questions.context:
Mueller: 75, 15-year life expectancy, portfolio $3.5M. Goal 3: leave **$1M** to charity after death, **60%** required probability of success. 15-year annualized minimum expectation returns:

| Required success | A | B | C | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 99% | 4.10% | 3.50% | 4.40% | 4.20% |
| 95% | 4.30% | 3.70% | 4.50% | 4.40% |
| 75% | 4.50% | 3.80% | 4.55% | 4.60% |
| 60% | 4.90% | 4.00% | 4.65% | 4.70% |
questions.stem: Determine which sub-portfolio module would offer the lowest funding cost for Mueller's Goal 3. (Module A, B, C, D) Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Module A.** At 15 years and 60% success, A has the highest annualized minimum expectation return (4.90%), so it has the lowest funding cost.

*Check (my recompute): PV of $1M over 15 years at 4.90% = $487,941 vs. $555,265 at 4.00% (Module B).*
questions.keyPrinciple: Higher minimum expectation return = higher discount rate = lower PV = lower funding cost.

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: Constraints on Yangs' PE Fund Investment
questions.context: Yangs: several children start college in two to three years, **$150,000 each**. Portfolio **$500,000**, mostly employer stock. Interested in reallocating a majority of the portfolio to a private equity fund run by a famous media personality.
questions.stem: Discuss two constraints the Yangs would most likely face regarding the fund investment to which they want to reallocate a majority of their portfolio. Note: Each discussion should be in a separate paragraph.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. **Asset size.** Smaller asset owners can have constrained access to private equity. Commingled vehicles usually require high minimums, and the Yangs' whole portfolio is $500,000.
2. **Liquidity.** College costs start in two to three years at $150,000 per child. PE is illiquid.
questions.keyPrinciple: Constraints: time horizon, liquidity, asset size, regulatory/other. PE: high minimums, illiquid.

questions.topic: Behavioral biases
questions.title: Representativeness in Yangs' Statements
questions.context:
Yangs' statements:
1. Volatility of gains doesn't bother us, but we would strongly prefer not to lose money in any given year.
2. We are highly confident in the prospects of the company where Bill works and would never consider selling our position.
3. We don't usually follow international stocks but read in the newspaper that EM stocks have been constantly rising over the past few months, so we'd like to invest in some.
questions.stem: Determine which of the Yangs' statements best exhibits representativeness bias. (Statement 1, Statement 2, Statement 3) Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Statement 3.** Wanting EM stocks after reading they've risen recently, without further research, is representativeness/recency: overweighting recent information over a longer, more comprehensive history (return chasing).

- Statement 1 = loss aversion.
- Statement 2 = illusion of control (holding concentrated legacy stock and overestimating control; can be amplified by overconfidence).
questions.keyPrinciple: Recent returns extrapolated = representativeness. Avoid-any-loss = loss aversion. Concentrated employer stock = illusion of control.

questions.topic: Safety-first / Monte Carlo
questions.title: Safety-First Portfolio for Brown
questions.context:
Brown: $5.0M windfall. Wants to withdraw **$120,000** in one year for a car **without drawing principal**. Tax-free withdrawals.

| Portfolio | Expected return | Std. dev. |
|---|---|---|
| A | 8.2% | 9.2% |
| B | 8.0% | 8.5% |
| C | 7.7% | 7.2% |
questions.stem: Determine the most appropriate portfolio for Brown based on a safety-first approach. (Portfolio A, Portfolio B, Portfolio C) Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Portfolio C.**

- Threshold return R_L = $120,000 / $5,000,000 = **2.4%**.
- Safety-first ratio = [E(Rp) − R_L] / σp:
  - A: (8.2 − 2.4) / 9.2 = **0.6304**
  - B: (8.0 − 2.4) / 8.5 = **0.6588**
  - C: (7.7 − 2.4) / 7.2 = **0.7361** (highest → lowest probability of falling below 2.4%)
questions.keyPrinciple: Safety-first: maximize (E(R) − threshold)/σ. Threshold = required withdrawal / portfolio value.

questions.topic: Safety-first / Monte Carlo
questions.title: Monte Carlo vs. MVO for Chu
questions.context: Chu: new retiree, $2.5M, funding 30 years of spending. Wants $90,000/yr spending funded **tax-efficiently** and an **estate** for heirs. Kim is **unsure of his risk tolerance** and is looking at **rebalancing** his existing portfolio tax-efficiently. She uses Monte Carlo rather than MVO.
questions.stem: Discuss two reasons why Monte Carlo simulation would be preferred over mean-variance optimization for Chu.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. **Unknown risk tolerance.** Monte Carlo shows a realistic picture of outcomes: the likelihood of meeting the spending and estate goals, the distribution of portfolio value over time, and potential maximum drawdowns.
2. **Rebalancing, trading costs and taxes.** Monte Carlo can model the effects of trading/rebalancing costs and taxes and the interaction of evolving markets with the allocation.

MVO is a single-period framework, which makes it inappropriate for portfolios that will be rebalanced over time, triggering gains and losses.
questions.keyPrinciple: Monte Carlo handles multi-period, path-dependent issues: cash flows, rebalancing, taxes, non-normal returns. MVO is single-period.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Limits of Two-Portfolio Approach for JMI
questions.context: JMI pension: closed to new beneficiaries. Liabilities set by the accumulated benefit obligation and **must keep pace with inflation**. Surplus is **slightly negative** and JMI won't raise contributions. Kim considers hedging/return-seeking with a **nominal government bond index** as the hedging portfolio.
questions.stem: Discuss two limitations regarding the use of the two-portfolio approach for JMI's pension plan.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. **Negative surplus.** A fully hedging portfolio can't be built unless a sufficiently large contribution is made, and JMI has declined.
2. **Basis risk.** Liabilities must keep pace with inflation but the nominal bond index isn't inflation-adjusted, so it isn't a true hedge.
questions.keyPrinciple: Two-portfolio approach needs a funding ratio ≥ 1 (or new contributions) and a hedge that matches the liability drivers.

questions.topic: Safety-first / Monte Carlo
questions.title: Safety-First Portfolio for Shipman
questions.context:
Shipman: $900,000 lottery win. Wants to withdraw **$54,000** in one year without reducing the initial $900,000.

| | Return | Std. dev. |
|---|---|---|
| Portfolio 1 | 10.50% | 20.0% |
| Portfolio 2 | 9.00% | 13.0% |
| Portfolio 3 | 7.75% | 10.0% |
questions.stem: Which of the portfolios provided in Exhibit 1 has the highest probability of enabling Shipman to meet his goal for the vacation home?

A.text: Highest return, but its ratio (0.225) is lower than P2's because of the 20% std. dev.

C.text: Lowest std. dev., but its ratio (0.175) is the lowest: excess over 6% is only 1.75%.

questions.keyPrinciple: Safety-first ratio = (E(R) − threshold)/σ. Threshold = withdrawal / initial principal.
questions.flag: Key's narrative swaps the P1 and P3 ratios (says P1 = 0.175, P3 = 0.225). Its own step list and my script give P1 = 0.225, P3 = 0.175.

questions.topic: Rebalancing ranges
questions.title: Corridor Width Statements
questions.context:
Remington: for a given asset class, the **higher the transaction costs** and the **higher the correlation** with the rest of the portfolio, the **wider** the corridor.
Montgomery: the **higher the volatility of the rest of the portfolio** (excluding the asset class), the **wider** the corridor.
questions.stem: When discussing asset allocation corridors with Shipman, which of Remington’s and Montgomery’s statements is the least accurate? The one regarding:

A.text: Montgomery's statement is the inaccurate one. Higher volatility of the rest of the portfolio makes large divergence from the SAA more likely → **narrower** corridor.

B.text: Accurate: higher correlation → wider corridor (assets move in sync, so divergence is less likely).

C.text: Accurate: higher transaction costs → wider corridor (a higher hurdle for rebalancing benefits).

questions.keyPrinciple: Wider: higher transaction costs, higher correlation. Narrower: higher volatility of the rest of the portfolio.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Model Behind Winfield's Allocation
questions.context: Winfield's allocation was established by **reverse optimization using investable global market weights**, with **adjustments to reflect Winfield's views** on expected returns.
questions.stem: The model on which Winfield’s current asset allocation is based is best characterized as:

A.text: Black–Litterman: start from reverse-optimized returns and alter them for the investor's views.

B.text: Pure reverse optimization takes market weights and solves for returns; it doesn't incorporate the investor's views.

C.text: MVO yields concentrated allocations; Winfield's would be spread across most classes.

questions.keyPrinciple: Reverse optimization + investor views = Black–Litterman.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Criticisms of Resampling
questions.context: Remington: resampling combines MVO with Monte Carlo, leading to more diversified allocations. Montgomery: criticisms include that **riskier allocations tend to be under-diversified** and the allocations **inherit the estimation errors** in the original inputs.
questions.stem: In Remington and Montgomery’s discussion with Winfield on resampling, Montgomery’s comment is most likely:

choices.text: incorrect regarding diversification of asset allocations.

C.text: The diversification part is wrong: riskier allocations are *over*-diversified. The estimation-error part is correct.

A.text: Fails: the under-diversification claim is wrong.

B.text: Fails: the estimation-error claim is correct.

questions.keyPrinciple: Resampling criticisms: inherits input error; riskier allocations over-diversified; complex.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Heuristics Comments (Montgomery)
questions.context:
1. The 60/40 stock/bond heuristic optimizes the growth benefits of equity and the risk reduction benefits of bonds.
2. The Norway model is a variation of the endowment model that **actively** invests in publicly traded securities with ESG considerations.
3. The 1/N heuristic allocates assets equally across asset classes with regular rebalancing without regard to return, volatility, or correlation.
questions.stem: In describing heuristics and other modeling techniques, Montgomery is most accurate with respect to:

C.text: Correct: 1/N treats all assets as indistinguishable in mean, volatility and correlation.

A.text: 60/40 isn't an optimization. It gives a growth foundation (60% equity) and risk reduction (40% fixed income).

B.text: The Norway model invests **passively** in public securities subject to ESG. The *endowment* model is the one with active management of alternatives for illiquidity premiums.

questions.keyPrinciple: Heuristics aren't optimizations. Norway model = passive public + ESG. Endowment = active + alternatives.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Sub-Portfolio Split for Sebastian
questions.context:
Sebastian: $2,900,000. Goal 1: $120,000/yr for 20 years, 90% success, 2.5% inflation, withdrawals at the **beginning** of each year starting immediately. Goal 2: $1,500,000 nominal in 10 years, 85% success.
Minimum expected returns (%) for sub-portfolios BY and CZ:

| Horizon / probability | BY | CZ |
|---|---|---|
| 10 yr, 99% | 2.90 | 2.50 |
| 10 yr, 90% | 3.40 | 2.80 |
| 10 yr, 85% | 3.60 | 3.00 |
| 20 yr, 95% | 5.10 | 5.40 |
| 20 yr, 90% | 5.20 | 5.70 |
| 20 yr, 85% | 5.60 | 5.90 |

*(Expected returns BY 5.70% / CZ 7.10% and current split 40/60 are ignored in the calculation. The 0% correlation line isn't needed.)*
questions.stem: Using Exhibit 2, which of the sub-portfolio allocations is most likely to meet both of Sebastian’s goals?

choices.text: A 43% allocation to sub-portfolio BY and a 57% allocation to sub-portfolio CZ
A 37% allocation to sub-portfolio BY and a 63% allocation to sub-portfolio CZ

A.text: Current 40/60: BY $1,160,000 covers Goal 2, but CZ $1,740,000 < $1,820,446. Goal 1 fails.

questions.keyPrinciple: Match each goal to its best module by horizon/probability, discount at that minimum return, then see which split funds both PVs.
questions.flag: The key's PV formulas didn't paste (only the conclusions). The dollar PVs above are my recompute and agree with the key's conclusions for all three choices.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: MVO Portfolio for XTR
questions.context:
XTR target return 5.7%, risk-free 1.8%. Each MVO portfolio is combined with the risk-free security to hit 5.7%.

| | E(R) | Std. dev. | Weight in risk-free |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 9.5% | 18.69% | 49.35% |
| B | 8.2% | 14.95% | 39.06% |
| C | 7.8% | 14.18% | 35.00% |
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, the most appropriateportfolio that meets the requirements of XTR Funds is:

B.text: Combined risk = σ × (1 − rf weight): A 9.47%, **B 9.11%**, C 9.22%. Sharpe = (5.7 − 1.8)/risk: A 0.412, **B 0.428**, C 0.423. B hits the target with the least risk (highest Sharpe).

A.text: Lowest weight in the risky portfolio, but highest combined risk (9.47%).

C.text: Least risky MVO portfolio on its own (14.18%), but not the least risky once combined with the risk-free asset (9.22%).

questions.keyPrinciple: Compare after combining with the risk-free asset. Highest Sharpe gets the target return with the least risk.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Criticisms of MVO Portfolios
questions.context:
- Swan: MVO portfolios are diversified with respect to risk factors such as value, size, and quality.
- Gruber: MVO portfolios are more sensitive to measurement errors in expected return than in correlation and risk.
- Morrison: Some MVO issues can be corrected by using reverse optimization to solve for **risk parameters** based on inputs for expected return and correlation.
questions.stem: In the discussion of the criticisms of MVO portfolios, the most accurate statement is made by:

B.text: Gruber is correct: MVO is most sensitive to errors in expected returns.

A.text: MVO diversifies on market risk only, not across risk factors.

C.text: Reverse optimization uses risk and correlation (covariance) inputs to solve for **expected returns**, not the other way around.

questions.keyPrinciple: Reverse optimization: inputs = weights + covariances + risk aversion; output = expected returns.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Illiquid Asset Statements (Gruber)
questions.context:
1. Illiquid assets offer both diversification benefits and an expected return **discount** relative to similar liquid assets as compensation for illiquidity.
2. Easily tracked indexes in asset classes similar to an illiquid asset often do not represent the **non-idiosyncratic** risk of the illiquid asset very accurately.
3. There are no low-cost passive investment vehicles to closely track the aggregate performance of less liquid asset classes.
questions.stem: Which of Gruber’s statements regarding illiquid assets is most accurate?

C.text: Correct: low-cost passive vehicles exist for liquid assets but not illiquid ones.

A.text: Illiquid assets typically carry a return **premium**, not a discount.

B.text: Easily tracked indexes usually don't capture the **idiosyncratic** risk of the illiquid asset. The statement says "non-idiosyncratic".

questions.keyPrinciple: Illiquid: return premium; idiosyncratic risk not captured by liquid proxies; no cheap passive vehicles.

questions.topic: Risk budgeting (MCTR)
questions.title: MCTR for Asset Class A
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the marginal contribution to total risk (MCTR) of the portfolio from asset class A is closest to:

C.text: MCTR = beta × portfolio std. dev. = 1.091 × 21.63% = **23.6%**.

A.text: 13.7% = weight × std. dev. (0.6334 × 21.63%). Not MCTR.

B.text: 14.9% = weight × MCTR (0.6334 × 23.6%). That is the *absolute* contribution to risk (ACTR).

questions.keyPrinciple: MCTR_i = β_i × σ_p. ACTR_i = w_i × MCTR_i.

questions.topic: Risk budgeting (MCTR)
questions.title: Excess Return / MCTR Ratio
questions.context: Same Exhibit 2 as the previous question. The portfolio is optimal.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the ratio of the excess return to the marginal contribution to total risk (MCTR) of the portfolio is closest to:

B.text: For an optimal portfolio the ratio of excess return to MCTR equals the portfolio Sharpe ratio: (9.5 − 1.8)/21.63 = **0.356**. I checked each class: (R − 1.8)/(β × 21.63) = 0.356 for A, B, C and D.

A.text: 0.077 is the Treynor measure: (9.5% − 1.8%)/1.0.

C.text: 0.439 = 9.5/21.63: uses total return, not excess return.

questions.keyPrinciple: Optimal risk budget: every asset's (R − Rf)/MCTR equals the portfolio Sharpe ratio.

questions.topic: Safety-first / Monte Carlo
questions.title: Harmon's Portfolio Comments
questions.context:
Harmon: deposit **$679,000**, goal **$775,000** in 10 years, 90% certainty, no excess risk. Equities and fixed income allowed.

| | Expected return | Volatility | Return at 90% success |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equity | 5.75% | 10.00% | 1.70% |
| Fixed income | 1.95% | 2.25% | 1.04% |

- Gruber: 100% fixed income is safest to meet the goal.
- Morrison: need some equity, but no further optimization required.
- Swan: need equity, and optimization will also be required.
questions.stem: In the discussion of Harmon’s portfolio asset allocation (Exhibit 3), the most accurate comment is made by:

A.text: Required return = (775,000/679,000)^(1/10) − 1 = **1.33%**. Fixed income's 1.04% at 90% falls short, so equity exposure is needed. Combinations must then be optimized (correlation drives how much risk reduction is possible) to reach 1.33% at 90% with the least risk.

B.text: Fixed income alone (1.04%) can't deliver 1.33% at 90% certainty.

C.text: Equity alone (1.70%) would clear 1.33% but at much more risk. Finding the lowest-risk blend that hits 1.33% requires further optimization.

questions.keyPrinciple: Required return = (goal/current)^(1/n) − 1. Compare to each sub-portfolio's return at the required success rate; blend to minimize risk.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Individual Investors in Goals-Based Approach
questions.stem: In a goals-based asset allocation approach, individual investors most likely:

choices.text: focus on a single long-term goal.
measure risk by the volatility of returns.
use minimum expectations to determine the funding cost of the goal.

C.text: Goals-based uses probability- and horizon-adjusted 'minimum expectations' (instead of average expected returns) to set the funding cost (discount rate) of each goal.

A.text: Individuals typically have *multiple* goals, each with its own horizon and urgency. Institutions have one overall objective set.

B.text: Individuals in goals-based frameworks define risk as the probability of not achieving a goal. Institutions use volatility.

questions.keyPrinciple: Goals-based: multiple goals · risk = probability of failure · minimum expectations set the discount rate.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Labeled Goal
questions.stem:
An individual client states the following three goals:

- **Goal 1:** Transfer $5 million to her children in 15 years
- **Goal 2:** Allocate any excess capital to a sub-portfolio module that preserves capital
- **Goal 3:** Maintain her current expenditure of $100,000 a year over the next 10 years

Which of the goals is best identified as a labeled goal?

B.text: Goal 2 ('preserve capital') names an investment feature (capital preservation) without articulating the underlying need. That is a **labeled goal**.

A.text: Goal 1 is a cash flow–based goal: a bullet payment of $5M in 15 years.

C.text: Goal 3 is cash flow–based: $100,000 a year for 10 years.

questions.keyPrinciple: Cash flow–based goals have identifiable amounts and dates. Labeled goals name features (minimal risk, capital preservation, purchasing power, long-term growth).

questions.topic: Risk budgeting (MCTR)
questions.title: Definition of MCTR
questions.stem: The marginal contribution to total risk for an asset class represents:

choices.text: the total amount of portfolio risk contributed by the asset class.
the rate of change in portfolio risk for a small change in the asset class weight.
the required change in asset class weights to maintain a target portfolio risk level.

B.text: MCTR is the rate at which portfolio risk changes for a small change in the asset class weight.

A.text: That describes ACTR (absolute contribution to total risk).

C.text: MCTR doesn't tell you the weight change needed to hold risk constant.

questions.keyPrinciple: MCTR = marginal (slope). ACTR = wᵢ × MCTRᵢ (total contribution).

questions.topic: Risk budgeting (MCTR)
questions.title: Absolute Contribution to Total Risk
questions.stem: The absolute contribution to total risk for an asset class can be calculated as the product of the asset class weight in the portfolio and:

choices.text: its marginal contribution to total risk.

C.text: ACTR = asset class weight × MCTR.

A.text: Beta alone times weight is not ACTR. MCTR = beta × portfolio volatility.

B.text: Portfolio volatility alone is not the multiplier; the weight is multiplied by the asset's MCTR.

questions.keyPrinciple: ACTR = w × MCTR, and ACTRs sum to portfolio volatility.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Asset Allocation Heuristics
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about asset allocation heuristics is most accurate?

choices.text: The 1/N rule exploits differences in marginal contribution to total risk
The endowment model characteristically seeks to earn illiquidity premiums
The "120 minus your age" rule is based on a hidden constant risk tolerance coefficient

B.text: The endowment model emphasizes large allocations to non-traditional investments and seeks illiquidity premiums, which long-horizon endowments can capture.

A.text: 1/N treats all assets as indistinguishable. Optimization methods exploit differences in characteristics, not 1/N.

C.text: '120 minus your age' infers an age-driven (not constant) risk tolerance.

questions.keyPrinciple: Endowment = illiquidity premium, alternatives, active. 120 − age = age-driven risk tolerance. 1/N ignores characteristics.

questions.topic: Rebalancing ranges
questions.title: Factor Leading to Narrower Corridor
questions.stem: Which of the following factors would most likely lead to a narrower optimal corridor width for an asset class?

choices.text: Higher volatility within the asset class
Higher volatility within the rest of the portfolio
Higher correlation of the asset class with the rest of the portfolio

B.text: Higher volatility of the rest of the portfolio makes large divergence from the SAA more likely → narrower corridor.

A.text: Per the key, an asset class's own higher volatility tends to point to a *wider* corridor (the effect is a trade-off between controlling transaction costs and risk; in practice width is proportional to volatility).

C.text: Higher correlation with the rest of the portfolio → *wider* corridor. In a two-asset mix, positively correlated classes move together, so the overweight class drifts less from target.

questions.keyPrinciple: Narrower: higher volatility of the rest of the portfolio, lower correlation. Wider: higher own volatility (in practice), transaction costs, correlation.
questions.flag: Key treats the asset class's *own* volatility as pointing to a wider corridor (practice, focused on transaction costs), while the *rest-of-portfolio* volatility points to narrower.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Liability-Relative Statements
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about liability-relative asset allocation is most accurate?

choices.text: Liquidity is one of the primary macro factors used to estimate the liability cash flows
A fully hedged portfolio can be constructed for a frozen pension plan with fixed liabilities
A factor-based approach cannot be implemented using the surplus optimization allocation method

B.text: A fully hedged portfolio can be built for a frozen plan with fixed liabilities. Liabilities affected by uncertain factors (inflation, salary growth, economy) can't be fully hedged.

A.text: The two primary macro factors for liability cash flows are future economic conditions and inflation, not liquidity.

C.text: A factor-based approach can be used with any of the three liability-relative methods (surplus optimization, hedging/return-seeking, integrated).

questions.keyPrinciple: Frozen plan with fixed liabilities → can be fully hedged.

questions.topic: Asset class specification / factor-based approaches
questions.title: Investment Factors
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the use of investment factors in asset allocation is most accurate?

choices.text: Investment factors generally have high correlations with each other
Investment factors generally have high correlations with the market
Investment factors are typically based on observed market premiums and anomalies

C.text: Factors are typically based on observed market premiums and anomalies, and are similar to fundamental/structural factors in multifactor models.

A.text: Factors generally have *low* correlations with each other.

B.text: Factors generally have *low* correlations with the market.

questions.keyPrinciple: Factors: low correlation with market and each other; based on observed premiums/anomalies.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Classifying a DB Pension Liability
questions.stem: A defined benefit pension plan whose benefit payments depend on the employees' retirement dates, longevity and cash payout rules is most likely considered a:

choices.text: contingent and legal liability to the company.
non-contingent and legal liability to the company.
non-contingent and quasi-liability to the company.

A.text: The sponsor has a legal commitment to pay, and the exact payment dates depend on uncertain events (retirement dates, longevity, payout rules) → **contingent** and **legal**.

B.text: The legal part is right; 'non-contingent' is wrong.

C.text: Quasi-liabilities are future cash payments essential to a mission but not legal obligations. A DB plan is legal.

questions.keyPrinciple: Legal vs quasi-liability = obligation vs mission-driven. Contingent = payment timing depends on uncertain events.

questions.topic: Liability-relative approaches
questions.title: Approach for Underfunded Conservative Pension
questions.stem: An investment manager needs to select a liability-relative asset allocation approach for a conservative pension fund. The funding ratio of the pension fund is less than one and is not expected to increase. If the investment manager is looking to implement a single period asset allocation model, which of the following models is most appropriate?

A.text: Surplus optimization is a single-period extension of MVO that works for any funding ratio.

B.text: Integrated asset–liability is multi-period; the question asks for single-period.

C.text: The basic hedging/return-seeking approach needs a funding ratio ≥ 1 (or a large enough contribution to fund a full hedge). With a ratio below 1 that isn't expected to improve, it doesn't apply.

questions.keyPrinciple: Single-period + any funding ratio → surplus optimization. Two-portfolio needs surplus/contributions.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: MVO Weight Constraints
questions.stem: Most real-world applications of Markowitz's mean–variance optimization allow for asset allocation weights:

choices.text: to sum to a value less than one.

A.text: Beyond weights summing to one, the next most common constraint is no negative (short) weights.

B.text: Real-world MVO is constrained.

C.text: Weights are typically constrained to sum to 100% (fully invested, non-leveraged).

questions.keyPrinciple: MVO constraints: weights sum to 1; long-only.

questions.topic: Economic balance sheet
questions.title: Assets to Include in MVO
questions.stem: An investor with moderate risk tolerance has $1,200,000 in liquid financial assets, $600,000 in residential real estate, and a net present value of $400,000 in human capital that is bond-like in nature. When performing mean–variance optimization to determine an appropriate asset allocation, the optimization should include:

choices.text: liquid financial assets and residential real estate only.
liquid financial assets, residential real estate and human capital.

C.text: Include liquid assets, real estate and human capital, with the non-tradable pieces (real estate, human capital) constrained at their current share of total wealth.

A.text: Liquid assets alone ignore real estate and human capital.

B.text: Omits the $400,000 human capital (bond-like).

questions.keyPrinciple: Optimize on total economic wealth, constraining non-tradable assets at their current weights.

questions.topic: Economic balance sheet
questions.title: Effect of Human Capital on Risk Capacity
questions.stem: Oliver Nolan is a 50-year-old tenured history professor with GBP 2,000,000 in liquid financial assets, GBP 1,000,000 in residential real estate, and a net present value of GBP 800,000 in human capital that provides bond-like cash flows. Compared to an asset allocation that only considers his liquid assets, including Nolan's real estate and human capital in the optimization would most likely:

choices.text: decrease his risk capacity in the liquid portfolio.
have no impact on his risk capacity in the liquid portfolio.
increase his risk capacity in the liquid portfolio.

C.text: Bond-like human capital and real estate are a large part of total economic worth → higher capacity for risk in the liquid portfolio.

A.text: Opposite direction.

B.text: They do change risk capacity.

questions.keyPrinciple: Large bond-like human capital → greater risk capacity in the financial portfolio.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Illiquid Assets and Return Premium
questions.stem: When determining an appropriate asset allocation to illiquid assets, an investor is most likely to:

choices.text: expect to earn a return premium as compensation for illiquidity.
invest in low-cost passive investment vehicles to lower investment management fees.
readily diversify their investments within each illiquid asset class to eliminate idiosyncratic risk.

A.text: Illiquid assets may offer a return premium plus diversification benefits.

B.text: There are no low-cost passive vehicles to closely track illiquid classes.

C.text: Illiquid classes can't be readily diversified to eliminate idiosyncratic risk.

questions.keyPrinciple: Illiquid assets: premium + diversification, but poor indexes, no passive vehicles, idiosyncratic risk.

questions.topic: Safety-first / Monte Carlo
questions.title: When Monte Carlo Is Needed
questions.stem: Under which of the following scenarios is a Monte Carlo simulation most likely required when estimating an investor's future wealth?

choices.text: There are no cash flows into or out of the portfolio over time
There are cash flows and terminal wealth is path dependent
There are cash flows but the terminal wealth is not path dependent

B.text: With cash flows in/out and path-dependent terminal wealth (sequence of returns matters), no analytical solution → Monte Carlo.

A.text: No cash flows → terminal wealth is path-independent; expected value and percentiles can be found analytically.

C.text: With cash flows, but not path-dependent (e.g. iid returns), an analytical approach is still feasible.

questions.keyPrinciple: Monte Carlo: cash flows + path dependence.

questions.topic: Asset-only models (MVO, reverse optimization, Black–Litterman, resampling, heuristics)
questions.title: Efficient Frontier Slope
questions.stem: A mean–variance optimization uses only risky assets and does not allow negative weights. Which of the following statements about the resulting efficient frontier is most accurate?

choices.text: The slope of the efficient frontier is flattest at the point representing the global minimum variance portfolio
The "kinks" in the slope of the efficient frontier represent the impact of leverage being applied and removed
The slope of the efficient frontier represents the rate at which the expected return increases per increase in risk

C.text: Slope = additional expected return per unit of additional risk. It is steepest at the far left (global minimum variance portfolio) and flattens moving right.

A.text: The slope is *steepest* at the minimum variance portfolio.

B.text: Kinks are corner portfolios, where an asset enters or leaves the efficient mix.

questions.keyPrinciple: Frontier slope falls from left to right. Kinks = corner portfolios.

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: Effect of Scholarship on Allocation
questions.context: Martins (44, retire at 62). Financial assets $600,000, of which 20% (= **$120,000**) is cash earmarked for Lara's university starting in one year. Lara just won a **four-year full scholarship**.
questions.stem: Given the change in funding of Lara’s education, the Martins’ strategic asset allocation would most likely decrease exposure to:

A.text: Much of the earmarked cash is no longer needed for near-term liquidity and can go toward the retirement goal (18 years away), so the cash allocation falls.

B.text: Nothing in the scholarship change argues for cutting bonds. *(Key silent.)*

C.text: Freed-up money goes to the long-horizon goal, which would raise (not cut) growth exposure.

questions.keyPrinciple: Change in liabilities (shorter/longer horizon, smaller liquidity need) → change in strategic allocation.

questions.topic: Goals-based approach
questions.title: Charitable Gift Sub-Portfolio
questions.context: The Martins redirect 15% of future retirement savings into a sub-portfolio for a **charitable gift from their estate**. It's a low-priority aspirational goal and they want the **highest return possible**.
questions.stem: The most appropriate asset allocation for the Martins’ new charitable gift sub-portfolio is:

C.text: Aspirational, low priority, long horizon (gift from the estate), highest return wanted → highest equity allocation.

A.text: 40/60 is too conservative for a goal that wants maximum return.

B.text: 70/30 is moderate; the goal calls for the most growth.

questions.keyPrinciple: Lower priority + long horizon → more risk in that sub-portfolio.

questions.topic: Taxes and asset location
questions.title: Neal's Tax Statements
questions.context:
Interest income is taxed at 35%; capital gains and dividends at 20%.
- Statement 1: The after-tax return volatility of assets in taxable accounts will be less than the pre-tax volatility.
- Statement 2: Assets that receive more favorable tax treatment should be held in tax-deferred accounts.
questions.stem: Which of Neal’s statements regarding the taxation of investments is correct?

A.text: Statement 1 is correct: taxes reduce the mean return and mute dispersion.

B.text: Statement 2 is wrong: assets eligible for lower tax rates and deferred gains should go first in the **taxable** account.

C.text: Fails on Statement 2.

questions.keyPrinciple: Favorable tax treatment (equities, LT gains) → taxable accounts. Tax-inefficient bonds/high turnover → tax-advantaged accounts.

questions.topic: Rebalancing ranges
questions.title: Rebalancing Taxable vs. Tax-Deferred
questions.context: Equity drifted from 60% to 71% (bonds 29%) in both a taxable and a tax-deferred portfolio after a 20% annualized equity return for three years. The Martins want the **same risk level** in both and want to **minimize taxes**.
questions.stem: Given the Martins’ risk and tax preferences, the taxable portfolio should be rebalanced:

choices.text: less often than the tax-deferred portfolio.
as often as the tax-deferred portfolio.
more often than the tax-deferred portfolio.

A.text: Rebalancing the taxable account realizes taxes. After-tax volatility is lower, so it takes larger moves to change its risk profile → wider ranges → rebalanced less often.

B.text: Same frequency ignores the tax cost.

C.text: More often would trigger more taxes for little added risk control.

questions.keyPrinciple: Taxable account: wider rebalancing range (after-tax range = pre-tax range / (1 − t)) → less frequent rebalancing.

questions.topic: Behavioral biases
questions.title: Neal's Bias
questions.context: Equities returned 20% annualized for three years. Neal is reluctant to sell stock, **confident strong returns will continue**.
questions.stem: During the rebalancing discussion, which behavioral bias does Neal exhibit?

C.text: Representativeness/recency: overweighting recent observations relative to a longer, more comprehensive history. Return chasing is a common result.

A.text: Framing bias is about how choices are presented. Not described. *(Key silent.)*

B.text: Loss aversion is a strong preference to avoid losses. Neal is sitting on gains. *(Key silent.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Recent strong returns assumed to continue = representativeness (recency).

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: New SAA for KCPF
questions.context: KCPF: 65% stocks / 35% bonds. After eight recession-free years the plan is **overfunded**. Early signs of weakening economy; Katt is in a **cyclical industry**. The committee fears risk to the high-priority goal of staying **fully funded** and may have trouble making contributions in a recession. McCall recommends a new IPS.
questions.stem: Given McCall’s IPS recommendation, the most appropriate new strategic asset allocation for the KCPF is:

A.text: 40/60: overfunded plan has less need for equity risk; cutting equities reduces risk, hedges liabilities better, and cuts contribution uncertainty.

B.text: No change doesn't address the concern about market and economic risk.

C.text: More equity raises risk.

questions.keyPrinciple: Overfunded + risk of sponsor distress → de-risk (more bonds).

questions.topic: Tactical / dynamic allocation
questions.title: Moving-Average Rule
questions.context: IPS revision: automatically **increase (decrease) equities by 5%** whenever the S&P 500 **50-day moving average crosses above (below) the 200-day** moving average.
questions.stem: The proposal for short-term adjustments to the KCPF asset allocation strategy is known as:

B.text: Rules-based, quantitative trend signal = systematic TAA.

A.text: De-risking is a shift toward lower risk; the rule works both ways.

C.text: Discretionary TAA relies on qualitative interpretation, not a mechanical rule.

questions.keyPrinciple: Systematic TAA = rules-based, quantitative signals (trend, value, momentum). Discretionary TAA = qualitative judgment.

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: Spending Rate Change and Liquidity
questions.context: KUE (large tax-exempt endowment) funded operations mainly from tuition. Enrollment is rising and expected to keep rising for five years, so **very modest endowment support** is needed. The committee approved a **lower annual spending rate**.
questions.stem: The change in the annual spending rate, in conjunction with the board’s expectations regarding future enrollment and the need for endowment support, could justify that KUE’s target weight for:

choices.text: private real estate equity be decreased.

A.text: Less need for liquidity → can raise strategic allocation to less liquid classes (infrastructure, private real estate) and cut liquid assets (IG bonds).

B.text: IG bonds are the liquid asset; lower liquidity need argues for *decreasing* them.

C.text: Private real estate is illiquid; lower liquidity need supports *increasing* it.

questions.keyPrinciple: Lower spending/liquidity need → more illiquid assets; higher need → more liquid.

questions.topic: Tactical / dynamic allocation
questions.title: Capara's TAA Statements
questions.context:
- Statement 1: The Sharpe ratio is suitable for measuring the success of TAA relative to SAA.
- Statement 2: Discretionary TAA attempts to capture asset-class-level return anomalies that have been shown to have some predictability and persistence.
- Statement 3: TAA allows a manager to deviate from the IPS asset-class upper and lower limits if the shift is expected to produce higher risk-adjusted returns.
questions.stem: Which of Capara’s statements regarding tactical asset allocation is correct?

A.text: Correct: compare the Sharpe ratio realized under TAA with the Sharpe ratio that would have been realized under the SAA.

B.text: Describes **systematic** TAA (rules-based, quantitative). Discretionary TAA relies on qualitative interpretation.

C.text: TAA bets must stay within IPS risk constraints (policy ranges, tracking-error budget). See the key to S3-41.

questions.keyPrinciple: Systematic = anomalies via quantitative signals. Discretionary = qualitative judgment. Both must stay within IPS limits.

questions.topic: Tactical / dynamic allocation
questions.title: Implementing TAA Within Limits
questions.context:
Exhibit 1:

| Asset class | Current | Target | Lower limit | Upper limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Developed markets equity | 30% | 30% | 25% | 35% |
| Emerging markets equity | 28% | 30% | 25% | 35% |
| Investment-grade bonds | 15% | 20% | 15% | 25% |
| Private real estate equity | 15% | 10% | 5% | 15% |
| Infrastructure | 12% | 10% | 5% | 15% |

Exhibit 2 (short-term expected excess returns): DM equity +2%, EM equity +5%, IG bonds −3%, private RE +3%, infrastructure −1%.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibits 1 and 2, to attempt to profit from the short-term excess return forecast, Capara should increase KUE’s portfolio allocation to:

choices.text: developed markets equity and decrease its allocation to infrastructure.
emerging markets equity and decrease its allocation to investment-grade bonds.
developed markets equity and increase its allocation to private real estate equity.

A.text: DM equity (+2%, room under 35%) up, infrastructure (−1%, room above 5%) down. Both moves are within the policy limits.

B.text: Signs match (EM +5%, IG −3%), but IG bonds are already at their 15% lower limit; cutting them breaches the policy limit. *(My reading of Exhibit 1; key doesn't explain B.)*

C.text: Private RE (+3%) is already at its 15% upper limit; adding breaches it. *(My reading of Exhibit 1; key doesn't explain C.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: TAA: overweight positive-forecast, underweight negative-forecast classes, but check each current weight against its policy limits first.
questions.flag: Key gives the reason for A only ('within KUE's lower and upper policy limits'). The limit breaches for B and C are my reading of Exhibit 1.

questions.topic: Taxes and asset location
questions.title: Tax-Efficient Reallocation for Koval
questions.context: Koval is in a high tax bracket. Interest income is taxed at progressively higher rates; dividends and long-term gains at lower rates. His taxable account holds equal weights of high-yield bonds, investment-grade bonds and domestic equities focused on long-term capital gains.
questions.stem: Given Koval’s current portfolio and the tax laws of the country in which he lives, Koval’s portfolio would be more tax efficient if he reallocated his taxable account to hold more:

choices.text: domestic equities focused on long-term capital gain opportunities.

C.text: Equities with long-term gain focus get the lowest tax rate and deferral, and their after-tax volatility is lower in a taxable account.

A.text: High-yield bond returns are mainly interest income, taxed at the highest rates.

B.text: Investment-grade bonds are also interest-based and tax-inefficient.

questions.keyPrinciple: Taxable account: assets with low-tax, deferred returns. Interest-heavy assets → tax-advantaged accounts.

questions.topic: Behavioral biases
questions.title: Koval's Aversion to EM Equity
questions.context: Koval refuses EM equity because he's **convinced it is too risky**, citing significant losses the family trust suffered in the recent economic crisis.
questions.stem: Koval’s attitude toward emerging markets equity reflects which of the following behavioral biases?

B.text: Availability bias: judging probability by how easily an outcome comes to mind. His personal experience of the crisis losses makes similar losses seem likelier.

A.text: Hindsight bias is the belief that past events were predictable. Not described.

C.text: Illusion of control is overestimating one's ability to control outcomes. Not described.

questions.keyPrinciple: Vivid personal experience driving probability estimates = availability.

questions.topic: Taxes and asset location
questions.title: Inputs Unaffected by Taxes
questions.context: Mayer recommends two MVO scenarios for Koval's taxable account: one pre-tax, one after-tax.
questions.stem: In both of Mayer’s optimization scenarios, which of the following model inputs could be used without adjustment?

B.text: Correlation of returns is unaffected by taxes → no adjustment needed.

A.text: After-tax optimization adjusts each class's expected return for expected taxes.

C.text: Taxes mute dispersion, so each class's standard deviation also needs adjusting.

questions.keyPrinciple: After-tax MVO: adjust returns and standard deviations; correlations unchanged.

questions.topic: Behavioral biases
questions.title: Young's Behavioral Biases
questions.context:
Young (47): sold a business for $5.5M net of taxes (in a money market account). Other assets: tax-deferred retirement account $3.0M, $500,000 after-tax account for her daughters' education, $400,000 after-tax account for unexpected needs, home owned outright. Daughters 7 and 10.
Living expenses covered by her job. Wants to retire in 15 years from existing assets. Orphaned at eight, with childhood financial hardships; places a high priority on retirement security and wants to **avoid losing money in any of her three accounts**.
questions.stem: Identify the behavioral biases Young is most likely exhibiting (from: loss aversion, illusion of control, mental accounting, representativeness, framing, availability). Justify each response.
questions.modelAnswer:
| Bias | Justification |
|---|---|
| **Loss aversion** | Strongly prefers avoiding losses to achieving gains; wants no losses in any account and stresses retirement security. May interfere with holding the ideal allocation through negative returns. |
| **Mental accounting** | Treats the $3M retirement account, $500,000 education account and $400,000 emergency account separately instead of as one investable total → risk of a sub-optimal allocation. |
| **Availability** | Mental shortcut based on how easily an outcome comes to mind. Strong memories of childhood hardship likely drive her emphasis on security and avoiding losses. |
questions.keyPrinciple: Loss aversion (avoid losses) · mental accounting (separate buckets) · availability (vivid past experience).

questions.topic: Safety-first / Monte Carlo
questions.title: Portfolio Selection with After-Tax Return Target
questions.context:
Young wants **at least 6.0% after tax** per year **without additional incremental risk**. Capital gains and overall tax rate 25%. Broker's alternative-asset minimum: **$500,000**. Funds available: $5.5M.

| Asset class | P1 | P2 | P3 | Pre-tax return |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Municipal bonds | 5% | 35% | 30% | 3% |
| Small-cap equities | 50% | 10% | 35% | 12% |
| Large-cap equities | 35% | 50% | 35% | 10% |
| Private equity | 10% | 5% | 0% | 25% |
| Post-tax std. dev. | 28.2% | 16.3% | 15.5% | |
questions.stem: Determine which proposed portfolio most closely meets Young's desired objectives. Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Portfolio 3.**

Post-tax returns by class: munis 3.00% (no tax), small-cap 9.00%, large-cap 7.50%, PE 18.75%.

| | P1 | P2 | P3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Post-tax return | 9.15%* | 6.64%* | **6.68%** |
| Post-tax std. dev. | 28.2% | 16.3% | 15.5% |
| PE exposure vs $500,000 min | $550,000 (met) | $275,000 (not met) | none needed |

*My recompute (the key shows only P3's 6.68%).

- P3 meets 6% with the lowest std. dev. of the three.
- P1 has the highest return but far more risk.
- P2 isn't viable: 5% × $5.5M = $275,000 is below the $500,000 private equity minimum.
questions.keyPrinciple: Read the objective: 'minimum return, no extra risk' = lowest σ that clears the threshold. Check practical constraints (minimums) before comparing.

questions.topic: Rebalancing ranges
questions.title: Rebalancing Range by Account Type
questions.context:
Young rebalances her **$5.5M money market account** (after-tax) and her **$3.0M tax-deferred retirement account**. Same risk profile for equities. Tax rate 25%.
- Alternative 1: 80% equities, ±8.0% range.
- Alternative 2: 75% equities, ±10.7% range.
questions.stem: Determine which alternative best fits each account. Justify each selection.
questions.modelAnswer:
| Account | Alternative | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| $5.5M (taxable, after-tax) | **2** | After-tax volatility is lower, so the range is wider. After-tax range = pre-tax range / (1 − t) = 8.0% / 0.75 = **10.67%**. Also, sales trigger taxes, so a wider range delays them. |
| $3.0M (tax-deferred) | **1** | Pre-tax volatility is higher, so the range is narrower (8.0%). |
questions.keyPrinciple: After-tax range = pre-tax range / (1 − tax rate). Taxable account → wider.
questions.flag: The circled alternatives didn't survive the paste. The assignment above (taxable → Alt 2, tax-deferred → Alt 1) follows from the key's own reasoning (8.0%/(1 − 0.25) = 10.67%).

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: Reason for Special Review (Young)
questions.context: Ten years later, Young is considering an **early-retirement package** with three years of continuing salary and benefits. The broker recommends a special review. She'd retire about five years sooner than planned.
questions.stem: Identify the primary reason for the broker's reassessment of Young's circumstances. (Change in goals / Change in constraints / Change in beliefs) Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Change in constraints.** Constraints cover time horizon, liquidity needs, asset size and regulatory/external limits. The time horizon has shortened.

- Change in goals: would be a change in personal circumstances altering risk appetite or capacity. Hers haven't.
- Change in beliefs: guiding investment principles haven't changed.
questions.keyPrinciple: Review triggers: goals · constraints (time horizon, liquidity, size, regulation) · beliefs.

questions.topic: Taxes and asset location
questions.title: Where to Add Equity (Young)
questions.context:
Young accepts the retirement offer. Very low liquidity needs. She wants to save part of the payout for **unforeseen costs more than a decade away**. The broker's long-term stock view is positive and recommends additional equity investment. Daughters are now 17 and 20.
Accounts: education, reallocated money market (taxable), retirement (tax-deferred), unexpected needs.
questions.stem: Determine which of Young's accounts (education, retirement, reallocated money market, or unexpected needs) is best suited for implementing the broker's recommendation. Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Reallocated money market account** (taxable).

- Equities, which are eligible for lower tax rates and deferred gains, belong in the taxable account. Taxable bonds and high-turnover strategies belong in tax-exempt/tax-deferred accounts.
- The retirement account is tax-deferred.
- The unexpected needs account requires liquidity, so it fits shorter-term positions.
- The education account is probably funding college now (daughters 17 and 20) and needs liquid assets.
questions.keyPrinciple: Location: tax-efficient equity → taxable. Tax-inefficient bonds → tax-deferred/exempt. Liquid needs stay liquid.
questions.flag: The circled account didn't survive the paste; the justification text sits on the 'Reallocated Money Market' row. Judgment call: the stem says the money is for costs >10 years out, which fits 'unexpected needs' on horizon. The key overrides that on liquidity and tax location.

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: Titan's Proposed Allocation
questions.context:
Titan: $10M. Must spend **3%** of beginning-of-year assets. Wants private equity exposure. Enrollment declining (revenue loss); regulatory sanctions → lower donations for five years.

| Fund | Existing | Proposed | Fund size (AUM) | Minimum |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global Equity Fund | 70% | 70% | $25B | $500,000 |
| Investment-Grade Bond Fund | 27% | 17% | $50B | $250,000 |
| Sun-Fin Private Equity Fund | 0% | 10% | $0.40B | $1,000,000 |
| Cash Equivalent Fund | 3% | 3% | $50B | $100,000 |
questions.stem: Discuss two reasons why the proposed asset allocation is inappropriate for Titan.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. **Liquidity.** Falling enrollment and lower donations mean higher likelihood of larger outflows to support operations. The proposal moves from bonds into riskier assets, increasing uncertainty about future value.
2. **Private equity is too big for Titan.** Smaller asset owners often lack access and expertise. The Sun-Fin fund's $1M minimum is 10% of the portfolio, which is inappropriate given Titan's weakened finances and potential liquidity need.
questions.keyPrinciple: Weaker finances → more liquidity, less illiquid alternatives. Check fund minimums against portfolio size.
questions.flag: Key says the proposal 'increases the relative equity holdings'; Exhibit 1 shows Global Equity unchanged at 70% (the increase in risky assets is the 10% PE).

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: Fordhart's Proposed Allocation
questions.context:
Fordhart: **$2B**. Must spend 3% of beginning-of-year assets. Enrollment strong and growing; a legal settlement **eliminated a $50M annual obligation**.

| Fund | Existing | Proposed | Fund size (AUM) | Minimum |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Large-Cap Equity Fund | 49% | 29% | $50B | $250,000 |
| Investment-Grade Bond Fund | 49% | 59% | $80B | $500,000 |
| CFQ Private Equity Fund | 0% | 10% | $0.5B | $5,000,000 |
| Cash Equivalent Fund | 2% | 2% | $50B | $250,000 |
questions.stem: Discuss two reasons why the proposed asset allocation is inappropriate for Fordhart.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. **Liquidity needs are falling.** Growing enrollment and the eliminated $50M obligation mean Fordhart can take more risk. The proposal moves the other way (equity down 49% → 29%, bonds up 49% → 59%).
2. **Concentration in the PE fund.** 10% × $2B = **$200M** = 40% of CFQ's $500M AUM. That is an undesirable level of operational risk for both sides.
questions.keyPrinciple: Check position size vs fund AUM: $ allocation / fund AUM.

questions.topic: Behavioral biases
questions.title: George's Lattice Shares
questions.context: George (62) owns over $1,000,000 of Lattice shares (long-term gains if sold) but views them separately from the Simpsons' overall portfolio and plans to start selling when he retires in three years.
questions.stem: Identify which behavioral bias best explains George's decision to delay selling his Lattice shares. Describe an asset allocation approach that would accommodate this bias.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Mental accounting.** He treats the shares as a separate bucket designated for retirement, ignoring their role in the family's total picture.

**Approach: goals-based investing.** It builds mental accounting into the allocation. Each goal gets a discrete sub-portfolio and an acceptable level of risk.
questions.keyPrinciple: Mental accounting → goals-based sub-portfolios.

questions.topic: Taxes and asset location
questions.title: Tax-Efficient Liquidity for the Simpsons
questions.context:
Liquidity needs: $50,000/yr for three years (daughter's education) and $150,000 in two years (son's wedding): **$300,000** total.
