Assets: Lattice shares over $1,000,000 (long-term gains), tax-deferred account $2,000,000 (withdrawals taxed as ordinary income), joint brokerage account $750,000 (mostly risky assets with short-term holding periods).
Taxes: **10%** on long-term capital gains; **25%** on ordinary income, short-term gains, interest and dividends.
questions.stem: Recommend an approach that would address the Simpsons' short-term liquidity needs in a tax-efficient manner.
questions.modelAnswer: **Gradually sell part of the Lattice shares over the next three years.** They've been held long-term, so gains are taxed at 10%.
questions.keyPrinciple: Raise liquidity from the lowest-taxed source first (long-term gains < ordinary income / short-term gains).

questions.topic: Tactical / dynamic allocation
questions.title: Risk and Benefit of Tactical Changes
questions.context: George is concerned about persistent inflation and volatility in global markets. He asks Casey for a few **tactical changes** to the joint brokerage account.
questions.stem: Identify one risk and one benefit of George's request related to the joint brokerage account.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Risk:** TAA can add costs (higher trading costs and taxes) and can concentrate risk relative to the policy portfolio.
- **Benefit:** TAA may raise returns or risk-adjusted returns if short-term conditions are correctly anticipated.
questions.keyPrinciple: TAA: potential alpha vs. costs, taxes, concentration.

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: OHF Phase 1 Constraint
questions.context: Phase 1 (1981–1991): initial $1B; **20-year accumulation, no distributions**; investments **restricted to cash and investment-grade bonds**; fund grew to $2.2B by 1991.
questions.stem: During Phase 1, the most significant constraint on OHF’s asset allocation choices was the result of:

B.text: Regulation: the mandate restricts investments to cash and investment-grade bonds.

A.text: Asset size isn't the binding constraint ($1B → $2.2B is low-range for a large institution but not the issue here).

C.text: No outflows were expected for 20 years and the portfolio was liquid anyway.

questions.keyPrinciple: Constraints: time horizon, liquidity, taxes, regulatory, asset size, unique.

questions.topic: Behavioral biases
questions.title: Phase 2 Manager Selection Bias
questions.context: Phase 2: external managers hired or retained if they **outperformed other active managers in at least the prior two years**.
questions.stem: During Phase 2,OHF’s external manager selection and retention policy was most likely susceptible to which of the following biases?

C.text: Representativeness/recency: assumes recent outperformance continues.

A.text: Endowment bias is valuing things more because you own them.

B.text: Loss aversion is about gains vs losses. The criterion was performance relative to peers.

questions.keyPrinciple: Selecting on short-term past performance = recency.

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: Phase 3 Change in Constraints
questions.context: Phase 3: **50%** public equities via passive index funds, **10%** cash and IG bonds, the remaining **40%** split equally among high-yield, real estate, PE and hedge funds, **managed externally**. Each external manager capped at about **$75M**. Fund grew from $6B (start) to $28B (end).
questions.stem: In Phase 3,the most likelychange in the constraints facing OHF’s ability to undertake asset allocation arose from an increased need for:

C.text: Governance resources: 40% externally managed ÷ $75M cap → about 32 managers at the start ($2.4B/75M) to about 149 at the end ($11.2B/75M = 149.3). Heavy demand for selecting and monitoring managers.

A.text: Liquidity needs hadn't changed; tax revenue flowed in again and 10% was in cash/bonds.

B.text: Risk wasn't being reduced; Phase 2 had already expanded risk.

questions.keyPrinciple: Many external managers → governance resources are the binding constraint.

questions.topic: Governance, IPS review, asset-owner constraints
questions.title: Phase 4 Change
questions.context: Phase 4: oil prices and production fell and management expects this to last through several cycles. It sought **lower withdrawals**, **higher equity** exposure (up to 65%), and ±5% flexibility around asset class policy weights. Government reaffirmed its commitment to the fund.
questions.stem: The changes that were allowed in OHF’s strategic asset allocation in Phase 4 are best classified as relating to changes in:

B.text: Beliefs: management's view of long-term inflows changed, so it adjusted spending and risk.

A.text: The fund's main goal hasn't changed; the government reaffirmed it.

C.text: No change in time horizon, liquidity needs, asset size or regulation.

questions.keyPrinciple: Review triggers: goals · constraints · beliefs.

questions.topic: Tactical / dynamic allocation
questions.title: Incremental Return from TAA
questions.context:
Exhibit 2 (weights %, period returns %):

| Asset class | Current | Policy | TAA | Period return |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Investment-grade bonds | 12 | 15 | 10 | 1.75 |
| High-yield bonds | 8 | 6.25 | 10 | 3.0 |
| Public equity | 63 | 60 | 65 | 7.0 |
| Private equity | 5* | 6.25 | 6.25 | 4.5 |
| Real estate | 6.25 | 6.25 | 2.5 | −4.0 |
| Infrastructure | 6.25 | 6.25 | 6.25 | 2.5 |

*As pasted. The key uses 4.5 so that Current sums to 100%.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, compared with the strategic asset allocation, the incremental return added to the fund through tactical asset allocation was closest to:

C.text: Incremental return = Σ (TAA weight − Policy weight) × period return: IG −5% × 1.75 = −0.0875; HY +3.75% × 3.0 = 0.1125; equity +5% × 7.0 = 0.35; real estate −3.75% × −4.0 = 0.15; PE and infrastructure 0. Total = **0.525% ≈ 0.53%**.

A.text: 0.13% compares Current weights with Policy weights (0.131%). Wrong benchmark for the TAA shift.

B.text: 0.39% compares Current weights with TAA weights (0.394%). The question is TAA vs the strategic allocation.

questions.keyPrinciple: TAA value added = Σ (w_TAA − w_SAA) × return. Benchmark is the SAA/policy portfolio.

questions.topic: Taxes and asset location
questions.title: Least Tax-Efficient Portfolio
questions.stem:
A taxable investor is considering the following portfolios invested in major economies with different sources of total return:

| Expected Contribution to Total Return | Portfolio 1 | Portfolio 2 | Portfolio 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interest income | 25% | 25% | 40% |
| Dividend income | 30% | 45% | 30% |
| Long-term capital gains | 45% | 30% | 30% |

Which portfolio is most likely to be considered least tax efficient?

C.text: Portfolio 3 has the highest share of return from interest income (40%), which is generally taxed highest. Versus P1 (same 30% dividends) it leans on interest instead of long-term gains. Versus P2 (same 30% long-term gains) it leans on interest instead of dividends.

A.text: P1 has 25% interest and 45% long-term gains (favorable), so it is more efficient than P3.

B.text: P2 has 25% interest and 45% dividends (taxed less than interest), so it is more efficient than P3.

questions.keyPrinciple: Tax burden ranking: interest (highest) > dividends > long-term capital gains (lowest, deferred).

questions.topic: Taxes and asset location
questions.title: After-Tax Optimization and HY Bonds
questions.stem:
A taxable investor is constructing a portfolio out of investment-grade (IG) bonds, high-yield (HY) bonds, and equity. Interest income is taxed at a higher rate than capital gains and dividends. The investor has also estimated the following correlations between asset classes:

- **Correlation between IG bonds and equity:** 0.05
- **Correlation between HY bonds and equity:** 0.72
- **Correlation between IG bonds and HY bonds:** 0.21

The most likely impact of considering after-tax returns rather than pretax returns in the portfolio optimization is a decrease in allocation to:

C.text: HY bonds have the heavier tax burden (interest income) and higher risk/correlation with equity (0.72), so after-tax optimization reduces them.

A.text: Equity is taxed more lightly (dividends, capital gains), so its allocation is not what falls.

B.text: IG bonds are taxed like HY, but they are lower-risk and have low correlation with equity (0.05), so they still diversify.

questions.keyPrinciple: After-tax optimization trims tax-inefficient assets unless they diversify enough to justify their tax cost.

questions.stem: Calculate the total cost of implementing a short seagull spread to hedge the WBIT position.

Short seagull = long ATM put + short OTM put + short OTM call.

questions.context: WBIT expires at $47.50. Strategy 1: collar using the $60 and $65 strikes. Strategy 2: bull call spread using the $55 and $65 strikes. Strategy 3: bear put spread using the $55 and $65 strikes. (Option prices as in DA-24.)
questions.stem: Determine which strategy is most profitable at expiration. Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Strategy 1 (collar)** is most profitable.
- **Strategy 1:** buy $60 put (3.11), sell $65 call (0.84): net premium 2.27. At 47.50 the put is worth 12.50 and the call expires worthless: profit = 12.50 − 2.27 = **$10.23**.
- **Strategy 2:** buy $55 call (9.23), sell $65 call (0.84): both calls expire worthless; loss = −(9.23 − 0.84) = **−$8.39**.
- **Strategy 3:** buy $65 put (8.21), sell $55 put (0.71): net premium 7.50. Payoff (65 − 47.50) − (55 − 47.50) = 10.00; profit = 10.00 − 7.50 = **$2.50**.
questions.keyPrinciple: Compute each option payoff at the expiry price, then subtract the net premium.
questions.flag: The key's figures cover the option legs only. The collar's share position is excluded. Including the stock bought at $60.25 (a −$12.75 loss), the collar would be about −$2.52 and Strategy 3 about −$10.25, so Strategy 1 is still best, but the profits quoted are option-only.

questions.modelAnswer:

questions.title: Best Strategy for Protection and Diversification
questions.context:
Reddy holds 50,000 CFT options (strike $8.50) and a concentrated position; CFT now $39.55. He wants downside protection and diversification at low cost and without a large short-term tax hit. Strategies: (1) long straddle with ATM options; (2) collar; (3) bear spread.

**Exhibit 1 — Six-month options**

| Call delta | Call premium | Exercise price | Put premium | Put delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.685 | 3.11 | 38.50 | 1.76 | −0.359 |
| 0.522 | 2.40 | 39.50 | 2.22 | −0.504 |
| 0.337 | 1.81 | 40.50 | 2.83 | −0.613 |
questions.stem: The option strategy Ramos should most likely recommend to Reddy is:

A.text: A long straddle is expensive and *increases* exposure to CFT, so it doesn't diversify.

B.text: **Strategy 2 (collar).** It protects the downside and effectively lets Reddy sell near the current price, cheaply, in exchange for giving up upside.

C.text: A bear spread is a directional bet; it protects less downside and is less cost-effective than a collar.

questions.keyPrinciple: Concentrated holder wanting cheap downside protection → collar.

questions.title: Gamma of a Straddle and Delta of a Collar
questions.context: S1: The gamma of the long straddle will be close to zero if the share price remains constant. S2: The delta of the collar will be close to zero if the share price increases significantly.
questions.stem: Is either of Ramos’s statements most likely correct?

A.text: Statement 2 is correct, so 'No' is wrong.

B.text: Statement 1 is wrong: if the price stays put, the straddle stays ATM and its gamma is at its highest, not near zero.

C.text: **Only Statement 2 is correct.** Collar delta = stock delta + put delta − call delta. After a big rise the call delta ≈ 1 and put delta ≈ 0: 1 + 0 − 1 ≈ 0.

questions.keyPrinciple: Collar delta → 0 after a large rally (call deep ITM offsets the stock). ATM options have the highest gamma.

questions.title: Synthetic Short Stock
questions.context: Cho: buy a put and sell a call with the same strike and expiration. Navarro: sell a put and buy a call. Lyons: sell a call and a put.
questions.stem: Who is most likely correct regarding the creation of the synthetic short stock position?

A.text: **Cho.** Long put + short call (same strike/expiry) = synthetic short stock.

B.text: Lyons: short call + short put is a short straddle.

C.text: Navarro: long call + short put is a synthetic *long* stock.

questions.keyPrinciple: Synthetic long = long call + short put. Synthetic short = long put + short call.

questions.title: Delta, Vega and Theta of Hedged Short Positions
questions.context:
Navarro, Cho and Lyons discuss synthetic positions. Patel has shorted 500 shares of Company A at $117.43 and is bearish. Navarro suggests buying five June 120 call contracts or writing five June 115 put contracts.

**Exhibit 1 — Company A options, 25 March 2019**

| Option | Expiration | Strike | Price | Delta | Vega | Theta |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Call | June 2019 | 120 | 3.65 | 0.439 | 0.221 | −0.027 |
| Put | June 2019 | 115 | 3.70 | −0.399 | 0.216 | −0.028 |

S1: the call position's delta is more bearish than the put position's. S2: stock + call is long vega (benefits from higher volatility); stock + put is short vega (benefits from lower volatility). S3: stock + call benefits from time decay; stock + put is exposed to it.
questions.stem: With respect to Company A, which of Navarro’s statements to Patel is most likely correct?

A.text: Statement 1 is wrong. Short stock delta = −500. Long 5 calls: +500 × 0.439 = +219.5 → −280.5. Short 5 puts: −(−0.399 × 500) = +199.5 → −300.5. The put position is *more* bearish.

B.text: **Statement 2 is correct.** Short stock + long call is long vega; short stock + short put is short vega.

C.text: Statement 3 is wrong. Short stock + long call has negative theta (exposed to decay); short stock + short put has positive theta (−(−0.028)) and benefits.

questions.keyPrinciple: Long option = long gamma/vega, negative theta. Short option = the reverse.

questions.title: Calendar Spread for Near-Term Stability, Long-Term Bearish
questions.context: **Company B ($139.81):** June and November 2019 $140 calls and puts. Outlook: stable near term, bearish long term.
questions.stem: Based on Patel’s outlook for Company B and using the information in Exhibit 2, the most appropriate strategy that Lyons could recommend to Patel is:

choices.text: buy the June 2019 call and buy the June 2019 put.
buy the June 2019 put and sell the November 2019 put.
buy the November 2019 put and sell the June 2019 put.

A.text: Buying a call and put at one strike is a straddle, which is directionally neutral.

B.text: Buying June and selling November puts is a short calendar spread, for an expected big move, not a stable outlook.

C.text: **Buy the November put, sell the June put** (long calendar spread with puts): stable near term, bearish later.

questions.keyPrinciple: Long calendar: short near-term, long longer-term, same strike. Short calendar: the reverse (expect a big move).

questions.topic: Implied volatility: skew, smile, term structure, risk reversals
questions.title: Cho's Statement on Skew and Risk Reversals
questions.context: Cho: implied volatility generally increases for puts struck below the stock price and decreases for calls struck above it (skew); sometimes the reverse (smile); if put implied vol is too high relative to call implied vol, a long risk reversal is to short the OTM call and go long the OTM put.
questions.stem: In her statement to Patel, Cho is most likely correct regarding the:

A.text: **Volatility skew.** Cho described it correctly: OTM puts have higher implied vol than ATM, and OTM calls lower.

B.text: Cho is wrong about the smile: a smile has *both* OTM calls and puts with higher implied volatility than ATM.

C.text: Cho described a *short* risk reversal. With put vol too high, a long risk reversal is short the OTM put and long the OTM call.

questions.keyPrinciple: Put vol rich vs calls → long risk reversal (short OTM put, long OTM call).

questions.title: Bear Spread at Minimum Cost
questions.context:
Kadakia expects XYZ ($117.43) to fall sharply, wants limited losses and minimum cost.

| Exercise | Call premium | Put premium |
|---|---|---|
| 115 | 5.40 | 2.85 |
| 120 | 2.70 | 5.22 |

Strategy 1: buy the Nov 120 call, sell the Nov 115 call. Strategy 2: buy the Nov 120 put, sell the Nov 115 put.
questions.stem: Are the strategies suggested by Dufu for Kadakia most likely correct?

A.text: Strategy 1 is correct.

B.text: **Strategy 2 is incorrect.** Strategy 1 is a bear call spread with a net *inflow* of 5.40 − 2.70 = $2.70 (max profit 2.70, max loss 5 − 2.70 = 2.30). Strategy 2 is a bear put spread with a net outflow of 5.22 − 2.85 = $2.37 (max profit 2.63, max loss 2.37), so it doesn't minimize cost.

C.text: Strategy 2 is wrong because of the initial cash outflow.

questions.keyPrinciple: Bear spread: buy higher strike, sell lower strike. Calls give a credit; puts a debit.

questions.title: Calendar Spread Statement
questions.context: Minkoff: a calendar spread suits an expectation that prices move in a certain direction but not immediately; it takes advantage of time-value decay; it is appropriate only when implied volatility is expected to increase.
questions.stem: In her statement, Minkoff is least likely correct with regard to:

choices.text: the time value decay of options.
the direction and timing of a price move.

A.text: **Implied volatility.** A long calendar spread suits stable markets or rising implied vol; a *short* calendar spread suits falling implied vol or a big, not-imminent move. So 'only when implied vol increases' is wrong.

B.text: Minkoff is right about capturing time value.

C.text: Minkoff is right about direction and timing.

questions.keyPrinciple: Calendar spreads: long = stable market or rising vol; short = falling vol or big later move.

questions.title: Skew vs Smile
questions.context: Exhibit 2, ABC three-month implied volatilities: ATM 17.60; Put 80% 26.31; Put 90% 22.40; Call 110% 15.54; Call 120% 14.65. Armitage: the exhibit depicts a volatility smile; if put vol is too high vs call vol, enter a long risk reversal and delta hedge by selling the underlying.
questions.stem: In his statement to Calzada, Armitage is least likely correct with regard to:

A.text: Armitage is right that the position is delta hedged by selling the underlying.

B.text: **Volatility smile.** The exhibit is a *skew*: vol rises for OTM puts and falls for OTM calls. A smile is U-shaped.

C.text: Armitage is right about a long risk reversal (sell the OTM put, buy the OTM call).

questions.keyPrinciple: Skew = downward-sloping vol across strikes; smile = U-shape.

questions.title: Strategies for a Range-Bound Market
questions.context: Dufu: if implied vol is expected to fall, write a straddle; if it rises, enter a short risk reversal; if unchanged, buy calls and write puts on the index.
questions.stem: In her response to Calzada, Dufu is most likely correct about:

A.text: **Writing a straddle** (narrow range, falling implied vol) is correct.

B.text: A short risk reversal (sell the OTM call, buy the OTM put) is used to exploit a skew when call-implied vol looks too high relative to put-implied vol, not for a rising-vol view.

C.text: Buying calls and writing puts is a bullish view with unchanged implied vol; the put sale lowers the cost of the calls. It isn't a range-bound strategy.

questions.keyPrinciple: Range-bound + falling vol → short straddle.

questions.title: Synthetic Positions via Put–Call Parity
questions.context: Example 1: a synthetic long stock = buy calls and sell puts, same strike and expiry. Example 2: a synthetic put = sell calls on the stock and short the stock.
questions.stem: Are the examples of synthetic positions provided by Manetti most likely correct?

A.text: Example 1 is correct.

B.text: **Example 2 is incorrect.** Put–call parity: p₀ = c₀ − S₀ + X/(1+r)ᵀ, so a synthetic put = **buy** a call + short the stock (not sell the call). Example 1 is correct: S₀ = c₀ − p₀ + X/(1+r)ᵀ.

C.text: Example 2 is incorrect.

questions.keyPrinciple: Parity: S + p = c + PV(X). Synthetic put = long call + short stock + bond.

questions.title: Covered Call Statement Check
questions.context:
Manetti (WTML) trains analysts. A client owns 2,000 shares of Company A (no dividend), priced at $139.81, expects the price to stay stable and doesn't want to sell.

**Exhibit 1 — Company A options, 25 November 2019**

| Option | Expiration | Strike | Premium | Delta | Theta |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Call | Feb 2020 | 140 | 5.40 | 0.510 | −0.035 |
| Call | Jul 2020 | 140 | 8.64 | 0.517 | −0.021 |
| Put | Feb 2020 | 140 | 6.15 | −0.508 | −0.034 |
| Put | Jul 2020 | 140 | 10.55 | −0.507 | −0.019 |

Fillizola suggests writing 20 Feb 2020 $140 call contracts (implied vol 21.05%). She says: if shares go to $140 and the call is exercised, she effectively sells at $145.40; if shares fall to $130, her effective sale price is $135.40; the strategy suits an expected volatility *higher* than 21.05%.
questions.stem: With regard to the strategy for Company A that Fillizola recommends, she is least likely correct regarding:

choices.text: the expectation of volatility of the underlying.
the effective sale price if share prices move lower, to $130.
the effective sale price if share prices trend higher than $140.

A.text: **Volatility expectation is wrong.** A covered call (short call, short vega) suits an expectation that volatility will be *lower* than the implied 21.05%.

B.text: Correct: at $130 the effective price = 130 + 5.40 = $135.40.

C.text: Correct: called away at $140; effective price = 140 + 5.40 = $145.40.

questions.keyPrinciple: Covered call = short volatility. Effective sale price = strike + premium (if called away).

questions.context:
Manetti (WTML) trains analysts. A client owns 2,000 shares of Company A (no dividend), priced at $139.81, expects the price to stay stable and doesn't want to sell.

**Exhibit 1 — Company A options, 25 November 2019**

questions.stem: If the client executes Fillizola’s suggested strategy at the current price, her position delta will most likely be the same as the position delta of a portfolio that is:

choices.text: long 2,000 shares and short forward 980 shares.
long 1,020 shares and short forward 980 shares.
long 2,000 shares and short forward 1,020 shares.

C.text: **Long 2,000 shares, short forward 1,020 shares.** Covered call delta = (1 − 0.51) × 2,000 = 980. Forward delta = 1.0 for a non-dividend stock; 2,000 − 1,020 = 980.

questions.keyPrinciple: Covered call delta = (1 − call delta) × shares. Forward on a non-dividend stock has delta 1.0.

questions.title: Put Purchase Statement Check
questions.context:
Manetti (WTML) trains analysts. A client owns 2,000 shares of Company A (no dividend), priced at $139.81, expects the price to stay stable and doesn't want to sell.

**Exhibit 1 — Company A options, 25 November 2019**

| Put | Feb 2020 | 140 | 6.15 | −0.508 | −0.034 |
| Put | Jul 2020 | 140 | 10.55 | −0.507 | −0.019 |

Manetti: buy the Feb 2020 put because it's cheaper than the July put and has the lowest time decay; a lower-strike Feb put would be cheaper but riskier.
questions.stem: Is Manetti most likely correct with regard to the strategy of purchasing put options?

choices.text: No, she is incorrect about the time decay of the option
No, she is incorrect about a strike price lower than $140

A.text: The decay statement is wrong, so she isn't correct.

B.text: **Wrong about time decay.** The Feb put theta is −0.034; the July put's is −0.019, so July has the *lowest* time decay (though it's more expensive).

C.text: She is right about the lower strike: cheaper but a greater risk of loss because protection starts lower.

questions.keyPrinciple: Longer-dated options cost more but decay more slowly (smaller negative theta).

questions.title: Synthetic Long Forward
questions.stem: A non-dividend-paying stock is currently trading at $50 per share. Which of the following option combinations could be used to create a synthetic long forward position in the stock?

choices.text: Buy a $50 strike call and sell a $50 strike put with the same maturity
Buy a $50 strike put and sell a $50 strike call with the same maturity
Buy a $50 strike call and buy a $50 strike put with the same maturity

A.text: **Buy a $50 call and sell a $50 put** (same maturity): long call + short put = synthetic long forward.

B.text: Long put + short call is a synthetic *short* forward.

C.text: Buying both is a long straddle (profits from large moves either way).

questions.keyPrinciple: Long call + short put = long forward; long put + short call = short forward.

questions.title: Long Put + Short Call Payoff
questions.stem: An investor who buys a put option on a stock and sells a call option with the same strike price and maturity will realize the same payoff as:

A.text: A covered call has an asymmetric payoff and needs the stock.

B.text: A long forward would be long call, short put.

C.text: **Short forward.** Buying a put and selling a call at the same strike and maturity replicates a short forward.

questions.keyPrinciple: Long put + short call = short forward.

questions.topic: Option strategies (covered call, protective put, collar, spreads, straddles/strangles, calendar, synthetics)
questions.title: Risk of a Covered Call for a Yield Enhancer
questions.stem: An investor has a long position in a stock that he intends to hold for the long term. He sells call options on the stock to enhance his yield. The risk exposure for this covered call position is most likely:

choices.text: the loss of upside exposure only.
limited protection from downside moves only.
both the loss of upside exposure and limited protection from downside moves.

A.text: **Loss of upside only.** The investor gives up capital gains above the strike. For a long-term holder seeking yield, the premium's limited downside cushion is a net gain, not a risk.

B.text: Limited downside protection isn't the risk exposure; downside exposure to the shares remains by intent.

C.text: The downside cushion is a benefit, not a risk, for a yield-seeking long-term holder.

questions.keyPrinciple: Covered call risk: gives up upside beyond the strike; downside exposure to the stock remains.

questions.title: Covered Call Profit at Expiration
questions.context: Stock $12.15; sell a $13.00 call at $1.25; stock ends at $14.30.
questions.stem: An investor owns shares of a stock priced at $12.15. She enters a covered call position using an option with a strike price of $13.00 trading at a premium of $1.25. When the option expires the shares are trading at $14.30. The profit at expiration is:

A.text: $0.90 = 14.30 − 1.25 − 12.15 (subtracts the premium).

C.text: $3.40 = 14.30 + 1.25 − 12.15 (ignores the strike, i.e., the capped gain).

questions.keyPrinciple: Covered call profit = S_T − max(S_T − X, 0) + c₀ − S₀ (max profit = X − S₀ + c₀).

questions.title: Lowering Position Delta
questions.context: Long 100 shares of a non-dividend-paying stock.
questions.stem: An investor who is long 100 shares of a non-dividend-paying stock wants to reduce the delta of his position. Which of the following transactions would result in the lowest delta?

choices.text: Buying at-the-money put options for 100 shares
Selling at-the-money call options for 100 shares

A.text: **Short futures on 100 shares.** Futures on a non-dividend stock have delta ±1.0, so 1.0 − 1.0 = 0.

B.text: Buying ATM puts adds ≈ −0.5 per share, leaving a position delta of about 50.

C.text: Selling ATM calls also adds ≈ −0.5 per share, leaving about 50.

questions.title: Short Stock: Buying a Call vs Writing a Put
questions.stem: An investor holds a short stock position and is considering a temporary position adjustment using options on the same number of shares. Compared to writing a put option, buying a call option would cause the combined position to:

choices.text: be exposed to potentially unlimited losses.
benefit from a reduction in implied volatility.
benefit from an increase in implied volatility.

A.text: The call's payoff offsets losses as the price rises, so losses aren't unlimited.

B.text: Writing the put (not buying the call) would benefit from a drop in implied vol.

C.text: **Benefit from an increase in implied volatility** (long option = long vega).

questions.keyPrinciple: Long options: long vega. Short options: short vega.

questions.context: Buy the October 40 call at $4.75; write the October 48 call at $2.30.
questions.stem: An investor establishes a bull call spread by buying an October 40 call for $4.75 and writing an October 48 call for $2.30. The maximum profit for this spread is:

A.text: $3.25 = 8.00 − 4.75 (ignores the credit from the short call).

C.text: $8.00 is the maximum value at expiration, not profit.

questions.keyPrinciple: Bull call spread max profit = width − net debit.

questions.topic: Option strategies (covered call, protective put, collar, spreads, straddles/strangles, calendar, synthetics)
questions.title: Where a Bear Put Spread Loses Most
questions.stem: The maximum loss on a bear put spread occurs when the underlying asset price at expiration is:

choices.text: less than or equal to the lower strike price.
greater than or equal to the higher strike price.

A.text: At or below the lower strike the spread earns its maximum profit.

B.text: Between the strikes the loss is less than the net cost.

C.text: **At or above the higher strike.** Both puts expire worthless and the net cost is lost.

questions.keyPrinciple: Bear put spread: max loss = net debit (at/above X_H); max profit = width − net debit (at/below X_L).

questions.topic: Option strategies (covered call, protective put, collar, spreads, straddles/strangles, calendar, synthetics)
questions.title: Motivation for a Long Calendar Spread
questions.stem: A primary motivation behind a long calendar spread with equal notional amounts is to:

choices.text: profit from a decrease in implied volatility.
profit from a large move in either direction.

A.text: **Take advantage of time decay** (the short near-term option decays faster than the long longer-term option).

B.text: Falling implied vol helps a *short* calendar spread.

C.text: A large move in either direction helps a *short* calendar spread.

questions.keyPrinciple: Long calendar: benefits from time decay, a stable market or rising implied vol.

questions.topic: Implied volatility: skew, smile, term structure, risk reversals
questions.title: Reading a Rise in Put Skew
questions.stem: An analyst observes increasing levels of implied volatility accompanied by sharp increases in the volatility skew of put options. Should this be interpreted as a change in market sentiment?

choices.text: Yes, it indicates increased bullish sentiment
Yes, it indicates increased bearish sentiment

A.text: It does indicate a change in sentiment.

B.text: Bullish sentiment would show up in increased *call* skew.

C.text: **Yes, increased bearish sentiment.** Hedgers buy puts, pushing up put prices and implied vol; a sharp rise in skew with higher overall implied vol signals bearish sentiment.

questions.keyPrinciple: Rising put skew + rising implied vol → bearish sentiment.

questions.topic: Implied volatility: skew, smile, term structure, risk reversals
questions.title: Term Structure in a Sell-Off
questions.stem: When equity markets experience large sell-offs, the term structure of implied volatility for equity index options typically:

A.text: The key says stress results in backwardation, not merely a flattening.

B.text: **Inverts.** In stress, demand for short-dated options pushes short-term implied vols above long-term.

C.text: Steepening is the normal-market pattern (longer-term vols higher).

questions.keyPrinciple: Market stress → inverted (backwardated) implied-vol term structure.

questions.topic: Option strategies (covered call, protective put, collar, spreads, straddles/strangles, calendar, synthetics)

A.text: A long straddle suits implied vol too low and a big move expected.

B.text: **Write puts** at the target price. With elevated implied vol the put premium is rich, so the effective purchase price is below the strike by the premium.

C.text: A long calendar spread profits from rising vol and is not suited to already-high vol.

questions.topic: Option strategies (covered call, protective put, collar, spreads, straddles/strangles, calendar, synthetics)
questions.title: Bullish View With Stable Volatility

C.text: A calendar spread is better for a neutral view.

questions.topic: Duration management with swaps

questions.topic: Duration management with swaps
questions.title: Constructing a Pay-Floating Swap to Convert Fixed Debt
questions.context: Wyalusing issued fixed-rate coupon bonds in Canada one year ago. The CFO expects Canadian rates to fall and stay low for three years and wants to use a par interest rate swap to convert the fixed coupon payments into floating-rate payments.
questions.stem: Explain how to construct the swap with regard to (i) tenor, (ii) cash flows, (iii) notional value and (iv) settlement dates.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **(i) Tenor:** three years, the period over which rates are expected to stay low.
- **(ii) Cash flows:** Wyalusing **receives fixed** and **pays floating**. Receiving fixed on the swap offsets the fixed bond coupons it pays, leaving floating-rate-based obligations. Reference rate and fixed rate are set at inception.
- **(iii) Notional:** set so that the fixed payments received equal the bond's fixed coupon payments.
- **(iv) Settlement dates:** the same dates as the bond's coupon payments.
questions.keyPrinciple: Convert fixed debt to floating: receive fixed/pay floating, notional and dates matched to the bond.

questions.topic: Cross-currency basis swaps
questions.title: Cross-Currency Basis Swap Cash Flows
questions.context: Wyalusing will borrow in CAD for a US plant but make interest payments in USD, using a cross-currency basis swap.
questions.stem: Describe, from Wyalusing's perspective, the swap's cash flows at inception, periodic cash flows and cash flows at maturity.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **At inception:** Wyalusing pays the CAD notional and receives USD at the USD/CAD rate agreed at inception.
- **Periodic:** Wyalusing receives CAD interest and pays USD interest. Both are on floating reference rates; the CAD side includes the quoted basis (CAD floating rate minus the basis, applied to the CAD notional), and the USD payment uses the inception exchange rate.
- **At maturity:** Wyalusing receives the CAD notional and pays USD at the inception exchange rate. These flows are the inverse of inception.
questions.keyPrinciple: Cross-currency basis swap: notionals exchanged at inception and maturity at one fixed rate; floating interest each currency, basis added to one leg.

questions.topic: Cross-currency basis swaps
questions.title: Notional Exchange in a Cross-Currency Basis Swap
questions.stem: A US institutional investor in search of yield decides to buy Italian government bonds for her portfolio but wants to hedge against the risk of exchange rate fluctuations. She enters a cross-currency basis swap, with the same payment dates as the bonds, where at inception she delivers US dollars in exchange for euros for use in purchasing the Italian bonds. The notional principals on the swap are most likely exchanged:

choices.text: both at inception and at maturity.

A.text: Exchange only at inception would leave the currency exposure unhedged at maturity.

B.text: Exchange only at maturity wouldn't provide the foreign currency needed at inception.

C.text: **Both at inception and at maturity**, at a single exchange rate.

questions.keyPrinciple: Cross-currency basis swap exchanges notionals at both ends.

questions.title: Positive Basis for Lending USD

questions.stem: Continuing from the previous question, assume demand for US dollars is strong relative to demand for euros, so there is a positive basis for “lending” US dollars. By hedging the position in Italian government bonds with the currency basis swap, the US investor will most likely increase the periodic net interest payments received from the swap counterparty in:

A.text: The basis affects the USD leg, not the euro payments.

B.text: **USD only.** The positive basis is included in the net periodic interest the counterparty pays to the investor, in USD.

C.text: Only the USD interest is increased.

questions.keyPrinciple: Strong USD demand → positive basis paid to those who lend USD via the swap.

questions.title: Shifting Large-Cap to Small-Cap With Futures
questions.stem: An equity portfolio manager is invested 100% in US large-cap stocks, but he wants to reduce the current allocation by 20%, to 80%, and allocate 20% to US small caps. sell Russell 2000 futures and purchase S&P 500 futures.

questions.topic: Variance swaps and volatility (VIX) trades
questions.title: VIX Carry Roll-Down Trade
questions.context: VIX 13.50; front-month futures 14.10; second-month futures 15.40 (upward sloping). Curve shape assumed constant over three months.
questions.stem: A volatility trader observes that the VIX term structure is upward sloping. In particular, the VIX is at 13.50, the front-month futures contract trades at 14.10, and the second-month futures contract trades at 15.40. Assuming the shape of the VIX term structure will remain constant over the next three-month period, the trader decides to implement a trade that would profit from the VIX carry roll down. She will most likely purchase the:

choices.text: VIX and sell the VIX second-month futures.
VIX and sell the VIX front-month futures.
VIX front-month futures and sell the VIX second-month futures.

A.text: You can't trade the VIX itself directly; trades use futures or options.

B.text: You can't trade the VIX itself directly.

C.text: **Buy the front-month and sell the second-month VIX futures.** The spread (1.30) narrows toward the front-month-to-spot gap (0.60) as futures converge to spot, earning roll-down gains.

questions.keyPrinciple: Contango + stable vol: VIX futures roll down toward spot; trade is a calendar spread in the futures.

questions.topic: Equity swaps
questions.title: Structuring an Equity Swap for a Concentrated Holder
questions.context: The CEO owns 100 million shares at €30 and wants to sell 10% of his position and earn a floating rate, via an equity swap.
questions.stem: Explain how to structure such a swap.
questions.modelAnswer: He **pays the total return on 10 million shares** (10% of his holding) and **receives a floating rate** (e.g., the market reference rate) on a notional of **€300 million** (€30 × 10 million shares).
questions.keyPrinciple: Pay equity / receive floating synthetically sells the stock and earns the floating rate.

questions.topic: Equity swaps
questions.title: Rebalancing Allocation Using Swaps
questions.context: $30 million account: one-third stocks, two-thirds bonds. Target 50/50, and within stocks 60% domestic / 40% foreign (currently 70/30); bonds all domestic corporate. Reference rate assumed flat.
questions.stem: Explain how swaps can be used to implement this adjustment.
questions.modelAnswer:
Current: $10 million stocks ($7 million domestic, $3 million foreign) and $20 million bonds. Target: $15 million stocks ($9 million domestic, $6 million foreign) and $15 million bonds.

Using swaps against the market reference rate:
1. **Receive** the return on **$2 million** of a domestic equity index and **$3 million** of a foreign equity index.
2. **Pay** the return on **$5 million** of a domestic corporate bond index.

The reference-rate flows on the equity swaps (paid) and the bond swap (received) net to zero because the notionals sum to the same $5 million.
questions.keyPrinciple: Receive equity/pay bond (vs MRR) shifts allocation toward equities synthetically.

questions.topic: Fed funds futures and rate probabilities
questions.title: Fed Funds Futures Probability of a Hike
questions.context: The fed funds futures contract expiring after the next FOMC meeting is priced at 97.175. The target range is 2.50%–2.75%.
questions.stem: Explain how the information can be used and calculate the probability of a 25 bp increase in the target range.
questions.modelAnswer:
Implied effective fed funds rate = 100 − 97.175 = **2.825%** (the expected average rate for the month).

Current target midpoint = (2.50 + 2.75)/2 = 2.625%. After a 25 bp hike the range is 2.75%–3.00% (midpoint 2.875%).

Probability of a hike = (2.825 − 2.625)/(2.875 − 2.625) = 0.200/0.250 = **80%**.
questions.keyPrinciple: Probability of move = (implied rate − current rate) / (rate after move − current rate).
questions.flag: The key's probability formula and result did not paste. The 80% comes from my calculation using range midpoints, the same method the key uses in DB-28 (86%); the key's own figure is unverified.

questions.topic: Variance swaps and volatility (VIX) trades
questions.title: Variance Swap Settlement
questions.context: Client B bought $90,000 vega notional of a 1-year variance swap on the Russell 2000 at a 15% strike a year ago; realized volatility was 17%.
questions.stem: Calculate the settlement amount at expiration and whether Client B pays or receives.
questions.modelAnswer:
Variance notional = 90,000/(2 × 15) = $3,000. Realized variance 17² = 289; strike variance 15² = 225.
Settlement = 3,000 × (289 − 225) = **$192,000**. Client B is long and realized vol exceeded the strike, so Client B **receives** $192,000.
questions.keyPrinciple: Variance swap payoff = N_var × (realized variance − strike variance); N_var = vega notional/(2K).

questions.topic: Equity swaps
questions.title: Equity Swap Gain/Loss for Client C
questions.context: Client C swaps the total return on 80,000 Kiwi shares ($21.50) for a floating rate of 1.00% (annualized) for three months; Kiwi pays a $0.25 dividend and the price falls 2%.
questions.stem: Calculate the gain or loss to Client C at expiration of the equity swap.
questions.modelAnswer:
Stock total return = (21.50 × 0.98 − 21.50 + 0.25)/21.50 = −0.18/21.50 = −0.8372%. Floating return = 1.00%/4 = 0.25%.
Client C pays the equity leg, receives the floating leg: gain = (21.50 × 80,000) × (0.25% − (−0.8372%)) = 1,720,000 × 1.0872% = **$18,700** received from the counterparty.
questions.keyPrinciple: Equity payer gains when the stock's total return is below the floating rate.

questions.stem: Which trade is Tryon most likely to implement to establish his equity market hedge?

questions.topic: Currency return decomposition and risk
questions.title: Direction of USD Against GBP (Portfolio A)
questions.context: Gupta evaluates two US-managed portfolios measured in USD. Portfolio A holds GBP bonds (19.5% domestic-currency return); Portfolio B holds EUR bonds (0% domestic-currency return). Portfolio A's foreign-currency return is 15%.
questions.stem: Analyze the movement of the USD against the foreign currency for Portfolio A (appreciated or depreciated). Justify your choice.
questions.modelAnswer:
**The USD depreciated against the GBP.** The 19.5% domestic-currency return exceeds the 15% foreign-currency return, so the currency must have added return.

R_DC = (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) − 1 → (1.15)(1 + R_FX) − 1 = 19.5% → **R_FX = +3.91%**. With the USD as the price currency (USD/GBP), the positive R_FX means the GBP appreciated, i.e., the USD depreciated.
questions.keyPrinciple: R_DC = (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) − 1, with R_FX = change in the foreign currency measured in domestic currency (domestic = price currency).

questions.topic: Currency return decomposition and risk

questions.context: Gupta evaluates two US-managed portfolios measured in USD. Portfolio A holds GBP bonds (19.5% domestic-currency return); Portfolio B holds EUR bonds (0% domestic-currency return). The EUR appreciated 5% against the USD.
questions.stem: Analyze the foreign-currency return for Portfolio B (positive or negative). Justify your choice.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Negative.** The domestic return is 0% and the EUR appreciated 5%, so the EUR return must have been negative to offset the gain.

(1 + R_FC)(1 + 5%) − 1 = 0% → **R_FC = −4.76%**.
questions.keyPrinciple: Flat domestic return with foreign currency up → foreign-currency return is negative.

questions.topic: Currency management strategies (passive, discretionary, active, overlay, FX as an asset class)
questions.title: Trading Costs of a 100% Hedge
questions.context: Portfolio B's manager is evaluating an internally managed 100% foreign-currency hedged strategy.
questions.stem: Discuss two forms of trading costs associated with this currency management strategy.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any two of:
- **Bid/offer spreads:** dealers earn the spread; keeping a 100% hedge needs frequent rebalancing, and 'churning' the hedge adds costs and erodes the benefit.
- **Option premiums:** a long option requires an upfront payment, an unrecoverable cost if it expires out of the money.
- **Rolling forwards:** forwards mature and must be rolled with FX swaps, generating cash flows (spot moves plus roll yield) that may require raising cash and become costlier as rates rise.
- **Infrastructure/overhead:** personnel and technology needed to trade can be a significant share of costs.
questions.keyPrinciple: Hedging costs: trading costs (spreads, premiums, rolling, infrastructure) and opportunity costs.

questions.topic: Currency management strategies (passive, discretionary, active, overlay, FX as an asset class)
questions.title: Opportunity Cost of a Full Hedge
questions.context: Gupta: *"We need to seriously consider the potential costs associated with favorable currency rate movements, given that a 100% hedge-ratio strategy is being applied."*
questions.stem: Explain Gupta's statement in light of the strategic choices in currency management.
questions.modelAnswer: Hedging costs are **trading costs** and **opportunity costs**. Gupta is referring to the **opportunity cost** of the 100% hedge: the forgone benefit of favorable currency moves. Accepting some currency risk could enhance return; a complete hedge eliminates that possibility.
questions.keyPrinciple: Full hedge removes currency risk and also any gain from favorable currency moves (opportunity cost).

questions.topic: Currency management strategies (passive, discretionary, active, overlay, FX as an asset class)
questions.title: Earning Currency Alpha Without In-House Expertise
questions.context: Portfolio A's IPS allows directional currency views. The manager can fully hedge internally but lacks expertise to generate currency alpha.
questions.stem: Recommend a solution that gives the manager the opportunity to earn currency alpha through active FX management.
questions.modelAnswer: Set up a **currency overlay program**: outsource currency exposure management to a **specialist sub-advisor**. That separates the hedging function (**currency beta**, done internally) from active currency management (**currency alpha**, done externally by an FX specialist).
questions.keyPrinciple: Currency overlay: internal beta hedging, external alpha via a specialist.

questions.topic: Currency management strategies (passive, discretionary, active, overlay, FX as an asset class)
questions.title: Matching Statements to Active Currency Approaches
questions.context: Three of Gupta's statements: (1) traders think it isn't necessary to examine current account deficits, inflation and interest rates because current exchange rates already reflect market views; (2) the six-month interest rate in India is 8% vs 1% in the US: a yield pick-up opportunity; (3) the overlay manager estimates fair value expecting spot rates to converge to long-run equilibrium values from parity conditions.
questions.stem: Evaluate each statement and select the active currency approach it best describes (carry trade, technical analysis, economic fundamentals). Justify each.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. **Technical analysis.** Technicians believe historical prices already contain all relevant information on future moves, so looking at macro data isn't needed.
2. **Carry trade.** Borrow the low-yield currency (USD at 1%) and invest in the high-yield currency (INR at 8%).
3. **Economic fundamentals.** Exchange rates are driven by modelable economic relationships; the approach estimates fair value and expects spot rates to converge to equilibrium implied by parity conditions.
questions.keyPrinciple: Technical = price history. Carry = borrow low-yield, hold high-yield. Fundamental = fair value from economics/parity.

| Franz Trading GmbH: exporter, high risk | Discretion to add alpha |
questions.stem: Based on Ostermann’s correlation forecast, the expected domestic-currency return (measured in EUR terms) on USD-denominated assets will most likely:

A.text: Higher correlation raises risk, not expected return.

B.text: Higher correlation doesn't lower expected return.

C.text: **Remain unchanged.** Correlation affects the *risk* of domestic-currency return (σ²(R_DC) ≈ σ²(R_FC) + σ²(R_FX) + 2σ(R_FC)σ(R_FX)ρ), not its expected level, given an unchanged foreign-currency return forecast.

questions.keyPrinciple: Higher correlation between asset return and FX raises domestic-currency return variance; expected return unchanged.

questions.topic: Currency return decomposition and risk
questions.title: Contribution of Currency to a Multi-Asset Portfolio's Return
questions.context: Bhatt's US-managed (USD) account returned 7.0% last year. Weights/asset returns/currency returns: US 50% / 10.0% / NA; Eurozone 25% / 5.0% / 2.0%; Japan 25% / −3.0% / 4.0%.
questions.stem: Calculate the contribution of foreign currency to the account's total return. Show your calculations.
questions.keyPrinciple: Currency contribution = total domestic return − weighted asset return = weighted currency return + weighted cross-product.

questions.topic: Currency management strategies (passive, discretionary, active, overlay, FX as an asset class)
questions.title: Strategy for a Client With ±25% Discretion
questions.context: Bhatt's IPS allows capturing USD/INR opportunities within ±25% of neutral (100% of the portfolio valued in USD). C&M has a currency overlay team.
questions.stem: Determine the most appropriate currency management strategy (passive hedging, discretionary hedging, active currency management). Justify.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Active currency management.**
- The manager is expected to take currency risk for profit, with the primary goal of adding alpha. Discretionary hedging's primary duty is protecting the portfolio, with alpha secondary and within limited bounds.
- ±25% from neutral is wide discretion, which points to active management over protection.
- Passive hedging is rules-based and removes all discretion (exposures close to the benchmark), which doesn't fit.
- Discretionary hedging fits limited discretion; ±25% is more than limited.
questions.keyPrinciple: Spectrum by discretion: passive (none) → discretionary hedging (limited bounds, protection primary) → active (alpha primary) → overlay → FX as an asset class.

questions.topic: Currency management strategies (passive, discretionary, active, overlay, FX as an asset class)
questions.title: Forward Strategy for a Bullish USD View Within IPS Bounds
questions.context: C&M expects the USD to appreciate vs the INR (interest and inflation differentials stable). Portfolio: USD 10,000,000. Neutral = 100% hedge; IPS allows ±25% around neutral.
questions.stem: Recommend the trading strategy C&M should implement. Justify.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Under-hedge**: sell USD forward against INR at a hedge ratio of **no less than 75%** of the USD 10,000,000 (i.e., between 75% and 100%).

- A hedge ratio below neutral (100%) leaves some unhedged USD exposure, which is expected to appreciate vs the INR, capturing that return.
- A 100% hedge would eliminate the alpha opportunity.
- 75% is the floor set by the IPS (100% − 25%).
questions.keyPrinciple: Expect the exposure (foreign) currency to **appreciate** → under-hedge (less than neutral), within IPS bounds; expect it to depreciate → over-hedge, within IPS bounds.

questions.topic: Currency management strategies (passive, discretionary, active, overlay, FX as an asset class)
questions.title: Approach for a Portfolio With a ±3% Hedge Band
questions.context: Wilson (Australian) prefers a neutral benchmark over a rules-based approach. IPS: hedge ratio between 97% and 103%. Portfolio currently in its flat natural neutral position because Lee lacks market conviction. Lee is a generalist managing many portfolios.
questions.stem: Identify the most likely approach (passive hedging, discretionary hedging, active currency management, currency overlay) and give two reasons.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Discretionary hedging.**
1. The portfolio is at its neutral position because Lee has no market conviction: consistent with discretionary hedging.
2. The 97–103% band gives some discretion, with exposures allowed to vary ±3% around neutral.

Why not the others:
- **Passive:** the ±3% band is discretion, and passive is rules-based (Wilson prefers otherwise).
- **Active:** a 3% band is too limited; the discretionary hedger's primary duty is protection, whereas active management takes currency risk for profit.
- **Overlay:** the band is too small for active overlay; overlays are typically run by FX-specialist sub-advisers (Lee is a generalist); overlays allow directional views and Lee has none.
questions.keyPrinciple: Narrow band around neutral, protection first → discretionary hedging.

questions.topic: Currency management strategies (passive, discretionary, active, overlay, FX as an asset class)
questions.title: Attribute That Supports Overlay as Strategic Positioning
questions.context: Wilson's IPS is revised: FX becomes a separate asset class and Lee hires an external FX sub-adviser for a currency overlay program.
questions.stem: Discuss a key attribute of the overlay that would increase the likelihood it is allowed in terms of strategic portfolio positioning.
questions.modelAnswer: **Low correlation (ideally uncorrelated) with the other asset classes and alpha programs in the portfolio.** With FX treated as its own asset class, the more the overlay's alpha is uncorrelated with the rest of the portfolio, the more it adds diversification and the more likely it fits strategic positioning.
questions.keyPrinciple: Overlay alpha should be uncorrelated with other portfolio return sources.

questions.topic: Currency management strategies (passive, discretionary, active, overlay, FX as an asset class)
questions.title: Strategy for a Long-Horizon Sovereign Wealth Fund
questions.stem:
Kalila Al-Khalili has been hired as a consultant to a Middle Eastern sovereign wealth fund. The fund’s oversight committee has asked her to examine the fund’s financial characteristics and recommend an appropriate currency management strategy given the fund’s Investment Policy Statement. After a thorough study of the fund and its finances, Al-Khalili reaches the following conclusions:

The fund’s mandate is focused on the long-term development of the country, and the royal family (who are very influential on the fund’s oversight committee) are prepared to take a long-term perspective on the fund’s investments.

The fund’s strategic asset allocation is tilted towards equity rather than fixed-income assets.

Both its fixed-income and equity portfolios have a sizeable exposure to emerging market assets.

Currently, about 90% of exchange rate exposures are hedged although the IPS allows a range of hedge ratios.

Liquidity needs of the fund are minimal, since the government is running a balanced budget and is unlikely to need to dip into the fund in the near term to cover fiscal deficits. Indeed, the expected lifetime of country’s large oil reserves has been greatly extended by recent discoveries, and substantial oil royalties are expected to persist into the future.

Based on her investigation, Al-Khalili would most likely recommend:

choices.text: a narrow discretionary band for currency exposures.

A.text: **Active currency management.** Long horizon, minimal liquidity needs, equity-tilted SAA (equity portfolios are typically hedged less than bond portfolios), and large EM exposure (higher yields → carry; volatile exchange rates) all support active management.

B.text: The fund's characteristics don't argue for a conservative strategy; a hedge ratio closer to 100% is not supported.

C.text: A narrow discretionary band is a more conservative design; the fund's profile suits more active management.

questions.keyPrinciple: Long horizon + low liquidity needs + equity tilt + EM exposure → more active currency management.

questions.topic: FX hedging mechanics (static/dynamic, forwards, rolling, cross-hedge, options)
questions.title: Key Consideration When Hedging With Futures
questions.context: Subscriber 1: French national holding USD 700,000, will repatriate to France and wants to hedge the EUR value with currency futures.
questions.stem: For Subscriber 1, the most significant factor to consider would be:

choices.text: transaction costs of using futures contracts.
different quoting conventions for future contracts.

A.text: **Margin requirements.** Futures require initial margin plus daily mark-to-market, so margin calls can force liquidation if liquidity is short. Most forwards have neither (though CSAs are changing this for large institutions).

B.text: Futures have low transaction costs.

C.text: Whether the EUR is the price or base currency in the quote doesn't affect the hedging process (CME quotes USD/EUR, with EUR as base).

questions.keyPrinciple: Futures hedges: initial margin + daily variation margin → liquidity risk.

questions.topic: Non-deliverable forwards
questions.title: Speculating on a KRW Depreciation With Capital Controls
questions.context: Subscriber 2 expects the KRW/USD rate to rise (KRW depreciation) and volatility to increase. KRW is subject to capital controls.
questions.stem: For Subscriber 2, and assuming all of the choices relate to the KRW/USD exchange rate, the best way to implement the trading strategy would be to:

A.text: A straddle is for a view on volatility, not direction. The subscriber expects the rate to rise, and writing it (short straddle) would suit low expected volatility, contradicting the expected volatility increase.

B.text: A put on KRW/USD profits from a fall in the rate, the opposite of the view; higher volatility also makes it more expensive.

C.text: **Long NDF position.** Expecting KRW/USD to increase means a long forward on the base currency (USD); with capital controls, an NDF is used. (The retail version is a contract for differences.)

questions.keyPrinciple: Currency with capital controls → NDF. Long base currency (USD) forward profits if price-currency (KRW) depreciates.

questions.topic: Carry trade, forward rate bias, roll yield, EM currency distributions
questions.title: Development That Favors a Carry Trade
questions.context: Subscriber 3 plans to borrow USD, convert to INR and invest in INR bonds unhedged, expecting persistently higher Indian rates.
questions.stem: Which of the following market developments would be most favorable for Subscriber 3’s trading plan?

choices.text: A higher forward premium for INR/USD.
Higher volatility in INR/USD spot rate movements.

A.text: A narrower differential reduces the carry and the compensation for unhedged currency risk.

B.text: **A higher forward premium for INR/USD.** The carry trade profits from the forward rate bias: buy currencies at a forward discount and sell those at a forward premium. A higher forward premium on the USD (the low-yield currency, and the base in INR/USD) reflects a wider interest rate differential in India's favor.

C.text: Higher spot volatility is bad for carry trades (riskier; rapid moves are associated with panicked unwinds).

questions.keyPrinciple: Carry trade wants a wide interest differential and low volatility.

questions.topic: Carry trade, forward rate bias, roll yield, EM currency distributions
questions.title: Emerging Market Currency Trading Opportunities
questions.context: Subscriber 4 asks whether EM currency trading offers more opportunities for superior returns via active management than DM currency trading.
questions.stem: Jiang’s best response to Subscriber 4 would be that active trading in trading in emerging market currencies:

choices.text: typically leads to return distributions that are positively skewed.
should not lead to higher returns because FX markets are efficient.
often leads to higher returns through carry trades, but comes with higher risks and trading costs.

A.text: Carry trade return distributions are typically negatively skewed (event risk, pegs re-set, panicked unwinds).

B.text: Even if FX markets are efficient, higher returns can reflect risk premia for unhedged currency risk and a favorable interest differential; the question is risk-adjusted return.

C.text: **Often higher returns through carry trades, but with higher risks and trading costs.** EM currencies are often the investment currencies in carry trades (higher yields); stressed markets bring panicked unwinds, illiquidity, wider bid/offer spreads, and leverage magnifies losses.

questions.keyPrinciple: Carry returns: positive carry, negative skew, crash risk.

questions.topic: Volatility trading in FX
questions.title: Speculative vs Hedger Views on Volatility
questions.context: Overlay manager statements: (1) several traders benefit because most options expire out of the money, so they are net short volatility; (2) traders wanting to minimize the impact of unanticipated price volatility are net long volatility.
questions.stem: Identify which statement best explains the view of a speculative volatility trader and which a hedger. Justify.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Statement 1 = speculative volatility trader.** If markets are expected to stay stable, the speculator is net short volatility: most options expire out of the money, so the writer keeps the premium as compensation for accepting volatility risk. (If a rise in volatility were expected, the speculator would go long.)
- **Statement 2 = hedger.** Hedgers buy protection from unanticipated price volatility; that is a long option position, like paying an insurance premium.
questions.keyPrinciple: Speculators can be short or long volatility; hedgers are net long volatility.

questions.topic: Volatility trading in FX
questions.title: Volatility Strategy for an 'FX as an Asset Class' Client
questions.context: Murimi (overlay manager, technician) serves institutions seeking to address currency risk; Konev is a hedge fund manager focused on option trading, wanting an 'FX as an asset class' approach for speculative gains and believing the long-term USD strength is peaking.
questions.stem: Describe how a volatility-based strategy for Konev would contrast with Murimi's other institutional investors.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Konev:** a speculator seeking gains (here on USD weakness). 'FX as an asset class' lets Murimi take exposure in any currency pair with value to capture. His volatility strategy would typically be **net short volatility**, earning the premium for absorbing volatility risk (options mostly expire out of the money).
- **Other institutional clients:** hedgers minimizing risk, typically **net long volatility** to buy protection from unanticipated volatility, so they are exposed to the time decay of the option's time value.

Volatility is cyclical: long calm periods punctuated by spikes. Ideally a short-volatility trader would flip to long ahead of spikes, but these are hard to time.
questions.keyPrinciple: Speculators: typically net short vol (collect premium). Hedgers: net long vol (pay time decay).

questions.topic: Volatility trading in FX
questions.title: Technical Analysis in Designing a Volatility Strategy
questions.context: Murimi is a market technician; Konev believes the long-term strength of the USD is peaking.
questions.stem: Discuss how Murimi can use her technical skills to devise the strategy.
questions.modelAnswer:
Technicians hold that (1) historical prices help project future moves, (2) historical price patterns tend to repeat and reveal profitable trades, and (3) analysis seeks where prices *will* trade, not where they should.

Murimi can use this to **time entry and exit points**. She can identify patterns in USD price history (overbought/oversold, trends stretched in one direction and vulnerable to reversal) to position USD trades and capture volatility shifts associated with the turning point (USD peaking).
questions.keyPrinciple: Technical analysis: timing of turning points, entries and exits from price patterns.

questions.topic: FX hedging mechanics (static/dynamic, forwards, rolling, cross-hedge, options)
questions.title: Why a Static Matched Hedge Eventually Leaves Currency Risk
questions.context: Portfolio B manager: a full hedge is a simple match of current market value of foreign-currency exposure with an equal, offsetting forward.
questions.stem: Explain how this hedge will eventually expose the portfolio to currency risk.
questions.modelAnswer: Foreign-asset market values change with market conditions, but the forward's notional is fixed. A **static hedge** accumulates unwanted currency exposure as asset values drift: the forward notional no longer matches the portfolio's foreign-currency value, creating a mismatch (currency risk). The manager generally has to rebalance, i.e., use a **dynamic hedge**.
questions.keyPrinciple: Static hedge → growing mismatch as asset values change. Dynamic hedge needed.

questions.topic: FX hedging mechanics (static/dynamic, forwards, rolling, cross-hedge, options)
questions.title: Dynamic Hedging and Its Main Disadvantage
questions.context: Same Portfolio B situation.
questions.stem: Recommend an alternative that keeps the hedge ratio near target. Identify its main disadvantage.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Dynamic hedging**: rebalance periodically, adjusting the size, number and maturities of the foreign-currency contracts.

**Disadvantage:** higher **transaction costs** than a static hedge.
questions.keyPrinciple: Dynamic hedge keeps hedge ratio near target but costs more to maintain.

questions.topic: FX hedging mechanics (static/dynamic, forwards, rolling, cross-hedge, options)
questions.title: Rebalancing a Forward Hedge After Asset Decline
questions.context: Björk (SEK reporting) hedges GBP assets with a short GBP 100,000,000 forward (SEK/GBP spot 10.6875), maturing Dec 1. Assets have declined by GBP 7,000,000.
questions.stem: To rebalance the SEK/GBP hedge, and assuming all instruments are based on SEK/GBP, Björk would buy:

A.text: A spot purchase would not reduce the forward position's net size; the offset has to be in the forward.

B.text: **Buy GBP 7,000,000 forward to December 1.** The exposure fell by GBP 7m, so the short forward must shrink; buying GBP forward nets the short to GBP 93m.

C.text: That sells GBP (buys SEK). Also, SEK 74,812,500 uses the spot rate (7,000,000 × 10.6875); the forward amount depends on the forward rate.

questions.keyPrinciple: Asset value falls → reduce the hedge: take an offsetting forward at the same maturity.

questions.topic: FX hedging mechanics (static/dynamic, forwards, rolling, cross-hedge, options)
questions.title: Option Hedge to Reduce Cost With a Limited-Upside View
questions.context: Björk holds CHF assets, wants some profit potential, lower hedging cost, and sees limited upside for SEK/CHF.
questions.stem: Given her investment goals and market view, and assuming all options are based on SEK/CHF, the best strategy for Björk to manage the fund’s CHF exposure would be to buy an:

choices.text: ITM call option and write an OTM call option.
OTM put option and write an OTM call option.

A.text: An ATM call doesn't protect against a fall in SEK/CHF, and ATM is expensive.

B.text: The long ITM call is expensive and gives no protection against a fall in SEK/CHF.

C.text: **Buy an OTM put and write an OTM call.** The fund fears CHF depreciation, a fall in SEK/CHF; the put protects, and the written OTM call finances it (the view is that the call expires worthless). This is a collar / short risk reversal.

questions.keyPrinciple: Foreign-asset holder protects with a put on the foreign currency; sell an OTM call to cut cost (collar).

questions.topic: FX hedging mechanics (static/dynamic, forwards, rolling, cross-hedge, options)
questions.title: Effect of a Forward Premium on a Rolling Hedge
questions.context: Riksbank tightening moved SEK/EUR forward points to a premium; EUR exposures are hedged with forwards.
questions.stem: Given the recent movement in the forward premium for the SEK/EUR rate, Björk can expect that the hedge will experience higher:

A.text: The hedge is in the same currency; basis (spot-forward gap) converges to zero near maturity when rolled.

B.text: **Higher roll yield.** She sells EUR forward at a higher all-in forward rate and, with a contango forward curve, closes out at a lower rate (all else equal).

C.text: Forwards don't earn premia; writing options does.

questions.keyPrinciple: Forward premium on the currency being sold forward → positive roll yield for the hedger.

questions.topic: FX hedging mechanics (static/dynamic, forwards, rolling, cross-hedge, options)
questions.title: Key Risk of a Cross-Hedge
questions.context: Björk considers hedging Latin American exposures with forwards on the MXN, which is correlated with those currencies vs SEK but more liquid.
questions.stem: The most important risk to Björk’s Latin American currency hedge would be changes in:

A.text: Forward points are not the key risk to a cross-hedge.

B.text: Volatility is not the main driver of cross-hedge effectiveness; correlation is.

C.text: **Cross-currency correlations.** A cross hedge has basis risk: if the correlation between the hedged currency and the hedging instrument changes, the hedge fails.

questions.keyPrinciple: Cross-hedge = basis risk from changing correlations.

questions.topic: FX hedging mechanics (static/dynamic, forwards, rolling, cross-hedge, options)
questions.title: Hedge Instrument Choice: Static/Dynamic, Forward/Futures
questions.context: Rivera's USD 2.5m portfolio (EUR reporting currency). IPS requires rebalancing at least monthly; Rivera and Delgado are risk averse; choice is between one-month forwards and futures.
questions.stem: Determine the most appropriate combination (static forward, static futures, dynamic forward, dynamic futures). Justify.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Dynamic forward hedge.**

*Dynamic vs static:*
1. Both Rivera and Delgado are risk averse.
2. The IPS requires monthly rebalancing.
A static hedge avoids transaction costs but accumulates a mismatch between asset value and forward notional (pure currency risk). More risk aversion → more frequent rebalancing back to the neutral hedge ratio; the frequency is a cost–benefit trade-off (risk aversion, market view, IPS).

*Forward vs futures:*
1. Forwards are more flexible (currency pair, settlement date, amount).
2. Forwards are simpler administratively (no margin requirements), lowering costs.
3. OTC forwards are more liquid for large sizes (daily volume dwarfs futures).
questions.keyPrinciple: Risk-averse + frequent rebalancing → dynamic; large, customized, no margin → forwards.

questions.topic: FX hedging mechanics (static/dynamic, forwards, rolling, cross-hedge, options)
questions.title: Net Cash Flow When Rolling a Forward Hedge (Bid/Offer)
questions.context:
Rivera's hedge was perfectly hedged a month ago (sold USD 2,500,000 one month forward vs EUR). Time to roll.

| | One month ago | Today |
|---|---|---|
| Portfolio value (USD) | 2,500,000 | 2,650,000 |
| USD/EUR spot (bid–offer) | 1.1713/1.1714 | 1.1575/1.1576 |
| One-month forward points (bid–offer) | 9/10 | 6/7 |
questions.stem: Calculate the net cash flow (in euros) today to maintain the desired hedge.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Net outflow of EUR 27,449.18.**

1. *Original forward (sold USD, i.e., bought EUR base currency)* uses the offer, with the points from a month ago: 1.1714 + 10/10,000 = **1.1724**. USD 2,500,000 / 1.1724 = **EUR 2,132,378.03** inflow.
2. *Offset: buy USD at today's spot*, i.e., sell EUR at the bid: USD 2,500,000 / 1.1575 = **EUR 2,159,827.21** outflow.
3. Net = 2,132,378.03 − 2,159,827.21 = **−EUR 27,449.18**.

Then enter a new forward to sell USD 2,650,000, with no cash flow today.
questions.keyPrinciple: Closing out a forward: transact in the opposite direction at today's spot, using bid/offer on the base currency (EUR) correctly.

questions.topic: Carry trade, forward rate bias, roll yield, EM currency distributions
questions.title: Strategies That Earn Positive Roll Yield
questions.context: USD trades at a forward premium and US rates are lower than Spanish rates. Delgado 'recommends trading against the forward rate bias' to earn a positive roll yield.
questions.stem: Identify two strategies Delgado should use to earn a positive roll yield and the steps for each.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. **Carry trade:** buy (invest in) the high-yield currency and sell (borrow) the low-yield currency.
2. **Trade the forward rate bias:** buy (invest in) the currency at a forward discount and sell (borrow) the currency at a forward premium.

The USD (base) is at a forward premium, so the hedge requires selling USD forward, producing a positive roll yield. The carry trade is equivalent to trading *the* forward rate bias (not against it).
questions.keyPrinciple: Carry trade ≡ trading the forward rate bias: sell the forward-premium (low-yield) currency, buy the forward-discount (high-yield) one.
questions.flag: The stem says Delgado trades 'against' the forward rate bias, yet the key's two strategies (carry trade, trade the forward rate bias) are the same trade and are the opposite of trading against the bias; the key itself notes trading against the bias would mean buying USD at a premium. Wording in the stem/key is inconsistent; I give the key's answer as is.

questions.topic: Carry trade, forward rate bias, roll yield, EM currency distributions
questions.title: Return Distributions: Emerging vs Developed Currencies
questions.context: CCM runs a 3-year 'model' EM currency portfolio using its developed-market approach; its standard deviation, Sharpe ratio and VaR look good, but markets have been stable throughout.
questions.stem: Evaluate the application of EM and DM return probability distributions to CCM's new product.
questions.modelAnswer:
- EM currency trades face frequent extreme events, so EM return distributions have **fatter tails** than the normal distributions customarily used for DM, and a pronounced **negative skew**.
- Tools that assume normality (VaR, Sharpe ratio) can be misleading in extreme conditions and understate risk; apparent outperformance during stable periods can vanish into deep losses faster than investors can react.
- Short-term stability gives false confidence and encourages over-positioning on the illusion of normal returns.
- CCM should **not assume normality** for the model EM portfolio; it should assume fat-tailed, negatively skewed returns.
questions.keyPrinciple: EM currencies: fat tails + negative skew → VaR/Sharpe on a stable-period track record overstate quality.

questions.topic: Carry trade, forward rate bias, roll yield, EM currency distributions
questions.title: Constructing a CNY/USD Carry Trade
questions.context: US yield 2.211%; China annual yield 5.667%.
questions.stem: Construct a CNY/USD carry trade and explain two risks.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Construction:** borrow in USD (low yield, 2.211%) and invest in CNY (high yield, 5.667%). Carry = 5.667% − 2.211% = **3.456%** (before any currency move).

**Risks (any two):**
- High-yielding currencies are typically from higher-risk countries.
- In global crises, funds flee high-risk currencies for low-risk ones, causing carry trade unwinds.
- Leverage can produce large losses quickly.
questions.keyPrinciple: Carry trade: borrow low-yield, invest high-yield; risks are crash/unwind and leverage.
