questions.title: Which of Beth's Statements Is Correct
questions.context: Statements: (1) Technical analysis projects moves by examining current interest rates, inflation and risk premium differentials. (2) Expansionary monetary policy in India has contributed to INR appreciation. (3) A long CNY/USD put would profit from a depreciation of the USD against the CNY.
questions.stem: Identify the statement most likely correct and justify with one reason.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Statement 3.** The USD is the base currency of CNY/USD, so buying a put on the rate profits when the USD depreciates.

- Statement 1 is wrong: technical analysis uses historical price data, not economic fundamentals.
- Statement 2 is wrong: expansionary policy lowers real rates, so the INR should depreciate.
questions.keyPrinciple: Put on X/Y profits if the rate (base-currency value) falls.

questions.topic: Volatility trading in FX
questions.title: Peters' Recommendations: Volatility and Inflation
questions.context: Recommendation 1: use options to move from net short to net long volatility given recent pandemic turmoil. Recommendation 2: Germany's inflation is rising rapidly, so increase exposure to Germany to benefit from the expected currency depreciation.
questions.stem: Identify which recommendation is most likely correct and justify.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Recommendation 1.** In stable conditions traders are often net short volatility (most options expire out of the money; writers keep the premium). In unstable conditions, traders go net long volatility to hedge uncertainty.

Recommendation 2 is wrong: rising German inflation depreciates the currency, lowering the value of German investments, so exposure should be **reduced**, not increased.
questions.keyPrinciple: Turmoil → net long vol. Higher inflation → currency depreciation → reduce that exposure.

questions.topic: Carry trade, forward rate bias, roll yield, EM currency distributions
questions.title: Constructing a Negative Carry Trade (MXN/USD)
questions.context: US 1-yr yield 2.21%; MXN 1-yr yield 4.50%; MXN/USD spot 18.90; 1-yr forward 19.72.
questions.stem: Construct a negative carry trade using MXN/USD.
questions.modelAnswer:
A negative carry trade borrows at the high rate and invests at the low rate, profiting only if the low-yield currency appreciates enough.

- Borrow MXN at 4.50%, invest in USD at 2.21%: net borrowing cost = 4.50% − 2.21% = **2.29%**.
- Exchange rate return = (19.72 − 18.90) / 18.90 = **4.34%**, which exceeds the net cost, so the trade is profitable: 4.34% − 2.29% ≈ **2.05%** (my subtraction; the key states only that the 4.34% exceeds the 2.29%).
questions.keyPrinciple: Negative carry: borrow high-yield, invest low-yield; works only if the low-yield currency appreciates by more than the yield gap.

questions.topic: Minimum-variance hedge ratio
questions.title: Minimum-Variance Hedge of HKD Exposure
questions.context: JI (GBP reporting) holds HKD 185m of assets. σ(R_GBP) = 5.10%; σ(R_HKD) = 2.73%; σ(R_GBP/HKD) = 3.61%; ρ(R_GBP; R_GBP/HKD) = 0.26.
questions.stem: Construct a minimum-variance hedge using a forward contract.
questions.modelAnswer:
h = ρ(R_GBP; R_GBP/HKD) × σ(R_GBP) / σ(R_GBP/HKD) = 0.26 × (5.10% / 3.61%) = **0.367**

Hedge position = 0.367 × HKD 185m = **HKD 67.95m**.

Direction: short HKD. The market quote is HKD/GBP, so go **long HKD/GBP** (buy GBP), i.e., **short a GBP/HKD forward** with notional HKD 67.95m.
questions.keyPrinciple: Min-variance hedge ratio h = ρ × σ(asset return in domestic currency) / σ(FX return); hedge = h × exposure.

questions.title: Cash Outflow to Close Out a Forward After 3 Months
questions.context: 200,000 shares × EUR 90 = EUR 18m hedged with a 6-month forward sold at bid. Three months later, close out. Spot 1.3935/1.3983 → 1.4106/1.4210; 6m fwd points at initiation −19.0/−18.3; 3m fwd points three months later −21.6/−21.0; USD MRR 1.266%.
questions.stem: Using Exhibit 1, if the Spanish shares had been sold after three months, the cash outflow (in US dollars) required to close out the forward contract would have been closest to:

A.text: Discounts with the EUR MRR (1.814%) instead of the USD rate; the cash flow is in USD.

B.text: **USD 489,850.** Original forward (sell EUR at bid): 1.3935 − 19/10,000 = 1.3916. Close-out forward (buy EUR at offer): 1.4210 − 21/10,000 = 1.4189. Settlement = EUR 18m × (1.4189 − 1.3916) = USD 491,400; discount 3 months at the USD MRR: 491,400 / (1 + 0.01266 × 90/360) = **USD 489,850**.

C.text: Undiscounted settlement amount.

questions.keyPrinciple: Forward close-out: opposite forward at the other side of the market; discount the net USD settlement at the USD rate (the currency of the cash flow).

questions.topic: FX hedging mechanics (static/dynamic, forwards, rolling, cross-hedge, options)
questions.title: Roll Yield on the Rolled EUR Hedge
questions.context: The hedge sells EUR (base currency) forward; the EUR trades at a forward discount (negative points). The EUR appreciated by the time of the roll.
questions.stem: If the 2009 forward hedge had been rolled forward at its maturity, using Exhibit 1, the roll yield would most likely have been:

choices.text: negative, but the currency change made it less negative.
positive, but the currency change reduced some of this effect.
negative, and the currency change made it even more negative.

A.text: The currency appreciation makes it more, not less, negative.

B.text: Roll yield is negative for a hedger selling a base currency at a forward discount.

C.text: **Negative, and the currency change made it even more negative.** Selling a base currency at a discount means selling low and buying back higher at settlement (negative roll yield); the EUR's appreciation makes the buy-back price even higher.

questions.keyPrinciple: Selling a currency at a forward discount = negative roll yield; spot appreciation of it worsens the hedge result.

questions.topic: Non-deliverable forwards
questions.title: Least Accurate Statement About NDFs
questions.context: Fournier on NDFs: (pricing) may differ from arbitrage-implied; (credit risk) greater than outright forwards because central banks in developing countries are weaker; (settlement) cash settled in the non-controlled currency.
questions.stem: Which of Fournier’s 2014 comments about non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) is least accurate? The one concerning:

A.text: Accurate: capital controls break covered interest parity arbitrage, so NDF pricing can differ.

B.text: **Credit risk is the inaccurate comment.** Credit risk relates to counterparty risk, not the central bank, and is **lower** than outright forwards since the notional isn't exchanged; only the net change is settled.

C.text: Accurate: the controlled currency can't be delivered; NDFs are cash settled in the non-controlled currency.

questions.keyPrinciple: NDFs: cash settled in the freely convertible currency; lower credit risk (net settlement); pricing can deviate from CIP.

questions.title: Hedging Two Long, Highly Correlated Currency Exposures
questions.context: Testa holds roughly equal USD-sized long positions in a New Zealand firm and an Australian firm; USD/AUD vs USD/NZD correlation ≈ 0.85; he wants to minimize FX exposure.
questions.stem: The most appropriate hedging strategy for the 2015 positions, in keeping with Testa’s wishes, is based on a:

choices.text: direct hedge on each currency separately.
cross-hedge of the two currencies in the portfolio.
minimum-variance hedge of the two currencies in the portfolio.

A.text: **Direct hedge on each currency.** Both positions are long, so both currencies are sold forward; the correlation doesn't help.

B.text: A cross-hedge/minimum-variance hedge exploits correlation when one asset is long and the other short.

C.text: A minimum-variance hedge doesn't need long/short positions, but the biggest risk reduction, which Testa wants, comes from the direct hedge.

questions.keyPrinciple: Both long, minimize exposure → hedge each currency directly.

questions.topic: Currency return decomposition and risk
questions.title: Domestic-Currency Return of a Two-Country Portfolio
questions.context: Dias's foreign assets (BRL reporting): UK 83.4m→86.0m GBP, BRL/GBP 3.8729→4.1025; Germany 55m→51m EUR, BRL/EUR 3.0359→3.5142.
questions.stem: Based on the information provided in Exhibit 1, the domestic currency value of Dias’s foreign investments most likely:

choices.text: decreased because of changes in the domestic currency value of foreign asset holdings.
increased because of changes in the domestic currency value of foreign asset holdings.
increased because of changes in the domestic currency value of UK assets but decreased because of changes in the domestic currency value of German assets.

A.text: The portfolio's BRL value, and both holdings' BRL values, increased.

B.text:
**Increased because of changes in the domestic-currency value of both holdings.** Weights (initial BRL value): UK 0.659, Germany 0.341.
R_DC = 0.659 × (86.0/83.4)(4.1025/3.8729) + 0.341 × (51/55)(3.5142/3.0359) − 1 = 0.659(1.0923) + 0.341(1.0734) − 1 ≈ **+8.6%**. Both the UK and German holdings rose in BRL terms.

C.text: The German holding's *EUR* value declined (55m → 51m) but its BRL value rose because the EUR appreciated.

questions.keyPrinciple: R_DC (multi-asset) = Σ w_i (1 + R_FC,i)(1 + R_FX,i) − 1, with weights on initial domestic values.
questions.flag: Key shows the result as 0.0858; unrounded I get 0.08585 (8.59%). Direction and answer unaffected.

questions.topic: Currency management strategies (passive, discretionary, active, overlay, FX as an asset class)
questions.title: Correlations and Overlay Value-Add
questions.context: Traldi: in the short run, if foreign asset and foreign currency returns are negatively correlated, hedge all exposure; a fully hedged overlay with separate alpha adds value only if the alpha has a high correlation with Brazilian equities/bonds.
questions.stem: In her response regarding hedging foreign currency exposure in Dias’s portfolio, Traldi is most likely:

choices.text: correct about the correlations and the currency overlay program.
incorrect about the correlations and the currency overlay program.
incorrect about the correlations, but correct about the currency overlay program.

A.text: She's wrong on both points.

B.text: **Incorrect on both.** With negative correlation, some currency exposure is desirable for diversification, so no need to hedge it all. An overlay adds value only if currency alpha has a **low** correlation with the other asset classes.

C.text: She's wrong on the overlay point too: alpha must be low-correlated, not high.

questions.keyPrinciple: Negative asset–currency correlation → leave some exposure unhedged. Overlay alpha should be low-correlation.

questions.topic: FX hedging mechanics (static/dynamic, forwards, rolling, cross-hedge, options)
questions.title: Risk-Neutral Hedge Ratios for AUD and CHF
questions.context:
FB is long AUD and CHF equities (BRL reporting).

| Pair | Spot | 6m forward | 6m forecast spot | Fwd prem/disc | Spot change |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BRL/AUD | 2.1046 | 2.1523 | 2.0355 | 2.27% | −3.28% |
| BRL/CHF | 2.5309 | 2.4641 | 2.5642 | −2.64% | 1.32% |
questions.stem: Based on the information provided in Exhibit 3, the most appropriate risk neutral strategy is for FB to:

choices.text: over-hedge AUD and not hedge CHF.
under-hedge CHF and not hedge AUD.

A.text: **Over-hedge AUD, don't hedge CHF.** AUD trades at a 2.27% forward premium (positive roll yield on a short hedge) and is expected to depreciate 3.28% (short gains); so hedge more than 100%. CHF trades at a −2.64% forward discount (negative roll yield on a short) and is expected to appreciate 1.32% (short loses); so don't hedge.

B.text: Under-hedging AUD and over-hedging CHF is the reverse of what both the roll yield and the forecast imply.

C.text: Under-hedging CHF and not hedging AUD ignores AUD's expected depreciation and positive roll yield.

questions.keyPrinciple: Short hedge earns the forward premium (roll yield) plus any expected spot depreciation; hedge more when both are positive.

questions.topic: Option strategies (covered call, protective put, collar, spreads, straddles/strangles, calendar, synthetics)
questions.title: Do the Option Structures Exploit Views and Cut Hedging Cost?
questions.context: Strategy 1 (AUD, exposure BRL/AUD): long put K=2.1046, short put K=2.1006, short call K=2.1456. Strategy 2 (CHF, BRL/CHF): long put K=2.5309, short put K=2.5049, short call K=2.5669. Forecasts: BRL/AUD 2.0355, BRL/CHF 2.5642.
questions.stem: Is Campos most likely correct that Strategy 1 and Strategy 2 will accomplish the goals of exploiting market views and reducing hedging costs?

choices.text: No, she is incorrect about reducing hedging costs
No, she is incorrect about exploiting market views

A.text: The costs are reduced, but the structures don't accommodate the market views.

B.text: She is right about reducing hedging costs: the short put and short call generate premium.

C.text: **No: she is wrong about exploiting market views.** Both structures reduce cost via premiums from the short options. But Strategy 1 (a short seagull on AUD) protects only down to 2.1006 (where the short put offsets the hedge), not to the forecast 2.0355; and in Strategy 2 the premium is pocketed if the rate doesn't reach the 2.5669 short call strike.

questions.keyPrinciple: Seagull/collar structures cut cost by selling options but give up protection (or upside) beyond the short strike.
questions.flag: The key's reasoning focuses on Strategy 1; for Strategy 2 it says the premium is pocketed and the option expires worthless, which doesn't clearly show how that strategy fails the 'exploit the view' test (the 2.5642 forecast is inside the 2.5669 short call strike). The answer (C) is per the key; I couldn't verify the Strategy 2 explanation.

questions.topic: Equity universe segmentation, ESG, shareholder engagement
questions.title: Barboa Fund — Segmentation Approach
questions.context: **Barboa Fund:** invests solely in the equity of companies in oil production and transportation industries in many countries.
questions.stem: The Barboa Fund can be best described as a fund segmented by:

A.text: The description says nothing about market cap or style (value, growth, blend). Size is usually market cap; style is scored on P/E, P/B, earnings growth, dividend yield, etc.

B.text: The fund invests in *many* countries, so it is not segmented by geography. Geographic segmentation is by stage of development (developed, emerging, frontier markets).

C.text: The fund groups companies by what they produce and the inputs they use (oil production and transportation). That is segmentation by **economic activity** (the production-oriented approach).

questions.keyPrinciple: Equity segmentation: **economic activity** (industry/sector), **size/style**, **geography**. Match the description to the dimension it actually uses.

questions.topic: Equity universe segmentation, ESG, shareholder engagement
questions.title: Caribou Fund — Size/Style Classification
questions.context: **Caribou Fund:** uses an aggressive strategy focusing on relatively new, fast-growing companies in emerging industries.
questions.stem: The Caribou Fund is most likely classified as a:

A.text: *(My reconstruction; the key explains only C.)* New companies are not large caps, and a fast-growth focus is not a value style. Wrong on both dimensions.

B.text: *(My reconstruction; the key explains only C.)* Size (small cap) fits, but an aggressive fast-growth focus is a growth style, not value.

C.text: New companies are generally small; an aggressive, fast-growth focus is a growth style. Size is usually market cap (large, mid, small) and style is value, growth or blend.

questions.keyPrinciple: New + fast-growing + aggressive = **small-cap growth**. Check both size and style before choosing.

questions.topic: Equity universe segmentation, ESG, shareholder engagement
questions.title: DoGood Fund — Screening Approach
questions.context: **DoGood Fund:** universe is US companies and sectors with favorable ESG ratings, and it **specifically excludes** companies with aerospace and defense products or services.
questions.stem: The DoGood Fund’s approach to the aerospace and defense industry is best described as:

A.text: Positive screening seeks the companies or sectors that score most favorably on ESG risks/opportunities. The aerospace and defense restriction is an exclusion, not a selection.

B.text: Excluding companies based on specified activities is **negative (exclusionary) screening**.

C.text: Thematic investing targets a specific sector or theme (e.g., energy efficiency, climate change). DoGood's universe is all companies and sectors with favorable ESG ratings, with specific exclusions.

questions.keyPrinciple: ESG approaches: **negative/exclusionary** (exclude), **positive/best-in-class** (select the best), **thematic** (one theme or sector).

questions.topic: Equity indexes, passive vs active, concentration (HHI)
questions.title: Elmer Fund — Management Strategy
questions.context: **Elmer Fund:** investments selected to track the S&P 500 Index. Minimizes trading based on the assumption that markets are efficient.
questions.stem: The Elmer fund’s management strategy is:

A.text: *(My reconstruction; the key explains only B.)* Active management seeks to outperform and does not assume efficiency; Elmer tracks an index with minimal trading.

B.text: Mimicking an index under an efficient-market assumption is an **index** strategy. Index strategies generally have lower turnover and generate a higher share of long-term gains.

C.text: *(My reconstruction; the key explains only B.)* A blended approach would combine index and active components. Nothing in the description mentions active management.

questions.keyPrinciple: Index fund = tracks a benchmark, low turnover, minimal rebalancing; fits investors who believe markets are efficient.

questions.topic: Equity income enhancement (lending, options, dividend capture), fees
questions.title: Caribou Fund — Fee Type
questions.context: **Note 1:** the fee on the Caribou Fund is a 15% share of any capital appreciation above a 7% threshold, with a high-water mark.
questions.stem: Based on Note 1, the fee on the Caribou Fund is best described as a:

A.text: A share of returns above a threshold, with a high-water mark, is a **performance fee**. These are usually "upward only": the manager earns when objectives are met and investors are not reimbursed when performance is negative.

B.text: Management fees cover direct research and portfolio management costs and are typically a percentage of assets under management.

C.text: Administrative fees cover corporate actions processing, performance and risk measurement, and voting at meetings. They are usually folded into the management fee.

questions.keyPrinciple: Performance fee = incentive fee above a hurdle, usually with a high-water mark. Management fee = % of AUM.

questions.topic: Equity universe segmentation, ESG, shareholder engagement
questions.title: DoGood Fund — Conflict of Interest vs Free Rider
questions.context:
**Note 2:** DoGood invests in Fleeker stock; Fleeker's pension fund has a significant investment in DoGood. The note says this creates a potential conflict of interest on the part of Fleeker, **but not** for the DoGood Fund.

**Note 3:** DoGood's PM has written policies stating the fund does not engage in shareholder activism, so it may be a free rider on other shareholders' activism.
questions.stem: Which of the following notes about the DoGood Fund is correct?

A.text: Note 2 is wrong. The conflict arises on the part of the **DoGood Fund**: it owns shares of a company (Fleeker) that is also an investor in the fund, so the PM may be influenced to support Fleeker's management to protect the mandate.

B.text: Note 3 is correct: a fund that does not engage but holds the stock benefits from other shareholders' engagement without bearing its cost (the free-rider problem). Note 2 is wrong (see C).

C.text: Wrong because Note 2 is wrong. Both notes would be correct only if the conflict note placed the conflict on the fund.

questions.keyPrinciple: Conflict of interest: the manager owns stock of a company that is also a client/investor. Free rider: benefits from others' engagement without paying for it.

questions.topic: Equity indexes, passive vs active, concentration (HHI)
questions.title: Elmer Fund — Fees and Bonds
questions.context:
**Note 4:** of the four funds, Elmer is most likely to appeal to investors who want to minimize fees and believe markets are efficient.

**Note 5:** adding investment-grade bonds to the Elmer Fund will decrease the portfolio's short-term risk.
questions.stem: Which of the notes regarding the Elmer Fund is correct?

A.text: Note 4 is correct: index funds have lower direct research and portfolio management costs, so fees are typically low. Note 5 is wrong (see C).

B.text: Note 5 is wrong, and Note 4 is correct, so "Only Note 5" has it backwards.

C.text: Note 5 is wrong. The key's reason is only: "the predictability of correlations is uncertain." The short-term risk reduction from adding bonds depends on the bond–equity correlation, which can't be assumed to hold.

questions.keyPrinciple: Diversification benefit depends on correlations, and correlations are unstable; adding bonds does not guarantee lower short-term risk.
questions.flag: Key's reason for rejecting Note 5 is one short sentence about correlation predictability.

questions.topic: Equity income enhancement (lending, options, dividend capture), fees
questions.title: Securities Lending vs Covered Calls
questions.context:
**Statement 1:** securities lending would increase income through reinvestment of cash collateral but would require the fund to miss out on dividend income from the lent securities.

**Statement 2:** writing covered calls would generate income but limit upside share price appreciation.
questions.stem: Which of Frey’s statements about securities lending and covered call writing is correct?

A.text: Statement 1 is wrong: the borrower "manufactures" the dividends and pays them to the lender, so the fund does **not** miss out on dividend income.

B.text: Statement 2 is correct: covered calls generate premium income but cap upside on the underlying shares.

C.text: Wrong because Statement 1 is wrong (manufactured dividends).

questions.keyPrinciple: Stock lending: fee + reinvestment of collateral, dividends are manufactured by the borrower. Covered call: premium income, capped upside.

questions.topic: Equity indexes, passive vs active, concentration (HHI)
questions.title: Index Investability — Free Float and Buffering
questions.context:
Tong's statements on investable indexes:
- **Statement 1:** a free-float adjustment to a market-cap-weighted index lowers its liquidity.
- **Statement 2:** an index provider that uses a buffering policy makes the index more investable.
questions.stem: Which of Tong’s statements regarding equity index benchmarks is correct?

A.text: Statement 1 is wrong. Without a free-float adjustment, shares held by founders, governments or other companies inflate the weight and make the index less investable. A free-float adjustment better reflects actual liquidity; it does not lower it.

B.text: Buffering makes index transitions more gradual and orderly, which makes the index more investable. The three requirements for an index to underpin a strategy are rule-based, transparent and investable.

C.text: Wrong because Statement 1 is wrong.

questions.keyPrinciple: Free-float adjustment improves investability (reflects tradable shares). Buffering reduces turnover at index reconstitution.

questions.topic: Equity indexes, passive vs active, concentration (HHI)
questions.title: Benchmark for Low-Beta, High-Yield, Low-P/E Preferences
questions.context: Winthrop wants a benchmark covering all sectors of the Canadian equity market and focused on highly liquid, well-known companies. Any stock purchased should have a relatively **low beta, high dividend yield, low P/E and low P/B**.
questions.stem: To satisfy Winthrop’s benchmark and security selection specifications, the equity index benchmark Tong selects should be:

choices.text: small capitalization with a core tilt.
large capitalization with a value tilt.

A.text: Small caps tend to be riskier than large caps, and Winthrop prefers low beta (also less liquid).

B.text: Large caps are the most liquid and well known. A value tilt matches high dividend yield, low P/E and low P/B.

C.text: Growth stocks have high momentum, high P/Es and high EPS growth, which conflicts with his low P/E preference.

questions.keyPrinciple: Value = high yield, low P/E, low P/B. Growth = high P/E, high EPS growth, momentum. Large cap = liquidity.

questions.topic: Equity indexes, passive vs active, concentration (HHI)
questions.title: Problem With the Benchmark Preference
questions.context: Winthrop desires exposure to **global** equity markets and asked Tong to select an equity benchmark holding all sectors of the **Canadian** equity market, with large, liquid, well-known companies.
questions.stem: What is a problem with Winthrop’s benchmark preference?

choices.text: The geographic limitation to Canadian equities
The exclusion of fixed-income securities given Winthrop’s significant exposure

A.text: He wants global equity exposure, so the equity benchmark should be global (e.g., MSCI All Country World Index), not Canadian only.

B.text: The benchmark request is for the equity allocation only. Adding fixed income to an equity benchmark would be inappropriate.

C.text: Including all sectors is appropriate because his strategy includes all sectors.

questions.keyPrinciple: The benchmark must match the mandate: global equity exposure → global equity index.

questions.topic: Equity income enhancement (lending, options, dividend capture), fees
questions.title: Explicit Trading Costs
questions.context:
Watson's fund trading costs (bps):

| Trading cost | bps |
|---|---|
| Brokerage commissions | 28 |
| Market impact | 13 |
| Delay costs | 5 |
| Exchange fees | 4 |
| Transaction taxes | 8 |
| Regulatory fees | 2 |
| Bid-offer spread | 7 |
questions.stem: Calculate the explicit trading costs incurred by Watson's fund.
questions.modelAnswer:
Explicit costs = brokerage commissions + transaction taxes + exchange fees + regulatory fees

= 0.28% + 0.08% + 0.04% + 0.02% = **0.42%** (42 bps).

*(My addition, from the same exhibit: the implicit costs are market impact + delay + bid-offer spread = 13 + 5 + 7 = 25 bps.)*
questions.keyPrinciple: Explicit = commissions, fees, taxes (visible). Implicit = market impact, delay, bid-offer spread.

questions.topic: Equity universe segmentation, ESG, shareholder engagement
questions.title: Weakness of Geographic Segmentation
questions.context: Watson has historically segmented her investment universe by the **geographic location** of prospective companies. She believes this best isolates the market in which the companies operate.
questions.stem: Describe one weakness in Watson's equity segmentation approach.
questions.modelAnswer:
The key gives two weaknesses (one is enough):
1. Investing in a particular country may not give the expected exposure to that market. A company's **domicile** does not necessarily reflect the geographic sources of its revenue.
2. **Currency risk** when investing internationally. Currency moves can help or hurt, and can be hedged, but managing currency adds complexity.
questions.keyPrinciple: Geographic segmentation weaknesses: domicile vs revenue exposure, and currency risk.

questions.topic: Equity universe segmentation, ESG, shareholder engagement
questions.title: Shareholder Engagement Statements
questions.context:
Watson's statements:
- **Statement 1:** shareholder engagement allows investors to quantify the return from promoted ideals around social and environmental policies.
- **Statement 2:** exercising voting rights is among the most influential tools available for shareholder engagement.
questions.stem: Determine whether each statement made by Watson is most likely correct or incorrect. (Correct, Incorrect) Justify each response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Statement 1 is incorrect.** Benefits of engagement on non-financial interests are difficult to quantify. Capital returns tied to governance, social or environmental activity have been mixed, and management quality and E&S practices may be correlated, making cause and effect hard to measure.

**Statement 2 is correct.** Voting is one of the most influential tools: it lets shareholders express views on strategy, capital allocation, governance, remuneration and board compensation.
questions.keyPrinciple: Engagement benefits are hard to quantify. Voting rights are a primary engagement tool.

questions.topic: Equity income enhancement (lending, options, dividend capture), fees
questions.title: Options Strategy for Income Without Cash Allocation
questions.context: Watson plans to leverage holdings she believes are trading **near their intrinsic values** with an options strategy to enhance income. She does **not** plan to set aside a separate cash allocation to execute it.
questions.stem: Describe an appropriate options strategy for Watson to present to the board.
questions.modelAnswer:
A **covered call** strategy. The manager owns the stock and sells a call on it; income comes from the premium. It limits upside, which is acceptable if the shares are near intrinsic value and not expected to appreciate much.

A cash-covered (cash-secured) **put** is not appropriate because it requires depositing money separately into a designated account, and Watson won't set aside a cash allocation.
questions.keyPrinciple: Covered call = long stock + short call: income, capped upside, no extra cash needed. Cash-covered put needs cash set aside.

questions.topic: Equity income enhancement (lending, options, dividend capture), fees
questions.title: Dividend Capture Strategy
questions.context: Cartwright and Rivers are doing due diligence on a **dividend capture** equity fund managed by Active Alpha.
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the equity strategy managed by Active Alpha?

choices.text: Automatically reinvest dividends received back into the same company’s stock, purchasing more shares
Purchase stock just before record date, hold the stock through record date, and subsequently sell the shares
Purchase stock just before ex-dividend date, hold the stock through ex-dividend date, and subsequently sell the shares

A.text: That describes a dividend reinvestment strategy.

B.text: The relevant date is the ex-dividend date, not the record date.

C.text: Dividend capture: buy just before the **ex-dividend date**, hold through it to earn the dividend, then sell.

questions.keyPrinciple: Dividend capture = buy before ex-date, hold through ex-date, then sell.

questions.topic: Equity income enhancement (lending, options, dividend capture), fees
questions.title: Active vs Index Fees — Least Accurate Statement
questions.context:
Why does the active fund carry a high fee relative to index peers?
- **Statement 1:** actively managed funds typically have higher research and portfolio management costs.
- **Statement 2:** active fees are higher due to potential hidden costs attributable to predatory trading.
- **Statement 3:** active fees incorporate marketing and other administrative costs.
questions.stem: Which of Cartwright’s statements is least accurate?

A.text: Accurate. Active funds have higher portfolio management and research costs.

B.text: Statement 2 is least accurate. The hidden cost from predatory trading hits **index** funds, not active funds: a predatory trader may buy (or short) shares ahead of their inclusion in (or deletion from) an index.

C.text: Accurate. Active fees incorporate marketing and administrative costs.

questions.keyPrinciple: Index funds face predatory-trading (front-running of reconstitution) costs; active funds face higher research/management costs.

questions.topic: Equity indexes, passive vs active, concentration (HHI)
questions.title: HHI and Effective Number of Stocks
questions.context:
Active Alpha holds 40 stocks. Cartwright wants a diversified vehicle that minimizes stock-specific risk relative to its benchmark. The **benchmark's concentration equals 28 equally weighted stocks**.

| Stock | Weight |
|---|---|
| 1 | 0.074 |
| 2 | 0.068 |
| 3 | 0.062 |
| 4 | 0.048 |
| 5 | 0.031 |
| 6 to 40 | 0.717 |

Stocks 6 to 40 have a sum of squared weights of **0.01554**.
questions.stem: Given Cartwright’s preference, should his firm invest in the Active Alpha fund?

choices.text: No, due to its HHI statistic of 0.0172
No, due to its HHI statistic of 0.0327
Yes, due to its HHI statistic of 0.0327

A.text: 0.0172 is the sum of squares of the top five only (0.017209). It leaves out the 35 other stocks' 0.01554.

B.text: HHI is 0.0327 and 1/0.0327 ≈ 31 effective stocks is *more* diversified than the benchmark's 28, so the fund meets Cartwright's preference.

C.text: HHI = 0.074² + 0.068² + 0.062² + 0.048² + 0.031² + 0.01554 = 0.005476 + 0.004624 + 0.003844 + 0.002304 + 0.000961 + 0.01554 = **0.0327**. Effective number of stocks = 1/0.0327 = 30.6 ≈ **31**, above the benchmark's 28. The fund is less concentrated than the benchmark, so invest.

questions.keyPrinciple: HHI = Σ wᵢ². Effective number of stocks = 1/HHI. More effective stocks than the benchmark = less concentration.
questions.flag: Key's text for A writes the top-five sum as 0.172; the choice (0.0172) is the correct value.

questions.topic: Equity universe segmentation, ESG, shareholder engagement
questions.title: What Shareholder Engagement Assists Companies With
questions.stem: Shareholder engagement most likely assists companies:

choices.text: in developing a more effective corporate governance culture.
to have full transparency in their disclosure of important information to all shareholders.
to remain focused on long-term decisions instead of deviating to achieve near-term earnings targets.

A.text: From the company's perspective, engagement can help develop a more effective corporate governance culture.

B.text: Engagement can lead to **selective** disclosure to a subset of shareholders, risking insider-trading breaches. It does not guarantee full transparency.

C.text: Engagement can pressure management toward near-term share price or earnings targets at the expense of long-term decisions (a disadvantage).

questions.keyPrinciple: Engagement: pro = governance culture; cons = selective-disclosure risk and short-termism pressure.

questions.topic: Equity indexes, passive vs active, concentration (HHI)
questions.title: When an Advisor Should Not Use a Strategy
questions.stem: An investment advisor should not engage in:

choices.text: active management when a client mandate is to eliminate "key person" risk.
index-based strategies when a client mandate is to minimize tax consequences of gains.
active management when a client mandate is ESG considerations with continual exclusionary screening process.

A.text: Key-person risk is relevant to active managers whose firm depends on one or a few star managers who might leave. A mandate to eliminate key-person risk argues *against* active management.

B.text: Index strategies have lower turnover and more long-term gains, so they *fit* a mandate to minimize taxes on gains. The advisor would not avoid them.

C.text: ESG mandates with continual exclusionary screening are typically managed actively, because an index may not efficiently meet desired holdings or exclusions. The advisor would not avoid active here.

questions.keyPrinciple: Question asks what NOT to do. Active + 'eliminate key-person risk' conflict; index + tax-minimization and active + ESG screening both fit.

questions.topic: Equity indexes, passive vs active, concentration (HHI)
questions.title: Equal-Weighted vs Cap-Weighted Index
questions.stem: When creating a new index, an index provider is most likely to choose an equally weighted index over a capitalization-weighted index when it is willing to accept:

A.text: Equal weighting imparts a **small-cap** bias (and higher volatility than cap weighting), not a large-cap bias.

B.text: Equal weights drift immediately after trading starts, so equal-weighted indexes need regular rebalancing (S&P offers an equal-weighted S&P 500 rebalanced quarterly). A provider choosing equal weighting accepts frequent rebalancing.

C.text: Equal weighting is chosen when the provider is *unwilling* to tolerate single-stock concentration. Weights are 1/n, the least concentrated option.

questions.keyPrinciple: Equal weight: small-cap bias, frequent rebalancing, least concentrated. Cap weight: large-cap bias, concentration, low turnover.

questions.topic: Equity indexes, passive vs active, concentration (HHI)
questions.title: Correlations in a Crisis
questions.context: High-net-worth portfolio of equities, REITs and treasuries, allocated on correlations to diversify market risk. A political crisis could intensify and hit the market.
questions.stem: A high net worth individual has a portfolio which contains equities, REITs and treasury securities. The allocation to these asset classes was based on their correlations with the objective of diversifying market risk. The country is currently experiencing a political crisis. If the crisis were to intensify and impact the market, the diversification benefits of the portfolio is most likely to:

A.text: In crises, correlations across asset classes and among equities often rise, so diversification benefits decrease.

B.text: Correlations are expected to increase, reducing diversification benefits.

C.text: Correlations (not diversification benefits) increase in a crisis.

questions.keyPrinciple: Correlations go up in crises → diversification benefit goes down.

questions.topic: Equity universe segmentation, ESG, shareholder engagement
questions.title: Disadvantage of Economic-Activity Segmentation
questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely a disadvantage when an equity portfolio manager segments her investment universe using an economic activity approach?

choices.text: The portfolio may include large companies whose businesses span multiple industries
It is difficult to construct a performance benchmark to measure investment performance

A.text: Better industry representation (diversification across sectors) is an *advantage* of this approach.

B.text: Large, diversified companies with business lines in several industries are hard to classify into one industry or sub-industry.

C.text: Constructing sector/industry benchmarks is an *advantage* of this approach, not a challenge.

questions.keyPrinciple: Economic-activity segmentation: pro = sector diversification and benchmarks; con = multi-industry companies are hard to classify.

questions.topic: Equity income enhancement (lending, options, dividend capture), fees
questions.title: Stock Lending — Index vs Active Fund
questions.context: An index fund and an active fund both lend stocks that are on "special" (some pay significant dividends).
questions.stem: An index fund and an active fund both lend stocks that are on "special." Some of these stocks pay significant dividends. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.text: Both funds do not receive any cash collateral for lending stocks on "special"
Both funds' income from stock lending includes interest earned less dividends received
The manager of the index fund is less concerned the borrowed stock will be used to facilitate short-selling

A.text: Stock loans are collateralized with cash or high-quality securities. Lenders earn fees (including on specials) and can earn more by reinvesting cash collateral.

B.text: Dividends are "manufactured" by the borrower and paid to the lender, so lending income is not "interest earned less dividends received".

C.text: Index-fund managers are normally not concerned that borrowed stock may facilitate short selling that pressures the stock's price. Active funds, endowments and large institutions are more concerned about the effect on returns.

questions.keyPrinciple: Stock lending income = lending fees + collateral reinvestment; dividends manufactured by the borrower. Index funds worry less about short-sale impact than active funds.

questions.topic: Fixed-income expected return, rolling yield, leverage
questions.title: Highest Inflation Protection for Coupons
questions.context:
Bond type, % of each fund (Exhibit 1):

| | Aschel | Permot | Rosaiso |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed-coupon | 95% | 38% | 62% |
| Floating-coupon | 2% | 34% | 17% |
| Inflation-linked | 3% | 28% | 21% |
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, which fund provides the highest level of protection against inflation for coupon payments?

B.text: Coupon inflation protection = floating-coupon % + inflation-linked %. Permot = 34% + 28% = **62%**. Floaters protect interest income because the reference rate adjusts for inflation; inflation-linked bonds protect both coupon and principal.

questions.keyPrinciple: Coupon inflation protection ≈ % floating + % inflation-linked.

questions.topic: Fixed-income expected return, rolling yield, leverage
questions.title: Rolling Yield — Aschel
questions.context: Aschel: current average bond price $117.00; expected price at end of Year 1 $114.00; average annual coupon $3.63. Assume no reinvestment income and an unchanged yield curve.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, the rolling yield of Aschel over a one-year investment horizon is closest to:

A.text: 2.56% is the size of the rolldown, with the sign dropped and the coupon income left out. *(My reconstruction.)* The price falls from 117 to 114, so rolldown is negative.

B.text: Rolling yield = coupon income + rolldown return. Coupon income = 3.63/117.00 = **3.10%**. Rolldown return = (114.00 − 117.00)/117.00 = **−2.56%** (a premium bond pulls to par). Rolling yield = 3.10% − 2.56% = **0.54%**.

C.text: 5.66% = 3.10% + 2.56%: the rolldown loss added instead of subtracted. *(My reconstruction.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Rolling yield = coupon/price + (end price − start price)/start price. A premium bond has negative rolldown.
questions.flag: The key states the rolldown figure (−2.56%) but does not show the arithmetic; I recomputed it.

questions.topic: Fixed-income expected return, rolling yield, leverage
questions.title: Leveraged Portfolio Return — Aschel
questions.context: Aschel: PV of assets $136.33m; value of equity $94.33m; borrowed funds $42.00m; borrowing rate 2.80%; return on invested funds 6.20%.
questions.stem: The leveraged portfolio return for Aschel is closest to:

A.text: 7.25% = 6.20% + (42.00/136.33) × (6.20% − 2.80%): borrowed funds divided by total assets instead of by equity. *(My reconstruction.)*

C.text: 8.96% = 6.20% + (42.00/94.33) × 6.20%: the extra return on borrowed money is added but the 2.80% borrowing cost is never subtracted. *(My reconstruction.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Leveraged return = rI + (V_B/V_E) × (rI − r_B). Divide by equity, and subtract the cost of debt.

questions.topic: Fixed-income expected return, rolling yield, leverage
questions.title: Effective Duration for Embedded Options
questions.context: **Note 2:** Rosaiso is the only fund of the three that holds a significant number of bonds with embedded options.
questions.stem: Based on Note 2, Rosaiso is the only fund for which the expected change in price based on the investor’s views of yields to maturity and yield spreads should be calculated using:

A.text: Convexity alone isn't the full estimate, and for option-embedded bonds the convexity measure must be effective convexity.

B.text: Modified duration is used for bonds without embedded options.

C.text: For bonds with embedded options, the price change from yield/spread views must use **effective duration** (and effective convexity).

questions.keyPrinciple: Option-free → modified duration and convexity. Embedded options → effective duration and effective convexity.

questions.topic: Liability-based mandates, immunization, duration
questions.title: Features of Liability-Based Mandates
questions.context:
Cécile's key features of a liability-based mandate:
- **Feature 1:** matches expected liability payments with future projected cash inflows.
- **Feature 2:** can minimize the risk of deficient cash inflows for a company.
questions.stem: Is Cécile correct with respect to key features of liability-based mandates?

A.text: Both are correct. Liability-based mandates are managed to match expected liability payments with projected inflows and to minimize shortfall risk (deficient cash inflows).

B.text: Feature 2 is also correct.

C.text: Feature 1 is also correct.

questions.keyPrinciple: Liability-based mandate: match asset cash flows to liability payments; minimize shortfall risk.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Which Bond to Sell for a Tax-Exempt Client
questions.context:
Villash Foundation is **tax-exempt** and needs $5 million in cash.

| | Bond 1 | Bond 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Market value | $5,000,000 | $5,000,000 |
| Capital gain/(loss) | +$400,000 | −$400,000 |
| Investment view | Overvalued | Undervalued |
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the optimal strategy to meet Villash Foundation’s cash needs is the sale of:

A.text: Sell 100% of Bond 1. For a tax-exempt investor, taxes (and the gain/loss) are irrelevant; the investment view drives the trade, and Bond 1 is overvalued.

B.text: Bond 2 is undervalued, so it would be held. Its loss has no tax value to a tax-exempt foundation.

C.text: Splitting would sell half of an undervalued bond. The view favors selling only the overvalued one.

questions.keyPrinciple: Tax-exempt investors trade on investment views; taxable investors also weigh gains/losses.
questions.flag: The tax-rate rows under Exhibit 2 pasted scrambled (39% / 30%). They don't matter here because Villash is tax-exempt.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Domestic Bond Portfolio — Total Return Approach
questions.context: Domestic bond portfolio mandate: long-term return objective of **25 bps over the benchmark**; small deviations in sector weightings permitted; risk factors such as duration must **closely match**; tracking error expected **< 50 bps** per year.
questions.stem: Which approach to its total return mandate is the fund’s domestic bond portfolio most likely to use?

A.text: Pure indexing replicates the index with no outperformance target, and no sector deviations.

B.text: **Enhanced indexing**: modest outperformance target, benchmark-like risk factors (duration), small sector deviations, small tracking error.

C.text: Active management runs larger deviations in duration, sectors and other risk factors, with larger tracking error.

questions.keyPrinciple: Pure indexing: replicate. Enhanced indexing: small deviations, modest alpha, low tracking error. Active: larger mismatches.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Strategy 2 vs Strategy 1
questions.context:
Objectives: fund future liabilities, protect interest income from short-term inflation, minimize correlation with the equity portfolio (currently 0.14).

- **Strategy 1:** AAA fixed-coupon corporate bonds, modified duration two years, correlation with equity −0.15.
- **Strategy 2:** US government agency floating-coupon bonds, modified duration one month, correlation with equity −0.10.
questions.stem: Strategy 2 is most likely preferred to Strategy 1 for meeting the objective of:

choices.text: minimizing the correlation of the fund’s domestic bond portfolio and equity portfolio.

A.text: Floating-coupon bonds protect interest income because the reference rate adjusts for inflation. Fixed-coupon bonds in Strategy 1 give no protection for interest or principal.

B.text: Strategy 1 is better for funding liabilities: fixed coupons give more predictable cash flows.

C.text: Strategy 1 is better for diversification: its correlation (−0.15) is lower than Strategy 2's (−0.10).

questions.keyPrinciple: Floaters → inflation protection for income. Fixed coupons → predictable liability funding.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Taxable Investors — Selling Bonds
questions.context:
Dan only sold overvalued bonds with capital gains. His statements:
- **Statement 1:** taxable investors should prioritize selling overvalued bonds and always sell them before selling bonds viewed as fairly valued or undervalued.
- **Statement 2:** taxable investors should never intentionally realize capital losses.
questions.stem: Are Dan’s statements to Celia that support Dan’s choice of bonds to sell correct?

choices.text: Neither Statement 1 nor Statement 2 is correct.

A.text: Statement 1 is wrong: because of taxes, overvalued bonds are not *always* sold first; loss-harvesting trades can take priority.

B.text: Statement 2 is wrong: intentionally realizing losses to offset gains is a core tax-management technique.

C.text: Both are wrong. For taxable investors there is value in harvesting tax losses, which offset capital gains that would otherwise be distributed and taxed. The fund must weigh total after-tax value, which can mean selling bonds that are not overvalued.

questions.keyPrinciple: Taxable investors: harvest losses to offset gains. Tax-exempt investors: views only.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Highest Liquidity Premium
questions.context:
| | Bond 1 | Bond 2 | Bond 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Credit quality | AA | AA | A |
| Issue size ($m) | 100 | 75 | 75 |

questions.title: Which Manager Is Active
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 3, which manager is most likely to have an active management total return mandate?

questions.title: Scotia Fund — Total Return Mandate

questions.title: ETFs for a Bond Ladder

questions.topic: Fixed-income expected return, rolling yield, leverage
questions.title: Rolling Yield — EZ Company
questions.context: EZ Company portfolio (Exhibit 1): coupon $6.75 per $100 par (annual); current price $94.20; expected price in 1 year (unchanged curve) $97.35; convexity 18; modified duration 3.70; expected Δ benchmark YTM +0.26%; expected Δ spread −0.10%.
questions.stem: The expected rolling yield of EZ Company’s bond portfolio over the one-year investment horizon is closest to:

questions.topic: Fixed-income expected return, rolling yield, leverage
questions.title: Yield and Spread Effects — EZ Company
questions.context: Same EZ data: modified duration 3.70, convexity 18, Δ benchmark YTM = +0.26%, Δ spread = −0.10%.
questions.stem: The combined expected return for EZ Company’s bond portfolio due to the expected changes in benchmark YTM and spread is closest to:

A.text: The ΔSpread is not squared in the convexity term (−1.49%): spread term becomes (3.7 × 0.001) + ½ × 18 × (−0.001) = −0.53%, and −0.96% − 0.53% = −1.49%.

C.text: Sign on modified duration omitted (0.60%): +0.97% from the yield term and −0.37% from the spread term.

questions.keyPrinciple: Price effect = (−MD × Δy) + (½ × Convexity × Δy²). Do the same for spread; squared term uses Δ².

questions.topic: Liability-based mandates, immunization, duration
questions.title: Balancing Reinvestment and Price Risk
questions.context: Wayne wants a strategy that best balances **cash flow reinvestment risk** and **market price risk**, the two main sources of interest rate risk.
questions.stem: Given his objective related to the two main sources of interest rate risk, which of the following strategies should Wayne recommend to his clients?

A.text: Not the balanced choice. The key credits the ladder's time diversification as the balance; the bullet doesn't provide it.

B.text: Not the balanced choice. The barbell is the highest-convexity structure (see FI-19), not the balanced one.

C.text: A **laddered** portfolio diversifies across time and gives a balanced position between reinvestment risk and market price risk.

questions.keyPrinciple: Ladder = diversification over time; balanced exposure to reinvestment risk and price risk.

questions.topic: Liability-based mandates, immunization, duration
questions.title: Brown's Comments on Duration and Convexity
questions.context:
- **Comment 1:** effective duration must be used to estimate the interest rate sensitivity of Type II, III and IV liabilities.
- **Comment 2:** to maximize convexity, a manager should use a laddered strategy rather than a bullet or barbell.
questions.stem: Is either of Brown’s comments most likely correct?

A.text: Wrong: Comment 1 is correct.

B.text: Comment 1 is correct: effective duration is used for Type II, III and IV liabilities.

C.text: Comment 2 is wrong: a **barbell** (not a ladder) maximizes convexity, because its cash flows have the widest dispersion around the portfolio duration.

questions.keyPrinciple: Convexity: barbell > ladder > bullet. Type II–IV liabilities → effective duration.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Role of Fixed Income — Incorrect Point
questions.context:
Moynahan's page 1 points:
- **A:** adding fixed income is an effective way to get diversification benefits, especially because correlations with other asset classes are low.
- **B:** the regular nature of fixed-income cash flows lets investors fund future obligations, unless there is a credit event.
- **C:** fixed-income securities can *always* provide a hedge for inflation, resulting in superior risk-adjusted real returns.
questions.stem: Which of the points outlined on page 1 of Moynahan’s presentation is least likely correct?

A.text: Accurate. Fixed income has diversification benefits.

B.text: Accurate. Regular cash flows fund obligations unless there is a credit event.

C.text: Wrong: only some fixed income (e.g., inflation-linked bonds) hedges inflation. Not all fixed-income securities do.

questions.keyPrinciple: 'Always' is the red flag: only inflation-linked (and some floating) bonds hedge inflation.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Labeling Portfolios 1–3 by Management Approach
questions.context:
Exhibit 1: features of total return portfolios.

| | Benchmark | Portfolio 1 | Portfolio 2 | Portfolio 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quality AAA/AA/A (%) | 76.0 | 74.9 | 75.8 | 76.3 |
| Quality BBB/BB (%) | 24.0 | 25.1 | 24.2 | 23.7 |
| Average quality | AA– | AA– | AA– | AA |
| Key rate duration 1–5 yrs | 2.5 | 2.4 | 2.4 | 2.5 |
| Key rate duration 5–10 yrs | 1.8 | 1.9 | 1.9 | 1.8 |
| Key rate duration 10–15 yrs | 1.5 | 1.4 | 1.5 | 1.5 |
| Credit spread duration | 1.45 | 1.55 | 1.43 | 1.50 |
| Turnover | — | 8% | 5% | 6% |
| Developed markets (%) | 90.0 | 86.4 | 91.2 | 87.0 |
| Emerging markets (%) | 10.0 | 14.0 | 9.8 | 13.0 |
| Securities lending | N/A | Not allowed | Allowed | Not allowed |
questions.stem: How should Moynahan most likely label the management approaches for each of the portfolios described in Exhibit 1 on page 2 of his presentation?

choices.text: Portfolio 1 = Active Management, Portfolio 2 = Pure Indexing, Portfolio 3 = Enhanced Indexing
Portfolio 1 = Active Management, Portfolio 2 = Enhanced Indexing, Portfolio 3 = Pure Indexing
Portfolio 1 = Enhanced Indexing, Portfolio 2 = Pure Indexing, Portfolio 3 = Active Management

A.text:
Portfolio 1 = Active (largest mismatches: credit spread duration 1.55, EM 14%, turnover 8%). Portfolio 2 = Pure indexing (closest to benchmark: credit spread duration 1.43, EM 9.8%, turnover 5%). Portfolio 3 = Enhanced indexing (modest tilts: credit spread duration 1.50, EM 13%, turnover 6%).

The key's grid, by criterion:

| | P1 | P2 | P3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quality | Enhanced or Active | Pure | Enhanced or Active |
| Duration | Active | Pure or Enhanced | Enhanced or Active |
| Credit spread | Active | Pure | Enhanced |
| Turnover | Active | Pure | Enhanced |
| Country exposure | Active | Pure | Enhanced |
| Securities lending | No impact | No impact | No impact |
| **Determination** | **Active** | **Pure** | **Enhanced** |

B.text: Swaps P2 and P3. Portfolio 2 is the closest to the benchmark (Pure), not Portfolio 3.

C.text: Swaps P1 and P3. Portfolio 1 has the largest mismatches (Active), not Portfolio 3.

questions.keyPrinciple: Rank deviations from the benchmark: smallest = pure indexing, modest = enhanced, largest = active. Securities lending does not decide it.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Fixed-Income Liquidity Comments
questions.context: Moynahan says: liquidity varies greatly across fixed-income securities and is generally lower than for equities; liquidity influences pricing but **illiquidity enhances the portfolio's yield to maturity**; and **dealers will narrow bid–ask spreads** on thinly traded securities because of their illiquidity.
questions.stem: Are Moynahan’s comments regarding fixed-income liquidity most likely correct?

choices.text: No, with respect to the bid–ask spread
No, with respect to fixed-income pricing and yield to maturity

A.text: Not all comments are correct (spread comment is wrong).

B.text: Wrong on the bid–ask spread: dealers **widen** spreads on thinly traded securities to reflect illiquidity.

C.text: The pricing/YTM comment is correct: liquidity influences pricing and illiquidity (the liquidity premium) enhances yield.

questions.keyPrinciple: Less liquid → wider bid–ask spreads, higher liquidity premium and higher yield.

questions.topic: Fixed-income expected return, rolling yield, leverage
questions.title: Roll Down Return Footnote
questions.context: Moynahan's footnote: "The roll down return demonstrates how the price of a bond typically moves closer to par **regardless of yield curve changes** over the strategy horizon." The example is a $100 par bond bought at a premium.
questions.stem: Is the footnote Moynahan includes on page 4 most likely correct?

choices.text: No, with respect to bond prices
No, with respect to roll down return

A.text: The footnote is not correct.

B.text: The statement about bond prices is accurate: as time passes, a bond's price typically moves closer to par.

C.text: Wrong on roll down return: it is the bond's percentage price change **assuming an unchanged yield curve** over the horizon, not regardless of curve changes.

questions.keyPrinciple: Roll down return assumes an unchanged yield curve.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Increasing Exposure of a Fully Invested Portfolio
questions.context: Page 5: the portfolio is fully invested. Given an outlook for a **decline in interest rates**, they want to increase the portfolio's investment exposure. Portfolio and benchmark durations are equal.
questions.stem: What trades can Moynahan most likely make to accomplish the objective outlined on page 5 of his presentation?

choices.text: Enter into a fixed-rate payer swap contract

A.text: Buying long bond futures adds exposure (leverage): futures give exposure to a large quantity of the underlying without transacting in it.

B.text: Selling an overnight repo would not increase the portfolio's exposure (per the key).

C.text: Per the key, entering a fixed-rate payer swap would not increase investment exposure. *(My addition: a fixed-rate payer is short a fixed-rate bond, which is the wrong direction for a view that rates will fall.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Add duration/exposure without cash: long bond futures, or receive-fixed swaps. Payer swaps cut duration.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Taxable Fixed-Income Considerations
questions.context:
Moynahan's key considerations for taxable portfolios:
- **A)** minimize interest income relative to capital gains.
- **B)** minimize capital gains relative to capital losses.
- **C)** forego an attractive trading opportunity because of tax implications.
questions.stem: Which of the considerations outlined by Moynahan on page 6 of the presentation is least likely correct?

A.text: A is a valid consideration: capital gains are typically taxed at a lower effective rate than interest income.

B.text: Least likely correct. The key: capital losses are generally only used to offset capital gains, so one shouldn't aim to minimize gains *relative to* losses.

C.text: Valid too: a taxable investor may dismiss an attractive relative value trade because of its tax implications.

questions.keyPrinciple: Taxable: favor capital gains over interest; defer gains, harvest losses; sometimes skip trades because of tax.
questions.flag: Key's reason for B is brief and the wording of B ('minimize gains relative to losses') is awkward. I follow the key.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Best Addition for Real Risk-Adjusted Returns
questions.stem: A portfolio manager manages a diversified portfolio of equity and fixed-rate bonds. Adding which of the following to the portfolio would best improve the risk-adjusted real returns of the portfolio?

choices.text: Both floating rate bonds and inflation-linked bonds

A.text: Floating-rate bonds adjust the coupon (if at all), not the par value as TIPS-type bonds do.

B.text: Adding **inflation-linked** bonds to a diversified stock/bond portfolio typically improves risk-adjusted real returns: they behave like a separate asset class and add to market completeness.

C.text: Only inflation-linked bonds give the improvement; floaters don't.

questions.keyPrinciple: Inflation-linked bonds protect coupon and principal and improve risk-adjusted real returns; floaters protect coupon only.

questions.topic: Fixed-income expected return, rolling yield, leverage
questions.title: Convexity When Yield Volatility Rises
questions.stem: Which of the following portfolio measures of risk and return is more valuable for bonds with no embedded options when yields become highly volatile?

A.text: Convexity captures the deviation of the yield/price relationship from linear and is more valuable when interest rate volatility is expected to increase (for option-free bonds).

B.text: Spread duration measures sensitivity to credit spread changes.

C.text: Portfolio dispersion measures the variance of cash flow timing around the duration, used in immunization.

questions.keyPrinciple: Higher yield volatility → convexity is worth more.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Factors That Raise the Liquidity Premium
questions.stem: Which of the following factors most likely increases liquidity premium associated with bonds?

choices.text: More acceptability as collateral in the repo market

A.text: Smaller issues are less liquid (and often excluded from major indexes with minimum size rules), so they carry a larger liquidity premium.

B.text: Higher credit quality means *more* liquid, so a lower premium.

C.text: Acceptability as repo collateral means higher liquidity and a lower premium.

questions.keyPrinciple: Liquidity premium ↑: small issue, lower credit quality, long maturity, old issue. ↓: benchmark status, repo collateral.

questions.topic: Liability-based mandates, immunization, duration
questions.title: Active Management With Liability-Based Management
questions.stem: Can active bond portfolio management be combined with a liability-based management?

A.text: Wrong: they can be combined.

B.text: Cash flow matching has no active management; it matches all future liability payouts with bond (or derivative) cash flows.

C.text: **Contingent immunization** combines immunization with active management when assets exceed the PV of liabilities.

questions.keyPrinciple: Contingent immunization = active management while a surplus exists; switch to immunization if the surplus runs out.

questions.topic: Fixed-income expected return, rolling yield, leverage
questions.title: Price Change From Rate Decline
questions.context: Modified duration 5.6, convexity 62; expected yield change −80 bps.
questions.stem: A bond portfolio has a modified duration of 5.6 and a convexity of 62. If the bond portfolio manager expects interest rates to decrease by 80 basis points over the next year, the expected change in the portfolio's value due to the change in interest rates is closest to:

A.text: −4.28% leaves modified duration positive, so falling rates produce a loss: sign error.

C.text: 4.88% omits the ½ in the convexity term (62 × 0.008² = 0.00397).

questions.keyPrinciple: ΔP/P ≈ −MD×Δy + ½×C×(Δy)². Rates down → gain.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Leverage When Rates Are Expected to Fall
questions.stem: A fixed-income portfolio manager believes interest rates will decline and would like to use leverage to increase portfolio returns. The most appropriate action for the portfolio manager is to enter a(n):

choices.text: short futures contract on a treasury note.
interest rate swap as a fixed-rate receiver.
long futures contract on a floating rate bond.

A.text: Shorting T-note futures cuts duration, which helps when rates rise.

B.text: A **fixed-rate receiver** swap is long a fixed-rate bond and short a floating-rate bond. If rates fall, the fixed leg's PV rises and the floating payments fall.

C.text: A long futures contract on a *floating-rate* bond gives floating-rate exposure, which doesn't benefit from falling rates.

questions.keyPrinciple: Expect falling rates → add duration: long bond futures or receive-fixed swap.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Tax-Efficient Fixed-Income Strategy
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most tax efficient strategy when managing a fixed-income portfolio for taxable clients?

choices.text: Realizing capital losses as they occur and deferring gains when possible
Holding all bonds to maturity to avoid realizing capital gains and paying taxes
Realizing more short-term capital gains in the portfolio when investments have a pass-through treatment

A.text: Tax-loss harvesting: realize losses as they occur and defer gains. Deferral lets investors accumulate gains pretax and raises present value.

B.text: Holding to maturity avoids realizing gains but is too restrictive and forgoes realizing losses to offset gains.

C.text: Realizing more short-term gains under pass-through treatment creates more taxes: net realized gains are treated as distributed in the year they arise.

questions.keyPrinciple: Defer gains, realize losses early. Pass-through funds distribute realized gains each year.

questions.topic: Liability-based mandates, immunization, duration
questions.title: Term Life Insurance Liability Type
questions.stem: Which of the following is most accurate about a term life insurance policy?

choices.text: The amount and timing of cash outflows are uncertain
Macaulay duration is the most appropriate measure for interest rate sensitivity
The amount of cash outflows is known and the timing of cash outflows are uncertain

A.text: Wrong: the amount is known; only the timing is uncertain.

B.text: Macaulay duration suits Type I liabilities. For Type II, effective duration is the right measure.

C.text: A term life policy is a **Type II** liability: the amount of the payout is known, the timing is uncertain.

questions.keyPrinciple: Type I: amount and timing known. Type II: amount known, timing uncertain (term life, callable/putable bonds).

questions.topic: Liability-based mandates, immunization, duration
questions.title: Accounting Defeasance
questions.stem: Accounting defeasance is the process of:

choices.text: selling the dedicated asset portfolio to pay off the debt liabilities.
replacing the debt liabilities with equity to improve the company's credit rating.
removing both the dedicated asset portfolio and the debt liabilities from the balance sheet.

A.text: The dedicated portfolio isn't sold; assets are set aside to repay the debt.

B.text: Defeasance doesn't replace debt with equity.

C.text: Accounting (in-substance) defeasance sets aside enough high-quality securities to repay the debt, letting the firm remove both the dedicated assets and the debt from the balance sheet.

questions.keyPrinciple: Accounting defeasance: set aside high-quality securities; remove assets and debt from the balance sheet.

questions.topic: Fixed-income mandates, liquidity, taxes, derivatives
questions.title: Bond Fund vs Direct Bonds
questions.stem: Compared to investing in bonds directly, investing in a fixed-income mutual fund holding the same bonds:

choices.text: results in less diversification of default risk.
facilitates faster redemption at a better price.

A.text: Direct bonds can entail a *higher* cost of acquisition.

B.text: A fund provides *greater* diversification of default risk.

C.text: Fund shares can be redeemed faster than bonds can be sold, and likely at a better price.

questions.keyPrinciple: Bond funds: diversification, liquidity, lower transaction costs, but with fees.

questions.topic: Alternatives: functional roles, classification, expected behavior
questions.title: Alternative That Hedges Inflation and Diversifies Equities
questions.context: SMC pension plan: 60% public equities / 40% bonds, fully funded. **Statement 1:** the committee wants the alternative asset that would best mitigate risks from **unexpected inflation** and also have a **relatively low correlation with public equities**.
questions.stem: Based on Statement 1, Park should recommend:

A.text: Hedge funds are not the inflation hedge here, and the key says commodities have much lower correlation with public equities than hedge funds do.

B.text: Private equity is not an inflation hedge, and the key says commodities have much lower correlation with public equities than private equity does.

C.text: Real assets (energy, infrastructure, timber, commodities, farmland) are generally believed to mitigate unexpected-inflation risk. Commodities hedge a core component of inflation measures and have much lower correlation with public equities than private equity or hedge funds do. They can be held through commodity futures (managed futures).

questions.keyPrinciple: Inflation hedge + low equity correlation → real assets (commodities). PE and hedge funds correlate more with public equities.

questions.topic: Alternatives: functional roles, classification, expected behavior
questions.title: Best Balance of Portfolio With 60% Public Equity
questions.context: Public equity stays at 60%. **Statement 2:** which single asset class for the rest of the portfolio gives the **greatest probability of maintaining the plan's funded status** over a long horizon (target return 5.5%)? Options: bonds, hedge funds, private equities.
questions.stem: In answering the question raised in Statement 2, Park would most likely recommend:

A.text: **Bonds** have the lowest expected return of the three and fill the safety role, not growth. With yields expected to stay low, they are least likely to reach the 5.5% target.

B.text: Hedge funds rank second on expected return, below private equity.

C.text: Expected returns rank private equities > hedge funds > bonds, so private equity gives the highest probability of reaching the return needed to hold funded status. Private equity has a high potential for capital growth; fixed income's strong role is safety.

questions.keyPrinciple: Roles: private equity = capital growth; bonds = safety. Expected return ranking: PE > hedge funds > bonds.

questions.topic: Alternatives: allocation approach (traditional vs risk-based, MVO vs CVaR)
questions.title: Limitation of the Traditional (Regime) Approach
questions.context: The committee has used a **traditional approach** that defines the opportunity set based on distinct macroeconomic regimes. Park proposes a risk-based approach.
questions.stem: A limitation of the existing approach used by the committee to define the opportunity set is that it:

choices.text: is sensitive to the historical look-back period.

A.text: The traditional approach is *easier* to communicate than risk-based approaches (see AL-35).

B.text: The primary limitations of the traditional approach are that it **overestimates portfolio diversification** and obscures the primary drivers of risk.

C.text: Sensitivity to the historical look-back period is a weakness of the **risk-based** approach (see the AL-38 key: factor sensitivities are sensitive to the period examined). *(This is my cross-reference; AL-3's own key doesn't explain C.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Traditional approach: intuitive and easy to communicate, but overestimates diversification and obscures risk drivers. Risk-based: look-back sensitivity, less explanatory power for private assets.

questions.topic: Alternatives: private investment structure, liquidity planning, NAV, monitoring
questions.title: Greatest Risk From the Early Retirement Program
questions.context: Proposed allocation (Exhibit 1): public equities 45%, broad fixed income 25%, private equities 10%, hedge funds 10%, public real estate 10%. SMC will offer an **early retirement incentive program (ERIP)** within two years: eligible employees can retire 10 years early.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1 and the proposed asset allocation, the greatest risk associated with the ERIP is:

A.text: *(My reconstruction.)* The ERIP does pull benefit payments forward, but the key frames the risk as an asset-side liquidity problem from the alternatives.

B.text: *(My reconstruction.)* Nothing in the vignette or Exhibit 1 adds leverage.

C.text: ERIP means the plan will pay benefits earlier than scheduled, so near-term **liquidity** is the main risk from adding private equity, hedge funds and real estate. Private equity can take about five years to reach full commitment and possibly another decade to unwind.

questions.keyPrinciple: Early payouts + illiquid alternatives (PE takes years to deploy and unwind) = liquidity risk.

questions.topic: Alternatives: private investment structure, liquidity planning, NAV, monitoring
questions.title: Suitability Concern — Blind Pool and Reporting
questions.context: Kroll notes alternatives won't offer daily reporting; reports come after monthly/quarter-end deadlines. Park notes that in a typical private equity structure the fund commits capital to a **blind pool**.
questions.stem: The suitability concern discussed by Kroll and Park most likely deals with:

A.text: *(My reconstruction.)* Governance concerns the decision-making and monitoring framework; the blind pool and reporting lag point to transparency.

B.text: A blind pool means capital is committed to a portfolio not specified in advance, and reporting is less transparent than for stocks and bonds: a **transparency** concern.

C.text: *(My reconstruction.)* Nothing described deals with the plan's time horizon.

questions.keyPrinciple: Blind pool + lagged, less detailed reporting = limited transparency.

questions.topic: Alternatives: allocation approach (traditional vs risk-based, MVO vs CVaR)
questions.title: Risk-Factor Approach vs MVO — Park's Statements
questions.context:
- **Statement 3:** risk factor-based approaches to asset allocation produce more robust asset allocation proposals.
- **Statement 4:** a mean–variance optimization typically overallocates to the private alternative asset classes due to stale pricing.
questions.stem: Which of Park’s statements regarding the asset allocation approaches is correct?

A.text: Statement 4 is also correct.

B.text: Statement 3 is also correct (together with Statement 4).

C.text: Both are correct. Risk-factor approaches can produce more robust allocations. MVO tends to overallocate to private alternatives because stale (appraisal) pricing understates risk and returns are assumed normal.

questions.keyPrinciple: MVO overallocates to alternatives (understated risk from smoothing, normality assumed). Risk-factor approaches are more robust.

questions.topic: Alternatives: private investment structure, liquidity planning, NAV, monitoring
questions.title: GP Behavior in a Forecast Bear Market
questions.context: Park notes that the current macro environment could lead to a **bear market within a few years**.
questions.stem: Based on the forecasted environment, liquidity planning should take into account that general partners may:

choices.text: call capital at a slower pace.
make distributions at a faster pace.
exercise an option to extend the life of the fund.

A.text: *(From the AL-36 key.)* In downturns, depressed prices create investment opportunities, so capital calls can **accelerate**, not slow.

B.text: *(From the AL-36 key.)* Mature funds' GPs extend fund life to avoid selling at depressed prices, which *reduces* distributions.

C.text: If public equities and fixed income are expected to perform poorly, general partners may exercise an **option to extend the life of the fund** (rather than sell into depressed prices).

questions.keyPrinciple: Downturn: capital calls can speed up, distributions slow down, fund lives can be extended.

questions.topic: Alternatives: private investment structure, liquidity planning, NAV, monitoring
questions.title: Private Equity Fund Selection With Due Diligence
questions.context: 5-year IRRs: Fund A 12.9%, Fund B 13.2%, Fund C 13.1%. Due diligence: **Fund A** retains administrators, custodians and auditors with impeccable reputations; **Fund B** achieved performance in a way that appears to conflict with its reported philosophy; **Fund C** recently lost three key persons.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2 and Park’s due diligence, the pension committee should consider investing in:

A.text: IRR is comparable across the funds and sensitive to cash-flow timing, so qualitative factors decide. Fund A has a positive factor (reputable service providers); B and C each have a negative.

B.text: Fund B shows **style drift**: returns not consistent with the manager's stated edge.

C.text: Fund C lost three **key persons**, which puts future returns in jeopardy.

questions.keyPrinciple: Monitor PE managers beyond IRR: key person risk, style drift, service providers, alignment, risk management, turnover.

questions.topic: Alternatives: functional roles, classification, expected behavior
questions.title: Diversifying Dominant Equity Risk
questions.context: The Benziger University Endowment is invested primarily in public equities (the rest in fixed income) and wants the asset class that provides the **highest diversification against its dominant equity risk**.
questions.stem: Which asset class would best satisfy the Fund’s diversification strategy?

A.text: Private equity provides only moderate diversification vs public equity. Its primary advantage is capital growth.

B.text: Private real estate provides only moderate diversification; its primary advantage is income generation.

C.text: **Absolute return hedge funds** have the greatest potential to diversify public equity risk: their equity beta is often lower than that of private equity or private real estate.

questions.keyPrinciple: Diversifying public equity: absolute return HF (high) > equity L/S, PE, private RE (moderate).

questions.topic: Alternatives: functional roles, classification, expected behavior
questions.title: Short-Biased Equity Strategies
questions.context:
- **Statement 1:** short-biased equity strategies generally provide alpha when used to diversify public equities.
