questions.keyPrinciple: DB required return: tied to the liability discount rate (market yields); don't double count inflation and salary growth.

questions.topic: Banks, insurers, sovereign wealth funds
questions.title: Missing Bank Investment Objective
questions.context: Pure Mobilebank takes deposits; assets are consumer/small-business variable-rate loans, high-quality debt securities and cash. Exhibit 1 objective: manage assets and liabilities by investing in high-quality debt securities with a longer-term orientation.
questions.stem: Which of the following investment objectives would Chan most likely recommend adding to Exhibit 1?

choices.text: Generate a positive real rate of return above a threshold
Manage liquidity and risk relative to the non-security assets
Outperform a long-term policy benchmark with a specific tracking error budget

A.text: A positive real return above a threshold is an endowment or foundation objective.

B.text: Loans (non-security assets) are the largest bank asset, so a central objective is to manage liquidity and risk relative to the non-security assets.

C.text: Outperforming a policy benchmark with a tracking error budget is a private foundation objective.

questions.keyPrinciple: Bank objective: manage liquidity and risk of the securities portfolio relative to loans and deposits.

questions.topic: Banks, insurers, sovereign wealth funds
questions.title: Institution Similar to Pure's Objective and Risk Tolerance
questions.stem: Li’s description of Pure Mobilebank’s investment objective and risk tolerance in Exhibit 1 could most likely also apply to:

A.text: An endowment doesn't manage liabilities in this way, and a bank's external regulatory constraints don't apply.

B.text: A private foundation doesn't manage liabilities in this way either.

C.text: Managing both assets and liabilities with high-quality debt and a liability-driven investment strategy also applies to a **DB plan**.

questions.keyPrinciple: LDI objective: DB plans, insurers, banks. Endowments/foundations: asset-only.

questions.topic: Banks, insurers, sovereign wealth funds
questions.title: Bank Constraint Not Applicable to a Life Insurer
questions.context: Pure's external constraints: **I.** reporting and transparency requirements; **II.** investing in higher-quality, liquid securities to meet net stable funding ratios; **III.** balance sheet comprehensive income accounts mandated by statutory accounting rules.
questions.stem: Which of Pure Mobilebank’s external constraints would least likely apply to the portfolio of a life insurance company?

A.text: Both banks and life insurers have reporting and transparency requirements.

B.text: Net stable funding ratios are a liquidity requirement for **banks**, not life insurers.

C.text: Both are subject to versions of statutory accounting.

questions.keyPrinciple: NSFR/LCR-type liquidity ratios → banks. Statutory accounting and reporting → insurers and banks.

questions.topic: Banks, insurers, sovereign wealth funds
questions.title: Rising Rates and Non-Interest-Bearing Checking Deposits
questions.context: Pure funds variable-rate loans mainly with **non-interest-bearing checking deposits**; it makes little use of wholesale funding. Its checking clients are insensitive to interest rate changes (and stay at Pure).
questions.stem: Assuming a rising interest rate environment, what would most likely be the impact on Pure’s balance sheet from the behavior of Pure’s checking account clients?

choices.text: A decrease in the value of the assets
An increase in the value of residual equity

A.text: Stable deposits mean no increase in liabilities.

B.text: Per the key, stable deposits don't cause a decrease in asset value. *(My caution: a bank's fixed-rate securities can lose value when rates rise; the key frames the question around the effect of deposit behavior.)*

C.text: Loans reset at higher rates, while the cost of funds (stable, non-interest-bearing checking) stays flat. Margins widen, so residual equity increases.

questions.keyPrinciple: Rate-insensitive, non-interest-bearing funding + floating-rate loans → asset-sensitive bank; margins and equity rise as rates rise.
questions.flag: The key's explanation for B is thin; I follow its framing.

questions.topic: DB pension plans
questions.title: Least Significant Risk in the Deferred Compensation Plan
questions.context: Non-qualified deferred compensation plan mimicking a DB plan: annual credit as a % of compensation plus a fixed 4% interest credit; vests gradually over years 3–6; forfeited benefits reduce future contributions; trust portfolio entirely fixed income; about 20% of staff leave in the first four years; average tenure 5.5 years.
questions.stem: Based on Li’s description of the deferred compensation plan, which of the following risks should she least likely consider significant?

choices.text: Correlation between the sponsor’s business and plan investments

A.text: Plan design is relevant: forfeitures create excess funding and the design limits runaway accumulated benefits as employees tend to leave after limited tenure.

B.text: Workforce characteristics are relevant: the ability to withdraw vested benefits after separation limits accumulation, and the design motivates staying at least six years.

C.text: Least significant. No apparent correlation between the sponsor (banking) and the plan's fixed-income investments, and Li expressed no concern about it.

questions.keyPrinciple: Check each risk against the facts: here, no sponsor–plan correlation was described.

questions.topic: DB pension plans
questions.title: Why the Deferred Comp Plan Has a Surplus
questions.context: Exhibit 2: market value of plan assets $5,820,300; current value of vested benefits $5,675,000; portfolio effective duration 4.95; current yield 2.95%; annualized return since inception 4.00%. The plan credits a fixed 4% annually; about 20% of staff leave before vesting and their forfeited benefits reduce future contributions.
questions.stem: Based on Li’s description of the deferred compensation plan and the data in Exhibit 2, the funding status of the plan is most likely explained by the difference between the:

choices.text: portfolio’s current yield and the return inception to date.
average employee tenure and the portfolio’s effective duration.
amount of the contributions and the growth rate of the vested benefits.

A.text: The current yield (2.95%) is below the 4% interest credit, and the return since inception (4.00%) only equals the required rate, so these wouldn't produce a surplus.

B.text: A portfolio duration (4.95) shorter than average tenure (5.5 years) wouldn't contribute to a surplus, especially when short-term rates are below long-term rates.

C.text: Assets exceed vested benefits (surplus of $145,300). Contributions made for the 20% of employees who leave before vesting provide excess funding when benefits are forfeited, so the surplus comes from the contributions vs the growth of vested benefits.

questions.keyPrinciple: Surplus source: forfeitures from unvested leavers, not asset returns beating the credit rate.

questions.topic: Institutional investment models (Norway, Endowment, Canada, LDI)
questions.title: Diseconomies of Scale for Large Investors
questions.stem: Large institutional investors are most likely to face dis-economies of scale when:

choices.text: directly purchasing property and private companies.
accessing niche investments that do not generate returns to justify the costs.
faced with multiple regulatory frameworks that frequently vary by jurisdiction and complexity.

A.text: Buying property and private companies directly is a *solution* some large institutions use to overcome diseconomies of scale.

B.text: Very large investors can't use niche strategies (e.g., venture capital) effectively: a small allocation may not justify its costs, and capacity-constrained managers can't absorb much capital.

C.text: Multiple regulatory frameworks add operational complexity; large institutions generally have the resources to handle it, so it isn't a scale diseconomy.

questions.keyPrinciple: Large size → hard to deploy into niche or capacity-constrained strategies.

questions.topic: Institutional investment models (Norway, Endowment, Canada, LDI)
questions.title: Alts + Active + External Managers
questions.stem: An institutional investor that has a large allocation to hedge funds and private investments, a high degree of active management, and reliance on external managers is most consistent with the:

A.text: The Canada model also has a high alternatives allocation but relies more on internally managed assets.

B.text: The Norway model relies on public equities and fixed income, largely passive, with little to no alternatives.

C.text: Large allocation to hedge funds and private investments, high active management, external managers = **endowment model**.

questions.keyPrinciple: Alts-heavy: external → Endowment; internal → Canada.

questions.topic: DB pension plans
questions.title: Fiduciary Duty in DC Plans
questions.stem: Do plan sponsors have a fiduciary responsibility in the case of a defined contribution plan where plan participants make contributions and investment decisions?

choices.text: Yes, to reduce plan participants' longevity risk
Yes, to ensure suitable investment options are offered to plan participants

A.text: Even though participants make the investment decisions, the sponsor still has important fiduciary responsibilities.

B.text: In a DC plan, participants bear the investment and longevity risk, so sponsors don't have a fiduciary duty to reduce longevity risk.

C.text: DC plan sponsors still have fiduciary duties, including overseeing the appropriate investment of plan assets, offering suitable investment options and selecting administrative providers.

questions.keyPrinciple: DC sponsor fiduciary duty: suitable options and providers, not guaranteeing outcomes.

questions.topic: DB pension plans
questions.title: Stakeholders in DB but Not DC Plans
questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely a stakeholder in a corporate defined benefit plan but not a stakeholder in a corporate defined contribution plan?

A.text: The government is a stakeholder in both: taxpayers may need to cover shortfalls (DB) or retirees who outlive savings (DC).

B.text: Participants are stakeholders in both plans (they bear investment and longevity risk in a DC plan).

C.text: Company shareholders are stakeholders in a corporate DB plan: an underfunded plan is a balance sheet liability, contributions reduce net income, and underfunding raises financial risk. A DC plan has no shortfall for the company.

questions.keyPrinciple: Shareholders care about DB plans because funded status hits the balance sheet and earnings.

questions.topic: DB pension plans
questions.title: What Raises the DB Obligation
questions.stem: An increase in which of the following will most likely increase the defined benefit pension obligation?

A.text: A higher discount rate lowers the PV of the liability.

B.text: Longer life expectancy lengthens the expected payment period, raising the obligation (longevity risk).

C.text: Higher turnover reduces expected vesting, which reduces the obligation.

questions.keyPrinciple: Obligation ↑: longer life expectancy, lower discount rate, lower turnover. Obligation ↓: higher discount rate, higher turnover.

questions.topic: DB pension plans
questions.title: What Raises DB Plan Liquidity Needs
questions.stem: The liquidity needs of a defined benefit pension plan will increase if the:

choices.text: funded status of the plan increases.
plan participants have the ability to switch to a defined contribution plan.

A.text: Liquidity needs rise as the workforce *ages* (nearer to benefit payments), not as it gets younger.

B.text: A higher funded status reduces the need for contributions and increases the assets available to pay benefits; it doesn't raise liquidity needs.

C.text: If participants can switch to a DC plan or withdraw on short notice, the plan must hold more liquid assets to pay out those withdrawals.

questions.keyPrinciple: Liquidity needs ↑: older workforce, ability to switch/withdraw, retiree-heavy plan.
questions.flag: The key's explanation for B is contradictory in places (it first says higher funding may create a need for more liquid balances, then says it reduces needs). The answer (C) is clear.

questions.topic: DB pension plans
questions.title: Older Workforce DB Plan
questions.stem: Compared to a plan with a young workforce, a similar defined benefit pension plan with a much older workforce should:

choices.text: increase allocations to more liquid assets.
increase allocations to higher-returning asset classes.

A.text: An older workforce has *shorter* liability duration, so asset duration should shorten, not extend.

B.text: An older workforce needs liquidity to pay benefits that will come due soon.

C.text: With benefit payments near, the plan should prioritize liquid assets over higher-returning ones.

questions.keyPrinciple: Older workforce → shorter liability duration, more liquidity, lower risk tolerance.

questions.topic: DB pension plans
questions.title: Trend in US Pension Fund Allocations
questions.stem: The trend in strategic allocations of US pension funds in recent years has been to reduce their allocations to public equities and reallocate to:

A.text: Some funds increased fixed income to reduce funded-status volatility, but most of the reallocation went to alternatives.

B.text: Pension funds have mainly moved from public equities into alternatives (and to some extent into bonds).

C.text: There has been no meaningful increase in cash allocations.

questions.keyPrinciple: Pension trend: equities → alternatives (private equity/debt, real assets, hedge funds).

questions.topic: Banks, insurers, sovereign wealth funds
questions.title: Sovereign Wealth Fund With Largest Fixed-Income Share
questions.stem: The fixed-income asset allocation is most likely to be the largest for which type of sovereign wealth fund?

A.text: Savings funds have very long horizons and tilt toward equities and alternatives.

B.text: Pension reserve funds tilt toward equities with large alternatives allocations (real assets, infrastructure, PE, private debt, hedge funds).

C.text: Budget stabilization funds are defensive and dominated by fixed income for stable returns and diversification against cyclically sensitive factors.

questions.keyPrinciple: SWF types: budget stabilization = most fixed income; savings and pension reserve = growth and alts.

questions.topic: Banks, insurers, sovereign wealth funds
questions.title: Modified Duration of a Bank's Equity
questions.context: Equity capital ratio 10%; modified duration of assets 2.0; modified duration of liabilities 1.0. For a 50 bps change in asset yield, liability yield moves 45 bps.
questions.stem:
An analyst gathers the following information about a bank's assets and liabilities:

- **Equity capital ratio for financial assets:** 10%
- **Modified duration of bank assets:** 2.0
- **Modified duration of bank liabilities:** 1.0

The analyst estimates that for a 50bps change in yield, the yield on liabilities is expected to move 45bps. The modified duration of the bank's equity capital is closest to:

A.text: Uses A/E instead of (A/E − 1) for the liabilities: 20 − 10×1×0.9 = 11.0 (not 9.0 or 9.1; see flag).

B.text: 11.1 = 10/(0.45/0.5) — the asset-to-equity ratio divided by the yield-change ratio.

questions.keyPrinciple: Equity duration = (A/E)·D_A − (A/E − 1)·D_L·(Δi/Δy). Liabilities are funded by A − E, i.e., (A/E − 1) × E.
questions.flag: The key's text for A says the calculation gives 9.0, but the choice reads 9.1, and by the key's own formula it would be 20 − 10×0.9 = 11.0. The key's A explanation doesn't match the choice, so I can't reproduce 9.1.

questions.topic: Wealth planning: IPS, goals, risk tolerance
questions.title: Where ESG Preferences Go in the IPS
questions.context:
Cree (45, attorney, EUR300,000 salary, EUR2.5m portfolio, three children) "prefers to have his environmental and social concerns reflected in his investment choices."
Pending IPS sections: investment parameters, investment objectives, duties and responsibilities.
questions.stem: Which of the following investment parameter categories of the IPS is most likely to include Cree’s preference for investments that reflect his environmental and social concerns?

A.text: **Investment parameters.** These contain limitations on how the portfolio can be invested; sustainability preferences go here.

B.text: Investment objectives cover short- and long-term goals.

C.text: Duties and responsibilities cover the wealth manager's role and the IPS review process.

questions.keyPrinciple: IPS parameters: risk tolerance, constraints, asset class and other preferences (incl. ESG). Objectives = goals.

questions.topic: Wealth planning: IPS, goals, risk tolerance
questions.title: Missing Component of Cree's Financial Background
questions.stem: Identify and discuss at least one important missing component of Cree's financial background necessary to preparing the IPS.
questions.modelAnswer:
Two items the key gives:
1. **Tax status** of the portfolio (taxable vs tax-deferred). It drives the after-tax return needed for capital sufficiency analysis.
2. **Pension:** whether his employment provides a pension and the expected income, which is a future income source.
questions.keyPrinciple: Financial background items often missing: tax status of accounts, pension/other income sources.

questions.topic: Wealth planning: IPS, goals, risk tolerance
questions.title: Unplanned Goal
questions.context: Cree's goals: retire in 17 years on EUR200,000/yr; **medical expenses** in retirement (amount not stated); buy an apartment building within three years; fund children's university from year 10; philanthropy; antiques.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would most likely be described as an unplanned goal for Cree?

A.text: **Medical expenses.** Unplanned goals are hard to quantify: the amount, the timing, or both can't be estimated.

B.text: The apartment purchase can be reasonably estimated and has an expected time horizon.

C.text: University expenses can be estimated and have a known time horizon.

questions.keyPrinciple: Planned goal = quantifiable amount and timing. Unplanned goal = amount and/or timing uncertain (medical).

questions.topic: Wealth planning: IPS, goals, risk tolerance
questions.title: Goals Needing Better Quantification
questions.stem: Identify and discuss two areas in which Cree needs to improve goal quantification.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. **Children's university expenses**, which may compete with retirement funding.
2. **Scope of the apartment purchase** (budget and expected rental income, net of maintenance).
questions.keyPrinciple: Quantify the education goal and the apartment purchase to test consistency with retirement.

questions.topic: Wealth planning: IPS, goals, risk tolerance
questions.title: Capital Sufficiency and Goal Prioritization
questions.stem: Discuss how a capital sufficiency analysis may assist Zhao in helping Cree with goal prioritization across his identified goals.
questions.modelAnswer: Capital sufficiency analysis tests whether current and future resources can support the quantified goals (retirement, education, apartment, philanthropy, antiques). If capital is insufficient, Cree can choose which goals to reduce or eliminate and which to protect. If it doesn't support the objectives, the manager works with the client to revise them.
questions.keyPrinciple: Capital sufficiency fails → revise or prioritize goals.

questions.topic: Wealth planning: IPS, goals, risk tolerance
questions.title: Risk Tolerance for the Retirement Goal
questions.stem: Determine Cree's degree of risk tolerance (lower versus higher) with respect to his retirement goal. Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer: **Higher.** Retirement is long-term (17 years); Cree accepts a moderate (10%) drop in retirement spending; and the planned rental property (stable income) supports medical expenses.
questions.keyPrinciple: Long horizon + acceptance of spending shortfall → higher risk tolerance for that goal.

questions.topic: Taxes and after-tax returns
questions.title: Distributions vs Retirement Income Shortfall
questions.context: Patel (60): needs EUR200,000/yr (inflation-adjusted); pension EUR50,000; business income EUR120,000; securities EUR4m (basis EUR1m), yield 2%, taxed at 40% annually.
questions.stem: Determine whether the distributions from Patel's portfolio are expected to be sufficient to cover the expected shortfall between his retirement needs and his anticipated income.
questions.keyPrinciple: After-tax income = yield × (1 − tax) × value; compare with shortfall.

questions.topic: Taxes and after-tax returns
questions.title: Selling Half the Portfolio to Buy the Vacation Home
questions.stem: Determine whether Patel should sell half of his securities portfolio to buy the vacation home.
questions.modelAnswer:
Sale: EUR2.0m sold, basis 0.5m, gain 1.5m, tax 0.3m → EUR1.7m for the home.
After-tax terminal value: FV_AT = MV₀(1+r)^T − t_cg[MV₀(1+r)^T − CB₀], with MV₀ = initial market value or purchase price, CB₀ = tax cost basis, r = pretax appreciation rate, T = holding period, t_cg = capital gains rate.

- Vacation home (8%): 1,700,000(1.08)^10 − 0.20[1,700,000(1.08)^10 − 1,700,000] = **EUR3,276,138**
- Retained securities (6.5%, basis 500k): 2,000,000(1.065)^10 − 0.20[2,000,000(1.065)^10 − 500,000] = **EUR3,103,420**
- Home higher by **EUR172,718** (reproduced).

But selling half cuts annual after-tax distributions from EUR48,000 to EUR24,000, which is **EUR6,000 below** the EUR30,000 shortfall. The comparison also leaves out the home's costs, liquidity, risk and consumption value.
questions.keyPrinciple: Compare after-tax terminal values; then check the income effect of selling.

questions.topic: Taxes and after-tax returns
questions.title: Retirement Income in 10 Years After Inflation
questions.stem: Evaluate Patel's ability to generate his retirement needs in 10 years after accounting for the effects of inflation on his small business income and his securities portfolio value. Assume that Patel does not purchase the vacation house and we are purely looking at the first year of retirement.
questions.modelAnswer:
Real need from portfolio + business = 200,000 − 50,000 (pension is indexed) = 150,000.
Real business income = 120,000/1.05^10 = **73,670**; remainder 76,330.
Portfolio real growth factor: FVIF = [(1 + r(1 − t_x))/(1 + π)]^T with r = 6.5% + 2%×(1 − 0.4) = 7.7%, t_x = 0 (gains deferred), T = 10, π = 5%: (1.077/1.05)^10 = **1.289** → 4,000,000 × 1.289 = ~5,156,000.
Real cash distribution = 1.2% × 5,156,000 ≈ **61,872**.
Shortfall ≈ 76,330 − 61,872 ≈ **EUR14,500** (my unrounded calc gives 14,457).
questions.keyPrinciple: Real value of nominal income = X/(1+π)^T. Pension is indexed; business income isn't.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Appropriate Early-Career Investments for Sili
questions.context: Sili (22): new data science analyst at a start-up. USD96,000 after-tax salary; annual stock options worth USD50,000 in her employer; saves 25% of after-tax salary into a taxable account and maxes out a DC account.
questions.stem: Which of the following investments would be most appropriate for Sili during the beginning years of her career?

choices.text: Lower-risk equity funds and fixed-income funds

A.text: Technology equity funds add to the same risk as her employer; they give little diversification of her compensation risk.

B.text: **Lower-risk equity funds and fixed-income funds.** Her human capital is large and she can take risk, but her options already give an undiversified, riskier position in her employer, and start-up pay is riskier; so she needs diversified equity plus some fixed income.

C.text: Fixed income alone ignores her high human capital and ability to take risk, and would limit equity exposure.

questions.keyPrinciple: Diversify away from employer/industry risk, but a young earner with large human capital can still hold equity.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Roles of Financial Assets and Real Estate
questions.stem: Discuss the expected roles of Sili's financial asset portfolio and her plan to purchase real estate at the age of 30 in terms of the value of her future wealth.
questions.modelAnswer: Her human capital is expected to decline as she progresses in her career. Financial assets and real estate are expected to rise to **offset the decline in human capital** and so protect the value of her total wealth.
questions.keyPrinciple: Over time: human capital ↓, financial capital ↑; total wealth is preserved.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Sili's Assumptions Between Ages 28 and 35
questions.context: At 28: expects ≥USD5m option payoff, financial assets ~USD300,000 (per the vignette). At 35: investable net worth >USD20m; net worth ≥USD100m.
questions.stem: Explain the assumptions that Sili is making regarding the change in her wealth between the ages of 28 and 35.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. One or more start-up ventures she invests in will become very valuable but remain **illiquid** over the seven years; these business interests explain the USD80m gap between net worth and investable net worth.
2. Her financial assets will keep growing strongly to reach USD20m investable.
3. Secondary: real estate equity rises significantly.
questions.keyPrinciple: Net worth − investable net worth = illiquid holdings (here ~USD80m of business interests).
questions.flag: Vignette gives the ≥USD5m payoff and ~USD300,000 of financial assets at 28 but not an exact investable total; 'quadruple' can't be checked.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Sili's Retirement Plan and the Life Cycle
questions.stem: Discuss the implications of Sili's retirement plan with respect to the value of her human capital, financial capital, and total wealth, as well as with respect to the decumulation phase of her economic life cycle.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Human capital:** declines with age, but investing and advisory income may offset big drops; falls more once she scales back.
- **Financial capital:** keeps increasing while she picks winning start-ups.
- **Decumulation:** starts later, when she donates her wealth to endowments; total wealth begins to decline only then.
questions.keyPrinciple: Retirement ≠ decumulation if the portfolio keeps compounding; decumulation starts when she spends or gives wealth away.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Investable Wealth
questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely considered investable wealth for an individual?

choices.text: Checking account used for day-to-day expenses
Savings account representing funds not needed for day-to-day needs
Defined benefit pension plan participation with payments only after reaching age 60

A.text: A checking account for day-to-day expenses is a transactions account, not investable.

B.text: **Savings account** for funds not needed day to day: investable.

C.text: DB pension participation: the individual doesn't make investment decisions until payments begin.

questions.keyPrinciple: Investable wealth = readily available financial assets (excludes transaction accounts, residence, business, DB entitlements).

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Investable Net Worth Calculation
questions.context:
| Item | EUR/USD thousands |
|---|---|
| Checking | 50 |
| Savings | 100 |
| Taxable investment | 200 |
| Tax-advantaged investment | 150 |
| Vehicles | 80 |
| Primary residence | 500 |
| Business assets | 800 |
| Credit card debt (short-term) | 25 |
| Business liabilities | 250 |
questions.stem:
A client reports the following assets and liabilities in thousands:

- **Checking account:** 50
- **Savings account:** 100
- **Taxable investment account:** 200
- **Tax-advantaged investment account:** 150
- **Vehicles:** 80
- **Primary residence:** 500
- **Business assets:** 800
- **Short-term credit card debt:** 25
- **Business liabilities:** 250

The client’s investable net worth in thousands is closest to:

B.text: 975 adds business assets and liabilities (+800 − 250).

C.text: 1,105 also adds checking and vehicles (+50 +80).

questions.keyPrinciple: Investable NW = savings + taxable + tax-advantaged − short-term personal debt. Excludes checking, vehicles, residence, business.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Gini Coefficient
questions.stem: A Gini wealth coefficient of 0.50 most likely indicates that there is:

choices.text: greater inequality compared to a Gini coefficient of 0.35.
less inequality compared to a Gini coefficient of 0.35.

A.text: Perfect equality is 0.

B.text: Greater inequality than a coefficient of 0.35. Range: 0 = perfect equality; 1 = perfect inequality.

C.text: 0.50 is closer to 1, so it shows more, not less, inequality.

questions.keyPrinciple: Gini: 0 equal, 1 unequal.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Longevity Risk and the Life Cycle
questions.stem: Longevity risk is most likely associated with which phase in the wealth life cycle?

A.text: Pre-retirement is early: assets are still accumulating.

B.text: Early retirement has a longer remaining life than later, but the risk of running out is highest later (when assets are depleted).

C.text: **Later retirement.** Longevity risk is the risk of outliving resources; it's greatest when the client is oldest.

questions.keyPrinciple: Longevity risk peaks in later retirement.
questions.flag: The key's explanations for A and B repeat the definition and don't say why; my wording for B is my own reading.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Discount Rate for Human Capital
questions.stem: The estimation of the value of human capital, the future income, is discounted at the:

choices.text: nominal risk-free rate plus a premium for inflation.
nominal risk-free rate plus a premium associated with occupational income volatility.

A.text: Real risk-free rate would be right only for real income.

B.text: The nominal rate already includes an inflation premium.

C.text: **Nominal risk-free rate plus a premium for occupational income volatility.** Future income is in nominal terms.

questions.keyPrinciple: HC = PV of expected future income (survival-adjusted, wage growth) at nominal rf + occupational risk premium.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Human Capital Over Time
questions.stem: The value of human capital tends to:

A.text: Fewer future years of income remain.

B.text: It doesn't stay the same for the same reason.

C.text: Decreases: less remaining income to include as time passes.

questions.keyPrinciple: Human capital falls over time; financial capital rises to compensate.

questions.topic: Taxes and after-tax returns
questions.title: Average Tax Rate
questions.context: Taxable income EUR1,500,000. Schedule: ...over 500k–1m: 150,000 + 40%; over 1m: 400,000 + 50% on the excess.
questions.stem:
Suppose a client has taxable income of EUR1,500,000. Based on the tax rate schedule, what is the client’s average tax rate?

| Taxable income (EUR) | Tax on  column 1 | Percentage on excess over column 1 |  |
|---|---|---|---|
| Over | Up to |  |  |
| 0 | 30,000 | — | 5 |
| 30,000 | 60,000 | 1,500 | 10 |
| 60,000 | 90,000 | 6,000 | 15 |
| 90,000 | 250,000 | 13,500 | 20 |
| 250,000 | 500,000 | 50,000 | 30 |
| 500,000 | 1,000,000 | 150,000 | 40 |
| 1,000,000 |  | 400,000 | 50 |

C.text: 50% is the marginal rate.

questions.keyPrinciple: Average rate = total tax / income; marginal ≠ average.

questions.topic: Taxes and after-tax returns
questions.title: Deferred vs Accrual Taxes
questions.stem: Deferred taxes on income, relative to accrual taxes,

A.text: Deferred taxes **decrease** tax drag.

B.text: Accrual taxes create more drag.

C.text: Accrual tax drag compounds over time.

questions.keyPrinciple: Deferral reduces tax drag; accrual taxation compounds the drag.

questions.topic: Wealth planning: IPS, goals, risk tolerance
questions.title: IPS Parameter Least Likely to Hold ESG Preferences
questions.stem: Which of the following investment parameters categories of an IPS is least likely to include a client’s preferences for investments that reflect his environmental and social concerns?

A.text: **Asset class preferences** are least likely to reflect ESG preferences.

B.text: Other investment preferences may include ESG.

C.text: Constraints may include ESG.

questions.keyPrinciple: ESG: constraints and other preferences, not asset class choice.

questions.topic: Wealth planning: IPS, goals, risk tolerance
questions.title: Parameter Zhong Missed With the Desais
questions.context: Zhong collects Desai info for an IPS but "fails to ask the couple about their volatility preferences." Desais: 40 and 35, two children, combined salary $550,000.
questions.stem: Identify the investment parameter Zhong failed to understand when meeting with the Desais. Describe the two components of this investment parameter.
questions.modelAnswer: **Risk tolerance**, made up of the client's **ability** and **willingness** to withstand portfolio volatility.
questions.keyPrinciple: Risk tolerance = ability (capacity) + willingness.

questions.topic: Taxes and after-tax returns
questions.title: Desais' Average Tax Rate
questions.context: Salary $550,000; real estate income $60,000; liquid investments: $850,000 tax-deferred, $700,000 brokerage; **10% dividend yield** on liquid accounts; interest $15,000. Tax on first $500,000 = $120,000; 35% from $500,000 to $1m.
questions.stem: Calculate the current average tax rate on the Desais' taxable income.
questions.keyPrinciple: Average tax rate = total tax / taxable income; exclude tax-deferred account income.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Silva's Stage in the Wealth Life Cycle
questions.context: Silva: 60-year-old cardiologist, retiring "in the coming months"; after-tax salary $800,000; portfolio $16m.
questions.stem: Determine the current stage of Silva's financial wealth life cycle. (Peak accumulation, Pre-retirement, Early retirement) Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer: **Pre-retirement.** The few years before retirement: maximum career income and the highest point of wealth. She hasn't retired, so she isn't in early retirement (65–75, per the key); peak accumulation is typically 50–60.
questions.keyPrinciple: Stages (key): career development 35–50; peak accumulation 50–60; pre-retirement (few years before retirement); early retirement 65–75.

questions.topic: Taxes and after-tax returns
questions.title: Silva — Are Returns Sufficient?
questions.context: Silva needs $800,000/yr after tax and inflation-adjusted; $16m portfolio; capital gains 8% taxed at 25%; dividends and interest 3% taxed at 35%; inflation 3%.
questions.stem: Determine whether the returns from Silva's portfolio will be sufficient to cover her retirement needs. (Sufficient, Not sufficient) Justify your response.
questions.keyPrinciple: After-tax real return = (1 + Σ after-tax components)/(1 + π) − 1.
questions.flag: Key rounds 4.806% to 4.80%, so $768,000/$32,000 are slightly off the exact $768,932/$31,068; the conclusion is unchanged.

questions.topic: Wealth planning: IPS, goals, risk tolerance
questions.title: Choosing a Rebalancing Strategy for Lemoine
questions.context:
Lemoine (55, retail entrepreneur, $10m portfolio, big drawdown last year) wants rebalancing to mitigate future losses.
- **Rec 1:** time-based rebalancing to reduce drift during significant, sudden market changes.
- **Rec 2:** threshold-based rebalancing during changing market conditions for swift adjustments.
- **Rec 3:** threshold-based rebalancing to define target weights and adjust on a preset frequency.
questions.stem: Which of Habib’s recommendations is most appropriate for Lemoine’s portfolio?

A.text: Time-based follows a preset schedule and doesn't respond to sudden moves between dates.

B.text: **Recommendation 2.** Threshold-based rebalancing reacts when weights deviate from targets by a set percentage, so it suits a portfolio sensitive to sudden shifts.

C.text: Threshold-based rebalancing isn't done on a preset frequency; it's dynamic.

questions.keyPrinciple: Time-based = calendar schedule; threshold-based = deviation triggers, more responsive to volatility.

questions.topic: Taxes and after-tax returns
questions.title: Tax Erosion of Inflation-Adjusted Value
questions.context: $10m; 11% pretax return for 10 years; flat 25% tax annually on all income; inflation 3%.
questions.stem: Over the next 10 years, taxes are expected to erode the inflation-adjusted value of Lemoine’s portfolio by an amount closest to:

C.text: $11.96m mixes nominal no-tax FV (28,394,209) with real after-tax FV: 28,394,209 − 16,440,188 = 11,954,021.

questions.keyPrinciple: Erosion = real FV (no tax) − real FV (after tax); keep inflation in both.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Campbell's Life Cycle Stage
questions.context: Campbell: senior executive, married, two children, $5m taxable portfolio; retires at 65 in 15 years (so she is 50); plans to start her own manufacturing facility.
questions.stem: Campbell’s financial wealth life cycle stage is most likely:

A.text: Pre-retirement is the few years before 65; she's 15 years away.

B.text: Peak accumulation is not yet reached: she still has significant human capital and is starting a new business.

C.text: **Career development** (ages ~35–50): upward mobility, income growth, human capital still a large share of wealth.

questions.keyPrinciple: Career development: 35–50. Peak accumulation: 50–60.
questions.flag: The key places a person 15 years from a retirement at 65 in career development (age 50). That sits on the boundary with peak accumulation (50–60) in the key's own age ranges; I can only follow the key's reasoning.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Human Capital Definition
questions.stem: Human capital is best described as the:

choices.text: sum of an individual’s personal property and productive wealth.
expected present value of an individual's future income streams.
value of an individual's financial and real assets that are readily available for investment.

A.text: Describes aggregate wealth components (personal property, productive wealth).

B.text: PV of future income streams (survival-adjusted, wage growth, discounted at a rate reflecting occupational income risk).

C.text: Describes investable wealth.

questions.keyPrinciple: Human capital = PV of expected future earnings.

questions.topic: Life cycle, human capital, balance sheet
questions.title: Economic Balance Sheet Statements
questions.context:
Two individuals with the same total assets and surplus. Individual 1 has more short- and long-term debt than Individual 2.
- **Statement 1:** the sum of bequests and PV of future consumption is lower for Individual 1.
- **Statement 2:** human capital is the same for both because it equals the surplus.
questions.stem:
The following relates to two individuals having the same amount of total assets and surplus in their economic balance sheet:

- **Statement 1:** The sum of bequests and the present value of future consumption is lower for Individual 1.
- **Statement 2:** Human capital is the same for both individuals as it is equal to the surplus in the balance sheet.

If Individual 1 has more short term and long term debt than Individual 2, which of the following is accurate?

A.text: **Statement 1 only.** Liabilities = debt + bequests + PV of consumption + surplus. Equal assets and equal surplus with more debt means lower bequests + consumption for Individual 1.

B.text: Surplus isn't human capital: it is total assets (including human capital) minus liabilities.

C.text: Statement 2 is wrong.

questions.keyPrinciple: Economic balance sheet: assets (financial + human capital) = liabilities (debt, consumption, bequests) + surplus.

questions.topic: Taxes and after-tax returns
questions.title: After-Tax Real Return
questions.context: 6% nominal; marginal tax 30%; inflation 2%.
questions.stem: An investment has 6% nominal annual return. If the investor's marginal tax rate is 30% and the annual inflation is 2%, the annual after-tax real return is closest to:

B.text: 3.9% = pretax real return, 1.06/1.02 − 1 (reproduced 3.92%).

C.text: 4.2% is after-tax nominal.

questions.keyPrinciple: After-tax real = (1 + r(1 − t))/(1 + π) − 1.
questions.flag: The key's text for B says '2.9% is the before-tax real return'; the calculation it shows gives 3.9%, so '2.9%' is a typo.

questions.topic: Taxes and after-tax returns
questions.title: Tax Drag
questions.context: 6% nominal, 30 years, taxed annually at 15%; initial $200,000.
questions.stem: An investor earns a nominal return of 6% on investments over a 30-year horizon and returns are taxed annually at 15%. If her initial investment was $200,000, the tax drag at the end of her investment horizon is closest to:

A.text: 22.6% divides the reduction by the untaxed ending value (1,148,698): 22.57%.

B.text: **27.3%.** FV untaxed = 200,000 × 1.06^30 = 1,148,698; FV taxed = 200,000 × (1 + 0.06 × 0.85)^30 = 889,429; reduction 259,269 per my calc (the key prints 259,698); divided by untaxed gain 948,698 → **27.3%** (I reproduced 27.33%).

C.text: 29.2% divides the reduction by the taxed ending value (889,429): 29.15%.

questions.keyPrinciple: Tax drag = (untaxed FV − taxed FV) / (untaxed FV − initial investment).
questions.flag: Key's reduction figure of $259,698 doesn't match its own FVs (1,148,698 − 889,429 = 259,269); typo in the key, the percentages still reproduce.

questions.topic: Wealth planning: IPS, goals, risk tolerance
questions.title: Different Risk Levels for Different Goals
questions.context: An investor accepts higher risk to buy a vacation home but not for retirement savings.
questions.stem: An investor is willing to invest in a higher risk portfolio to achieve the goal of purchasing a vacation home but not to achieve the retirement savings goal. This scenario best illustrates a varying:

A.text: Risk capacity is the ability to bear risk; the scenario gives no information on that.

B.text: **Risk tolerance** varies by goal.

C.text: Risk perception is the subjective assessment of risk; the scenario describes different tolerances, not perceptions.

questions.keyPrinciple: Risk tolerance can differ across goals; capacity is objective; perception is subjective.

questions.topic: Wealth planning: IPS, goals, risk tolerance
questions.title: Primary vs Secondary Objectives
questions.context: Goal 1: retire in 25 years with at least $5m in the fund. Goal 2: donate to a favorite charity after her lifetime. Long-term view.
questions.stem:
The client of a private wealth manager has the following financial goals:

- **Goal 1:** Retire in 25 years’ time with at least $5 million in her investment fund
- **Goal 2:** Donate to her favorite charitable organization after her lifetime

The client has a long-term view of all investment-related decisions. Which of the following best describes the client’s investment objectives in an IPS?

choices.text: Goal 1 is a primary objective and Goal 2 is a secondary objective
Goal 2 is a primary objective and Goal 1 is a secondary objective

A.text: Both can't be primary.

B.text: Goal 1 is primary (quantified with a time horizon); Goal 2 is secondary.

C.text: Goal 2 is unquantified and not time-specific, so not primary.

questions.keyPrinciple: Primary objective = quantified, time-specific, needed; secondary = remaining.
questions.flag: The key's reasoning for A ('both goals cannot be primary') is thin.

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: Inside Bid–Ask Spread
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, the inside bid–ask spread for the limit order book for Light Systems is closest to:

A.text: **$0.04.** Inside spread = lowest ask − highest bid = 17.19 − 17.15.

B.text: *(My reconstruction; the key doesn't explain.)* $0.07 = 17.22 − 17.15, which mixes the highest ask with the best bid.

C.text: *(My reconstruction.)* $0.10 = 17.22 − 17.12, the widest quoted spread (the outermost bid and ask), not the inside.

questions.keyPrinciple: Inside spread = best ask − best bid across all dealers.

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: Proceeds from a Market Sell Order
questions.context: Same book as TR-1. SAMN sells 1,100 shares at market.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, the total amount that SAMN will receive, on a per share basis, for executing the market sell order is closest to:

A.text: *(My reconstruction.)* $17.14 is only the second bid price.

B.text: Sell into bids: 900 at $17.15 (Dealer B), then 200 at $17.14 (Dealer C). Average = (900 × 17.15 + 200 × 17.14)/1,100 = **$17.1482 ≈ $17.15** (reproduced).

C.text: *(My reconstruction.)* $17.22 is the highest ask; a seller receives bids, not asks.

questions.keyPrinciple: Market sell order walks down the bid side of the book.

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: Market Impact of Trade 2
questions.context: Buy order for 5,000 shares in three trades. Trade 1: 9:45, $25.20, 1,200 sh, bid 25.17/ask 25.20. Trade 2: 9:55, $25.22, 1,300 sh, bid 25.19/ask 25.22. Trade 3: 11:30, $25.27, 2,500 sh, bid 25.22/ask 25.26.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the market impact relating to Trade 2, on a per share basis, is closest to:

A.text: **$0.02.** Trade 1 executed at $25.20; Trade 2 executed at $25.22: price impact = $0.02 per share.

B.text: *(My reconstruction.)* $0.03 = Trade 2 price − its bid (25.22 − 25.19).

C.text: *(My reconstruction.)* $0.07 = Trade 3 price − Trade 1 price (cumulative, not Trade 2's).

questions.keyPrinciple: Market impact = change in price caused by the previous trades (here, Trade 2 price − Trade 1 price).

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: Average Effective Spread — Buy Trades
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the average effective spread of the three trades is closest to:

A.text: *(My reconstruction.)* $0.0333 = average **quoted** spread: (0.03 + 0.03 + 0.04)/3.

B.text: *(My reconstruction.)* $0.0367 = average (trade price − bid), without doubling and not using the midpoint.

C.text: **$0.0400.** Effective spread (buy) = 2 × (trade price − midpoint). T1 = 0.03; T2 = 0.03; T3 = 2 × (25.27 − 25.24) = 0.06. Average = 0.12/3 = **0.04** (reproduced).

questions.keyPrinciple: Effective spread = 2 × |trade price − midpoint| (buy: trade − mid; sell: mid − trade). Average across trades.

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: Why SAMN Had to Adapt
questions.stem: The reason for SAMN having to adapt its trading strategies is a result of:

A.text: Latency is the delay in communication or decision.

B.text: **Market fragmentation.** Trading in an instrument is spread across many venues, so each exchange has only a small share of liquidity; large trades need to be adapted to avoid market impact.

C.text: High frequency trading isn't what Johnson describes as the cause.

questions.keyPrinciple: Fragmentation → liquidity split across venues → aggregation and smart order routing.

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: Statements on Electronic Markets
questions.context:
- **1:** once built, electronic systems are more efficient and cheaper to operate than floor-based.
- **2:** electronic trading attracted many new buy-side traders and the increased competition narrowed spreads.
- **3:** electronic markets had a much greater impact on corporate and municipal bonds than on equities.
questions.stem: Which of Martin’s statements relating to the introduction of electronic markets is correct?

A.text: **Statement 1 is correct.** Less physical space; no exchange officials to record prices; lower costs for buy-side, dealers and arbitrageurs.

B.text: The key attributes narrower spreads to competition among **dealers and arbitrageurs** passing on cost savings, not to new buy-side traders.

C.text: Impact has been much greater on equities; bond markets still trade largely over the counter.

questions.keyPrinciple: Electronic trading: cheaper, narrower spreads from dealer competition; bigger effect on equities than bonds.

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: Increasing SAMN's Communication Speed
questions.stem: Which of the following changes should SAMN make to address its key priority?

choices.text: Upgrade to more complex operating systems
Move the trading desk physically closer to the exchanges it works with

A.text: SAMN already has a large, experienced team.

B.text: More complex operating systems don't address distance.

C.text: **Move the desk closer to the exchanges** (collocation where exchanges allow servers in their rooms). Shorter distance = faster communication.

questions.keyPrinciple: Speed = fast communication (distance, collocation) + fast computation.

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: When Machine Learning Models Work Best
questions.stem: The model that Martin is tasked with designing will likely be most effective:

choices.text: during periods of higher than normal market volatility.

A.text: New markets have little history to learn from.

B.text: **Well-understood market environment.** Problems that repeat regularly and often suit ML.

C.text: Volatility episodes are rare with few precedents; ML often fails and traders shut systems down.

questions.keyPrinciple: ML works with abundant repeated data; it fails in unusual/high-volatility regimes.

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: Limiting Systemic Risk From an Algorithm
questions.stem: Which of Martin’s suggestions will most likely be effective in limiting the systemic risk introduced by his algorithm?

A.text: Suggestion 2 is also effective.

B.text: Suggestion 1 is also effective.

C.text: **Both.** Extensive pre-launch testing reduces programming-error risk; mandatory trading halts on large price moves limit undesired results.

questions.keyPrinciple: Systemic-risk controls: testing, access/review controls, halts/circuit breakers, broker surveillance.

questions.topic: Manipulation and high-frequency strategies
questions.title: Manipulation Targeted by News Validation
questions.stem: Which market manipulation strategy is most likely the target of the new rule suggested by Martin?

A.text: **Rumormongering:** disseminating false information about values or other traders' intentions. Validating news before trading helps.

B.text: Gunning the market: buying/selling quickly to trigger stops.

C.text: Trading for market impact: trading to deliberately move prices.

questions.keyPrinciple: Rumormongering = false information; validate news before acting.

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: Comments on Fragmentation
questions.context:
- **Comment 1:** liquidity aggregation and smart order routing help traders manage fragmentation.
- **Comment 2:** traders filling large orders search for liquidity across venues and across time to control market impact.
questions.stem: Which of Riley’s comments related to market fragmentation is accurate?

A.text: Comment 2 is also correct.

B.text: Comment 1 is also correct.

C.text: **Both are correct.** Liquidity aggregators build 'super books' across venues; smart order routers send orders to venues with the best quoted prices and sizes; large-order traders search across venues and time.

questions.keyPrinciple: Fragmentation tools: aggregators, smart order routing, spreading orders across venues and time.

questions.topic: Manipulation and high-frequency strategies
questions.title: Bloomfield's BYYP Strategy
questions.context: 500-share BYYP trades every 20 minutes for an hour, same pattern the previous day. Bloomfield buys ahead on the assumption that a trader is filling a large buy order in pieces.
questions.stem: Bloomfield’s strategy to purchase BYYP shares is best classified as electronic:

A.text: Arbitrageurs trade across markets: buy the undervalued, sell the similar overvalued.

B.text: **Electronic front running.** Order anticipation: identify predictable order patterns and trade ahead of liquidity *demanders*.

C.text: Quote matchers trade ahead of liquidity *suppliers* (standing orders).

questions.keyPrinciple: Front running → ahead of liquidity demanders. Quote matching → ahead of liquidity suppliers (standing orders).

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: Average Effective Spread — BYYP
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, the average effective spread of the BYYP trades is closest to:

A.text: *(My reconstruction.)* $0.018 ≈ half of the correct answer (0.0175): it forgets the factor of 2.

B.text: **$0.035.** Effective spread = 2 × (trade price − midpoint of market at time of order entry). T1 = 2 × (41.50 − 41.475) = 0.05; T2 = 2 × (41.75 − 41.74) = 0.02; average **0.035**.

C.text: *(My reconstruction.)* $0.070 = sum of the two effective spreads (0.05 + 0.02), not averaged.

questions.keyPrinciple: Average the per-trade effective spreads; don't sum.

questions.topic: Manipulation and high-frequency strategies
questions.title: Bloomfield's AXZ Strategy
questions.context: AXZ: narrow bid–ask spread, high volatility. Bloomfield buys using a strategy that does not include standing orders.
questions.stem: Bloomfield’s trading strategy for the purchase of AXZ shares most likely includes the use of:

A.text: **Flickering quotes:** exposed limit orders submitted and cancelled quickly (often within a second); the trader doesn't want the order to stand.

B.text: ML isn't suited to a high-volatility period.

C.text: Leapfrogging is used when spreads are **wide**; AXZ's spread is narrow.

questions.keyPrinciple: Flickering quotes: show, then cancel. Leapfrogging: improve quotes when spreads are wide.

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: Structural Change Consistent With Bloomfield's Claim
questions.stem: Which structural change for the market associated with electronic trading systems is most consistent with Bloomfield’s claim?

choices.text: Delaying order processing by random intervals
Exchanges using trade halts when prices move too quickly
Slowing markets by running call markets once a second or more often instead of trading continuously

A.text: Random processing delays reduce the speed advantage.

B.text: **Trade halts** when prices move too quickly: reduce systemic risk while 2Fast stays faster than rivals once trading resumes.

C.text: Frequent call markets slow trading and reduce the speed advantage.

questions.keyPrinciple: Halts keep speed advantage; random delays and call markets remove it.

questions.topic: Manipulation and high-frequency strategies
questions.title: Competitor's Manipulation Strategy
questions.context: Competitor buys stock to raise its price, encouraging momentum traders to buy, then sells to them at higher prices. No standing limit orders and no commonly controlled accounts were used.
questions.stem: The competitor company’s trading is best described as:

A.text: **Bluffing:** submitting orders and arranging trades to influence perceptions of value; preys on momentum traders.

B.text: Spoofing uses exposed standing limit orders, which regulators confirmed weren't used.

C.text: Wash trading uses commonly controlled accounts, also ruled out.

questions.keyPrinciple: Bluffing: momentum traders. Spoofing: exposed standing orders. Wash trading: commonly controlled accounts.

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: VWAP Transaction Cost Estimate — ABC
questions.stem: Calculate the volume-weighted average price (VWAP) transaction cost estimate for the ABC shares sold by MMM.
questions.keyPrinciple: VWAP cost estimate (sell) = (day VWAP − own VWAP) × shares.
questions.flag: Key's $3,930 uses VWAPs rounded to 4 decimals; unrounded is $3,931.58.

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: Average Effective Spread — MMM's Sells
questions.stem: Calculate the average effective spread of MMM's three ABC trades.
questions.keyPrinciple: Effective spread: buy = 2(price − mid); sell = 2(mid − price).

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: Incorrect Statement About Costs
questions.stem:
Determine which statement made by Anosov is most likely incorrect. (Statement 1, Statement 2) Justify your response.

1: The effective spread is a poor estimate of actual transaction costs when small orders receive price improvement.
2: Implementation shortfall compares the actual portfolio with a paper portfolio assuming trades at VWAP.
questions.modelAnswer: **Statement 2** is incorrect. Implementation shortfall compares the actual portfolio with a paper portfolio at the **decision (arrival) price**, usually the midquote at the time of the decision, not VWAP. Statement 1 is correct.
questions.keyPrinciple: IS benchmark = decision price (arrival/strike). VWAP is a separate benchmark.

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: Davis's Alternatives for Selling the MDS Stake
questions.stem: Which of Davis’s alternatives would most likely be appropriate for selling the stake in MDS?

A.text: Alternative 2 is also appropriate.

B.text: Alternative 1 is also appropriate.

C.text: **Both.** Searching across venues and time controls market impact; smart order routing sends orders to the best displayed prices and sizes.

questions.keyPrinciple: Fragmentation responses: search across venues and time; smart order routing; liquidity aggregation.

questions.topic: Manipulation and high-frequency strategies
questions.title: Wong's Strategy
questions.context: Wong: place hidden MDS sell orders, then place exposed standing limit buy orders to suggest prices may rise; after others buy into the sells, cancel the buy orders.
questions.stem: The trading strategy suggested by Wong is best described as:

A.text: **Layering (spoofing):** exposed standing limit orders create a false impression of demand while a hidden order on the other side executes.

B.text: Rumormongering spreads false information.

C.text: Gunning the market: buying/selling quickly to trigger stop orders. Wong doesn't want his buy orders to execute.

questions.keyPrinciple: Spoofing = layering: exposed fake orders + hidden real order on the opposite side.

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: Average Effective Spread — TECH
questions.stem: The average effective spread for the TECH shares sold by Creative is closest to:

A.text: $0.0940 omits the factor of 2.

C.text: $0.9400 is the sum; it must be divided by five.

questions.keyPrinciple: Average effective spread = mean of the per-trade 2×|mid − price|.

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: VWAP Transaction Cost Estimate — TECH
questions.stem: The volume-weighted average price (VWAP) transaction cost estimate for the TECH shares sold by Creative is closest to:

B.text: $71,500: I can't reproduce this figure from the data.

C.text: $188,000 = the average effective spread (0.188) × 1,000,000 shares: wrong measure (I reproduced this).

questions.keyPrinciple: VWAP cost = (day VWAP − own VWAP) × shares (sell); day VWAP includes others' trades.
questions.flag: Key's $44,600 is rounded (unrounded $44,633). Choice B ($71,500) can't be reproduced; the key doesn't explain it.

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: Inside Spread
questions.stem:
A trader observes the following limit order book for a company’s stock:

| Bid | Ask |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dealer | Time Entered | Price | Size | Dealer | Time Entered | Price | Size |
| A | 11.15 am | $50.38 | 700 | C | 11.15 am | $51.35 | 300 |
| B | 11.15 am | $50.36 | 600 | A | 11.15 am | $51.38 | 900 |
| C | 11.10 am | $50.34 | 800 | B | 11.10 am | $51.42 | 650 |

The inside spread is:

choices.text: the average of all the dealers' spread.
the lowest spread among the three dealers.
narrower than at least one individual dealer's spread.

A.text: The inside spread isn't the average of dealer spreads.

B.text: The inside spread isn't the lowest dealer spread; it is the spread between the best bid and best ask in the market.

C.text: **Narrower than at least one dealer's spread.** The inside spread (best ask − best bid = 51.35 − 50.38 = 0.97) is narrower than a dealer's own spread if the best bid and best ask come from different dealers.

questions.keyPrinciple: Inside spread = best ask − best bid; ≤ every dealer's own spread.

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: Effective Spread as a Cost Estimate
questions.context: Fund sells 4,000 shares at market; quote $25.27–$25.41; the whole order fills at $25.27.
questions.stem: A mutual fund enters a market sell order for 4,000 shares when the prevailing bid–ask spread is $25.27–$25.41. The entire order fills at the bid price of $25.27. Is the effective spread a reasonable estimate of transaction costs?

A.text: **Yes.** No price improvement and no price impact beyond the quote, so the effective spread represents the cost.

B.text: No delay costs: the order filled at the bid.

C.text: No market impact: the whole order traded at the quoted bid.

questions.keyPrinciple: Effective spread misleads when orders get price improvement or are split/delayed.

questions.topic: Trading costs, spreads, VWAP, implementation shortfall
questions.title: What Implementation Shortfall Captures
questions.stem: Implementation shortfall measures the cost of implementing an investment decision by capturing a trade's:

choices.text: both explicit costs and implicit costs.

A.text: It also includes implicit costs (opportunity cost).

B.text: It also includes explicit costs. *(The key's text calls market impact and delay costs 'explicit', which is a mistake; I have not corrected the answer.)*

C.text: **Both explicit and implicit costs:** it includes market impact and delay costs plus opportunity costs.

questions.keyPrinciple: IS = explicit (commissions, fees) + implicit (impact, delay, opportunity costs).
questions.flag: The key's text for A/B mislabels market impact and delay costs as 'explicit'; they are implicit costs. Answer C is unaffected.

questions.topic: Manipulation and high-frequency strategies
questions.title: Quote Matcher's Main Risk
questions.context: A slow trader bids $40; a fast quote matcher buys, expecting the price to rise.
questions.stem: A slow trader is bidding on a stock at $40. A fast quote matcher buys the stock, expecting the price to rise. The main risk for the fast quote matcher is that:

choices.text: standing buy orders may be unavailable.
many standing sell orders may be available.
standing sell orders they are leaning on may be canceled.

A.text: **Standing buy orders may be unavailable.** The matcher relies on standing bids to exit; they vanish when filled or cancelled.

B.text: If prices move against them, matchers exit by trading with standing orders, so the loss is limited to exit costs; many standing sell orders isn't the main risk.

C.text: The matcher who bought (long) leans on standing **buy** orders to get out, not sell orders.

questions.keyPrinciple: Quote matcher long → relies on standing bids to exit; risk = bids disappear.

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: Trading Tactic Definition
questions.stem: A trading tactic can best be described as a(n):

choices.text: algorithmic approach to filling large orders while minimizing price impact.
strategy involving the submission of multiple orders to execute a specific function.
plan to maintain a bid or an offer at a specified distance relative to some benchmark.

A.text: This describes an **algorithm**.

B.text: A tactic is a plan for executing a simple function, generally by submitting multiple orders.

C.text: This describes an **advanced order** (e.g., pegged limit order).

questions.keyPrinciple: Order → advanced order → tactic → algorithm (increasing complexity).

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: Minimizing Decision Latency
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most effective technique used by electronic traders to minimize decision-making latency?

choices.text: Coding critical functions using high-level, interpreter languages
Deferring complex analyses until after a relevant market event occurs
Generating and storing optimal responses in advance using contingency tables

A.text: Low-latency traders avoid interpreted languages (e.g., Python) for latency-sensitive code.

B.text: Deferring analysis until after the event adds delay; do it beforehand.

C.text: **Pre-compute optimal responses and store them in contingency tables**, then look them up when the event occurs.

questions.keyPrinciple: Low latency: precompute, avoid interpreted languages, collocate.

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: Accurate Statement on Electronic Trading
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is most accurate? Electronic trading systems:

choices.text: facilitate hidden orders in an efficient manner.
have had a greater impact on bond trading than equity trading.
have resulted in an integration of financial markets and trading across the globe.

A.text: **Electronic systems keep hidden orders hidden**, unlike floor brokers who may reveal them.

B.text: Electronic trading has had more impact on equities than on bonds.

C.text: Markets became more **fragmented**, not integrated, as venues proliferated.

questions.keyPrinciple: Electronic trading → hidden orders work reliably; markets more fragmented; bonds still mostly OTC.

questions.topic: Market structure, electronic trading, fragmentation
questions.title: Mitigating Systemic Risk of Electronic Trading
questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to mitigate the systemic risk problems associated with electronic trading systems?

choices.text: The requirement that all software be read, understood, and vouched for by at least one developer besides its author
Allow brokers' clients to enter orders directly into exchange trading systems to promote market efficiency and liquidity
Allow automatic conversion of limit orders into marketable market orders to ensure that brokers trade at reasonable prices

A.text: **Code review by a second developer** (with access controls on who can change software) is a best practice.

B.text: Brokers must not allow sponsored naked access: they must surveil client orders.

C.text: The option has it backwards: brokers convert **market** orders into **marketable limit** orders to avoid unreasonable prices, not limit orders into market orders.

questions.keyPrinciple: Controls: access control and peer review of code, broker surveillance (no naked access), marketable limit orders, halts.

questions.topic: Manipulation and high-frequency strategies
questions.title: Wash Trading
questions.stem: Trades arranged among commonly controlled accounts to create the impression of market activity at a particular price best describes:

A.text: Spoofing (layering) uses exposed standing limit orders to give a false impression of liquidity or value.

B.text: **Wash trading:** trades among commonly controlled accounts to create an impression of activity at a price.

C.text: Trading for market impact: deliberately trading to move prices.

questions.keyPrinciple: Wash trading = commonly controlled accounts; spoofing = fake exposed orders.

questions.topic: Performance evaluation framework (measurement, attribution, appraisal)
questions.title: Effective Performance Attribution
questions.context:
Jones (senior adviser, Federalist Investors) asks Bragg (junior analyst) to describe an effective attribution process. Bragg's monthly evaluation of a fixed-income manager covers measurement, attribution and appraisal.
- **Response 1:** attribution draws conclusions regarding the quality of a portfolio manager's investment decisions.
- **Response 2:** attribution should help explain how performance was achieved by breaking apart the return or risk into different explanatory components.
questions.stem: Which of Bragg’s responses regarding effective performance attribution is correct?

A.text: Response 1 is wrong: drawing conclusions about the quality of the manager's decisions is **appraisal**, not attribution. *(My reading; the key explains only why B is right.)*

B.text: Attribution explains *how* performance was achieved by breaking return or risk into components. Effective attribution accounts for all return/risk exposure, reflects the investment decision process, quantifies the manager's active decisions and fully explains excess return/risk.

C.text: Response 1 is wrong, so 'both' can't be right.

questions.keyPrinciple: Measurement = what; attribution = how; appraisal = judging the quality of the manager's decisions.

questions.topic: Risk attribution and factor exposures
questions.title: Risk Attribution for a Top-Down Fixed-Income Manager
questions.context: Bragg notes the fixed-income manager has strong views about the effects of macroeconomic factors on credit markets and follows a top-down investment process. The portfolio is managed against a benchmark.
questions.stem: The most appropriate risk attribution approach for the fixed-income manager is to:

choices.text: decompose historical returns into a top-down factor framework.
evaluate the marginal contribution to total risk for each position.
attribute tracking risk to relative allocation and selection decisions.

A.text: Decomposing historical returns into a top-down factor framework is return-based factor attribution, not risk attribution relative to the benchmark. *(My reading; the key doesn't discuss A and B.)*

B.text: Marginal contribution to total risk by position is an absolute-risk, bottom-up measure; the portfolio is managed against a benchmark. *(My reading.)*

C.text: The portfolio is benchmark-relative, so use relative-risk attribution. For a top-down process, attribute **tracking risk** to allocation and selection decisions relative to the benchmark.

questions.keyPrinciple: Benchmarked manager → relative risk (tracking risk) attribution; top-down → allocation and selection decisions.

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Target Semideviation from the Sortino Ratio
questions.context:
**Exhibit 1 — 10-Year Trailing Risk-Adjusted Performance**

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Average annual return | 8.20% |
| Minimum acceptable return (MAR) | 5.00% |
| Sharpe ratio | 0.95 |
| Sortino ratio | 0.87 |
| Upside capture | 0.66 |
| Downside capture | 0.50 |
| Maximum drawdown | −24.00% |
| Drawdown duration | 4 months |
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, the target semideviation for the portfolio is closest to:

A.text: *(My reconstruction.)* 2.78% doesn't come from any simple rearrangement I tried; I can't reproduce it.

B.text: **3.68%.** Target semideviation is the denominator of the Sortino ratio: Sortino = (average return − MAR)/target semideviation, so TSD = (8.20% − 5.00%)/0.87 = **3.678% ≈ 3.68%** (reproduced).

C.text: *(My reconstruction.)* 4.35% doesn't come from any simple rearrangement I tried; I can't reproduce it.

questions.keyPrinciple: Sortino = (R − MAR) / target semideviation. Solve for TSD = (R − MAR)/Sortino.

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Interpreting the Capture Ratios
questions.context: Exhibit 1 (see Q3): upside capture 0.66; downside capture 0.50.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, the capture ratios of the portfolio indicate:

choices.text: that the portfolio generates higher returns than the benchmark during all market conditions.

A.text: A ratio above 1 is convex, not concave.

B.text: **Positive asymmetry.** Capture ratio = upside capture / downside capture = 0.66/0.50 = **1.32**. A ratio above 1 means positive asymmetry (a convex return profile).

C.text: Upside capture of 0.66 means the portfolio captured only 66% of the benchmark's up-market return, so it did not beat the benchmark in all conditions. *(My reading.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Capture ratio = upside capture / downside capture. > 1 → positive asymmetry (convex).

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Maximum Drawdown and Drawdown Duration
questions.context: Exhibit 1 (see Q3): maximum drawdown −24.00%; drawdown duration 4 months; 10-year period.
questions.stem: The maximum drawdown and drawdown duration in Exhibit 1 indicate that:

choices.text: the portfolio recovered quickly from its maximum loss.
over the 10-year period, the average maximum loss was −24.00%.
a significant loss once persisted for four months before the portfolio began to recover.

A.text: Maximum drawdown is the cumulative peak-to-trough loss over a continuous period. Drawdown duration is the total time from the start of the drawdown until the cumulative drawdown recovers to zero (drawdown phase + recovery phase). A 24% maximum loss recovered in a total of four months, within a 10-year window, is a quick recovery.

B.text: Maximum drawdown is the single largest peak-to-trough loss, not an average. *(My reading; the key doesn't discuss B and C.)*

C.text: Four months is the *total* duration from the start of the drawdown to full recovery, not the time before recovery began. *(My reading.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Max drawdown = worst peak-to-trough loss. Drawdown duration = start to full recovery (decline + recovery).

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Attribution Approach Requested by the Committee
questions.context: Tolmach (consultant) uses three approaches to attribution: return-based, holdings-based and transaction-based. The Plan's investment committee asks her to (1) apply the attribution method that uses only each fund's total portfolio returns over the last 12 months to identify the return-generating components of the investment process, and (2) include the impact of specific active decisions and the attribution effects of allocation and security selection.
questions.stem: Of the three attribution approaches referenced by Tolmach, the method requested by the committee:

choices.text: uses the underlying holdings of the actual portfolio.
is the most difficult and time consuming to implement.

A.text: The committee described **return-based** attribution, which is the **least accurate** of the three approaches. It uses only total portfolio returns over a period to identify the components of the investment process that generated returns.

B.text: Using the underlying holdings describes holdings-based attribution. *(My reading from the key's definition of return-based.)*

C.text: Transaction-based attribution is the most demanding to implement; return-based is the simplest. *(My reading; the key doesn't discuss C.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Accuracy/effort: return-based (least) < holdings-based < transaction-based (most).
questions.flag: The committee's request has two parts: (1) returns only, and (2) allocation and selection effects. The key's answer follows part (1).

questions.topic: Risk attribution and factor exposures
questions.title: Fund 1 Style Tilt from the Carhart Exhibit
questions.context:
**Exhibit 1 — Fund 1 Factor Model Attribution**

| Factor* | Portfolio (1) | Benchmark (2) | Difference (3) | Factor return (4) | Absolute (3) × (4) | Proportion of active return |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RMRF | 1.22 | 0.91 | 0.31 | 16.32% | 5.06% | −126.80% |
| SMB | 0.59 | 0.68 | −0.09 | −3.25% | 0.29% | −7.33% |
| HML | −0.17 | 0.04 | −0.21 | −9.60% | 2.02% | −50.53% |
| WML | −0.05 | 0.07 | −0.12 | 3.38% | −0.41% | 10.17% |
| | | | **A. Factor tilt return** | | **6.96%** | **−174.49%** |
| | | | **B. Security selection** | | **−10.95%** | **274.49%** |
| | | | **C. Active return (A + B)** | | **−3.99%** | **100.00%** |

*RMRF = excess market return; SMB = small minus big; HML = high minus low; WML = winners minus losers.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1 and relative to the benchmark, the manager of Fund 1 most likely used a:

A.text: **Growth tilt.** The fund's HML sensitivity is −0.17 vs +0.04 for the benchmark (difference −0.21): negative HML exposure = growth tilt.

B.text: SMB difference is −0.09 (0.59 vs 0.68): a slight tilt toward *larger* caps, not small. *(My reading.)*

C.text: WML difference is −0.12 (−0.05 vs +0.07): a tilt *away* from momentum. *(My reading.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Factor tilt = portfolio sensitivity − benchmark sensitivity. Negative HML = growth; negative SMB = large-cap; negative WML = anti-momentum.

questions.topic: Risk attribution and factor exposures
questions.title: Smallest Contributor to Active Return
questions.context: Fund 1 factor attribution — Exhibit 1 (see Q7).
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, which of the following factors contributed the least to active return?

A.text: HML contributed 2.02%, more than SMB.

B.text: **SMB** contributed the least: 0.29% absolute (7.33% of active return in magnitude) vs HML 2.02% (50.53%) and RMRF 5.06% (126.80%).

C.text: RMRF contributed 5.06%, the most.

questions.keyPrinciple: Contribution = (portfolio − benchmark sensitivity) × factor return.

questions.topic: Risk attribution and factor exposures
questions.title: Factor Weighting That Would Have Added Value
questions.context: Fund 1 factor attribution — Exhibit 1 (see Q7). Factor returns: SMB −3.25%; HML −9.60%; WML +3.38%.
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, the manager could have delivered more value to the portfolio during the investment period by weighting more toward:

A.text: HML (value minus growth) returned −9.60%; more value would have detracted.

B.text: SMB returned −3.25%; more small-cap would have detracted.

C.text: **Momentum stocks.** WML's factor return was +3.38%; more weight there would have contributed positively.

questions.keyPrinciple: Adding exposure to a factor helps only if that factor's return was positive.

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Brinson–Fachler Allocation Effect — South America
questions.context:
**Exhibit 2 — Fund 2 Performance — Allocation by Region**

| Region | Portfolio weight | Benchmark weight | Portfolio return | Benchmark return |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| North America | 10.84% | 7.67% | 16.50% | 16.47% |
| Greater Europe | 38.92% | 42.35% | 23.16% | 25.43% |
| Developed Asia and Australasia | 29.86% | 31.16% | 11.33% | 12.85% |
| South America | 20.38% | 18.82% | 20.00% | 35.26% |
| **Total** | 100.00% | 100.00% | 18.26% | 22.67% |
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the allocation effect for South America is closest to:
