A.text: *(My reconstruction.)* −0.04% doesn't come from the formula; I can't reproduce it.

B.text: *(My reconstruction.)* 0.03% is the **total** allocation effect for the fund (0.0329%), not South America's.

questions.keyPrinciple: Brinson–Fachler allocation = (portfolio weight − benchmark weight) × (segment benchmark return − total benchmark return).

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Region Whose Weighting Decision Helped
questions.context: Exhibit 2 (see Q10).
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the decision to overweight or underweight which of the following regions contributed positively to performance at the overall fund level?

A.text: North America: (10.84% − 7.67%)(16.47% − 22.67%) = **−0.20%** (overweighted a below-average region).

B.text: Greater Europe: (38.92% − 42.35%)(25.43% − 22.67%) = **−0.09%** (underweighted an above-average region).

C.text: **Developed Asia and Australasia.** Underweighting it was good because its benchmark return (12.85%) was below the total benchmark (22.67%). Allocation = (29.86% − 31.16%)(12.85% − 22.67%) = **+0.13%**, the only positive one of the three.

questions.keyPrinciple: Overweight a segment that beat the total benchmark, or underweight one that lagged → positive allocation.

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Source of Fund 2 Underperformance
questions.context:
Exhibit 2 (see Q10). Fund return 18.26% vs benchmark 22.67%.

| Region | Allocation | Selection + interaction | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| North America | −0.1966% | 0.0033% | −0.1934% |
| Greater Europe | −0.0946% | −0.8835% | −0.9781% |
| Developed Asia and Australasia | 0.1277% | −0.4539% | −0.3262% |
| South America | 0.1964% | −3.1100% | −2.9136% |
| **Total** | 0.0329% | −4.4441% | −4.4112% |
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the underperformance at the overall fund level is predominantly the result of poor security selection decisions in:

A.text: **South America.** Of −4.44% from selection + interaction, South America contributed −3.11%: its portfolio return was 20.00% vs 35.26% for the benchmark.

B.text: Greater Europe selection + interaction was −0.88%.

C.text: Developed Asia and Australasia selection + interaction was −0.45%.

questions.keyPrinciple: Selection + interaction = W_i(R_i − B_i) + (w_i − W_i)(R_i − B_i).

questions.topic: Benchmarks and misfit
questions.title: Valid-Benchmark Characteristic Fund 3's Benchmark Has
questions.context: Fund 3 is a domestic fixed-income strategy. Its benchmark is a cap-weighted bond index with **daily reported performance**; the index is **rebalanced frequently, making it difficult to replicate**, and has a meaningful investment in **foreign bonds**, whereas Fund 3 invests only in domestic bonds.
questions.stem: The benchmark for Fund 3 has which of the following characteristics of a valid benchmark?

A.text: Not investable: a frequently rebalanced cap-weighted bond index is hard to replicate. To be investable, the benchmark must be possible to replicate and hold (at least gross of expenses), so the sponsor could move assets from active management to a passive benchmark.

B.text: **Measurable.** Daily performance is reported, so the benchmark's return can be measured frequently and in a timely way.

C.text: Not appropriate: the index holds meaningful foreign bonds but Fund 3 is domestic-only. The benchmark must be consistent with the manager's style or area of expertise.

questions.keyPrinciple: Valid benchmark traits shown here: measurable (frequent returns) (met); investable (not met) (hard to replicate); appropriate (not met) (foreign bonds vs domestic fund).

questions.topic: Benchmarks and misfit
questions.title: Benchmark Type for the Pension Plan
questions.context: Tolmach's review of the Plan: a **defined benefit** plan whose benefits are no longer indexed to inflation; the workforce is, on average, younger than when the current allocations were approved. She recommends a change in the asset allocation policy.
questions.stem: Based on the final section of Tolmach’s report, the Plan should use:

A.text: **Liability-based benchmark.** Given the Plan is a DB plan, a liability-based benchmark fits best: these are used most often when assets must pay a specific future liability.

B.text: The key doesn't discuss B. An absolute-return benchmark doesn't tie to the Plan's liabilities. *(My reading.)*

C.text: The key doesn't discuss C. A manager-universe benchmark compares to peers, not to liabilities. *(My reading.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: DB plan → liability-based benchmark.

questions.topic: Performance evaluation framework (measurement, attribution, appraisal)
questions.title: When Risk Enters Performance Evaluation
questions.context: Autland Quantitative Inc. (AQI) evaluates fund investment vehicles. Timmon interviews Richard. Richard answers that **risk is considered only within performance appraisal**, which determines the quality of a fund manager's performance.
questions.stem: Richard’s answer in regard to risk and performance evaluation is best described as:

choices.text: incorrect in regard to what is assessed through performance appraisal.
incorrect in regard to when risk enters into the performance evaluation process.

A.text: Not correct: risk belongs to all phases of performance evaluation.

B.text: Appraisal does determine the quality of the manager's performance, so he is right about that; he is wrong that risk enters only there.

C.text: Incorrect about **when** risk enters. Risk is part of all three phases: measurement, attribution and appraisal.

questions.keyPrinciple: Risk is part of performance measurement, attribution and appraisal, not only appraisal.

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Residual Term in Holdings-Based Attribution
questions.context: Timmon asks why holdings-based attribution can generate a residual between portfolio and benchmark performance. Richard: the residual **cannot be explained by an action taken by the fund manager**, but could result from **transactions occurring more frequently than the holdings assessments**.
questions.stem: Richard’s answer with respect to holdings-based attribution is best described as:

choices.text: incorrect in regard to the fund manager’s action affecting the residual term.
incorrect in regard to the frequency of measuring holdings relative to transactions.

A.text: Correct. The residual isn't caused by manager actions; it arises when holdings are measured less often than transactions occur (the trading effect).

B.text: The residual cannot be explained by the manager's actions, so Richard was right on that point.

C.text: He was right: the residual can come from measuring holdings less frequently than the fund trades.

questions.keyPrinciple: Holdings-based residual (trading effect) = transactions between holding snapshots.

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Brinson Model With Interaction Term
questions.context:
Timmon: AQI uses the Brinson model with an interaction term, and asks how it incorporates fund manager sector weights and benchmark sector weights.

Notation: w_i = manager's sector weight; W_i = benchmark sector weight; R_i = fund sector return; B_i = benchmark sector return.
questions.stem: The best answer to Timmon’squestion in regard to AQI’s use of the Brinson model is that the:

choices.text: fund manager’s sector weights are incorporated into the selection effect.
fund sponsor’s allocation of capital will affect the fund manager’s sector weights, which influence the results of the model.
differences between the fund manager’s and the benchmark’s sector weights are incorporated into the allocation effect and the interaction term.

A.text: The selection effect uses only the benchmark's sector weights: S_i = W_i × (R_i − B_i).

B.text: The fund sponsor's allocation of capital doesn't affect the manager's allocation of capital.

C.text: Differences between manager and benchmark sector weights show up in the **allocation effect** A_i = (w_i − W_i) × B_i and in the **interaction term** I_i = (w_i − W_i) × (R_i − B_i).

questions.keyPrinciple: Brinson: Allocation = (w − W)×B; Selection = W×(R − B); Interaction = (w − W)×(R − B).

questions.topic: Risk attribution and factor exposures
questions.title: Explaining AQI's Risk Assessment Process
questions.context: Timmon: AQI considers risk allocation based on **sector allocation followed by within-sector security selection**; the risk assessment is **relative to a benchmark**.
questions.stem: An improvement in the explanation of AQI’s risk assessment process to a client is most likely to include that the:

choices.text: fund manager’s risk assessment is the tracking risk relative to the benchmark.
fund manager’s risk assessment incorporates only risk associated with security selection.

A.text: It is top-down, not bottom-up.

B.text: Sector allocation then security selection is a **top-down** approach; because it is relative to a benchmark, the manager's risk is measured as **tracking risk** vs the benchmark.

C.text: Both sector allocation and security selection create risk relative to the benchmark.

questions.keyPrinciple: Top-down + benchmark-relative → tracking risk from allocation and selection.

questions.topic: Benchmarks and misfit
questions.title: Hedge Fund Benchmark Challenges
questions.context: Richard: it is difficult to find an appropriate benchmark for hedge funds. Despite hedge funds generally holding **liquid assets that can be readily valued**, each fund's strategy is unique, making it difficult to find an appropriate **peer group**.
questions.stem: Which of Richard’scomments about benchmarks for hedge funds is most accurate? The comment in regard to:

A.text: **Peer group.** Hedge funds are unique in their investment process, so an appropriate peer group is hard to build. Hedge fund data are frequently self-reported.

B.text: Wrong: hedge funds can hold **illiquid** assets.

C.text: Wrong: illiquid hedge fund assets can be **subjectively priced** because market prices aren't available.

questions.keyPrinciple: Hedge fund benchmarking: unique strategies (no peer group), self-reported data, illiquid and subjectively priced assets.

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Identifying the Appraisal Ratio
questions.context: Richard describes a ratio that computes the **expected return on an investment less a target return, divided by a standard deviation measure based on performance below the target return**.
questions.stem: Richard’s preferred appraisal measure is best described as the:

A.text: Sharpe = (return − risk-free rate)/standard deviation of returns.

B.text: **Sortino ratio** = (return − target return)/target semideviation.

C.text: Capture ratio = upside capture / downside capture.

questions.keyPrinciple: Sortino uses downside deviation below a target; Sharpe uses total standard deviation and Rf.

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Brinson–Fachler Allocation Effect — Steel
questions.context:
**Exhibit 1 — Hunter Capital Sector Fund (HCSF)**

| Sector | Portfolio weight | Benchmark weight | Portfolio return | Benchmark return |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive | 30% | 10% | 7.85% | 9.10% |
| Electronics | 15% | 30% | 3.50% | 4.50% |
| Machinery | 20% | 35% | 7.65% | 5.65% |
| Steel | 35% | 25% | 8.50% | 3.75% |

questions.stem: Calculate the arithmetic Brinson–Fachler allocation effect for the steel sector.
questions.modelAnswer:
Allocation effect = (w_i − W_i) × (B_i − B), where w_i = portfolio sector weight, W_i = benchmark sector weight, B_i = benchmark sector return, B = overall benchmark return.

Steel = (35% − 25%) × (3.75% − 5.18%) = **−0.14%** (exact −0.143%).
questions.keyPrinciple: Brinson–Fachler allocation = (w − W)(B_i − B).

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Correct Statement on Attribution Methods
questions.context:
Clark's statements:
- **Statement 1:** transactions-based attribution is the most accurate because it uses both holdings and transactions during the evaluation period, but is very difficult and time-consuming to implement.
- **Statement 2:** returns-based attribution is the most reliable because it uses total portfolio returns and is the least vulnerable to data manipulation.
- **Statement 3:** holdings-based attribution yields accurate results for both shorter and longer measurement periods because it eliminates the trading effect.
questions.stem: Determine which of Clark's statements is most likely correct. (Statement 1, Statement 2, Statement 3) Explain why each of the other two statements is incorrect.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Statement 1 is correct.** Transactions-based attribution uses the portfolio's holdings and the transactions during the period (including transaction costs). It is the most accurate, and also the most difficult and time-consuming.

**Statement 2 is incorrect.** Returns-based attribution uses only total portfolio returns. It is the easiest to implement, but because it doesn't use underlying holdings it is the **least accurate** and the **most vulnerable to data manipulation**. It suits cases where holdings data aren't available at the required frequency and detail.

**Statement 3 is incorrect.** Holdings-based attribution uses beginning-of-period holdings and improves with shorter intervals. Over longer periods it misses transactions made during the period; that residual is the **trading effect**, which it does **not** eliminate.
questions.keyPrinciple: Accuracy/effort: returns-based (least accurate, easiest) < holdings-based < transactions-based (most accurate, hardest).

questions.stem: Which of Zlotnikov’s statements is most likely correct?

questions.stem: The most appropriate performance allocation method to evaluate the effectiveness of the big data strategy is:

B.text: Holdings-based fits low-turnover strategies (e.g., passive) because it ignores individual transactions. This is a very active strategy.

C.text: **Transactions-based.** It is most effective for active stock-selection portfolios because it captures both holdings and the purchases/sales within the period, which explains the whole excess return.

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Least Accurate Reason for Preferring Sortino
questions.context:
Rao's reasons the Sortino ratio is better than the Sharpe ratio. The Sortino ratio:
- **Reason 1:** is preferred when the investor's goal is to preserve capital.
- **Reason 2:** can more accurately assess performance when the return distribution is not symmetrical.
- **Reason 3:** uses a target return based on market conditions rather than individual investor preferences.
questions.stem: Which of Rao’s reasons for preferring the Sortino ratio over the Sharpe ratio is least accurate?

A.text: Reason 1 is right: Sortino penalizes returns below the MAR, which suits a capital-preservation goal.

B.text: Reason 2 is right: Sortino handles asymmetric return distributions better; the Sharpe ratio assumes symmetric returns.

C.text: **Reason 3 is wrong.** Sortino uses the investor's own target (MAR), i.e., individual preferences, not market conditions.

questions.keyPrinciple: Sortino: investor-specific MAR, downside only, suits asymmetric distributions and capital preservation.

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Fund C Downside Capture
questions.stem: Based on the information provided in Exhibit 2, Fund C’s manager has a downside capture closest to:

A.text: **83%.** Use periods when the benchmark return is negative (2, 3, 6). Geometric mean: manager −3.14%, benchmark −3.77%. Downside capture = (−3.14%)/(−3.77%) = **0.8328 ≈ 83%** (reproduced).

B.text: 108% is the **upside** capture: periods 1, 4, 5; manager 12.03% / benchmark 11.17% = 1.0771.

questions.keyPrinciple: Upside capture = manager geo-mean / benchmark geo-mean over benchmark-up periods; downside capture likewise over benchmark-down periods; CR = UC/DC.

questions.stem: Based on the capture ratio Rao calculated for Fund B, the fund’s return profile can most accurately be described as:

A.text: **Convex.** A capture ratio above 1 indicates positive asymmetry (convex profile).

B.text: Concave would need a capture ratio below 1 (negative asymmetry).

C.text: A symmetric profile would be a capture ratio of exactly 1.

questions.keyPrinciple: CR > 1 convex (positive asymmetry); CR < 1 concave; CR = 1 symmetric.

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Macro vs Micro Attribution
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the difference between macro attribution and micro attribution?

choices.text: Macro attribution is conducted at the total portfolio level, while micro attribution is conducted at the individual security level
Macro attribution evaluates the asset owner's decisions, while micro attribution evaluates the portfolio manager's decisions
Macro attribution measures the impact of asset allocation decisions, while micro attribution measures the impact of security selection decisions

A.text: Both macro and micro can be done at the total portfolio level; the difference is whose decisions are evaluated.

B.text: **Macro** attribution evaluates the **asset owner's** decisions (tactical asset allocation and manager selection); **micro** attribution evaluates the **portfolio manager's** decisions on the asset owner's total fund performance.

C.text: Micro attribution measures *both* the manager's allocation and selection decisions, not only selection.

questions.keyPrinciple: Macro = asset owner (allocation across asset classes/managers). Micro = portfolio manager (allocation + selection).

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Transactions-Based vs Holdings-Based Attribution
questions.stem: Compared to holdings-based attribution, transactions-based attribution is:

choices.text: easier and less time-consuming to implement.
more likely to reconcile to the actual portfolio return.
more appropriate when an investment strategy has low turnover.

A.text: Transactions-based is the most difficult and time-consuming.

B.text: More likely to **reconcile to the actual portfolio return**. Transactions-based uses holdings and transactions, so it captures trades during the period; holdings-based doesn't and may not reconcile.

C.text: Low-turnover (e.g., passive) strategies suit holdings-based attribution.

questions.keyPrinciple: Transactions-based: most accurate, reconciles to actual return, hardest. Holdings-based: best for low turnover.

questions.topic: Performance evaluation framework (measurement, attribution, appraisal)
questions.title: What Makes Attribution Effective
questions.stem: An effective attribution analysis most likely:

choices.text: uses a holdings-based rather than returns-based approach.
quantifies the impact of the manager's active investment decisions.

A.text: It must measure all active decisions, not only allocation. For a bottom-up stock picker who ignores sector benchmark weights, sector allocation effects are just a by-product, not a decision.

B.text: Holdings-based is generally more accurate than returns-based, but the key is reflecting the manager's actual process; either can do so. The choice depends on data availability and quality, client reporting needs and the complexity of the decision process.

C.text: An effective attribution **quantifies the impact of the manager's active investment decisions**. If it doesn't reflect the decision-making process, it has little value to the manager or client.

questions.keyPrinciple: Attribution must mirror the manager's investment process and quantify active decisions.

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Transactions-Based vs Holdings-Based Attribution (2)
questions.stem: Compared to holdings-based attribution, transactions-based attribution:

choices.text: excludes transaction costs during the measurement period.
provides a less accurate analysis but is easier to implement.
uses both portfolio holdings data and transactions data to provide the most accurate analysis.

A.text: Transactions-based **includes** transaction costs: weights and returns reflect all transactions in the period.

B.text: Reverse: it is *more* accurate but harder to implement.

C.text: Uses **both holdings and transactions data** to provide the most accurate analysis.

questions.keyPrinciple: Transactions-based = holdings + trades + costs; most accurate, most work.

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: BHB Allocation Effect Sign
questions.context: Manager overweights a sector. Sector return 4%; overall benchmark return 6%. Model: Brinson–Hood–Beebower (BHB).
questions.stem: An equity portfolio manager is overweight a sector relative to the benchmark. The sector return is 4% while the overall benchmark return is 6%. Using the Brinson–Hood–Beebower (BHB) model for return attribution analysis, the allocation effect for this sector will be:

A.text: That would be the Brinson–Fachler answer (4% < 6%), not BHB.

B.text: An overweight times a nonzero return is not zero.

C.text: **Positive.** BHB allocation A_i = (w_i − W_i) × B_i uses the sector's benchmark return (not return minus total benchmark). An overweight in a sector with a positive return always gives a positive allocation effect.

questions.keyPrinciple: BHB allocation = (w − W) × B_i. Brinson–Fachler allocation = (w − W) × (B_i − B).

questions.topic: Return attribution (Brinson, holdings/returns/transactions-based, fixed income)
questions.title: Yield-Curve Shape from Exposure Decomposition
questions.context:
Fixed-income portfolio; yields increased and benchmark returns were negative in every duration bucket.

| Bucket | Portfolio weight | Benchmark weight | Portfolio duration | Benchmark duration | Duration effect | Curve effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Short | 30% | 35% | 4.41 | 4.41 | 0.40% | 0.12% |
| Mid | 30% | 35% | 7.42 | 7.44 | 0.23% | 0.03% |
| Long | 40% | 30% | 10.12 | 10.14 | −1.12% | 0.29% |
| **Total** | 100% | 100% | 8.17 | 7.19 | −0.49% | 0.45% |
questions.stem:
An analyst conducting an exposure decomposition analysis gathers the following information regarding the performance of a fixed income portfolio during a period when yields increased and benchmark returns were negative in each duration bucket:

| Duration Bucket | Portfolio Weight (%) | Benchmark Weight (%) | Portfolio Duration (Years) | Benchmark Duration (Years) | Duration Effect (%) | Curve Effect (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Short | 30 | 35 | 4.41 | 4.41 | 0.40 | 0.12 |
| Mid | 30 | 35 | 7.42 | 7.44 | 0.23 | 0.03 |
| Long | 40 | 30 | 10.12 | 10.14 | –1.12 | 0.29 |
| Total | 100 | 100 | 8.17 | 7.19 | –0.49 | 0.45 |

During the performance review period, the shape of the yield curve most likely:

A.text: **Flattened.** The manager overweighted the long-duration bucket (40% vs 30%) and the curve effect is largest there (+0.29%), so long yields rose less than short/benchmark yields: the curve flattened. The duration effect (−0.49%) is the cost of the longer duration while yields rose; the curve effect (+0.45%) is the gain from the curve's shape change.

B.text: Unchanged would give no meaningful curve effect.

C.text: Steepening would hurt a long overweight, not add 0.29%.

questions.keyPrinciple: Duration effect = parallel shift; curve effect = shape change. Overweight long + positive curve effect with rising yields → flattening.
questions.flag: The exhibit's portfolio total duration of 8.17 doesn't match the weighted average of its buckets: 0.30×4.41 + 0.30×7.42 + 0.40×10.12 = 7.60. The benchmark total of 7.19 does reconcile (7.1895). The curve effects sum to 0.44%, shown as 0.45%. The answer doesn't depend on these.

questions.topic: Risk attribution and factor exposures
questions.title: Risk Attribution for a Benchmark-Relative Mandate
questions.stem: A portfolio is managed relative to a benchmark. An appropriate risk attribution model will identify the sources of:

A.text: **Tracking error.** For benchmark-relative mandates, risk attribution identifies the sources of tracking risk.

B.text: Portfolio volatility is what risk attribution identifies for **absolute** mandates.

C.text: Overall portfolio risk likewise applies to absolute mandates (explained by exposures to market, size and style factors plus stock-specific risk).

questions.keyPrinciple: Absolute mandate → sources of volatility. Relative mandate → sources of tracking risk.

questions.topic: Benchmarks and misfit
questions.title: Older Workforce and a Liability-Based Benchmark
questions.stem: When constructing a liability-based benchmark for a company's defined benefit pension plan portfolio, an older workforce would most likely justify a higher allocation to:

A.text: **Nominal bonds.** An older workforce has fewer years to retirement and shorter remaining life expectancy: less salary growth, more predictable cash outflows and shorter-duration cash flows. The plan is DB with no inflation indexing specified, so nominal bonds fit.

B.text: A younger workforce means more equities.

C.text: Real return bonds fit when benefits are inflation-indexed; indexing isn't specified here.

questions.keyPrinciple: Liability-based benchmark mix: older workforce → more nominal bonds; younger → more equity; inflation-indexed benefits → real return bonds.

B.text: Factor-model benchmarks come from regressing the portfolio's return on factors (market, industry, leverage).

C.text: Custom security-based benchmarks are built from the manager's actual process and securities.

questions.title: Misfit Active Return
questions.context: Manager return 11.0%; normal portfolio return 8.0%; investor benchmark return 13.0%.
questions.stem:
An analyst gathers the following information about a portfolio:

- **Manager return:** 11.0%
- **Normal portfolio return:** 8.0%
- **Investor benchmark return:** 13.0%

The portfolio manager's misfit active return is:

A.text: **−5.0%.** Misfit active return = normal portfolio return − investor benchmark = 8.0% − 13.0% = **−5.0%**.

B.text: −2.0% is the investor's (mismeasured) active return: 11.0% − 13.0% = true active + misfit = 3.0% + (−5.0%).

C.text: 3.0% is the **true active return**: manager − normal portfolio = 11.0% − 8.0%.

questions.keyPrinciple: Mismeasured active = true active (manager − normal) + misfit (normal − investor benchmark).

questions.topic: Benchmarks and misfit
questions.title: Real Estate Benchmarks
questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding real estate benchmarks for performance evaluation is most accurate?

choices.text: They are based on the entire real estate opportunity set
Property valuations are primarily based on actual transaction prices
They fail to capture the impact of illiquidity on investment performance

A.text: They cover only a subset of the real estate opportunity set.

B.text: Valuations are typically **appraisals**, because transactions are infrequent.

C.text: They **fail to capture the impact of illiquidity**: indexes don't reflect the high transaction costs, limited transparency and illiquidity that drive actual real estate returns.

questions.keyPrinciple: Real estate indexes: subset of the universe, appraisal-based, ignore illiquidity and transaction costs.

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Asymmetry from Upside/Downside Returns
questions.context: Geometric averages: manager upside 0.55%; benchmark upside 0.70%; manager downside −0.55%; benchmark downside −0.60%.
questions.stem:
An analyst gathers the following geometric average performance of an investment portfolio:

- **Manager upside return:** 0.55%
- **Benchmark upside return:** 0.70%
- **Manager downside return:** –0.55%
- **Benchmark downside return:** –0.60%

The asymmetry of the capture ratio is:

A.text: **Negative.** Capture ratio = (0.55%/0.70%) / (−0.55%/−0.60%) = 0.7857/0.9167 = **0.857 ≈ 86%** (reproduced). Below 1 → negative asymmetry (concave).

B.text: Zero asymmetry would need a ratio of exactly 1; equal manager up and down magnitudes don't make it symmetric versus the benchmark.

C.text: Positive would need a ratio above 1.

questions.keyPrinciple: CR = UC/DC. CR < 1 → negative asymmetry (like negative convexity/gamma).

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Sharpe Ratio
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the Sharpe ratio is most accurate?

choices.text: It measures the additional return for bearing risk above the market return
It is commonly used on an ex ante basis to evaluate risk-adjusted returns
It assumes investors are indifferent between upside and downside volatility

A.text: It measures excess return over the **risk-free rate**, not the market return.

B.text: It is commonly used **ex post** (historical).

C.text: It assumes investors are **indifferent between upside and downside volatility** (standard deviation counts both).

questions.keyPrinciple: Sharpe: (R − Rf)/σ, ex post, treats up and down volatility the same.

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Evidence of Manager Skill
questions.stem: Which of the following would be most indicative of manager skill?

choices.text: An annual portfolio return 8.1% above benchmark
An annual portfolio volatility 3.3% below benchmark

A.text: **An information ratio of 0.43.** It accounts for return versus the benchmark and for the volatility of that active return, so it can indicate skill, especially over longer periods.

B.text: An 8.1% excess return on its own isn't necessarily skill (it ignores the risk taken).

C.text: Volatility 3.3% below the benchmark on its own isn't necessarily skill.

questions.keyPrinciple: Information ratio = active return / tracking error: risk-adjusted evidence of skill.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Choosing Among Zeta, Eta and Theta
questions.context:
Connell inherited $700,000. Three funds earned similar returns over five years and are expected to earn similar returns going forward; all publish results on a timely, routine basis.

**Exhibit 1 — Fund characteristics**

| | Zeta | Eta | Theta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Organization | Independent investment fund | Part of a medium-sized firm with multiple funds | Part of a large firm that rotates investment professionals among funds |
| Team size | Small | Small | Small |
| Staff turnover | High | Medium | Low |
| Incentive compensation | Salary adjustment when returns exceed benchmark | Annual salary adjustment | Annual salary adjustment and performance-based bonus |
| Key people | Founder directs all trades and decisions | Fund manager and assistant make decisions | Fund manager and assistant lead team in selecting investments |
| Longevity/experience | Founder > 25 years | Manager > 15 years; assistant > 12 years | Manager > 20 years; assistant > 10 years; fund family > 50 years |
questions.stem: Based on the Exhibit 1 data, which fund is most appropriate for Connell's needs? Justify your selection with two reasons.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Theta.** The key's reasons:
1. **Lower key-person risk:** it is run by an investment team rather than one manager (Zeta) or two (Eta). If the single Zeta manager or either Eta manager leaves, performance could suffer.
2. **Lowest staff turnover:** more continuity limits loss of institutional knowledge and experience.
3. **Better compensation:** annual salary adjustment plus a performance-based bonus keeps people longer, and unlike the others it directly increases rewards when performance beats benchmark, aligning interests with Connell's.
questions.keyPrinciple: Manager selection factors: key-person risk, staff turnover/continuity, compensation alignment.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Type I and Type II Errors for Connell
questions.context:
A year later, Connell reviews one-year results vs the benchmark (assume performance is mean reverting): **Zeta** in line; **Eta** underperforms; **Theta** outperforms.
- **Alternative 1:** keep the inheritance in the money market account to avoid the Eta fund.
- **Alternative 2:** place the inheritance in the Theta fund.
questions.stem: Identify the type of error Connell is at risk of committing and its associated cost for each alternative. Justify your selection.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Alternative 1 → Type II error.** Avoiding Eta because of recent underperformance, with performance reverting to the mean, risks failing to hire/retain a skilled manager. A Type II error is failing to detect a true relationship; its cost is the **opportunity cost** of not hiring Eta and seeing its performance improve.

**Alternative 2 → Type I error.** Choosing Theta because of recent outperformance, with performance reverting to the mean, risks hiring a manager who then underperforms expectations. The cost is **explicit and relatively easy to measure**.

The goal is to avoid deciding on short-term performance (trend following) and to look for behavioral biases in manager evaluation.
questions.keyPrinciple: Type I = hire/retain a manager who underperforms (explicit cost). Type II = fail to hire/retain a skilled manager (opportunity cost).

questions.topic: Style analysis (returns-based vs holdings-based)
questions.title: When Style Analysis Is Most Useful
questions.context: Connell asks the adviser under what conditions style analysis would be useful in understanding the funds. The funds hold US equities, global equities, venture capital, corporate bonds, government bonds and cash.
questions.stem: Identify the conditions under which the adviser would find style analysis most useful.
questions.modelAnswer:
Style analysis, returns-based (RBSA) or holdings-based (HBSA), is most useful for strategies that hold **publicly traded securities with frequent pricing**. It can be applied to other strategies (hedge funds, private equity), but there the results mostly suggest further lines of due diligence inquiry rather than confirm the investment process.

It must also be **meaningful, accurate, consistent and timely**. For Connell it would be most useful for the equities and bonds, and less meaningful for the **venture capital** assets, which are not traded and are illiquid.
questions.keyPrinciple: Style analysis works best with liquid, frequently priced holdings.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Qualitative and Quantitative Manager Selection Components
questions.context: Grimmett (EUR850,000 bonus) asks a financial adviser how to select a manager. The adviser says both qualitative and quantitative components are involved in identifying, evaluating and selecting a manager.
questions.stem: Describe two considerations for each type of component recommended to Grimmett for her manager selection process.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Qualitative**
- **Process and people:** the manager's philosophy, process, people and portfolio (investment due diligence).
- **Operational due diligence:** infrastructure and firm: accuracy of the track record and whether it reflects risks; back-office processes; profitability, culture and survival. Related items: investment vehicle suitability, terms, and ongoing monitoring of fit.

**Quantitative**
- **Attribution and appraisal:** whether the manager has displayed skill.
- **Capture ratio:** performance in up vs down markets.
- **Drawdown:** whether the return distribution has large drawdowns.
questions.keyPrinciple: Qualitative = investment due diligence + operational due diligence. Quantitative = attribution/appraisal, capture ratio, drawdown.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Steps Before Manager Selection
questions.context: Grimmett asks whether other preparatory steps should be taken before choosing managers; the adviser produces a checklist.
questions.stem: List the preparatory tasks that should be completed before manager selection.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Decide that **outside support** is necessary.
- Complete an **investment policy statement (IPS)**.
- Determine the appropriate **asset allocation**.

Without these, she can't identify managers who fit her needs, confirm they suit her IPS, or be confident they will act on the appropriate asset allocation.
questions.keyPrinciple: Before selecting managers: decide to outsource, write the IPS, set the asset allocation.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Qualitative Factor for Repeatable Performance
questions.stem: Which of the following qualitative considerations is most associated with determining whether investment manager selection will result in superior repeatable performance?

A.text: The key doesn't discuss A. Transparency is part of operational due diligence rather than repeatability of the process. *(My reading.)*

B.text: **Investment process.** A critical element of manager selection is whether the investment process is superior, repeatable and can be applied consistently.

C.text: The key doesn't discuss C. Operational process concerns infrastructure and back office, not the repeatability of investment results. *(My reading.)*

questions.keyPrinciple: Repeatable skill → assess the investment process (philosophy, process, people, portfolio).

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Defining the Manager Universe
questions.stem: The manager selection process begins by defining the universe of feasible managers. When defining this manager universe, the selection process should avoid:

choices.text: excluding managers based on historical risk-adjusted returns.
identifying the benchmark against which managers will be evaluated.
using third-party categorizations of managers to find those that might fill the desired role in the portfolio.

A.text: The initial screen builds a universe that could satisfy the portfolio need and shouldn't focus on historical performance, so avoid **excluding managers on historical risk-adjusted returns**.

B.text: Identifying the benchmark is a key part of defining the manager's role, so do it.

C.text: Third-party categorizations are an efficient way to build the initial universe, to be refined later.

questions.keyPrinciple: Universe definition: role + benchmark + third-party categories; don't screen on past performance.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Why Investors Worry More About Type I Errors
questions.stem: A decision-making investor is most likely to worry more about making a Type I error than a Type II error because:

choices.text: Type II errors are errors of mistaken rejection.
Type I errors are more easily measured.
Type II errors are more likely to have to be explained as to why a skilled manager was fired.

A.text: Type I (not Type II) errors are errors of mistaken rejection.

B.text: **Type I errors are more easily measured** (explicit costs). They may also be tied to the decision maker's compensation. Firing a skilled manager (Type II) is less transparent.

C.text: Type II errors are *less* transparent, so they're less likely to have to be explained.

questions.keyPrinciple: Type I: explicit, transparent, painful. Type II: opportunity cost, less visible.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Type I and Type II Errors Together
questions.context:
| Manager | Large-cap skill | Small-cap skill |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Skilled | Unskilled |
| 2 | Skilled | Skilled |
| 3 | Unskilled | Unskilled |
questions.stem:
An investor is considering hiring three managers who have the following skill levels:

| Manager | Large-cap skill level | Small-cap skill level |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Skilled | Unskilled |
| 2 | Skilled | Skilled |
| 3 | Unskilled | Unskilled |

Type I and Type II errors both occur when the investor is:

choices.text: hiring Manager 1 for large-cap stocks and not hiring Manager 3 for small-cap stocks.
hiring Manager 3 for large-cap stocks and not hiring Manager 2 for small-cap stocks.
hiring Manager 3 for large-cap stocks and not hiring Manager 1 for small-cap stocks.

A.text: Hiring Manager 1 for large-cap (skilled) is correct, and not hiring Manager 3 for small-cap (unskilled) is correct: no error.

B.text: Hiring unskilled Manager 3 for large-cap is a **Type I** error; not hiring skilled Manager 2 for small-cap is a **Type II** error.

C.text: Hiring Manager 3 for large-cap is a Type I error, but not hiring Manager 1 for small-cap (unskilled) is correct: only one error.

questions.keyPrinciple: Type I = hire an unskilled manager. Type II = pass on a skilled manager.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Skilled vs Unskilled Return Distributions
questions.stem: A return distribution of skilled managers that is highly distinct from the return distribution of unskilled managers, most likely implies a:

choices.text: low opportunity cost of not hiring a skilled manager.
high opportunity cost of not hiring a skilled manager.

A.text: Efficient markets show *smaller* differences between skilled and unskilled managers.

B.text: Distinct distributions imply a high, not low, opportunity cost.

C.text: **High opportunity cost of not hiring a skilled manager.** When the two distributions are very distinct, unskilled managers significantly underperform skilled ones.

questions.keyPrinciple: Wide gap between skilled and unskilled return distributions → high opportunity cost of missing skill.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Boinic's Type I and Type II Errors
questions.context:
Boinic set aside $20 million for a new pension plan. After assessing five firms (A–E), all expected to perform in line with benchmarks, it hired **A, D and E**.

**Exhibit 1 — Year 1 performance vs benchmark**

| | A | B | C | D | E |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Performance vs benchmark | Above | Above | Below | Below | Above |

Boinic has made both a Type I and a Type II error.
questions.stem: Identify the firm associated with Boinic's Type I and Type II error. Justify your selection for each error type, discussing the psychological effects of its Year 1 performance on Boinic.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Type I: Firm D.** Hired, then underperformed. It is an active decision that turned out wrong with explicit costs. Boinic is likely to find it psychologically troubling: people avoid regret, opportunity costs get less weight than explicit costs, and Type I errors are more transparent, so there is also the pain of explaining it to the investor.

**Type II: Firm B.** Not hired, then outperformed. Its cost is an opportunity cost and is typically less psychologically troubling (less transparent unless the investor tracks the rejected managers).

The other decisions weren't errors (hired A and E outperformed; didn't hire C, which underperformed).
questions.keyPrinciple: Type I: hired D (below). Type II: skipped B (above). Regret and transparency make Type I feel worse.

questions.topic: Style analysis (returns-based vs holdings-based)
questions.title: Style Analysis Inconsistent with Stated Process
questions.stem: Suppose that the results of a style analysis for an investment manager are not consistent with the stated philosophy of the manager and the manager’s stated investment process. These facts suggest the:

choices.text: investment process may not be repeatable.
manager should be included in the universe of potential managers.

A.text: Results consistent over time but different from the stated style would point to drift; the key says if results *track over time* they may suggest style drift.

B.text: **The investment process may not be repeatable** (or not consistently implemented). Style analysis results should be consistent with the manager's stated philosophy and process.

C.text: The key says such a manager should *not* be included in the universe of potential managers.

questions.keyPrinciple: Style analysis should match stated philosophy; mismatch → process may not be repeatable.

questions.topic: Style analysis (returns-based vs holdings-based)
questions.title: Returns-Based vs Holdings-Based Style Analysis
questions.stem: Compared with holdings-based style analysis (HBSA), a returns-based style analysis (RBSA):

choices.text: requires less effort to acquire data.
is more accurate when illiquid securities are present.

A.text: HBSA (a snapshot at one date) is subject to window dressing, not RBSA.

B.text: **RBSA requires less effort to acquire data.** HBSA needs data on every security held.

C.text: Both are difficult to interpret with illiquid securities; RBSA is not more accurate there.

questions.keyPrinciple: RBSA: easy data, top-down. HBSA: security data, bottom-up, snapshot (window dressing).

questions.topic: Style analysis (returns-based vs holdings-based)
questions.title: What Is Not Style Drift
questions.context: Mandate: fully invested; benchmark a blend of large-cap stocks and investment-grade bonds.
questions.stem: A manager has a mandate to be fully invested with a benchmark that is a blend of large-cap stocks and investment-grade bonds. Which of the following is not an indication that style drift has occurred? The manager:

choices.text: initiates an allocation to small-cap stocks.
decreases investments in investment-grade corporate bonds.
increases allocation to cash in anticipation of a market decline.

A.text: Initiating small-cap stocks violates the large-cap equity style.

B.text: **Not drift.** Reducing exposure to some class of investment-grade bonds is normal portfolio management within the style.

C.text: Raising cash violates the fully-invested mandate.

questions.keyPrinciple: Style drift = moving outside the stated mandate (asset class, cap range, cash).

questions.topic: Style analysis (returns-based vs holdings-based)
questions.title: Advantage of Returns-Based Style Analysis
questions.stem: An advantage of a returns-based style analysis is that such analysis:

choices.text: is suitable for portfolios that contain illiquid securities.
can effectively profile a manager’s risk exposures using a short return series.

A.text: **Comparable across managers** (and through time).

B.text: Illiquid securities lack current prices, which can understate volatility in RBSA.

C.text: Longer return series give more accurate estimates; a short series is not effective.

questions.keyPrinciple: RBSA: comparable, easy; weak with illiquid assets and short histories.

questions.topic: Style analysis (returns-based vs holdings-based)
questions.title: Bottom-Up Style Analysis
questions.stem: Which of the following types of style analysis use(s) a bottom-up approach to estimate the risk exposures in a portfolio?

choices.text: Both return-based and holdings-based style analysis

A.text: RBSA is top-down: it estimates sensitivities to market indexes from portfolio returns.

B.text: **Holdings-based only.** HBSA estimates exposures from the securities held (bottom-up).

C.text: Only HBSA is bottom-up.

questions.keyPrinciple: HBSA = bottom-up. RBSA = top-down.

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Capture Ratio for a Manager Weaker in Downturns
questions.stem: A manager whose relative performance is worse during market downturns most likely has a capture ratio that is:

A.text: **Less than one.** Downside capture exceeds upside capture, i.e., more participation in falling than rising markets.

B.text: Equal to one is symmetric.

C.text: Greater than one means better relative performance in downturns.

questions.keyPrinciple: CR < 1 → worse relative performance in down markets (negative asymmetry).

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Upside 75% and Downside 125%
questions.stem: In a quarter, an investment manager’s upside capture is 75% and downside capture is 125%. We can conclude that the manager underperforms the benchmark:

choices.text: only when the benchmark return is positive.
only when the benchmark return is negative.
when the benchmark return is either positive or negative.

A.text: Also underperforms when the benchmark is negative.

B.text: Also underperforms when the benchmark is positive.

C.text: **Underperforms in both.** Up markets: gained only 75% of the benchmark's gain. Down markets: lost 125% of the benchmark's loss.

questions.keyPrinciple: Upside capture < 100% lags in up markets; downside capture > 100% lags in down markets.

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Choosing a Fund by Return Profile for a Near-Retiree
questions.context:
Yang (59) hopes to retire within three years and hates investment losses.

| Fund | Upside capture | Downside capture | Most recent drawdown loss | Drawdown duration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha | 80 | 20 | 57% | 21 months |
| Beta | 55 | 45 | 38% | 15 months |
| Gamma | 50 | 50 | 28% | 12 months |
questions.stem: Select the best fund for Yang, using only the information provided. Justify your selection.
questions.modelAnswer: **Gamma.** With retirement in three years Yang has little time to recover from losses, so she should seek a **shallower and shorter expected drawdown**. Gamma has the smallest drawdown (28%) and the shortest drawdown duration (12 months).
questions.keyPrinciple: Near retirement → favor smaller, shorter drawdowns (less time to recover).
questions.flag: Computed capture ratios (upside ÷ downside) are Alpha 4.00, Beta 1.22, Gamma 1.00, so Alpha has the best capture ratio and the key still picks Gamma because it judges on drawdown. The key doesn't say why drawdown outranks capture ratio here beyond the shorter time horizon.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Is Aspen's Investment Philosophy Consistent?
questions.context: Aspen's stated philosophy: *"We pursue a passive investment strategy, which seeks to identify and exploit structural inefficiencies through identifying mispricings created by loss aversion. Our strategy and philosophy have evolved over time in response to fund and market performance."*
questions.stem: Determine whether Yang is likely to judge that Aspen follows a consistent investment philosophy, using only the information provided. Justify your response with two reasons.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Not consistent.**
1. It calls its strategy **passive** but describes an **active** one. Passive strategies earn risk premiums (return above the risk-free rate for bearing systematic risk). Active strategies assume markets are inefficient enough that mispricings can be found and exploited. Aspen can't articulate its philosophy clearly or consistently.
2. It has **changed its philosophy over time in response to market performance**. This suggests it is reacting to markets rather than following a consistent philosophy, so its results may not be repeatable.
questions.keyPrinciple: Philosophy test: clearly and consistently articulated, passive vs active coherent, not changed in response to performance.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Repeatability of Exploiting a Structural Inefficiency
questions.stem: Which of the following is consistent with the expectation that exploiting a structural inefficiency is repeatable?

choices.text: The inefficiency is a unique event that occurs infrequently.
The level of gross return is equal to the amount of transaction costs and expenses.
The aggregate value of all assets affected by the inefficiency is larger than the AUM of the manager and its competitors.

A.text: A unique, infrequent event is probably not worth pursuing.

B.text: Gross return equal to transaction costs and expenses is zero marginal return, so probably not worthwhile.

C.text: **Aggregate value of inefficient assets exceeds the AUM of the manager and its competitors.** That gives some assurance the inefficiency is repeatable; it would take time to converge to efficient valuation.

questions.keyPrinciple: Repeatable inefficiency: large relative to the capital chasing it, recurring, and net of costs worthwhile.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Choosing a Manager from Philosophy for Predictable Income
questions.context:
Patnode (66, widowed) received £2,000,000 and wants predictable income for living expenses. All three managers are active.

| Manager | Philosophy/approach |
|---|---|
| Laurbær Partners | Seeks returns by investing in new investment themes and emphasizes measuring the contribution of each to performance. |
| Alcanfor Limited | Seeks returns by investing in securities that appear mispriced in their industry sectors and tracks their ultimate performance against market benchmarks. |
| Mylesten Management | Seeks returns by investing with maximum flexibility to the most popular investor sentiments worldwide. |
questions.stem: Identify which investment manager is most suitable for Patnode. Justify your response based solely on each manager's investment philosophy and approach.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Laurbær.** The key says it recognizes its strategy is exposed to being arbitraged away and is more likely to evolve to deliver the ongoing returns Patnode needs.

**Alcanfor** is weaker: it judges within industry sectors but measures effectiveness against broad market benchmarks, which doesn't give evidence of success within its own selection domain.

**Mylesten** is ad hoc, reacting to changing conditions and investor flows, which suggests a lack of repeatability and robustness.
questions.keyPrinciple: Prefer a philosophy that measures success within its own selection domain and is repeatable.
questions.flag: The key says Laurbær 'recognizes its strategy is exposed to potentially being arbitraged away', but the Exhibit 1 wording for Laurbær doesn't say that. The key's reasoning goes beyond the exhibit text.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Consistent with Adhering to Philosophy and Process
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is consistent with the manager adhering to a stated investment philosophy and investment decision-making process?

choices.text: Senior investment team members have left to form their own firm.
A senior employee has been cited by the SEC for violating insider trading regulations.
A large drawdown occurs because of an unforeseen political event in a foreign country.

A.text: Senior team members leaving to form their own firm calls into question the firm's ability to adhere to its philosophy and process.

B.text: An SEC insider-trading citation of a senior employee also calls that ability into question.

C.text: **A large drawdown from an unforeseen political event** is explainable as an isolated event and doesn't prevent the manager from adhering to its philosophy and process.

questions.keyPrinciple: Isolated, explainable events are consistent with adherence; loss of key people or compliance breaches are not.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Portfolio Construction Features and Costs
questions.context: Parade University endowment (≈GBP1.6bn); IPS prefers **low turnover and trading costs**. Manager A uses hard-stop losses to manage risk. Manager B's portfolio can be liquidated within five business days or less. Manager C's portfolio turnover is greater than the frequency of signals generated.
questions.stem: Identify which manager is most appropriate for Parade. Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Manager B.** All else equal, a liquid portfolio reduces trading costs relative to illiquid securities. Illiquid portfolios are more costly to change and to trade. Strategies not seeking a liquidity premium must watch portfolio liquidity.

**Manager A** is not best: hard-stop losses can close positions too frequently, raising turnover and trading costs.

**Manager C** is problematic: for an active portfolio, turnover should agree with (not exceed) the frequency of signals and the securities' liquidity.
questions.keyPrinciple: Low turnover/cost mandate → liquid portfolio; turnover should match signal frequency; hard stops raise turnover.

questions.topic: Investment vehicles (SMA vs pooled, liquidity, lockups)
questions.title: SMA vs Pooled Vehicle by Characteristic
questions.context: Parade must choose between a customized separately managed account (SMA) and a pooled vehicle called Diversified. Its IPS prioritizes: transparency, investor behavior, cost, liquidity and tracking risk.
questions.stem: Identify which investment vehicle best addresses each characteristic highlighted in Parade's IPS. Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Transparency: SMA.** Real-time, position-level detail and accurate attribution. Even if Diversified gives position-level detail, it is likely delayed.
- **Investor behavior: Diversified.** Less susceptible to investor micromanagement; decisions are set by the manager and the value is determined by the strategy.
- **Cost: Diversified.** Pooled vehicles are typically cheaper because operational costs are spread across investors (stated in the key's answer to a related question, PB-30).
- **Liquidity: SMA.** The investor owns individual securities directly, which adds safety in a liquidity event; manager decisions aren't influenced by other investors' redemptions.
- **Tracking risk: Diversified.** Lower than an SMA, whose customization increases tracking risk vs the benchmark and can confuse attribution because results reflect investor constraints, not manager decisions.
questions.keyPrinciple: SMA: transparency, liquidity, customization, tax, direct ownership. Pooled: cost, less investor interference, lower tracking risk.
questions.flag: The key's explanation under 'Cost' is a copy of the 'Liquidity' paragraph (SMA direct ownership). The conclusion 'Cost: Diversified' is stated, but the key's own reason is missing; the reason above comes from the key's answer to PB-30.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Benefits and Drawbacks of Strategy Details
questions.context: Brickridge reviews Lyon Management. Detail 1: long and short positions are paired. Detail 2: the strategy relies on unique information. Detail 3: AUM connected with the strategy have grown substantially, while the number and characteristics of positions have stayed the same. Moore: *"The regulatory environment is strong and seeks to decrease information asymmetries."*
questions.stem: Identify whether each detail from Moore's summary is most likely a benefit or a drawback of the strategy. Justify your selection.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Detail 1: Benefit.** Pairing captures alpha as prices converge while offsetting market risk, if positions are well matched and sized correctly.
- **Detail 2: Drawback.** Hard to keep an informational edge when regulation seeks to reduce information asymmetries.
- **Detail 3: Drawback.** With significant asset growth, Lyon should adjust the number and/or characteristics of positions to accommodate the larger AUM.
questions.keyPrinciple: Strategy review: pairing helps; info edge fades with regulation; capacity requires adjusting positions as AUM grows.

questions.topic: Manager selection process, due diligence, Type I/II errors
questions.title: Key Investment Due Diligence Consideration
questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely a key consideration in investment due diligence?

choices.text: Depth of expertise and experience of investment personnel

A.text: Suitability of the investment vehicle is part of operational due diligence.

B.text: Back-office processes are part of operational due diligence.

C.text: **Depth of expertise and experience of investment personnel** is a key aspect of investment due diligence.

questions.keyPrinciple: Investment DD: philosophy, process, people, portfolio. Operational DD: infrastructure, vehicle, terms, back office.

questions.topic: Fee structures and performance-based fees
questions.title: Vehicle and Fee Fit for Circue
questions.context: Circue's IPS: some tolerance for lower liquidity, moderate sensitivity to management fees, heightened sensitivity to closet indexing. Options: hedge funds with a soft lock; open-end funds with an incentive fee; closed-end funds with no incentive fee.
questions.stem: Determine which of the three investment vehicles is most appropriate for Circue's IPS. Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Open-end funds with an incentive fee.**
- Slightly less liquid than closed-end funds per the key, but still daily liquidity, and Circue tolerates some lower liquidity.
- Mutual fund assets are "sticky" and investors accept lower returns, which reduces manager motivation and leads to closet indexing. An incentive fee motivates managers to work harder, which fits Circue's heightened sensitivity to closet indexing.
- **Closed-end with no incentive fee:** without an incentive fee, the manager may lack the motivation of the open-end manager.
- **Hedge funds with a soft lock:** least liquid of the three; the soft-lock redemption fee (paid into the fund) is inconsistent with moderate fee sensitivity.
questions.keyPrinciple: Closet indexing concern → incentive fee. Soft lock = redemption fee; hard lock = no redemptions.
questions.flag: The key calls closed-end funds the most liquid of the three and open-end funds slightly less liquid. I did not verify that ranking independently; PB-29 only compares open-end funds against private equity funds and limited partnerships.

questions.topic: Fee structures and performance-based fees
questions.title: Bonus-Style Fees and Risk Estimation
questions.context: Porter: *"More managers are applying a bonus structure in which the manager is not fully exposed to the downside but is fully exposed to the upside."* Smith: *"Circue's current market view is that there are increasing risks to the downside."*
questions.stem: Discuss how Smith's stated expectation would be reflected in estimated portfolio risk under the fee structure identified by Porter.
questions.modelAnswer: It would be reflected in a **misestimation (underestimate) of portfolio risk**. Performance-based fees convert symmetrical gross active-return distributions into asymmetrical net active-return distributions: variability is reduced on the upside but not the downside. A single standard deviation computed on a series of active returns above and below the base fee can therefore **underestimate downside risk**. By contrast, fully symmetric fees (manager exposed to both sides) align risk and effort more closely than bonus-style fees.
questions.keyPrinciple: Bonus-style fees → asymmetric net returns → standard deviation understates downside risk.

questions.topic: Fee structures and performance-based fees
questions.title: Net Active Return Under a Sharing Fee Schedule
questions.context:
| Fee structure | Fee (%) |
|---|---|
| Standard fee | 0.35 |
| Base fee | 0.20 |
| Sharing (on active return beyond base fee) | 25 |
| Breakeven active return | 0.80 |
| Maximum annual fee | 0.90 |
questions.stem: Calculate the net active return for gross active returns of ≤0.20%, 0.75%, 0.80% and 1.75%. Show your calculations.
questions.modelAnswer:
Billed fee = base fee + sharing × (gross active return − base fee), when gross active return exceeds the base fee. Net active return = gross active return − billed fee.

| Gross active return | Billed fee | Net active return |
|---|---|---|
| ≤ 0.20% | 0.20% (base fee only) | 0.00% |
| 0.75% | 0.20 + 0.25 × (0.75 − 0.20) = 0.3375% | 0.75 − 0.3375 = 0.4125 → **0.41%** |
| 0.80% (breakeven; standard fee applies) | 0.35% | 0.80 − 0.35 = **0.45%** |
| 1.75% | 0.20 + 0.25 × (1.75 − 0.20) = 0.5875% | 1.75 − 0.5875 = 1.1625 → **1.16%** |

Check: at 0.80%, 0.20 + 0.25 × 0.60 = 0.35, equal to the standard fee, which is why 0.80% is the breakeven. The 0.90% maximum is not reached in any case.
questions.keyPrinciple: Billed fee = base + sharing × (active − base). Net = active − billed fee.

questions.topic: Fee structures and performance-based fees
questions.title: AUM-Based vs Performance-Based Fees
questions.context: Vaudreuil's fees are AUM-based; Pourtir's are performance-based. Comparable net-of-fee performance.
questions.stem: Discuss one advantage and one disadvantage to the client of each manager's contracted fee structure.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Vaudreuil (AUM-based)**
- *Advantage:* the fee's impact on the client is lower as assets grow in a rising market.
- *Disadvantage:* the client may not get the same returns as under another structure; Vaudreuil may not work to generate returns to retain assets once they are large, since assets tend to be "sticky".

**Pourtir (performance-based)**
- *Advantage:* aligns interests because both share in investment results; the client pays lower fees when active returns are low; Pourtir may work harder.
- *Disadvantage (any of):* tension, since the client pays the base fee even if Pourtir underperforms; the structure can lead to misestimates of portfolio risk and may incentivize higher risk; bonus-style fees give different incentives for client and manager; Pourtir may hold assets until a profit can be realized even if the client would benefit from selling at a loss.
questions.keyPrinciple: AUM fees: cheaper as assets grow, weak performance incentive. Performance fees: aligned, but risk-taking and misestimated risk.

questions.topic: Fee structures and performance-based fees
questions.title: Fee Structure That Lowers Net Return Volatility
questions.stem: Which of the following fee structures most likely decreases the volatility of a portfolio’s net returns?

choices.text: Neither incentive fees nor management fees

A.text: **Incentive fees only.** A fee that is a percentage of returns reduces net gains in positive months and net losses in negative months, lowering the standard deviation of realized returns.

B.text: A management fee (fixed % of assets) lowers the level of return without changing the standard deviation of the return series.

C.text: With neither fee, the standard deviation is unchanged.

questions.keyPrinciple: Incentive fee (% of returns) scales returns → lower volatility. Management fee only shifts the mean.

questions.topic: Fee structures and performance-based fees

questions.context: Tree Fallers fee schedules (see Appendix): Red Grass = higher of base or base + sharing of positive performance (base 1.00%, sharing 20%, on return net of base fee, no cap). Blue Water = same form, base 0.50%, sharing 20% on active return, max 2.50%. Yellow Wood = base + sharing of both positive and negative performance (base 1.50%, 20%).
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, which fund has a symmetrical fee structure?

A.text: Red Grass has a floor at the base fee (bonus-style, asymmetric).

B.text: Blue Water has a floor at the base fee and a cap.

C.text: **Yellow Wood.** Its profit-sharing component is negative when return is negative and positive when it is positive.

questions.keyPrinciple: Symmetrical: Computed fee = Base + Sharing of performance (positive and negative).

B.text: Blue Water's maximum annual fee caps the upside incentive.

C.text: Yellow Wood participates in the downside, which restrains risk taking.

questions.topic: Fee structures and performance-based fees
questions.title: High-Water Mark Effect on Red Grass
questions.context: Red Grass gross returns: 2016 +8.00%, 2017 −2.00%, 2018 +5.00%. Base 1.00%, sharing 20% on return net of base fee. High-water mark: sharing only charged to the extent losses have been recouped.
questions.stem: In which year would the Red Grass Fund’s investment management fee be affected by Summer’s recalculation using the high-water mark?

A.text: 2016 has no prior losses.

B.text: 2017 has no sharing fee because the return was negative.

C.text: **2018.** 2016 is the first year with a positive return, no prior losses (fee 1.00 + 0.20 × 7.00 = 2.40%). 2017 return is negative, so the sharing fee is zero (fee 1.00%). In 2018 the gain must first offset the 2017 loss, so only the remaining gain is shared. 2018 is the only year in which a positive return follows a negative one.

questions.keyPrinciple: High-water mark: no sharing fee until prior losses are recouped.

questions.topic: Fee structures and performance-based fees
questions.title: Fee Structure Resembling a Call Option
questions.context:
| Fee | Hidden Lake | Carpenter Management |
|---|---|---|
| Base fee | 0.30% | 0.18% (minimum fee) |
| Sharing (on active return beyond base fee) | 15% | 20% |
| Maximum annual fee | N/A | 0.80% |
questions.stem: Identify which manager's fee structure is most similar to a call option on a share of active return. Justify your selection.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Carpenter Management.** It has a bonus-style fee with a maximum fee. Bonus-style fees are close to the manager holding a call option on a share of active return, with the base fee as the strike. Here that is the 18 bp base fee, plus a long call on active return struck at the minimum (base) fee, minus another (less valuable) call struck at the maximum fee.

**Hidden Lake** is a symmetrical structure (as the key describes it), in which the manager is fully exposed to both downside and upside, so it is not option-like.
questions.keyPrinciple: Bonus-style fee ≈ manager's call option on active return; base fee ≈ strike; cap = short call at the maximum.
questions.flag: The key calls Hidden Lake 'symmetrical', but the exhibit shows only base fee 0.30% and sharing 15% on active return beyond the base fee, with no stated computed-fee rule. I cannot confirm from the exhibit whether it is symmetrical.

questions.topic: Behavioral biases
questions.title: Behavioral Bias in Directing the Team
questions.context: Jacob (CIO, Astro Investments) attended a conference, views alternatives as an emerging trend, and directs her team to begin investing in alternatives.
questions.stem: Identify the behavioral bias Jacob exhibits (groupthink, authority bias, or aversion to complexity). Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Authority bias.** She is in a position of authority and makes the decision independently; authority bias is groups deferring to a member who is an expert or in authority.

**Groupthink** is wrong: this is an individual decision by the person in authority; groupthink is a team minimizing conflict and dissent to reach consensus.

**Aversion to complexity** is wrong: she is not giving disproportionate attention to trivial issues at the expense of harder topics.
questions.keyPrinciple: Authority bias: defer to the expert/boss. Groupthink: suppress dissent for harmony. Aversion to complexity: dwell on trivia.

questions.topic: Style analysis (returns-based vs holdings-based)
questions.title: Style Analysis Type and Additional Benefit
questions.context: Jacob wants additional due diligence using style analysis that does not require a large amount of difficult-to-acquire data and is not subject to window dressing.
questions.stem: Determine the type of style analysis (holdings-based or returns-based) and discuss one additional benefit of this approach.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Returns-based style analysis (RBSA).** It is top-down: it estimates the portfolio's sensitivities to security market indexes representing distinct factors. Its advantages per the key: no large amount of additional or hard-to-acquire data; can be estimated even for complicated strategies; not subject to window dressing; comparable across managers and through time.

*Additional benefits beyond the two in the vignette:* it can be estimated for complicated strategies, and it is comparable across managers and through time.
questions.keyPrinciple: RBSA: top-down, easy data, no window dressing, comparable, works for complex strategies.

questions.topic: Fee structures and performance-based fees
questions.title: Net Active Return for Schwinn Capital
questions.context: Gross return 3.50%; standard fee 0.50%; base fee 0.25%; sharing on active return beyond base fee 20%; breakeven active return 1.50%; maximum annual fee 1.00%.
questions.stem: Calculate the net active return for Schwinn Capital.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Return subject to sharing = 3.50% − 0.25% = 3.25%
- Sharing fee = 3.25% × 20% = 0.65%
- Billed fee = 0.25% + 0.65% = 0.90% (below the 1.00% maximum)
- **Net active return = 3.50% − 0.90% = 2.60%**

Check: the 0.90% billed fee is above the 0.50% standard fee, consistent with a gross active return above the 1.50% breakeven.
questions.keyPrinciple: Net active = gross active − (base + sharing × (gross active − base)), subject to the cap.
questions.flag: The exhibit labels the 3.50% 'Gross return' and the key treats it as gross active return. I followed the key.

questions.topic: Behavioral biases
questions.title: Incorrect Type I/II Statement
questions.context: S1: Type I errors are more transparent and create explicit costs. S2: Type II errors create opportunity costs and are psychologically less painful than Type I errors. S3: Type II errors are relatively easy to measure.
questions.stem: Determine which of the team's statements is most likely incorrect. Justify your response.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Statement 3.** Type II errors are *less* likely to be measured: the performance impact of not selecting a manager is often not tracked and is hard to measure.

Statement 1 is correct: Type I errors create explicit costs and are more transparent; the manager feels regret plus the pain of explaining it. Statement 2 is correct: Type II errors create opportunity costs, which people weight less.
questions.keyPrinciple: Type I: explicit, transparent. Type II: opportunity cost, hard to measure, less painful.
