B.text: Positive asymmetry is a bonus structure (higher of base or base + sharing of positive performance).

C.text: The key doesn't discuss negative asymmetry separately.

questions.keyPrinciple: Symmetric: Base + Sharing. Bonus-style: Higher of Base or Base + positive sharing (cap optional).

questions.topic: Style analysis (returns-based vs holdings-based)
questions.title: When Holdings-Based Style Analysis Fits
questions.context:
| | Turnover | Liquidity | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Manager 1 | Low | Low | High |
| Manager 2 | High | High | High |
| Manager 3 | Low | High | Low |
questions.stem:
A pension plan sponsor conducts an annual review of its three external hedge fund managers and collects the following information regarding each manager's investment style:

|  | Turnover | Liquidity | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Manager 1 | Low | Low | High |
| Manager 2 | High | High | High |
| Manager 3 | Low | High | Low |

Based only on this information, a holdings-based style analysis is most appropriate for evaluating the performance of:

A.text: Manager 1 has low turnover but low liquidity and high complexity.

B.text: Manager 2 has high liquidity but high turnover and high complexity.

C.text: **Manager 3.** HBSA works best with low turnover, a not-overly-complex style, and high liquidity (so accurate pricing can be obtained).

questions.keyPrinciple: HBSA: low turnover, liquid, simple. It is a snapshot; stale pricing understates risk for illiquid holdings.

questions.topic: Risk-adjusted measures, capture ratios, drawdown
questions.title: Capture Ratio and Drawdown Risk
questions.context:
| | Upside capture (%) | Capture ratio |
|---|---|---|
| Manager 1 | 75 | 1.0 |
| Manager 2 | 120 | 2.0 |
| Manager 3 | 90 | 3.0 |

Downside capture = upside capture ÷ capture ratio.
questions.stem:
An investor nearing retirement age considers replacing her existing manager. She gathers the following information on three potential managers:

|  | Upside Capture (%) | Capture Ratio |
|---|---|---|
| Manager 1 | 75 | 1.0 |
| Manager 2 | 120 | 2.0 |
| Manager 3 | 90 | 3.0 |

With which manager is the investor least likely to experience a large drawdown?

C.text: **Manager 3.** Downside capture = 90 ÷ 3 = **30%**, the lowest.

questions.keyPrinciple: CR = UC ÷ DC, so DC = UC ÷ CR. Near retirement, minimize downside capture.

questions.topic: Investment vehicles (SMA vs pooled, liquidity, lockups)
questions.title: Taxable vs Non-Taxable Account Vehicle
questions.stem: A private wealth manager meets with a client to discuss potential investment options for two accounts: a taxable account and a non-taxable account. Both accounts have large unrealized gains. Compared to a separately managed account (SMA), is a pooled vehicle the most appropriate for both accounts?

choices.text: No, the taxable account should be invested in an SMA
No, the non-taxable account should be invested in an SMA

A.text: Pooled is appropriate for the non-taxable account, but not for both.

B.text: **No, the taxable account should be in an SMA.** Selling large unrealized gains to move into a pooled vehicle triggers taxable income. An SMA keeps existing holdings and allows tax-efficient management (e.g., in the US, tax only on realized gains).

C.text: The non-taxable account is the one for which a pooled vehicle is fine.

questions.keyPrinciple: Large unrealized gains in a taxable account → SMA.

questions.topic: Investment vehicles (SMA vs pooled, liquidity, lockups)
questions.title: Lockups and Withdrawal in Two Years
questions.context:
| | Lockup type | Lockup period | Notification (days) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hedge Fund 1 | Soft | 6 years | 180 |
| Hedge Fund 2 | Hard | 3 years | 360 |
| Hedge Fund 3 | Hard | 3 years | 90 |

The investor may need to withdraw in two years and is willing to pay a fee.
questions.stem:
An investor considers investing in one of three hedge funds:

|  | Lockup Type | Lockup Period | Notification Period (Days) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hedge Fund 1 | Soft | 6 years | 180 |
| Hedge Fund 2 | Hard | 3 years | 360 |
| Hedge Fund 3 | Hard | 3 years | 90 |

The investor may need to withdraw funds in two years and is willing to pay a fee to do so. Which manager should the investor choose?

A.text: **Hedge Fund 1.** A soft lock allows redemption for a fee (paid into the fund); the investor can withdraw after the initial investment.

B.text: A hard lock allows no redemptions until it expires (3 years). The notification period doesn't change the lockup.

C.text: Same: hard lock for 3 years.

questions.keyPrinciple: Hard lock = no redemptions. Soft lock = redemption fee paid into the fund.

questions.topic: Fee structures and performance-based fees
questions.title: Base Fee 0% and Sharing 20%
questions.stem:
An analyst evaluates a hedge fund manager's fee schedule:

- **Base fee:** 0%
- **Sharing:** 20%

The manager's fee structure is fully exposed to:

choices.text: the upside but not the downside.
both the downside and the upside.
neither the downside nor the upside.

A.text: With a zero base fee the manager is exposed to the downside (no fee in poor performance).

B.text: **Both downside and upside.** With a 0% base fee the manager earns nothing if performance is poor and 20% of strong performance with no cap.

C.text: There is no annual maximum, so the upside exposure is full.

questions.keyPrinciple: Three structures: symmetric (Base + Sharing), bonus uncapped (higher of Base or Base + positive sharing), bonus capped (with limit).

questions.topic: GIPS: firm definition and objectives
questions.title: Defining Company C as a Firm
questions.stem: Company C manages retail and institutional money through two autonomous groups, 'Company C Institutional Investment Management' and 'Company C Retail Investors'. How should Company C define itself as a firm to comply with the GIPS standards?
questions.modelAnswer: The GIPS standards encourage the **broadest, most meaningful definition of a firm**. Company C should consider defining the firm to include assets managed by **both** entities. It could define them as **separate firms** only if each is held out to clients and prospects as a distinct business unit.
questions.keyPrinciple: Firm = broadest definition; a division/subsidiary can be its own firm only if held out as a distinct business entity.

questions.topic: GIPS: firm definition and objectives
questions.title: Can the US Entity Claim Compliance?
questions.stem: Firm A is a multinational investment firm with offices in Japan, Australia, the UK and the US. Each office is registered with its national regulator and held out to clients and prospects as a distinct business entity. Firm A (United States) claims compliance. Can the US entity claim compliance?
questions.modelAnswer: **Yes.** The US entity is a distinct business entity and so meets the GIPS definition of a firm.
questions.keyPrinciple: Distinct, held-out entity (e.g., separately registered) = a firm for GIPS.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Composite Inclusion Requirement
questions.stem: Which statement most accurately expresses a requirement of the GIPS standards?

choices.text: Non-fee-paying portfolios must not be included in composites.
All actual fee-paying discretionary segregated accounts must be included in at least one composite.
All actual fee-paying discretionary segregated accounts must be included in only one composite.

A.text: Non-fee-paying discretionary accounts *may* be included in a composite, with appropriate disclosure.

B.text: **All actual, fee-paying, discretionary segregated accounts must be included in at least one composite.** Non-discretionary accounts must not be included in composites.

C.text: 'At least one', not 'only one': an account that fits several composites must go in all of them (see GP-11).

questions.keyPrinciple: All actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolios → at least one composite; non-discretionary → none.

questions.topic: GIPS: return calculation
questions.title: Revaluing for Large Cash Flows
questions.stem: Calculate the rate of return for January, February, March and Q1 2019 using revaluing for large cash flows.
questions.keyPrinciple: Large flow → revalue on the flow date, compute sub-period TWRs, link geometrically.

questions.topic: GIPS: valuation
questions.title: What GIPS Does Not Require in Valuation
questions.stem: The GIPS standards do not require firms to value portfolios in accordance with:

choices.text: generally accepted principles of financial accounting.

A.text: Portfolios must be valued in accordance with the definition of fair value.

B.text: Firms must value portfolios in accordance with the composite-specific valuation policy.

C.text: **Generally accepted principles of financial accounting.** Not required.

questions.keyPrinciple: Required: fair value + valuation policy. Not required: GAAP-style accounting principles.

questions.topic: GIPS: return calculation
questions.title: Cash in Return Calculations
questions.context: Convenable manages an equity portfolio for Flender; cash is invested by Flender's existing custodial bank.
questions.stem: Convenable Capital Management manages an equity portfolio for the Flender Company. Cash held in the portfolio is invested by Flender’s existing custodial bank. Must Convenable include cash and cash equivalents in the portfolio return calculations?

choices.text: No, the cash is not invested by Convenable
No, Convenable does not have discretion over the selection of the custodian

A.text: **Yes.** 'Returns from cash and cash equivalents must be included in all return calculations, even if the firm does not control the specific cash investment(s).'

B.text: Not controlling the cash investment doesn't exclude it.

C.text: Discretion over selecting the custodian doesn't matter.

questions.keyPrinciple: Cash and equivalents are always in the return, even if the firm doesn't control them.

questions.topic: GIPS: return calculation
questions.title: What Transaction Costs Exclude
questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, the most accurate statement is that transaction costs do not include:

A.text: Bid–offer spreads from internal or external brokers are transaction costs.

B.text: Brokerage commissions are transaction costs.

C.text: **Custody fees charged per transaction** are custody fees, not transaction costs.

questions.keyPrinciple: Transaction costs: commissions, exchange fees/taxes, bid–offer spreads. Per-transaction custody fees are custody fees.

questions.topic: GIPS: return calculation
questions.title: Modified Dietz Returns for Three Portfolios
questions.context:
European equity composite (€ millions); cash flow weighting factors given.

| | Weight | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FV 31 July | | 74.9 | 127.6 | 110.4 |
| 8 Aug | 0.742 | | −15 | |
| 12 Aug | 0.613 | 7.5 | | |
| 19 Aug | 0.387 | | −5 | 15 |
| FV 31 Aug | | 85.3 | 109.8 | 128.4 |
questions.stem: Calculate the August returns of Portfolios A, B and C using the Modified Dietz formula.
questions.keyPrinciple: Modified Dietz: (End − Begin − Net flows) ÷ (Begin + Σ flow × weight), weight = remaining days ÷ total days.

questions.topic: GIPS: return calculation
questions.title: Composite Return, Beginning-Value Weighted
questions.context: Uses the portfolio returns from GP-8: A 3.65%, B 1.92%, C 2.58%.
questions.stem: Calculate the August composite return by asset-weighting the portfolio returns using beginning-of-period values.
questions.keyPrinciple: Beginning-value weighting: weight = portfolio BMV ÷ composite BMV.

questions.topic: GIPS: return calculation
questions.title: Composite Return, Beginning Value Plus Cash Flows Weighted
questions.context: Uses the portfolio returns from GP-8 and the Modified Dietz denominators.
questions.stem: Calculate the August composite return by asset-weighting using a method that reflects both beginning values and external cash flows.
questions.modelAnswer:
Weights use the Modified Dietz denominators: A 79.5, B 114.535, C 116.205; total 310.24.

| | Weight | Return |
|---|---|---|
| A | 79.5 ÷ 310.24 = 25.6% | 3.65% |
| B | 114.535 ÷ 310.24 = 36.9% | 1.92% |
| C | 116.205 ÷ 310.24 = 37.5% | 2.58% |

Composite = 0.0365 × 0.256 + 0.0192 × 0.369 + 0.0258 × 0.375 = **2.61%**.

The same answer results from the **aggregate return** method: sum beginning assets and flows for the composite and apply Modified Dietz once (I computed 2.611%).
questions.keyPrinciple: Beginning assets + weighted cash flows weighting ≡ aggregate method.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: One Portfolio in Several Composites
questions.stem: Can a firm include a single portfolio in more than one of the firm's composites?
questions.modelAnswer: **Yes.** All actual, discretionary, fee-paying segregated accounts must be in at least one composite. If an account meets the criteria for more than one (e.g., large-cap and large-cap growth), it must be included in all the appropriate composites.
questions.keyPrinciple: Account fits several composite definitions → include in all.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Linking Backtested Returns to Actual Performance
questions.stem: Tan/Lim began running live portfolios on a new model in June 2016 (after backtesting). In 2019 it linked the backtested returns to the actual composite record and presented 3-, 5- and 10-year performance as continuous in GIPS Reports. Does this comply?
questions.modelAnswer: **No.** Composites must include only **actual assets** under management within the defined firm, and the standards expressly prohibit **linking model/simulated performance to actual performance**. Tan/Lim may not claim compliance if it does this.
questions.keyPrinciple: Never link simulated/model performance with actual composite performance.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Discretion and the SMERF Portfolio
questions.stem: Midwest's Institutional Equity composite holds portfolios 'actively managed for long-term capital appreciation'. SMERF's IPS requires Investment Committee approval of all transactions in advance, anticipates regular substantial net withdrawals, and requires the manager to disburse funds per a withdrawal schedule. Can Midwest justify including SMERF in the composite?
questions.modelAnswer: Non-discretionary portfolios must not be in composites. IPS restrictions don't automatically make a portfolio non-discretionary; the firm defines discretion. Here, **pre-approval of every transaction** and the **liquidity/withdrawal needs** most likely prevent Midwest from implementing long-term active capital appreciation. If so, Midwest **must classify the portfolio as non-discretionary and exclude it from all composites**.
questions.keyPrinciple: If client restrictions prevent implementing the strategy → non-discretionary → out of all composites.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Likely Non-Discretionary Fixed-Income Portfolio
questions.stem: A fixed-income portfolio is most likely to be considered non-discretionary if the client’s investment policy states that:

choices.text: securities held at a gain must not be sold.
the average credit quality must be investment grade.
securities held in the portfolio must be issued in developed markets.

A.text: **Securities held at a gain must not be sold.** This would likely make the portfolio differ materially from the firm's other fixed-income portfolios.

B.text: Average investment-grade credit quality is a normal strategy constraint.

C.text: Developed-market issuers is a normal strategy constraint.

questions.keyPrinciple: Restrictions that stop the strategy from being implemented → non-discretionary.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Including a New Portfolio That Is Slow to Invest
questions.context: Taurus received securities in kind and expects five months to invest in bank loans.
questions.stem: A charitable foundation transfers securities in kind to Taurus Asset Management Ltd. to fund a new bank loan portfolio. Taurus estimates that after liquidating the transferred securities, it will take five months to invest the foundation’s assets in bank loans. Which statement best describes a requirement of the GIPS standards? Taurus must include the foundation’s portfolio in the appropriate composite:

choices.text: on a timely and consistent basis.
when the assets are substantially invested.
as of the beginning of the next full measurement period.

A.text: **On a timely and consistent basis**, per the firm's documented policy (e.g., as of the first full measurement period fully invested).

B.text: Not stated as the requirement.

C.text: Not stated as the requirement.

questions.keyPrinciple: New portfolios enter composites on a timely, consistent basis per documented policy.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Terminated Portfolio: Last Period Included
questions.context: Ord uses monthly returns. Notified 15 April that it will be terminated at end of April, and told to stop trading immediately.
questions.stem: Ord Capital Management, an investment management firm that claims compliance with the GIPS standards, manages a global equity portfolio for a pension plan sponsored by Chimie Bio-Industrielle. On 15 April, the plan sponsor notifies Ord that the firm will be terminated as of the end of the month and instructs the manager to stop trading immediately. Assuming Ord calculates composites using monthly portfolio returns, Ord must include the Chimie portfolio in the historical returns of the composite to which it belongs up to:

A.text: **31 March.** Terminated portfolios stay in historical composite performance through the last full measurement period during which the firm had discretion.

B.text: 15 April is not a full measurement period end.

C.text: 30 April is when the contract ends, but discretion ended with the instruction.

questions.keyPrinciple: Terminated portfolio: include through the last full period under management.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Switching a Portfolio Between Composites
questions.context: A family-office portfolio in an enhanced-indexing composite can no longer hold high-yield or emerging-market bonds (client wrote to say so). Southwest moves it to another composite.
questions.stem: Southwest Capital Advisors LLC manages a fixed-income composite in accordance with an enhanced indexing strategy that makes strategic use of high-yield and emerging market bonds in addition to investment grade bonds issued in developed markets. The Merrimack Company, a family office, has a portfolio that is included in the firm’s fixed-income enhanced indexing composite. Merrimack informs Southwest in writing that, because of changes in its investment policy, the portfolio can no longer hold high-yield or emerging market bonds. In accordance with the GIPS standards, Southwest decides to switch the Merrimack portfolio to another composite. The historical performance of the portfolio must be:

choices.text: retained in the enhanced indexing composite.

A.text: Not reflected in both.

B.text: History isn't moved.

C.text: **Retained in the enhanced indexing composite.** History stays with the original composite. Portfolios may switch only after documented changes in mandate, objective or strategy, or composite redefinition.

questions.keyPrinciple: Switch composites only with documented mandate change; history stays with the original.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Bida Portfolio History After Policy Change
questions.context: Bamako's core-plus fixed-income composite: all discretionary portfolios over $10 million with a strategy that includes domestic high-yield; benchmark 75% Barclays US Gov/Credit and 25% Barclays US High Yield, rebalanced monthly. The Bida endowment can no longer hold below-investment-grade securities, so it moves to the core composite.
questions.stem: The core-plus fixed-income composite includes a portfolio managed on behalf of the Bida Academy endowment fund. The trustees of Bida inform Bamako in writing that because of a change in investment policy, the endowment fund is no longer permitted to hold below-investment-grade securities. Bamako determines that henceforth, the Bida portfolio should be included in the core fixed-income composite rather than the core-plus fixed-income composite. The historical record of the portfolio must be:

choices.text: kept in the core-plus fixed-income composite.
excluded from the core-plus fixed-income composite.

A.text: Not included in both.

B.text: **Kept in the core-plus composite.** Historical performance stays with the original composite.

C.text: Not excluded from the core-plus composite.

questions.keyPrinciple: History stays with the original composite.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Portfolio Falls Below the Minimum
questions.context: Bouwa's portfolio falls below the $10 million composite minimum for nine months, then returns above it.
questions.stem: After an extended period of rising interest rates, the value of Bouwa Special Equipment Company’s core-plus fixed-income portfolio falls below the composite minimum of $10 million. The Bouwa portfolio remains below the composite-specific minimum asset level for nine months, at which point the client makes an additional contribution that brings it back above $10 million in assets. During the nine months the portfolio is below the composite minimum asset level, Bamako must:

choices.text: temporarily switch the Bouwa portfolio to the firm’s miscellaneous composite.
include the Bouwa portfolio in the core-plus fixed-income composite in all measurement periods.
exclude the Bouwa portfolio from the core-plus fixed-income composite for the period it was below the minimum asset level.

A.text: There should be no 'miscellaneous' composite: composites reflect similar mandates, objectives or strategies.

B.text: Including it in all periods would violate the minimum.

C.text: **Exclude it from the composite for the period below the minimum.** Firms must not include portfolios below the composite minimum. Unless policy sets separate add/remove levels, remove it when below and return it when it qualifies again.

questions.keyPrinciple: Below composite minimum → excluded for those periods.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Client Requires Pre-Approval of Trades
questions.context: Mahe (a core-plus client) now requires its controller to approve all security transactions in advance.
questions.stem: Mahe Manufacturing Company, a core-plus fixed-income client, informs Bamako in writing that, in the future, all security transactions must be approved in advance by Mahe’s controller. The most likely consequence is that Bamako must prospectively exclude the Mahe portfolio from:

A.text: **All composites.** Prior approval likely renders the portfolio non-discretionary, and non-discretionary portfolios must not be in composites.

B.text: Total firm assets must include discretionary and non-discretionary assets.

C.text: It's excluded from all composites, not only core-plus.

questions.keyPrinciple: Non-discretionary: excluded from composites, but stays in total firm assets.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Minimum Portfolios in a Composite
questions.stem: What is the minimum number of portfolios a composite must contain? Must a firm disclose the number of portfolios in a composite?
questions.modelAnswer: There is **no minimum or maximum**. The number of portfolios must be disclosed for each annual period presented, **unless there are five or fewer** portfolios.
questions.keyPrinciple: No minimum count; disclose number of portfolios unless ≤5.

questions.topic: GIPS: presentation and disclosure
questions.title: Dropping Poor Early Years
questions.stem: Macondo has managed accounts since 2007, became GIPS-compliant on 1 January 2012 and has GIPS-compliant composite reports for 2007–2019. A new marketing director in June 2020 proposes showing only 2015–2019 (the improved years). Does this comply?
questions.modelAnswer: **No.** On initial compliance a firm must show at least five years of GIPS-compliant performance, then add a year each period, building to a minimum of **10 years**. In 2020 Macondo must present **2010 through 2019**. Dropping pre-2015 years also isn't fair representation and full disclosure. Years older than 10 may be removed, though showing the whole record is recommended.
questions.keyPrinciple: Minimum 5 years, building to 10; cannot cherry-pick the good years.

questions.topic: GIPS: portability
questions.title: Portability of a Manager's Track Record
questions.stem: O'Connor made all decisions for JEMStone's Emerging Market composite. Acella hires him to start an emerging-market strategy. Can Acella link his JEMStone performance to its new strategy and comply?
questions.keyPrinciple: Portability: records, primary decision maker, strategy intact, and no gap (to link).
questions.flag: The key's explanation is conditional and never states a plain yes/no; I've presented it as 'only if the requirements are met'.

questions.topic: GIPS: verification
questions.title: What Verification Does
questions.stem: It is most accurate to say that verification:

choices.text: makes the claim of compliance more credible.
certifies that the firm has adequate internal controls.
ensures the accuracy of specific composite presentations.

A.text: **Makes the claim of compliance more credible.**

B.text: Verification does not provide assurance on the adequacy of internal controls.

C.text: It 'does not provide assurance on the accuracy of any specific performance report'.

questions.keyPrinciple: Verification: firm-wide, credibility only; no assurance on a specific composite or controls.

questions.topic: GIPS: verification
questions.title: Verifying Only Some Composites
questions.stem: Renner, Williams & Woods wants its equity and balanced composites verified but not a small fixed-income composite. Can it obtain a firm-wide verification covering only those composites?
questions.modelAnswer: **No.** A firm cannot have only a portion of the firm verified. Verification cannot be carried out on selected composites, pooled funds or portfolios. A firm may have a performance examination on specific composites, but must not state that a particular composite has been 'verified'.
questions.keyPrinciple: Verification = whole firm only. Single-composite assurance = performance examination.

questions.topic: GIPS: firm definition and objectives
questions.title: Objectives of the GIPS Standards
questions.stem: Describe three objectives of the GIPS standards.
questions.modelAnswer:
The key lists five; any three suffice:
1. Promote investor interests and instill investor confidence.
2. Ensure accurate and consistent data.
3. Obtain worldwide acceptance of a single standard for calculating and presenting performance.
4. Promote fair, global competition among investment firms.
5. Promote industry self-regulation on a global basis.
questions.keyPrinciple: Five GIPS objectives: investor interest, accurate/consistent data, one global standard, fair competition, self-regulation.

questions.topic: GIPS: presentation and disclosure
questions.title: GIPS-Compliant Items in the Delta Report
questions.context: Delta's Equities World MSCI Composite report (Jul 2017–Dec 2023) includes: definition of the firm; composite assets and % of firm assets (each year); reporting currency CHF; composite creation date 01 July 2017; gross-of-fee returns net of trading expenses with fee schedule; dispersion shown only when more than five portfolios; and 'a complete list and description of all composites is available upon request'. (Full report in Appendix.)
questions.stem: Explain, for three of the statements or disclosures in the report, why each is GIPS-compliant.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any three of (key's list):
- **Definition of the firm:** clearly defines Delta Asset Management.
- **Composite asset values:** shows composite assets and their % of total firm assets.
- **Reporting currency:** shown.
- **Creation date:** shown.
- **Fee disclosure:** fee disclosures provided for the performance figures.
- **Dispersion:** shown when the number of portfolios exceeds five.
- **Composite list:** 'complete list and description of all composites is available upon request'.

The key notes this list may not be complete.
questions.keyPrinciple: GIPS Report items: firm definition, assets, currency, creation date, fees, dispersion (>5 portfolios), composite list.

questions.topic: GIPS: return calculation
questions.title: When Money-Weighted Returns Are Allowed
questions.stem: Describe two instances under the GIPS standards in which firms may use money-weighted returns instead of time-weighted returns.
questions.modelAnswer:
A firm may present money-weighted returns if it **has control over the external cash flows** and:
1. the portfolios are **closed-end, fixed life or fixed commitment**; or
2. **illiquid investments are a significant part** of the investment strategy.
questions.keyPrinciple: Money-weighted returns: firm controls flows AND (closed-end/fixed-life or significant illiquid investments).

questions.topic: GIPS: presentation and disclosure
questions.title: Non-Compliant Elements in the Sonesta Report
questions.context: Sonesta's Fixed Income Fund report (2015–2023) shows gross and net returns, benchmark, number of accounts, internal dispersion and total firm assets (£bn). Notable footnotes: Sonesta is a subsidiary of Sonesta LLC; composite created 01 Jan 2010; benchmark is the FTSE Fixed Income Sustainable Finance index; dispersion is asset-weighted; accounts include fixed-income returns carved out of a balanced composite. (Full report in Appendix.)
questions.stem: Identify three elements of Exhibit 1 and the related footnotes that are not GIPS-compliant. Justify each with one reason.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any three of (key's list; it notes the list may be incomplete):
- **Firm definition missing.** The footnote only notes a parent relationship.
- **Composite assets missing.** Must show composite assets and either % of firm assets or total firm assets at each period end.
- **Only nine years shown (2015–2023).** At least 10 years are needed once five years have been met, so one more year is required.
- **Management fee schedule not disclosed.**
- **Dispersion missing for 2017, 2018, 2019.** Required when the composite has more than five portfolios for the full year; 2015–2016 (<5 accounts) are fine.
- **List of composites disclosure missing.**
- **Composite description missing.**
- **Benchmark may be misspecified:** nothing indicates the composite invests only in sustainable investments.
- **Valuation policy disclosure missing.**
questions.keyPrinciple: Missing: firm definition, composite assets, 10-year record, fees, dispersion (>5), composite list/description, valuation policy.
questions.flag: The key's 'benchmark may be misspecified' item is hedged ('may'), and the key's 'Note that the answers ... may not be a complete list'. Treat that item as the key's judgment, not a clear rule. I didn't independently check the nine-year count beyond the exhibit (2015–2023 = nine years).

questions.topic: GIPS: verification
questions.title: Non-Compliant Verification Statement
questions.context: Sonesta states: 'The Fixed Income Fund results for 2023 were independently verified. The Fixed Income Fund was found to be in compliance with the GIPS standards. The verification report is available upon request.'
questions.stem: Identify two elements of Sonesta's statement that are not GIPS-compliant.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Verification must be **firm-wide**; the statement covers only the Fixed Income Fund.
- It is limited to **2023**; the key says verification must cover all periods shown in Exhibit 1.
- A firm **cannot claim a single composite is 'in compliance'**.
questions.keyPrinciple: Verification: whole firm, not one composite; a composite can't be 'in compliance'.
questions.flag: The key says verification 'must be done for all periods shown'. The key's own answer to GP-31 says covering all periods is only recommended, not required. The two answers conflict; I report both as the key states them.

questions.topic: GIPS: verification
questions.title: WCM's Verification Claim
questions.context: Wryte Capital Management (WCM) says its US Large-Cap Equity Composite has been independently verified; the verification report was issued only for the composite, not WCM, and states that during 2009–2011 WCM complied with composite construction requirements and that its policies are designed to comply. (Full text in Appendix.)
questions.stem: Is WCM most likely correct in claiming compliance based on the verification report?

choices.text: No, because of the level at which verification is claimed
No, because of the time frame for which verification is claimed

A.text: Not correct: see B.

B.text: **No, because of the level at which verification is claimed.** A single verification report must cover the whole firm; verification cannot be done on a composite, and firms must not state a composite is 'verified'.

C.text: The minimum initial verification period is one year (or since inception if shorter); covering all periods is recommended, not required.

questions.keyPrinciple: Verification is firm-wide; minimum period one year; all periods recommended.

questions.topic: GIPS: return calculation
questions.title: WCM Calculation Methodology
questions.context: WCM's Note 1: time-weighted returns; sub-period returns geometrically linked; cash equivalents included; returns calculated quarterly or when large external cash flows (as defined by WCM) occur.
questions.stem: WCM’s methodology for calculating performance, as disclosed in Note 1, is least likely consistent with GIPS standards for:

A.text: Calculating returns when a large external cash flow occurs is compliant.

B.text: Geometric linking of sub-period returns is required and done.

C.text: **Frequency of return calculations.** GIPS requires monthly returns for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2001.

questions.keyPrinciple: Monthly returns required (post-2001); large flows → revalue; link geometrically.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: WCM Composite Construction
questions.context: WCM's Note 2: the composite includes all actual fee-paying portfolios holding large-cap stocks; non-discretionary portfolios are not in any composite; the large-cap model portfolio is not in any composite.
questions.stem: Is WCM most likely compliant with GIPS standards required for composite construction as disclosed in Note 2?

choices.text: No, because of how the large-cap model portfolio is treated
No, because of how non-discretionary portfolios are treated

A.text: **Yes.** It includes all actual fee-paying portfolios managed on a discretionary basis.

B.text: The model portfolio's exclusion is compliant (not actual assets).

C.text: Excluding non-discretionary portfolios is compliant.

questions.keyPrinciple: Composites: actual, fee-paying, discretionary only.

questions.topic: GIPS: return calculation
questions.title: Gross-of-Fees Treatment in WCM Note 4
questions.context: WCM's Note 4: gross-of-fees returns are before investment management fees but after trading expenses, which include custodial fees. Clients pay a flat 75 bp on month-end account value plus a 10 bp performance fee when the composite beats the benchmark by 100 bp.
questions.stem: With respect to gross-of-fees returns, Note 4 is least likely compliant with GIPS required standards in its treatment of:

A.text: **Trading expenses.** Only direct trading expenses should be deducted in gross-of-fees returns. Custodial fees are not a component of direct trading expenses.

B.text: The key says performance fees are a component of the investment management fee and must not be part of the gross-of-fees return. Note 4 does present gross returns before management fees. *(Key's wording is ambiguous; see flag.)*

C.text: Month-end account value may be used to calculate fees.

questions.keyPrinciple: Gross-of-fees: deduct direct trading expenses only; custody fees are not trading expenses.
questions.flag: The key's reasoning for B is ambiguous: it says performance fees must not be part of gross returns, and Note 4 says gross returns are before management fees, so B reads as compliant. A is the key's answer.

questions.topic: GIPS: presentation and disclosure
questions.title: Internal Dispersion Measures
questions.context: Walter: *"Standard deviation has the advantage of comparability across investment firms. Other measures, such as the high/low range and the interquartile range, are skewed by outliers."*
questions.stem: With respect to the relative merits of internal dispersion measures, Walter is least likely correct about:

A.text: Walter is right that the high–low range is skewed by outliers.

B.text: Walter is right that standard deviation allows comparability across firms.

C.text: **Interquartile range.** It covers only the middle 50% of portfolio returns, excluding extremes, so it is not affected by outliers.

questions.keyPrinciple: Dispersion: SD comparable across firms; range skewed by outliers; interquartile range robust to outliers.

questions.topic: GIPS: valuation
questions.title: WCM's Valuation Hierarchy
questions.context: WCM's hierarchy: (1) observable quoted prices for similar investments in active markets; (2) quoted prices for similar investments in markets that are not active; (3) market-based inputs other than quoted prices that are not observable; (4) estimates from quantitative models and assumptions when no quotes or market inputs exist.
questions.stem: Is Walter’s response to McGourn’s inquiry regarding WCM’s valuation hierarchy most likely correct?

choices.text: No, Item 4 from the valuation hierarchy should be excluded
No, the valuation hierarchy should be reordered as Item 2, Item 1, Item 3, and Item 4

A.text: **Yes.** The key says the hierarchy is GIPS-compliant.

B.text: Item 4 is part of the GIPS hierarchy (subjective, unobservable inputs).

C.text: Reordering is not needed.

questions.keyPrinciple: Valuation order: identical quoted → similar active → inactive-market quotes → observable market inputs → subjective inputs.
questions.flag: WCM's Item 3 says 'not observable'; the key's own hierarchy in GP-41 says 'observable' for that step. The key still marks WCM's hierarchy as compliant.

questions.topic: GIPS: firm definition and objectives
questions.title: Entities That May Claim GIPS Compliance
questions.stem: Which of the following entities may claim compliance with the GIPS standards?

choices.text: A division of an investment management firm
A custodian that provides performance measurement services
A firm that provides software used to calculate composite returns

A.text: **A division of an investment management firm** (if held out as a distinct business entity).

B.text: Custodians and other third-party performance measurement providers can't claim compliance.

C.text: Software firms can't claim compliance.

questions.keyPrinciple: Only investment firms (or subsidiaries/divisions held out as distinct) may claim; consultants, software and custodians can't.

questions.topic: GIPS: verification
questions.title: What Clients Can Be Confident About
questions.stem: According to the GIPS standards, prospective clients and investors evaluating the historical performance of GIPS-compliant firms can be confident that:

choices.text: the performance presented is guaranteed to be accurate.
input data and methodologies used by the firms have been reviewed and approved by CFA Institute.
rates of return have been calculated using a common set of valuation principles and methodological guidelines.

A.text: The standards do not guarantee accuracy.

B.text: CFA Institute doesn't review or approve firms' data and methodologies.

C.text: **Rates of return were calculated using a common set of valuation principles and methodological guidelines.**

questions.keyPrinciple: GIPS compliance → comparability, not guaranteed accuracy or CFA Institute approval.

questions.topic: GIPS: return calculation
questions.title: Modified Dietz for April
questions.context: Beginning value $95,000 (1 April); ending $101,650 (30 April); $5,000 inflow at end of day 10 April (not large).
questions.stem: A portfolio has a beginning value of $95,000 on 1 April and an ending value of $101,650 on 30 April. It received a $5,000 cash inflow at the end of the day on 10 April that was not considered a large cash flow. Using the Modified Dietz method, the portfolio's return for April is closest to:

B.text: 1.74% = 1,650 ÷ 95,000, i.e., cash flow not weighted in the denominator (1.737%).

questions.keyPrinciple: Modified Dietz weight = days flow was in portfolio ÷ days in period (end-of-day flow on day 10 → 20/30).

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Non-Fee-Paying Portfolios
questions.stem: A firm manages fee-paying and non-fee-paying portfolios using a similar strategy. According to the GIPS standards, the non-fee-paying portfolios:

choices.text: must be excluded from the composite.
must be included in a separate composite from the fee-paying portfolios.
may be included in the composite, but additional disclosures may be required.

A.text: They need not be excluded.

B.text: No separate composite is required.

C.text: **May be included, but additional disclosures may be required.** Non-fee-paying discretionary segregated accounts and pooled funds may be included.

questions.keyPrinciple: Non-fee-paying discretionary portfolios: may be in composites, with disclosure.

questions.topic: GIPS: valuation
questions.title: Next Step in the Valuation Hierarchy
questions.stem: In the GIPS valuation hierarchy, if quoted prices for similar investments in active markets are not available or appropriate, which valuation input is recommended as the next to use?

choices.text: The most recent actual valuation for the investment
Quoted prices for similar investments in markets that are not active
Market-based inputs, other than quoted prices, that are observable for the investment

A.text: Most recent actual valuation is not the next step.

B.text: **Quoted prices for similar investments in markets that are not active.**

C.text: Observable market-based inputs come only after inactive-market quotes.

questions.keyPrinciple: Order: identical (active) → similar (active) → inactive-market quotes → observable inputs → subjective inputs.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Seed Money Portfolios
questions.stem: An investment management firm creates a new strategy and manages portfolios with its own assets using this strategy. These seed money portfolios:

choices.text: are not permitted to be included in the firm composites.
can only be included in appropriate firm composites after the strategy has an established track record of at least three years.
can be included from inception in appropriate firm composites, subject to any presentation and reporting requirements related to the inclusion of non-fee-paying portfolios in composites.

A.text: Internally funded portfolios aren't barred.

B.text: There's no minimum track record for inclusion.

C.text: **Can be included from inception**, subject to the presentation and reporting requirements for non-fee-paying portfolios.

questions.keyPrinciple: Seed capital portfolios can be in composites from inception (non-fee-paying rules apply).

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Too Few Composites vs Too Many
questions.stem: Compared to creating multiple specific composites, grouping diverse portfolios together into a single composite may:

choices.text: produce a wide dispersion of portfolio returns.

A.text: Unnecessary costs come from *too many* composites.

B.text: Compromising client confidentiality comes from too many (narrow) composites.

C.text: **Produce a wide dispersion of portfolio returns.** Too few composites can group diverse portfolios in an overly broad composite.

questions.keyPrinciple: Too few composites → wide dispersion; too many → cost, tiny composites, confidentiality risk.

questions.topic: GIPS: composite construction
questions.title: Terminated Portfolio Cut-Off (August)
questions.context: Monthly composite returns. Notified 15 August of termination effective 31 August, told to stop trading immediately.
questions.stem: An investment management firm that calculates composites using monthly portfolio returns is informed on 15 August that its management contract is being terminated effective 31 August and is instructed to stop trading immediately. According to the GIPS standards, the firm should include the portfolio in its composite through:

A.text: **31 July.** Terminated portfolios are included through the last full measurement period prior to notification.

B.text: 15 August is not a month-end.

C.text: 31 August is the contract end.

questions.keyPrinciple: Terminated portfolio included through last full period before discretion ended.

questions.topic: GIPS: presentation and disclosure
questions.title: Years of Performance Required
questions.context: A firm has claimed GIPS compliance for 12 years.
questions.stem: A firm has claimed compliance with the GIPS standards for the past 12 years. To meet the minimum requirements of the GIPS standards, the firm is required to present GIPS-compliant annual performance for:

A.text: Five years is the starting minimum, not the ongoing requirement.

B.text: **10 years.** At least 5 years initially, extended each year until 10 are presented.

C.text: Only the most recent 10 years are required.

questions.keyPrinciple: Minimum: 5 years, building to 10. More than 10 not required.

questions.topic: GIPS: verification
questions.title: Verification Statement That Is Most Accurate
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about verification of GIPS compliance is most accurate?

choices.text: A verification report may be issued only with respect to the entire firm
Verification provides assurance that specific composite returns are correctly calculated and presented
GIPS standards recommend that firms have a verification performed by the firm's internal audit department

A.text: **A verification report may be issued only for the entire firm.**

B.text: Verification doesn't give assurance that specific composite returns are correct.

C.text: GIPS recommends a qualified, independent third party, not internal audit.

questions.keyPrinciple: Verification: firm-wide, third-party, no composite-level assurance.

questions.topic: Index benchmarks: construction, requirements, selection by characteristics and HHI
questions.title: Requirements for an Index-Based Strategy
questions.context: Tong's statements: (1) a free-float adjustment to a market-cap weighted index lowers its liquidity; (2) an index provider using a buffering policy makes the index more investable.
questions.stem: Which of Tong’s statements regarding equity index benchmarks is (are) correct?

A.text: Statement 1 is wrong: a free-float adjustment excludes shares held by founders, governments or other companies, so index weights reflect true liquidity. It does not lower it.

B.text: **Only Statement 2.** An index must be rule based, transparent and investable. Buffering makes transitions gradual and orderly, so the index is more investable.

C.text: Statement 1 is wrong, so 'both' can't be right.

questions.keyPrinciple: Investable index = rule based + transparent + investable. Float adjustment and buffering improve investability.

questions.topic: Index benchmarks: construction, requirements, selection by characteristics and HHI
questions.title: Benchmark Matching Low Beta, High Yield, Low P/E and P/B
questions.context: Winthrop wants a Canadian equity benchmark covering all sectors, highly liquid well-known companies, low beta, high dividend yield, low P/E and low P/B.
questions.stem: To satisfy Winthrop’s benchmark and security selection specifications, the Canadian equity index benchmark Tong selects should be:

choices.text: small capitalization with a core tilt.
large capitalization with a value tilt.

A.text: Small caps are riskier than large caps; Winthrop wants low beta.

B.text: **Large cap with a value tilt.** Large caps are the most liquid and lower risk; value stocks have high yields and low P/E and P/B.

C.text: Growth stocks have high P/Es, high momentum and EPS growth, which conflicts with his low-P/E requirement.

questions.keyPrinciple: Large cap = liquid. Value = high yield, low P/E, low P/B. Growth = high P/E.

questions.topic: Replication methods: full replication, sampling, optimization, tracking error, ETFs vs mutual funds
questions.title: Which ETF Has the Highest Expected Tracking Error
questions.context: Full replication. Constituents: XIU 60 (expense 0.18%), SPY 506 (0.10%), EFA 933 (0.33%).
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1 and assuming a full-replication indexing approach, the tracking error is expected to be highest for:

A.text: XIU has the fewest constituents (60), so the lowest tracking error potential.

B.text: SPY has 506 constituents, fewer than EFA, and the lowest expense ratio (0.10%).

C.text: **EFA.** More constituents → higher tracking error under full replication (more trading, harder to hold every name at exact weights), and EFA also has the highest expense ratio (0.33%).

questions.keyPrinciple: Tracking error rises with number of constituents, and costs (fees) drag excess return.

questions.topic: Replication methods: full replication, sampling, optimization, tracking error, ETFs vs mutual funds
questions.title: Identifying Full Replication
questions.context: Method 1: requires all index constituents to be available for trading and liquid; significant brokerage commissions can occur when the index is large.
questions.stem: Method 1’s portfolio construction process is most likely:

A.text: Optimization uses sophisticated software and covariances to build a portfolio with fewer securities.

B.text: **Full replication.** The manager holds every index security at index weights, needing all constituents to be liquid and tradable, and sufficient assets. Commissions can be large when the index is large.

C.text: Stratified sampling holds only a sample from each strata, so it doesn't need all constituents.

questions.keyPrinciple: Full replication: hold all index securities at index weights; costly for large indexes.

questions.topic: Replication methods: full replication, sampling, optimization, tracking error, ETFs vs mutual funds
questions.title: Identifying Stratified Sampling
questions.context: Method 2: for an index with many constituents and/or low assets under management; simple and technically unsophisticated; fewer securities than the index, lower commissions.
questions.stem: Method 2’s portfolio construction process is most likely:

A.text: Optimization needs technical sophistication (software/algorithms), so it isn't 'simple'.

B.text: Full replication holds all securities.

C.text: **Stratified sampling.** Used for indexes with many constituents or when assets are small; the portfolio holds a sample from each stratum.

questions.keyPrinciple: Stratified sampling: simple, fewer securities. Optimization: sophisticated.

questions.topic: Replication methods: full replication, sampling, optimization, tracking error, ETFs vs mutual funds
questions.title: Revenue to Offset Costs: Securities Lending
questions.context: Tong adds that portfolio stocks may generate incremental revenue, offsetting administrative costs but creating counterparty and collateral risks.
questions.stem: The method that Tong suggests to add incremental revenue is:

A.text: Program trading is buying or selling many stocks at once; it doesn't generate revenue.

B.text: **Securities lending.** The lender earns fees that offset management costs, but is exposed to the borrower's credit risk (counterparty) and to market risk on the posted collateral.

C.text: Attribution analysis explains sources of return; it doesn't generate revenue.

questions.keyPrinciple: Securities lending income offsets fund costs; risks: counterparty and collateral.

questions.topic: Equity index futures: equitizing cash, risks, sizing
questions.title: Futures Needed to Equitize a USD Bonus
questions.context: USD 5,750,000 bonus arrives in one month; 15% policy weight to US equity; S&P 500 futures price 2,464.29; E-mini multiplier 50.
questions.stem: In preparation for receipt of the performance bonus, Tong should immediately:

choices.text: buy two US E-mini equity futures contracts.
sell nine US E-mini equity futures contracts.
buy seven US E-mini equity futures contracts.

A.text: Two contracts would cover only about 29% of the target exposure.

B.text: The view is bullish, so she buys, not sells.

questions.keyPrinciple: Contracts = (allocation × cash) / (futures price × multiplier).

questions.topic: Equity index futures: equitizing cash, risks, sizing
questions.title: Risk of Using Equity Index Futures
questions.context: Tong cautions that futures returns can differ from the underlying index, primarily because of dividends and splits.
questions.stem: The risk that Tong discloses regarding the equity futures strategy is most likely:

A.text: **Basis risk.** The hedging/overlay instrument doesn't match the exposure perfectly; futures track only the index price, so dividends cause differences. (Stock splits don't affect performance comparisons.)

B.text: Not the risk she described: the difference she cites comes from dividends and splits, not currency.

C.text: Not the risk she described: she cites differences between futures and index returns.

questions.keyPrinciple: Futures vs index differences (dividends, mismatches) = basis risk.

questions.topic: Factor-based and smart-beta strategies vs market-cap weighting
questions.title: Factor-Based Momentum vs Market-Cap Weighting
questions.context: McMahon suggests a factor-based momentum strategy for international stocks.
questions.stem: Compared with broad-market-cap weighting, the international equity strategy suggested by McMahon is most likely to:

choices.text: be based on the efficient market hypothesis.
overweight stocks that recently experienced large price decreases.

A.text: **Concentrate risk exposure.** Factor strategies concentrate risk in the chosen factor, leaving investors vulnerable when that factor is out of favor.

B.text: Momentum conflicts with market efficiency (it's not based on the EMH); cap weighting is the one closer to it.

C.text: Momentum overweights stocks that have recently gone up, not those that fell.

questions.keyPrinciple: Single-factor strategies concentrate risk (vs cap-weighted).

questions.topic: Factor-based and smart-beta strategies vs market-cap weighting
questions.title: Classifying a Momentum Strategy
questions.context: Factor-based momentum strategy (excess price return vs market over a period).
questions.stem: The international strategy suggested by McMahon is most likely characterized as:

A.text: Risk-based strategies reduce volatility (e.g., low volatility).

B.text: **Return oriented.** Momentum is a return-oriented factor.

C.text: Diversification-oriented strategies include equal weighting and similar.

questions.keyPrinciple: Factor strategy types: return oriented (momentum, value), risk oriented (low vol), diversification oriented (equal weight).

questions.topic: Index benchmarks: construction, requirements, selection by characteristics and HHI
questions.title: What a Price-Weighted Index Holds
questions.context: The US large-cap benchmark is price-weighted, 150 stocks.
questions.stem: The initial benchmark used for the US large-cap allocation:

choices.text: holds the same number of shares in each component stock.

A.text: Price-weighted indexes are affected by splits (a split cuts the price and weight).

B.text: Liquidity-weighted isn't a feature of price weighting.

C.text: **Holds the same number of shares in each stock.** Weight = price / sum of prices, i.e., a portfolio of one share of each constituent.

questions.keyPrinciple: Price-weighted index = one share of each stock; splits change weights.

questions.topic: Index benchmarks: construction, requirements, selection by characteristics and HHI
questions.title: Effective Number of Stocks From the HHI
questions.context: HHI of the benchmark = 0.0286.
questions.stem: Based on its HHI, the initial US large-cap benchmark most likely has:

choices.text: an effective number of stocks of approximately 35.
individual stocks held in approximately equal weights.

A.text: 4.29 isn't a concentration measure here; the HHI is 0.0286.

B.text: **≈35 effective stocks.** HHI = Σ w_i²; effective N = 1/HHI = 1/0.0286 = 34.97.

C.text: Equal weights across 150 stocks would give an HHI of 1/150 = 0.0067; 0.0286 means a concentrated cap/price structure, so weights are not approximately equal.

questions.keyPrinciple: HHI = Σ w²; effective number of stocks = 1/HHI.

questions.topic: Return attribution: sector and factor contributions to active return
questions.title: Sector Contributing Most to Underperformance
questions.context: Contribution = sector return × weight. Foundation vs benchmark weights: IT 18.71% vs 19.06%; Staples 16.52% vs 16.10%; Energy 9.38% vs 9.53%; Utilities 8.76% vs 8.25%; Financials 6.89% vs 6.62%.
questions.stem: Using a sector attribution analysis based on Exhibit 1, which US large-cap sector is the primary contributor to the portfolio’s underperformance relative to the benchmark?

A.text: Utilities difference is −0.02% (−0.34% vs −0.32%), smaller than IT's.

B.text: Consumer staples difference is +0.05%, positive.

C.text: **Information technology.** Contribution difference (foundation − benchmark) is −0.04% (2.01% vs 2.05%), the largest negative. IT had a positive return but was underweight.

questions.keyPrinciple: Simple sector attribution: (weight × return) difference vs benchmark; underweighting a positive-return sector hurts.

questions.topic: Replication methods: full replication, sampling, optimization, tracking error, ETFs vs mutual funds
questions.title: Lowest Tracking Error Portfolio
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, which portfolio will most likely have the lowest tracking error?

A.text: Highest cash (6.95%, cash drag) and highest fee.

B.text: Middle on both.

C.text: **Portfolio 3.** Lowest cash holding (2.13%) and lowest fee (0.07%).

questions.keyPrinciple: Cash drag and fees raise tracking error.

questions.topic: Factor-based and smart-beta strategies vs market-cap weighting
questions.title: Most Accurate Comment on Factor Approaches
questions.context: Parker: value factor funds seek to lower downside risk; fundamental weighting overweights overpriced and underweights underpriced stocks; single-factor funds concentrate risk relative to cap weighting.
questions.stem: Which comment by Parker regarding factor-based approaches is most accurate? The comment regarding:

A.text: Value funds focus on valuation measures, not volatility.

B.text: **Single-factor funds.** Relative to cap weighting they concentrate risk in the factor's characteristic.

C.text: Fundamental weighting is meant to do the opposite: overweight stocks priced below intrinsic value and underweight overpriced ones.

questions.keyPrinciple: Single-factor → concentrated risk. Fundamental weighting targets mispricing.

questions.topic: Replication methods: full replication, sampling, optimization, tracking error, ETFs vs mutual funds
questions.title: Manager Blending Stratified Sampling and Optimization
questions.context:
| | Manager A | Manager B | Manager C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Benchmark | S&P 500 | MSCI EAFE | Russell 3000 |
| Holdings fund/index | 498/500 | 800/928 | 1,200/3,000 |
| Futures | cash drag | currency overlay | none |
| Accounts for covariances | No | No | Yes |
| Tracking error | 0.06% | 1.97% | 0.34% |
| Excess return | 0.10% | 2.10% | −0.15% |
questions.stem: In Exhibit 1, the replication manager that most likely blends stratified sampling and optimization is:

A.text: Manager A holds 498 of 500 with tiny tracking error: full replication.

B.text: Manager B holds 800 of 928 (sampling) and ignores covariances (no optimization), with a large tracking error.

C.text: **Manager C.** Holds 1,200 of 3,000 (sampling) and accounts for covariances (optimization), giving lower tracking error than sampling alone.

questions.keyPrinciple: Covariances accounted for → optimization. Fewer holdings than index → sampling.

questions.topic: Replication methods: full replication, sampling, optimization, tracking error, ETFs vs mutual funds
questions.title: Evaluating Statements About Manager B
questions.context: Manager B (MSCI EAFE, tracking error 1.97%, excess return 2.10%, currency overlay). Parker: (1) he faced more volatile markets, from tracking errors; (2) he used currency overlays to lever returns; (3) his excess return looks like luck, not skill.
questions.stem: Which of Parker’s statements about Manager B in Exhibit 1 is most appropriate? The statement about:

A.text: **Excess return.** A replication manager aims to track the index; the proper measure of skill is tracking error, and B's is the highest of the three. Excess return of 2.10% is then luck, not skill.

B.text: Tracking error measures the volatility of excess return, not market volatility.

C.text: A currency overlay hedges foreign-currency returns; it doesn't lever them.

questions.keyPrinciple: Tracking error = volatility of (portfolio − index) return; high TE with high excess return suggests luck.

questions.topic: Factor-based and smart-beta strategies vs market-cap weighting
questions.title: Primary Strategy of a Multi-Factor Fund
questions.context: MultiFAK vs benchmark: Yield 28%/28%; Momentum 14%/17%; Low Volatility 31%/28%; Quality 27%/27%; 91 vs 100 stocks.
questions.stem: From Exhibit 2, MultiFAK’s primary strategy is most likely:

A.text: **Risk reduction.** Overweights low volatility, underweights momentum (return oriented), and holds fewer securities (not diversification).

B.text: Fewer securities than the index isn't a diversification approach.

C.text: It underweights momentum, the return-oriented factor.

questions.keyPrinciple: Overweight low volatility = risk-oriented strategy.

questions.topic: Return attribution: sector and factor contributions to active return
questions.title: Excess Return From Active Factor Weighting
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the excess return of MultiFAK arising from active factor weighting is closest to:

A.text: **0.04%.** Only Momentum and Low Volatility weights differ: (0.14 − 0.17)(8.1%) + (0.31 − 0.28)(9.3%) = −0.243% + 0.279% = 0.036% ≈ 0.04%. Quality's return gap (4.9% vs 4.1%) is security selection (0.216%), not factor weighting.

B.text: 0.25% is the total active effect (0.252%): factor weighting plus Quality selection.

C.text: 0.28% is the Low Volatility overweight alone and ignores the Momentum underweight.

questions.keyPrinciple: Factor weighting effect = Σ (w_p − w_b) × factor return (same return in both); selection = w × (R_p − R_b).

questions.topic: Equity index futures: equitizing cash, risks, sizing
questions.title: Cost-Efficient Fix After a Market Correction
questions.context: Allocation drifted to 51% equity, 2% cash, 47% fixed income vs policy 60/40 (±5%), cash max 2%. IPS permits active managers and derivatives (cash drag/allocation guidelines achievable with derivatives, notional ≤10% of assets); no index ETFs.
questions.stem: The most cost efficient strategy to deal with Dashe’s concerns following the equity market correction is a(n):

choices.text: rebalancing to policy weights by selling bonds and purchasing equities.
rebalancing by replacing the highest-tracking-error manager with low-cost index exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

A.text: **Overlay with equity index futures.** Brings equity exposure to the guideline range without disrupting the active managers and with low tracking error.

B.text: Selling bonds and buying equities incurs trading costs and disrupts managers.

C.text: The IPS doesn't allow index ETFs.

questions.keyPrinciple: Futures overlay = cheapest way to rebalance toward policy weights.

questions.topic: Replication methods: full replication, sampling, optimization, tracking error, ETFs vs mutual funds
questions.title: Sources of Positive Quarterly Excess Return for an Index ETF
questions.context: PGQ tracks the S&P 500 Top 50 (float-adjusted, quarterly rebalance with buffer) via replication; positive excess returns in some quarters with no constituent changes.
questions.stem: Discuss one potential source of positive quarterly excess returns for PGQ, including how it contributes.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any one of:
- **Securities lending:** long holders' shares are in demand by short sellers; lending income offsets costs and, for low-cost index funds, can make net expenses negative, so the fund earns more than the index.
- **Cash drag in a falling market:** equity indexes hold no cash, so cash from dividends, sale proceeds and investor contributions creates tracking error; when the market falls, uninvested cash doesn't suffer the index decline, giving positive excess return (negative when the market rises).
questions.keyPrinciple: Index fund excess return sources: securities lending income; cash drag in down markets.

questions.topic: Factor-based and smart-beta strategies vs market-cap weighting
questions.title: Factors Characterizing a Top-10 Index Product
questions.context: Exhibit 1: S&P 500 Top 10 vs S&P 500: P/E 32.8 vs 26.5; P/B 26.7 vs 4.6; yield 0.45% vs 1.19%; average market cap $880bn vs $97bn; 10-yr return 18.95% vs 13.06%; 10-yr volatility 19.04% vs 15.29%.
questions.stem: Identify two factors other than Market that could characterize the product and justify each with one reason.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any two of:
- **Growth (or value):** higher mean P/E than the S&P 500 (positive growth / negative value exposure).
- **Size:** larger mean float-adjusted market cap (negative relative exposure to size).
- **Yield:** lower dividend yield (negative exposure to yield).
- **Momentum:** return history showing greater momentum (positive exposure).
- **Volatility:** higher annualized volatility (negative exposure to low volatility).
questions.keyPrinciple: Characterize an index by its tilt on factors: size, value/growth, yield, momentum, volatility, quality.

questions.topic: Replication methods: full replication, sampling, optimization, tracking error, ETFs vs mutual funds
questions.title: Tracking an Index With No Listed Derivatives: Equity Swap
questions.context: Ultra-Cap 10 SMA ($12m) must track the S&P 500 Top 10; no full replication, sampling or optimization; and not by building a portfolio of the index's securities. No US ETFs, funds or listed derivatives track this index.
questions.stem: Discuss a portfolio management approach for the account and how it generates returns that track the index.
questions.modelAnswer:
**An equity index swap.** Futures/options don't exist for this index, and its tracking error vs listed-futures indexes is too large to proxy; a swap can be set up on virtually any index with a willing counterparty.

OTC contract for a set period: the account **receives the index return** and **pays** the counterparty a market reference rate (typically floating) plus an agreed fee. It needs no trading by PAM and little information beyond the index return.
questions.keyPrinciple: No listed derivatives and can't hold constituents → OTC equity index swap (receive index return, pay MRR + spread).

questions.context: LVEU ETF: 98 holdings; LVEUX mutual fund: 99 holdings; index tracks 205 stocks. Equity futures only for cash flows; no listed futures on the index.

questions.title: Why ETF Tracking Error Is Higher Than the Mutual Fund's
questions.context: Index and mutual fund (LVEUX) prices use European primary-market closes (converted at that time); the ETF (LVEU) trades in the US until the US close. Management fees: 0.22% vs 0.24%.
questions.stem: The factor that increases the published tracking error of the LVEU ETF but not the LVEUX mutual fund is most likely the:

choices.text: effect of market bid–ask spreads on trade prices.
difference in pricing practices between the index and the fund.

A.text: Fees differ by only 2 bp, minimal and in the ETF's favor.

B.text: ETF daily returns use closing prices that don't include spreads; authorized participant creations/redemptions are in kind with no spread cost to the fund.

C.text: **Pricing practices.** The index and the mutual fund use European closing prices and FX at that time; the ETF's price is its last US trade, reflecting later FX and sentiment moves, which raises its published tracking error.

questions.keyPrinciple: ETF price (US close) vs index (primary-market close) timing mismatch → published tracking error.

questions.topic: Replication methods: full replication, sampling, optimization, tracking error, ETFs vs mutual funds
questions.title: Investor Cost Unique to the ETF
questions.context: Purchase costs: ETF commissions ≈0.25%, mutual fund load 0.25%.
questions.stem: The factor that decreases a fund investor’s realized excess return in the LVEU ETF but not the LVEUX mutual fund is most likely the:

choices.text: effect of market bid–ask spreads on trade prices.
difference in pricing practices between the index and the fund.

A.text: Fees are lower for the ETF (0.22% vs 0.24%).

B.text: **Bid–ask spreads.** ETF investors trade at market prices and bear the spread; mutual fund shares trade directly with the fund at the daily price with no spread.

C.text: Pricing-practice differences affect tracking error randomly, not consistently negatively for investors.

questions.keyPrinciple: ETF investors pay bid–ask spreads; mutual fund investors transact at NAV.

B.text: Transparency claim is correct: factor selection, weighting and rebalancing are transparent (and replicable, causing crowding).

questions.topic: Return attribution: sector and factor contributions to active return
questions.title: Share of Excess Return From Active Factor Weighting
questions.context: River Valley vs benchmark (weight/return): Growth 0.22/7.9% vs 0.25/7.9%; Value 0.19/5.2% vs 0.19/5.2%; Quality 0.29/6.7% vs 0.26/6.7%; Momentum 0.30/3.9% vs 0.30/4.5%. Totals: 5.84% vs 6.06%.
questions.stem: In Exhibit 1, the percentage of the excess return of the River Valley Fund arising from active factor weighting is closest to:

A.text: −0.22% is the total active effect, not the share.

B.text: −0.04% is the factor-weight effect before dividing by the total effect.

C.text: **18.18%.** Factor-weighting effect: Growth (0.22 − 0.25)(7.9%) = −0.24%; Quality (0.29 − 0.26)(6.7%) = +0.20%; sum = −0.04%. Total effect = 5.84% − 6.06% = −0.22%. Share = −0.04/−0.22 = 18.18%. (Momentum's shortfall of −0.18% is security selection.)

questions.keyPrinciple: Share from factor weighting = factor-weight effect ÷ total active effect.
questions.flag: The key's 18.18% uses table values rounded to two decimals (−0.04 / −0.22). Unrounded I get −0.036 / −0.216 = 16.7%. The answer (18.18%) is still the only sensible choice among those offered.

questions.title: Which Manager Is Most Fundamental
questions.context: Furlings: head manager's discretionary sector views (10%+ sector deviations held 12–24 months) plus equal-weighted baskets of 7–10 high-conviction names per sector (~90 total). Asgard: bottom-up fundamental research on <125 stocks but heavy reliance on software, screening and a quantitative risk model. Tokra: factor-score ranking (P/B, 12-month price change, ROA), optimized with risk limits, ~400 holdings.
questions.stem: Which fund manager’s investing approach is most consistent with fundamental management?

A.text: **Furlings.** Top-down and bottom-up, but allocation rests on managers' discretion and judgment; strong emphasis on financial statements, valuation, competitive advantage and governance; a small number of names.

B.text: Asgard has both fundamental and quantitative traits; it depends heavily on technology for screening/ranking and its allocation depends heavily on a quantitative risk model.

C.text: Tokra is quantitative: ranks on quantitative metrics and uses portfolio optimization, with many positions.

questions.keyPrinciple: Fundamental = discretionary, few names, deep company analysis. Quantitative = systematic, many names, optimization.

questions.title: Which Statement About the Managers' Styles Is Incorrect
questions.context: Tokra scores securities on P/B, 12-month price increase, and return on assets.
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the approaches and styles of either Furlings, Asgard, or Tokra is incorrect?

choices.text: Furlings is a top-down sector rotator with a value orientation within sectors.
Asgard is a bottom-up manager with a GARP (growth at a reasonable price) style.
Tokra is a factor-based manager using value, growth, and profitability metrics.

A.text: A is a correct statement: Furlings is a top-down sector rotator, selecting within sectors on relative valuation.

B.text: B is a correct statement: Asgard is bottom-up, favoring reasonable valuations and above-average growth (GARP).

C.text: **C is the incorrect statement.** Tokra is factor based, but its metrics are value (P/B), momentum (12-month price change) and profitability (ROA); there is no growth proxy such as earnings growth.

questions.keyPrinciple: Read the stem: 'incorrect' questions — the keyed letter is the false statement.

questions.title: Manager Most Likely to Fall Into a Value Trap
questions.context: Value trap: a stock looks cheap on P/E or P/B only because its growth prospects are deteriorating.
questions.stem: Which manager is most likely to get caught in a value trap?

A.text: Furlings' analysts dissect financial statements and competitive landscape for a few names, so they are more likely to spot worsening prospects.

B.text: Asgard targets cash flow growth over the next three years and has tools to evaluate growth, so it is more aware of deteriorating prospects.

C.text: **Tokra.** A quantitative process using historical information and no forward-looking cash flow or profitability expectations may not detect deteriorating prospects.

questions.keyPrinciple: Value trap risk is highest for backward-looking, screen-based value processes.

questions.topic: Shareholder activism: tactics and target characteristics
questions.title: Activist Tactic Least Likely for a Long-Term Engaged Manager
questions.context: Asgard engages with companies as a long-term shareholder using its voice and vote; emphasizes governance and strong balance sheets.
questions.stem: Which activist investing tactic is Asgard least likely to use?

choices.text: Engaging with management by writing letters to management, calling for and explaining suggested changes, and participating in management discussions with analysts or meeting the management team privately
Launching legal proceedings against existing management for breach of fiduciary duties
Proposing restructuring of the balance sheet to better utilize capital and potentially initiate share buybacks or increase dividends

A.text: Engaging management through letters, calls, meetings is consistent with using its voice.

B.text: **Launching legal proceedings against management for breach of fiduciary duty.** Aggressive posturing doesn't fit a long-term, good-governance investor, which wouldn't hold companies with weak governance.

C.text: Proposing balance-sheet restructuring (buybacks, dividends) fits Asgard's strength in cash flow and capital structure analysis.

questions.keyPrinciple: Activist spectrum: constructive engagement → proposals → proxy fights/legal action; governance-focused long-term holders stay at the soft end.

questions.title: Portfolio Characteristics at Odds With Declared Style
questions.context: Key data (Index / Furlings / Asgard / Tokra): P/B 4.8 / 4.30 / 4.35 / 5.4; Net income/assets 2.8% / 4.5% / 4.3% / 3.2%; 12-month momentum 10.5% / 14.0% / 10.0% / 12.0%; EPS growth 11.9% / 11.0% / 13.1% / 10.8%.
questions.stem: Based on the information provided in Exhibits 1 and 2, which manager’s portfolio characteristics is most likely at odds with its declared style?

A.text: Furlings' lower P/B and P/E and higher net income/assets fit a relative-value orientation within sectors.

B.text: Asgard's P/B and expected growth (13.1%) fit reasonable valuation and above-average growth; lower yield, slightly higher P/E and lower momentum aren't inconsistent.

C.text: **Tokra.** It emphasizes P/B, momentum and ROA; momentum and ROA are favorable, but its average P/B (5.4) is higher than the index (4.8), at odds with a value metric. Sector tilts could explain this, but its sector deviation limit is only 3%, which weakens that explanation.

questions.keyPrinciple: Compare the portfolio's characteristics to the index for each declared factor; unexplained gaps need follow-up with the manager.

questions.title: Why Morningstar and Lipper Can Classify a Fund Differently
questions.context: Asgard is a blend fund per Morningstar and a value fund per Lipper.
questions.stem: Leonard is looking at the style classification from Asgard as reported by Morningstar and Thomson Reuters Lipper. He is surprised to find that Asgard is classified as a blend fund by Morningstar and a value fund by Lipper. Which of the following statements is correct?

choices.text: Although the Morningstar methodology classifies securities as either value, growth, or core, the Lipper methodology assumes a stock can have the characteristics of many styles. This approach can result in a different classification for the same portfolio.
The Lipper methodology can only lead to a value or growth classification. It does not offer a core/blend component.

The Morningstar methodology classifies securities as either value, growth, or core by looking at the difference between their respective growth and value scores. It is possible that the Asgard funds hold a balanced exposure to both value and growth and/or core stocks.

A.text: Neither Morningstar nor Lipper assumes a stock belongs to several styles; both place each stock in one category.

B.text: Lipper does have a core classification (sums Z-scores of six characteristics to give value, core or growth).

C.text: **Morningstar uses growth minus value scores.** Value and growth scores (0–100, five proxies each) are subtracted; strongly positive = growth, strongly negative = value, near zero = core. A blend fund can have balanced value/growth exposure and/or dominant core exposure.

questions.keyPrinciple: Morningstar: growth score − value score → growth/core/value. Lipper: sum of Z-scores → value/core/growth.

see risk at the company level rather than the portfolio level.

B.text: **Rebalance at more regular intervals.** Quant portfolios rebalance on a schedule (monthly/quarterly); fundamental managers monitor continuously and trade any time.
