questions.title: Expectations Implied by the Fund's Positioning
questions.context: Exhibit: IG 82% (bm 100); EM 5%; HY 3%; CDO senior (Class A) −10%; CDO subordinated (Class B) +10%; MBS 10%.
questions.stem: Based on Choate’s final comments and the COF portfolio positions in Exhibit 1, Choate is most likely expecting:

choices.text: improved real estate markets and higher interest rate volatility.
lower interest rate volatility and increasing default correlations.
lower interest rate volatility and decreasing default correlations.

A.text: An MBS buyer expects lower, not higher, volatility.

B.text: **Lower interest rate volatility and increasing default correlations.** MBS holders benefit from lower volatility; short Class A / long Class B profits if default correlation rises (mezzanine value rises relative to senior).

C.text: Short Class A / long Class B implies higher, not lower, default correlation.

questions.keyPrinciple: MBS: short volatility. Higher default correlation → mezzanine up relative to senior.

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Least Correct Risk Comment by West
questions.context: C1: IG bonds of the same duration are more sensitive to rates than HY; C2: the four Cs assess both PD and LGD; C3: spread duration is more useful for HY than IG.
questions.stem: Which of West’s comments regarding risk considerations in corporate bonds is least likely correct?

A.text: Correct: IG moves in lockstep with rates; HY is quoted in prices/yields and moves less with rates.

B.text: Correct: the four Cs assess creditworthiness, thus PD and LGD.

C.text: **Comment 3 is incorrect.** Spread duration measures sensitivity to credit spread changes, which is more relevant for IG, where spread volatility rather than outright default loss matters.

questions.keyPrinciple: IG: spread duration; HY: default loss and price level.

questions.topic: Credit spread measures: G-, I-, Z-spread, OAS, ASW and excess spread
questions.title: Spread Quoted to a Treasury of Non-Matching Maturity
questions.context: Dealers quote a spread to Treasuries whose maturity doesn't match the bond's.
questions.stem: In Island’s conversation with West, the spread measure that dealers often quote Island is most likely the:

A.text: I-spread uses same-currency swap rates.

B.text: G-spread uses an actual or interpolated government bond.

C.text: **Benchmark spread.** Yield minus the yield of a recent on-the-run benchmark bond; maturity mismatch is the problem.

questions.keyPrinciple: Benchmark spread = yield − nearest on-the-run govt yield.

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Most Useful Data Item With Unchanged Spreads
questions.context: Candidate items: expected PD, rating agency credit outlook, historical sector default rates.
questions.stem: Assuming no change in credit spreads, which data item that the analysts provide Stone would portfolio managers most likely find useful in their analysis?

A.text: The outlook doesn't enter the excess return formula.

B.text: **Expected probability of default.** EXR ≈ s·t − Δs·SD − t·p·L; with Δs = 0, p and L are the key unknowns.

C.text: Historical sector default rates are used in top-down analysis.

questions.keyPrinciple: Unchanged spreads: relative value = spread vs expected loss (PD × LGD).

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: West's Top-Down Report Structure
questions.context: Section 1 macro factors: corporate profitability, economic growth, currency movements, expected volatility changes, key rate durations, default rates. Section 2 risk measures: average rating, average spread duration, DTS, average OAS, duration, effective convexity.
questions.stem: Is West’s two-section report regarding the top-down approach most likely correctly structured?

choices.text: No. She is incorrect with respect to the macro factors
No, she is incorrect with respect to the risk measurement factors

A.text: Section 1 includes key rate durations.

B.text: **No, incorrect on macro factors.** Key rate durations measure exposure to non-parallel curve shifts; they aren't a macro factor.

C.text: The risk measurements are correct.

questions.keyPrinciple: Macro factors ≠ portfolio risk measures (KRD is a risk measure).

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Stone's Liquidity Comments
questions.context: Stone's three points: (1) trading volume has declined, so liquidity management is less relevant to alpha; (2) spread changes are more pronounced in HY outflows, so macro forecasting helps position for liquidity risk; (3) bid–ask spreads vary over time and are a good indicator of liquidity; wider bid–ask spreads in a downturn create opportunities for PMs to add value.
questions.stem: Stone’s comments to West regarding liquidity risk in credit markets is most likely correct with regard to:

A.text: **Spread changes** (his second point) is correct. Point 1 is wrong: liquidity management has become more relevant to generating alpha. Point 3 is right that bid–ask varies and indicates liquidity but wrong that wider spreads benefit PMs; trading costs are higher.

B.text: His third point is wrong: more volatile markets widen bid–ask spreads, so trading costs detract from performance.

C.text: His first point is wrong: liquidity management has become more relevant to adding alpha.

questions.keyPrinciple: Outflows hit HY spreads harder; wider bid–ask raises trading costs.

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Palma's Out-of-Benchmark Investment Suggestions
questions.context: Stone's three suggestions concern: (A) the credit cycle, (B) spread advantage, (C) local currency investment.
questions.stem: Which of the suggestions Stone outlines for Palma in selecting the proposed investments is most likely correct? The one regarding:

choices.text: the credit cycle is most likely correct.
spread advantage is most likely correct.
local currency investment is most likely correct.

A.text: Credit cycles vary across regions, which can be used to diversify.

B.text: **The spread advantage point is correct.** Hedging FX can offset much of the yield pickup; pegged currencies may not need hedging.

C.text: For pegged currencies, FX hedging may not be needed (exchange rate more stable).

questions.keyPrinciple: Foreign yield pickup must be net of hedging cost.

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Credit Spread Curve of High-Grade Issuers at Economic Peaks
questions.stem: During economic peaks, the credit spread curve of high-grade issuers will most likely:

A.text: **Steepen.** Peaks have stable profitability and defaults, and the spread curve steepens (long spread minus short spread widens).

B.text: Stable curves are typical for high-grade issuers in early expansion/recovery.

C.text: Inverted curves are for low-grade issuers in contraction or early expansion.

questions.keyPrinciple: Peak: IG curve steepens. Contraction: HY curve inverts.

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Lower Recovery Rate and the Credit Spread
questions.context: Spread ≈ LGD × POD; LGD = EE × (1 − RR).
questions.stem: If the recovery rate of an investment-grade bond falls, the bond's credit spread will most likely:

A.text: Spread widens, not contracts.

B.text: LGD changes, so spread changes.

C.text: **Widen.** A lower recovery rate raises LGD, so spread widens.

questions.keyPrinciple: ↓ RR → ↑ LGD → ↑ spread.

questions.topic: Credit spread measures: G-, I-, Z-spread, OAS, ASW and excess spread
questions.title: Yield Spread vs G-Spread
questions.stem: The yield spread for a corporate bond will be the same as the G-spread for that bond if the government benchmark yield curve is:

A.text: They differ if the curve is downward sloping.

B.text: **Flat.** Yield spread uses an on-the-run government bond of similar maturity; G-spread interpolates. Same if the curve is flat.

C.text: They differ if the curve is upward sloping.

questions.keyPrinciple: Flat government curve → yield spread = G-spread.

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Models Using Observable Company-Specific Financial Ratios
questions.stem: Which of the following statistical credit models solve for the probability of default using observable company-specific financial ratios?

choices.text: Both structural credit models and reduced form credit models

A.text: Structural models use market-based variables for asset value and volatility.

B.text: **Only reduced-form models.** They solve for default intensity from financial ratios, recovery assumptions and macro variables.

C.text: Only reduced-form models use company-specific ratios.

questions.keyPrinciple: Reduced-form: observable ratios + macro. Structural: asset value vs liabilities.

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Key Financial Ratios
questions.context: T1: Debt/Capital is more relevant for HY than IG. T2: EBITDA/Interest isn't suitable for firms with high cash flow variability. T3: EBITDA/Total Assets takes account of working capital changes.
questions.stem:
At a training workshop, the following comments are made in relation to key financial ratios:

| Trainee 1 | The Debt/Capital (or leverage) ratio is more relevant for analyzing high-yield issuers than investment-grade issuers. |
|---|---|
| Trainee 2 | The EBITDA/Interest Expense (or coverage) ratio is not suitable for analyzing firms with high cash flow variability. |
| Trainee 3 | The EBITDA/Total Assets (or leverage) ratio takes account of working capital changes. |

Which trainee’s statement is most accurate?

A.text: Debt/Capital is more relevant for IG than HY.

B.text: **Trainee 2.** The coverage ratio is volatile for firms with highly variable cash flow.

C.text: EBITDA ignores capital expenditures and working capital changes.

questions.keyPrinciple: Leverage ratios: IG. Coverage ratios: HY (but volatile when cash flows are variable).

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Rating Category to Underweight
questions.stem:
An investor has formed expectations for the following bond rating categories and intends to underweight the rating category with the lowest expected excess return over the coming year:

| Rating Category | Current OAS | Expected ∆OAS | Expected Loss (POD × LGD) | Effective Spread Duration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0.80% | −0.20% | 0.05% | 6.0 |
| Baa | 1.25% | −0.50% | 0.50% | 5.5 |
| Ba | 2.40% | −0.38% | 0.80% | 4.5 |

Assuming no change in spread duration over the coming year, which rating category ​​​​​​should the investor underweight?

A.text: **A.** E[excess] = OAS − SD × ΔOAS − EL: A 0.80 + 1.20 − 0.05 = 1.95%, the lowest.

questions.keyPrinciple: Underweight the lowest expected excess spread.

questions.stem:
An investor is considering an active portfolio decision across the following bond rating categories:

| Rating Category | Current OAS | Expected Loss (POD × LGD) | Effective Spread Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 1.5% | 0.2% | 4.0 |
| BBB | 2.0% | 0.8% | 5.0 |
| BB | 3.5% | 2.8% | 6.0 |

The credit spreads are expected to remain stable under the current market conditions. Which of the following active bond portfolios is the investor most likely to choose if the objective is to maximize the expected excess return across these rating categories?

choices.text: An equally weighted portfolio of A rated bonds and BB rated bonds
An equally weighted portfolio of A rated bonds and BBB rated bonds
An equally weighted portfolio of BBB rated bonds and BB rated bonds

questions.keyPrinciple: Stable spreads: excess spread = OAS − POD × LGD.

questions.topic: Credit spread measures: G-, I-, Z-spread, OAS, ASW and excess spread
questions.title: Disadvantage of the I-Spread
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the disadvantages of I-spread is most accurate? I-spread:

choices.text: fails to use the term structure of interest rates to estimate yield spreads.
uses government yields as benchmark and lacks consistency over time.

A.text: Maturity mismatch bias is a yield spread drawback; the I-spread addresses it.

B.text: **It fails to use the term structure of interest rates;** it uses a point on the curve, and is limited to option-free bonds.

C.text: Government-benchmark inconsistency over time is a yield spread drawback.

questions.keyPrinciple: I-spread: point on the swap curve, option-free only. Z-spread uses the full curve.

questions.topic: Credit spread measures: G-, I-, Z-spread, OAS, ASW and excess spread
questions.title: Why OAS Is the Most Appropriate Spread Measure
questions.stem: Option-adjusted spread (OAS) is the most appropriate yield spread measure for active fixed-income portfolios because:

choices.text: the measure is not dependent on volatility.
bonds with embedded options will realize the spread implied by the bond’s option-adjusted spread.
the measure provides a consistent basis for comparing yield spreads for option-free and structured fixed income instruments.

A.text: OAS depends heavily on volatility and model assumptions.

B.text: OAS is theoretical; bonds with options are unlikely to realize it.

C.text: **It gives a consistent basis for comparing option-free, callable, putable and structured bonds.**

questions.keyPrinciple: OAS: comparability across bonds with and without options; model-dependent.

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Strategy When Spreads Are Fair and Curves Stable
questions.context: Credit spreads are correctly priced; credit curves stable for six months.
questions.stem: An active credit manager believes that current credit spreads are correctly priced and that the credit curves will remain stable during the next six months. The most appropriate strategy is to:

choices.text: buy credit default swaps for longer maturities.
rebalance the portfolio to improve the portfolio's average credit rating.
increase the investment in longer-dated bonds with a similar rating to the current portfolio.

A.text: Should sell, not buy, longer-maturity CDS protection (adds spread duration).

B.text: Should lower, not improve, the average rating.

C.text: **Increase investment in longer-dated bonds of similar rating** (adds spread duration to earn carry).

questions.keyPrinciple: Static spreads: add spread duration or lower credit quality.

questions.topic: CDS and CDX: pricing, upfront payment, positioning
questions.title: CDX Positioning for HY Spreads Widening More Than IG
questions.stem: An active credit portfolio manager believes that high-yield credit spreads will rise more than investment-grade credit spreads in the next year due to an economic slowdown. To generate excess return, the manager's best course of action is to:

choices.text: sell protection on the high-yield credit default swap index.
buy protection on the investment-grade credit default swap index.
sell protection on the investment-grade credit default swap index and buy protection on the high-yield credit default swap index.

A.text: Should buy, not sell, HY protection.

B.text: Should sell, not buy, IG protection.

C.text: **Sell IG CDX protection and buy HY CDX protection.**

questions.keyPrinciple: Slowdown: short HY (buy protection), long IG (sell protection).

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Fixed Income in Emerging Markets
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about fixed-income investments in emerging markets is most accurate?

choices.text: External debt to GDP is a key measure of financial leverage
Geopolitical risk refers to the ability and willingness of issuers to repay debt
The largest company's credit rating in emerging markets is generally higher than the sovereign credit rating of its domicile

A.text: **External debt to GDP is a key leverage measure** (with reserves/GDP as a liquidity measure).

B.text: Describes sovereign credit risk, not geopolitical risk.

C.text: A sovereign ceiling normally caps corporate ratings at the sovereign's rating.

questions.keyPrinciple: EM: external debt/GDP, reserves/GDP; sovereign ceiling.

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Structured Products for an Economic Recovery With Fewer Defaults
questions.stem: An active fixed-income portfolio manager anticipates an economic recovery accompanied by lower than expected defaults. Which of the following portfolio positioning strategies involving structured products is the most appropriate?

choices.text: Underweight credit exposure using a higher-rated tranche of a collateralized loan obligation
Increase exposure to covered bonds and decrease exposure to mortgage-backed securities
Decrease exposure to A-rated asset-backed securities tranche and increase exposure to BBB-rated asset-backed securities tranche

A.text: Underweighting credit with higher-rated tranches is a downturn position.

B.text: Covered bonds over MBS reduces credit risk, wrong for a recovery.

C.text: **Reduce A-rated ABS tranche, add BBB-rated ABS tranche.** Overweights default risk, benefiting from greater spread tightening in lower-rated tranches.

questions.keyPrinciple: Recovery: add credit risk via lower-rated tranches.

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Structured Products Positioning Statements
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about portfolio positioning strategies involving structured products is most accurate?

choices.text: Covered bonds involve higher credit risk and higher yield than asset-backed securities
Collateralized loan obligation tranches benefit more from short-term rate rises than collateralized debt obligation tranches
Portfolio manager should overweight credit exposure using lower-rated asset-backed securities tranche in an economic downturn

A.text: Covered bonds have lower credit risk and lower yield than ABS.

B.text: **CLO tranches benefit more from short-term rate rises than CDO tranches.** CLOs hold leveraged loans paying MRR plus a spread.

C.text: In a downturn the manager would underweight, not overweight, credit via lower-rated tranches.

questions.keyPrinciple: CLO: floating-rate loans → benefit from rate rises.

questions.topic: Value at risk and tail risk
questions.title: Conditional VaR
questions.stem: A one-day Conditional Value at Risk (1%) of a portfolio can be best described as the:

choices.text: the minimum one-day loss expected to occur 99% of the time.
the average one-day loss if the Value at Risk cutoff is exceeded.
change in portfolio Value at Risk when a new position is added to the portfolio.

A.text: That describes VaR.

B.text: **Average one-day loss if the VaR cutoff is exceeded** (expected tail loss/expected shortfall).

C.text: That describes incremental VaR.

questions.keyPrinciple: CVaR = average loss beyond the VaR cutoff.

questions.topic: Credit strategies: top-down and bottom-up, liquidity, tail risk, structured products
questions.title: Instruments for Rapidly Changing Markets
questions.stem: An active bond manager expects market conditions to change rapidly. For short-term tactical positioning, the manager is most likely to prefer:

choices.text: corporate bonds with long records of successful coupon payments.

A.text: **Bond ETFs** (and CDS) are liquid alternatives for quick tactical moves.

B.text: Active managers favor on-the-run governments for tactical positioning.

C.text: Seasoned illiquid positions are for buy-and-hold.

questions.keyPrinciple: Tactical: liquid instruments (ETFs, CDS, on-the-run). Strategic: illiquid.

questions.topic: Value at risk and tail risk
questions.title: Effect of Index Derivatives Used for Downside Protection
questions.stem: The use of index derivatives to protect against downside risk in a fixed-income portfolio reduces:

choices.text: hedging costs in a distressed market.

A.text: Concentration is reduced by position limits and risk budgeting, not by derivatives.

B.text: **Reduces excess portfolio spread over time** (swaption/CDS-swaption premiums are a drag).

C.text: Hedging in distressed markets costs more because of higher option volatility.

questions.keyPrinciple: Option-based protection costs premium → lowers excess spread.

questions.topic: CDS and CDX: pricing, upfront payment, positioning
questions.title: Positioning for a Steepening Credit Curve
questions.stem: An active credit manager expects the credit curve slope to steepen. To benefit from the view, the manager will most likely:

choices.text: only sell long-term protection on a CDS subindex.
buy short-term protection on a CDS subindex and sell long-term protection on the same subindex.
sell short-term protection using a single-name CDS contract and buy long-term protection on that same reference entity.

A.text: To benefit from steepening you must buy long-term protection, not only sell it.

B.text: That is a flattening trade.

C.text: **Sell short-term protection and buy long-term protection on the same single-name reference entity.**

questions.keyPrinciple: Steepener: sell short-tenor, buy long-tenor protection. Flattener: the reverse.

questions.topic: CDS and CDX: pricing, upfront payment, positioning
questions.title: Positioning Near the End of a Growth Cycle
questions.stem: A credit portfolio manager believes the economy is nearing the end of a growth cycle. The manager will most likely:

choices.text: buy short-term CDS protection on a subindex and sell long-term protection on the same subindex.
sell short-term protection on a single-name CDS contract and buy long-term protection on that same reference entity.
buy five-year protection on a high-yield CDS index and sell protection on an investment-grade CDS index of the same tenor.

A.text: **Buy short-term protection and sell long-term protection on the same subindex.** Near-term spreads rise, flattening the CDS curve.

B.text: That capitalizes on a steepening view (falling near-term default probability).

C.text: That is a weaker-economy view: HY spreads widening vs IG.

questions.keyPrinciple: Late cycle: CDS curve flattening.

questions.topic: CDS and CDX: pricing, upfront payment, positioning
questions.title: CDX Pair When Slowdown Hurts Lower-Rated Issuers Most
questions.stem: An active fixed-income manager anticipates an economic slowdown in the coming year with a greater adverse impact on lower-rated issuers. There are two credit default swap index (CDX) contracts available, namely the investment-grade CDX and high-yield CDX contracts. If the manager chooses a tactical strategy combining positions in investment-grade CDX and high-yield CDX contracts to capitalize on this view, the manager will most likely:

choices.text: buy protection on both high-yield CDX contracts and investment-grade CDX contracts.
buy protection on high-yield CDX contracts and sell protection on investment-grade CDX contracts.
buy protection on investment-grade CDX contracts and sell protection on high-yield CDX contracts.

A.text: The key's feedback text for this choice says it is **incorrect**: buying protection on both contracts protects against the slowdown but doesn't capitalize on a greater impact on lower-rated issuers.

B.text: The key's feedback text for this choice says it is **correct**: buy HY protection and sell IG protection captures the greater hit to lower-rated issuers. This matches QF-73 and QF-30.

C.text: Buys IG and sells HY protection, the opposite of the view.

questions.keyPrinciple: Slowdown hitting low-rated issuers harder: buy HY protection, sell IG protection.
questions.flag: Key contradiction: the 'Correct answer' line lists A, but the feedback text calls A incorrect and B correct, and QF-73/QF-30 support B. I'd treat B as intended.

questions.topic: Trade strategy selection: urgency, size, liquidity and cost drivers
questions.title: Factors Affecting Trading Strategy Selection
questions.context: S1: greater urgency → lower execution risk. S2: larger orders with higher urgency reduce market impact. S3: high alpha decay requires less aggressive trading.
questions.stem: Which of Yellow’s statements regarding the factors affecting the selection of a trading strategy is correct?

A.text: **Statement 1.** Faster execution means less time exposed to price volatility and changing conditions.

B.text: Larger, more urgent orders raise (not reduce) market impact.

C.text: High alpha decay calls for more aggressive (faster) trading.

questions.keyPrinciple: ↑ urgency → ↓ execution risk, ↑ market impact.

questions.topic: Trade benchmarks: arrival, VWAP, close, decision price
questions.title: Benchmark That Excludes Trade Outliers
questions.context: Benchmark price computed from market prices during the trading period, excluding outliers.
questions.stem: Given the parameters for the benchmark given by Harding, Yellow should recommend a benchmark that is based on the:

A.text: Arrival price is a pre-trade benchmark.

B.text: **TWAP.** Intraday benchmark; chosen to exclude potential trade outliers.

C.text: VWAP is also intraday but isn't the one used to exclude outliers.

questions.keyPrinciple: Intraday: VWAP, TWAP (TWAP when outliers should be excluded).

questions.topic: Trading algorithms, venues and instruments
questions.title: Strategy for Filling the Rest of the ABC Order
questions.context: Buy 30,000 ABC (~1% of expected daily volume, very liquid); part at the open auction, the rest executed at prices close to the market price when the order was received.
questions.stem: To fill the remaining portion of the ABC order, Yellow is using:

A.text: **Arrival price strategy.** High urgency, liquid stock, small order vs volume.

B.text: A TWAP participation strategy spreads trades over time.

C.text: A VWAP participation strategy follows the volume schedule.

questions.keyPrinciple: Arrival price strategy: trade near the price when the order arrives.

questions.topic: Trading algorithms, venues and instruments
questions.title: Algorithm for a Liquid Stock With Market-Impact Priority
questions.context: XYZ shares are relatively liquid; priority is to minimize market impact/information leakage; no expected adverse price movements.
questions.stem: What type of algorithm should be used to purchase the XYZ shares given Harding’s priority in building the XYZ position and his belief about potential price movements?

A.text: **Scheduled algorithm.** Appropriate when no adverse price move is expected, with more tolerance for longer execution and priority on minimizing market impact; works for small orders in liquid securities.

B.text: Arrival price algorithms are for expected adverse price moves, trading aggressively.

C.text: Opportunistic algorithms aren't the keyed choice here.

questions.keyPrinciple: Scheduled (VWAP/TWAP/POV): no adverse move expected, minimize impact.
questions.flag: The key explains only the correct answer; the B reasoning is from QG-16's description of arrival price algorithms, and nothing is given for C.

questions.topic: Trade strategy selection: urgency, size, liquidity and cost drivers
questions.title: Non-Equity Trade Implementation
questions.context: S4: small currency and small exchange-traded derivatives trades typically use DMA. S5: high-touch agency approach is typically used for large, non-urgent trades in fixed income and exchange-traded derivatives.
questions.stem: Which of Yellow’s statements regarding the trade implementation of non-equity investments is correct?

A.text: **Only Statement 4.** Small currency trades are usually via DMA, and buy-side traders generally use DMA for exchange-traded derivatives, particularly smaller trades.

B.text: Statement 4 is also correct.

C.text: Statement 5 is not correct per the key.

questions.keyPrinciple: Small FX/ETD trades: DMA.
questions.flag: The key doesn't explain why Statement 5 is wrong.

questions.topic: Trade cost measurement: implementation shortfall, delay, arrival and market-adjusted cost
questions.title: Execution Cost of the BYYP Purchase
questions.context:
Order: buy 120,000 BYYP; decision price $40.00; limit $42.00; released at $40.50; commission $0.02/share; 90,000 filled at an average of $41.42; close $42.50.
| Trade | Price | Shares |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $40.75 | 10,000 |
| 2 | $41.25 | 30,000 |
| 3 | $41.50 | 20,000 |
| 4 | $41.75 | 30,000 |
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, the execution cost for purchasing the 90,000 shares of BYYP is:

A.text: Doesn't match.

B.text: Doesn't match.

C.text: **$127,500.** Execution cost = Σ(shares × price) − shares × decision price = $3,727,500 − 90,000 × $40.00 = $127,500.

questions.keyPrinciple: Execution cost = Σ s_j p_j − Σ s_j p_d (buy).

questions.topic: Trade cost measurement: implementation shortfall, delay, arrival and market-adjusted cost
questions.title: Opportunity Cost of the BYYP Purchase
questions.context:
Order: buy 120,000 BYYP; decision price $40.00; limit $42.00; released at $40.50; commission $0.02/share; 90,000 filled at an average of $41.42; close $42.50.
| Trade | Price | Shares |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $40.75 | 10,000 |
| 2 | $41.25 | 30,000 |
| 3 | $41.50 | 20,000 |
| 4 | $41.75 | 30,000 |
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, the opportunity cost for purchasing the 90,000 shares of BYYP is:

A.text: Doesn't match.

B.text: Doesn't match.

C.text: **$75,000.** Unexecuted shares × (closing price − decision price) = 30,000 × ($42.50 − $40.00).

questions.keyPrinciple: Opportunity cost = (S − Σs_j)(p_n − p_d).

questions.topic: Trade cost measurement: implementation shortfall, delay, arrival and market-adjusted cost
questions.title: Arrival Cost of the BYYP Purchase
questions.context:
Order: buy 120,000 BYYP; decision price $40.00; limit $42.00; released at $40.50; commission $0.02/share; 90,000 filled at an average of $41.42; close $42.50.
| Trade | Price | Shares |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $40.75 | 10,000 |
| 2 | $41.25 | 30,000 |
| 3 | $41.50 | 20,000 |
| 4 | $41.75 | 30,000 |
questions.stem: The arrival cost for purchasing the 90,000 shares of BYYP is:

A.text: 164.4 bp doesn't match.

B.text: **227.2 bp.** Arrival cost = side × (average price − arrival price)/arrival price × 10,000 = (41.42 − 40.50)/40.50 × 10,000.

C.text: 355.0 bp doesn't match.

questions.title: Market-Adjusted Cost of the LIM Trade
questions.context: Arrival price $23.09; average fill $23.45; index $2,150 at order entry, index VWAP $2,184; LIM beta 0.95.
questions.stem: Calculate the market-adjusted cost and discuss.
questions.modelAnswer:
Arrival cost = (23.45 − 23.09)/23.09 × 10,000 ≈ 155.9 bp.
Market move = (2,184 − 2,150)/2,150 × 10,000 ≈ 158.1 bp; beta-adjusted = 0.95 × 158.1 ≈ 150.2 bp.
Market-adjusted cost ≈ 155.9 − 150.2 ≈ **5.7 bp**.

This is far lower than the arrival cost: most of the cost of buying LIM came from buying in a rising market rather than from the order's own price pressure.
questions.keyPrinciple: Market-adjusted cost = arrival cost − β × market return over the horizon.

questions.title: Market-Adjusted Cost (6 bp Example)
questions.context: Buy at an average of $53.40; arrival $53.30; index $100 at entry, index VWAP $100.15; beta 0.85.
questions.stem: A portfolio manager executes a buy order at an average price of $53.40. The arrival price at the time the order was submitted to the market was $53.30. The index price at the time of order entry was $100, and market index volume weighted average price over the trade horizon was $100.15. If the stock has a beta to the index of 0.85, the market-adjusted cost is closest to:

B.text: 15 bp is the index cost.

C.text: 19 bp is the arrival cost.

questions.keyPrinciple: Market-adjusted cost = arrival cost − β × index cost.

questions.topic: Trade strategy selection: urgency, size, liquidity and cost drivers
questions.title: Trading Motive Where Alpha Decay Matters
questions.stem: With respect to motivations to trade, alpha decay is an important trading consideration for:

A.text: **Profit seeking.** Alpha decay matters for active managers maximizing net returns.

B.text: Margin calls drive urgency; alpha decay isn't the consideration.

C.text: For cash flow needs, liquidity is the key consideration.

questions.keyPrinciple: Alpha decay → profit-seeking trades.

questions.topic: Trade strategy selection: urgency, size, liquidity and cost drivers
questions.title: Trading Larger Orders More Quickly
questions.stem: All else being equal, trading larger order sizes more quickly will:

choices.text: decrease both market impact cost and execution risk.
increase both market impact cost and execution risk.
increase market impact cost and decrease execution risk.

A.text: Market impact rises.

B.text: Execution risk falls with urgency.

C.text: **Increases market impact cost and decreases execution risk.**

questions.keyPrinciple: Faster/larger → ↑ impact, ↓ execution risk.

questions.topic: Trading algorithms, venues and instruments
questions.title: Strategy for a Short-Term Alpha-Driven Buy
questions.stem: A trader plans to purchase a stock based on a short-term alpha-driven motivation. Which of the following is the most suitable trading strategy?

choices.text: Using dark pool venues to hide the order and minimize the impact
Participating in the opening auction and trading any residual using an arrival price strategy
Trading the order passively using volume-weighted average price participation strategy during the day

A.text: Dark pools risk unfilled executions.

B.text: **Trade part at the opening auction, then the residual with an arrival price strategy.**

C.text: Passive VWAP trading isn't appropriate given urgency.

questions.keyPrinciple: Short-term alpha → urgency: open auction + arrival price strategy.

questions.topic: Trading algorithms, venues and instruments
questions.title: Futures Implementation for a Large Index Mandate With No Closing Auction
questions.context: Track a benchmark (5% tracking error); futures have no closing auction; fully invest quickly using derivatives.
questions.stem: An investment manager has received a large mandate to track a market benchmark with a tracking error of 5%. The futures market on this benchmark does not have a closing auction. The client is open to using derivatives and requests that the mandate be fully invested as quickly as possible. The most appropriate trading strategy is to have the manager:

choices.text: send a market order for the futures contract at the market close.
trade futures using a volume-weighted average price algorithm into the market close.
skip the equitization-via-futures step and instead invest directly in the underlying securities.

A.text: A single market order at the close would have large price impact for a large mandate.

B.text: **Trade futures using a VWAP algorithm into the market close.**

C.text: For large mandates, equitizing via futures first usually reduces tracking error.

questions.keyPrinciple: Large futures trades with no closing auction: VWAP/TWAP into the close.

questions.topic: Trading algorithms, venues and instruments
questions.title: When Scheduled Algorithms Are Appropriate
questions.stem: Scheduled algorithms are appropriate for executing trades when the portfolio managers:

choices.text: are concerned with minimizing market impact.
have low risk tolerance for longer execution time periods.
have expectations of adverse price movement during the trade horizon.

A.text: **Concerned with minimizing market impact.**

B.text: Scheduled algorithms are for those with greater, not lower, risk tolerance for longer execution.

C.text: They're for no expected adverse price movement.

questions.keyPrinciple: Scheduled algorithms: low impact, no adverse view, tolerate longer execution.

questions.topic: Trade strategy selection: urgency, size, liquidity and cost drivers
questions.title: Market Commonly Using RFQs for Large Urgent Trades
questions.stem: Which of the following markets more commonly utilize request for quotes (RFQs) for large and urgent trades?

A.text: Large urgent small-cap equity trades are high-touch broker risk trades.

B.text: **Fixed income.** Broker risk trades via RFQs (broker as counterparty) are common for small and large urgent trades.

C.text: Large OTC derivative trades are generally high-touch agency trades per the key.

questions.keyPrinciple: FI: RFQs/broker risk trades. Large non-urgent: high-touch agency.
questions.flag: The key's explanation for A and C is not parallel to B (it says large urgent trades in OTC derivatives are agency trades, which conflicts with calling them 'urgent' in the stem). I've repeated it as given.

questions.topic: Trade cost measurement: implementation shortfall, delay, arrival and market-adjusted cost
questions.title: Opportunity Cost of a Partial Fill
questions.context: Buy 90,000 at decision price $29.95; 60,000 executed; close $30.75.
questions.stem: A portfolio manager decides to buy 90,000 shares of a stock, when the price is $29.95. At the end of the day, 60,000 shares are executed and the stock closes at $30.75. If no further attempt is made to buy the stock, the opportunity cost for this trade is:

A.text: Rising price makes the opportunity cost positive.

C.text: $48,000 uses the executed shares.

questions.keyPrinciple: Opportunity cost = (S − Σs_j)(p_n − p_d).

questions.topic: Trade cost measurement: implementation shortfall, delay, arrival and market-adjusted cost
questions.title: VWAP Cost in Basis Points
questions.context: Buy at average $59.80; VWAP $59.40.
questions.stem: A portfolio manager executes a buy order at an average price of $59.80. The volume-weighted average price (VWAP) over the trading horizon is $59.40. The VWAP cost benchmark (in bps) is closest to:

A.text: 66.9 divides by the execution price.

B.text: 67.1 divides by the average of price and VWAP.

questions.keyPrinciple: VWAP cost = side × (P − VWAP)/VWAP × 10,000.

questions.topic: Trade cost measurement: implementation shortfall, delay, arrival and market-adjusted cost
questions.title: Market-Adjusted Cost (17.6 bp Example)
questions.context: Buy at $50.70; arrival $50.00; index 4,900 at entry, VWAP 4,950; beta 1.2.
questions.stem: A portfolio manager executes a buy order at an average price of $50.70. The arrival price at the time the order was entered into the market was $50.00. The selected index level at the time of order entry was 4,900, and market index volume-weighted average price (VWAP) over the trade horizon was 4,950. If the stock has a beta to the index of 1.2, the market-adjusted cost (in bps) is closest to:

A.text: 15.6 uses the execution price as the arrival cost denominator.

C.text: 18.8 uses index VWAP as the index cost denominator.

questions.keyPrinciple: Denominators: arrival price and index arrival level.

questions.topic: Trade governance and policies: best execution, allocation, errors
questions.title: Best Execution as Good Trade Governance
questions.context: Short-term returns; concerned about impact costs.
questions.stem: An asset manager is seeking to generate returns in the short term. If the manager is concerned about impact costs, with respect to best order execution, which of the following is the most appropriate example of good trade governance?

choices.text: Maximizing the likelihood of execution and settlement
Obtaining the best price at the lowest possible trading cost
Identifying the most appropriate trade-off between nature of trade and speed of execution

A.text: Focusing only on execution and settlement may increase impact and give unfavorable prices.

B.text: Best execution isn't simply lowest cost; patient trading can be suboptimal when alpha decays quickly.

C.text: **Identify the most appropriate trade-off between the nature of the trade and speed of execution.** Best execution weighs price, costs, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, size and nature of trade.

questions.keyPrinciple: Best execution = trade-off among price, cost, speed, likelihood, size.
